question: A hardware refresh catalog item at a logistics company has a multi-row variable set (MRVS) called devices where requesters list each laptop they are returning (asset tag, model, condition). The parent form also has a return_method choice (courier or drop-off). Two bugs came in after go-live: an onChange script on the parent that counts rows with g_form.getValue('devices').length reports 160 devices for a request with two rows, and an onLoad script on the MRVS that should hide the 'pickup address' cell when return_method is drop-off never works. How do you read and write MRVS data correctly from the parent form, and how does a script running inside the MRVS row modal read a value from the parent form?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to hear that an MRVS value is a JSON string, not an array, so you parse it before you count or loop, and you stringify it before you write it back. They also want you to know that inside the row modal g_form points at the row, not the catalog item, and that the parent form is reached through g_service_catalog.parent.getValue(). You earn extra credit for spotting the type traps too: a string length instead of a row count, and the string "false" passed where a Boolean is expected.

The Answer

Bug 1: counting characters, not rows. The GlideForm reference says getValue() returns a String, and for an MRVS that string is the serialized array of rows. .length on it counts characters. The documented pattern is JSON.parse(g_form.getValue('mrvs_name') || '[]'); the || '[]' covers the empty case, where getValue() returns an empty string and JSON.parse('') would throw.

function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading) {
        return;
    }
    var rows = JSON.parse(g_form.getValue('devices') || '[]');
    var damaged = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
        if (rows[i].condition == 'damaged') {
            damaged++;
        }
    }
    g_form.setValue('device_count', String(rows.length));
    g_form.setValue('damaged_count', String(damaged));
}

Each row object is keyed by the MRVS variable names (here asset_tag, model, condition). To change rows from the parent, edit the parsed array and write it back with g_form.setValue('devices', JSON.stringify(rows)). The reference's salary example does exactly that.

Bug 2: reading the parent from inside the row. A catalog client script attached to the MRVS runs in the row modal. In that context g_form.getValue('return_method') looks for a variable on the row and finds nothing. The g_service_catalog API exists for this case: g_service_catalog.parent.getValue('return_method') returns the value from the catalog item form while the MRVS modal is open. The reference says the method can only be called through the parent object, and that the API works in Service Portal, the core platform UI, Workspace and Now Mobile.

function onLoad() {
    // runs in the MRVS row modal
    var method = g_service_catalog.parent.getValue('return_method');
    if (method == 'drop_off') {
        g_form.setMandatory('pickup_address', false); // clear mandatory first
        g_form.setVisible('pickup_address', false);   // Boolean, not 'false'
    }
}

The order of those two lines matters. Remember the reference note on setVisible() and setDisplay(): neither can hide a mandatory field that has no value. If pickup_address is mandatory by default, clear the mandatory flag first or the hide is ignored.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference example for g_service_catalog calls g_form.setVisible("ipv6_address", "false"). The string "false" is truthy in JavaScript. Whether a given g_form implementation coerces it back to a Boolean is not documented, so do not rely on it: pass the Boolean false, as the method signature says.
  • getValue() on an empty MRVS returns an empty string, not '[]'. Always default before JSON.parse.
  • Values inside the parsed rows are strings. A quantity column read from the JSON needs parseInt(value, 10) before arithmetic.
  • Writing the MRVS back with setValue fires onChange on the MRVS variable. If your onChange on that same variable rewrites it, guard against re-entry; the setValue note in the reference warns about onChange loops.
  • setVisible() leaves blank space on the desktop UI but collapses the space in Service Portal and mobile, so a layout that looks fine in one channel can look odd in the other.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating the MRVS value as an array and calling .length, .forEach or index access on the raw string.
  • Calling g_form.getValue() for a parent variable from a script that runs in the row modal and concluding the variable is empty.
  • Calling g_service_catalog.getValue() directly instead of g_service_catalog.parent.getValue().
  • Trying to hide a mandatory, empty cell and wondering why it stays visible.
Score points: Say out loud which form g_form refers to in each script (catalog item form or MRVS row). Most MRVS bugs come from assuming it is always the parent.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you stop a requester submitting more than five rows, and where would you enforce it so a crafted request cannot bypass the limit?
  • How would you read one MRVS from a script that runs inside another MRVS on the same item?
  • Would you do the device count in a client script at all, or compute it server-side when the request item is created?

Sources

  • GlideForm (g_form) - API reference
  • g_service_catalog - API reference

question: A university IT team is building its first Service Portal widget: students type part of a course name, press Search, and see up to ten matching tasks. The junior developer's server script queries the task table and fills data.tasks, the client controller sets c.data.textQuery and calls c.server.update(), and the HTML repeats over data.tasks. It works, but they are confused about three things: why the server script seems to run twice, why input is undefined when the page first loads, and why a value they set on a plain controller variable (c.clientText) never reaches the server. Walk them through how data and input move between the server script and the client controller, and fix the gaps in their mental model.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Describe the widget as a round trip. The server script builds a data object, the platform serialises it to the browser, and the client controller sees it as c.data. When the client calls c.server.update(), the client's current c.data is posted back, the whole server script runs again, and on that second run the posted values appear as input. The returned data then replaces c.data. You should also explain why only properties on c.data travel, and why the server script has to be written to handle both the first load and later updates.

The Answer

Developer Advocate Earl Duque's walkthrough of the data/input object describes it in four steps, and the confusions in this scenario map straight onto them.

  1. Page load. The server script runs once. Nothing has been posted from the browser yet, so input is undefined. That is expected, which is why the blog's examples always guard with if (input && input.textQuery).
  2. Delivery. Whatever the script put on data arrives in the browser as c.data (or $scope.data), and the template can bind to {{data.tasks}} directly.
  3. Client update. The controller sets properties on c.data and calls c.server.update(). The whole server script runs again from the top. This is the "runs twice" effect: one run for page load and one for each update.
  4. Return. On that second run, the posted values are read from input.*. The script rebuilds data, and the response refreshes c.data. The update returns a promise, so code that needs the new values goes inside .then().

The missing value is the clearest lesson. c.clientText is a controller property bound with ng-model. It is not part of c.data, so it is never posted. The blog's search example copies it across first:

// Client controller
api.controller = function() {
  var c = this;
  c.clientText = '';
  c.searchForText = function() {
    c.data.textQuery = c.clientText;      // move it onto data so it is posted
    c.server.update().then(function() {
      console.log(c.data.tasks);          // refreshed after the server re-ran
    });
  };
};

// Server script
(function() {
  var taskGr = new GlideRecord('task');
  if (input && input.textQuery) {
    data.textQuery = input.textQuery;
    taskGr.addEncodedQuery('short_descriptionLIKE' + input.textQuery);
  }
  taskGr.setLimit(10);
  taskGr.query();
  data.tasks = [];
  while (taskGr.next()) {
    data.tasks.push({
      number: taskGr.getValue('number'),
      short_description: taskGr.getValue('short_description')
    });
  }
})();

Point out the habits in this code. It uses getValue() to copy plain strings into the array instead of pushing GlideElement objects. The scoped GlideRecord reference warns that dot-walked objects in arrays or in Service Portal can give odd results. It also caps the result with setLimit(10), so a vague search cannot pull the whole task table into the browser.

Two related tools are worth knowing. For URL parameters (for example ?id=search&q=chem), the server script reads them with $sp.getParameter('q'), which returns null when there is no request or widget context. And spUtil.update($scope) and spUtil.refresh($scope) do the same job as server.update() and server.refresh() but let you say which scope to use. The spUtil reference uses this with recordWatch to re-fetch data when a watched record changes.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The full server script runs on every update. If it does expensive work that does not depend on input, such as loading reference lists for dropdowns, guard it with if (!input) or the cost is paid on every click.
  • input carries everything that was on c.data when the update was sent, including large arrays you sent down earlier. Trimming data keeps both directions light.
  • Anything the browser posts can be changed by the user. input.textQuery here is concatenated into an encoded query, so a user could add ^ conditions of their own. Use addQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', value) or a secure query when the input is untrusted.
  • Values set on data that the server does not rebuild on the second run are gone from c.data after the update. Rebuild them, or keep purely client-side state on the controller instead.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading c.data right after calling c.server.update() without waiting for the promise.
  • Expecting input on page load and throwing "cannot read property of undefined".
  • Pushing GlideRecord or GlideElement objects into data instead of plain values.
  • Setting values on c or $scope and expecting them on the server.
Score points: Draw the four-step loop (load, deliver, update, return) and say plainly that "data goes down, input comes up, and the server script runs top to bottom both times". Then point out that the blog's string-concatenated encoded query trusts user input, and say how you would close that gap.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you refresh the list automatically when another agent updates one of the tasks? (spUtil.recordWatch plus spUtil.update.)
  • How do widget options differ from input and data?
  • When would you move this logic into a Scripted REST API or GraphQL API instead of the widget server script?

Sources

  • Understanding the data/input object in Service Portal widgets (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GlideSPScriptable ($sp) - Scoped (API reference)
  • spUtil - Client (API reference)
  • GlideRecord - Scoped (API reference)
  • Widget API reference (ServiceNow Docs)

question: A logistics company wired generative AI into its instance in 2023, straight from the Developer Advocate "getting started" post. An after-insert business rule on incident calls sn_fd.FlowAPI.getRunner().action('sn_generative_ai.summarize').inBackground().withInputs(inputs).run(), then reads result.getOutputs()['response'] and writes it to work notes. Work notes are always empty, and finance has noticed IntegrationHub transaction counts climbing in production. A new architect wants to "rip it all out and rebuild in Skill Kit." Question: What is wrong with the existing code, and how do you decide whether a use case belongs on a direct Generative AI Controller call or in a custom AI Skill Kit skill?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Spot the background/foreground bug at once. Then explain the controller as the plumbing layer (provider connection, a handful of fixed capabilities callable from Flow, Virtual Agent and script) and AI Skill Kit as the place where you own the prompt, the inputs, the grounding and the deployment. A good answer doesn't say "always Skill Kit". It picks per use case and brings up cost, data leaving the instance and testability.

The Answer

The bug. The snippet the 2023 post generated has two modes, and the comments in it say so: inBackground() starts the action asynchronously and "will not have access to outputs"; inForeground() runs synchronously and is the only way to read outputs['response'] and outputs['provider']. The team took the background line and the output-reading lines from the same template. The action runs, the LLM is called (and billed), and the script reads nothing. Every insert pays for a summary nobody sees.

A minimal fix, run from an async business rule so the user's save is not held up by an LLM round trip:

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var inputs = {};
    inputs['texttosummarize'] = current.getValue('description');
    try {
        var result = sn_fd.FlowAPI.getRunner()
            .action('sn_generative_ai.summarize')
            .inForeground()
            .withInputs(inputs)
            .run();
        var outputs = result.getOutputs();
        var summary = outputs['response'];
        if (summary) {
            current.work_notes = 'AI summary (' + outputs['provider'] + '): ' + summary;
            current.update();
        }
    } catch (ex) {
        gs.error('Incident summary failed for ' + current.getValue('number') + ': ' + ex.getMessage());
    }
})(current, previous);

Put a condition on the rule (description is not empty, and only on insert) so it does not summarise one-line tickets or re-fire on its own update.

Why the transaction count climbs. The post's FAQ says the controller uses embedded IntegrationHub spokes to reach the provider, and LLM calls from a production instance count as IntegrationHub transactions (sub-prod calls do not). An after-insert rule with no condition on a busy incident table is a meter running on every record.

What the controller is. It connects the instance to an LLM provider and exposes a small set of capabilities: Summarize, Content Generation, QnA, Sentiment Analysis and Generic Prompt, usable from Flow Designer, Virtual Agent Designer, Mobile App Builder and script. At launch the prompts behind those capabilities were read-only, temperature defaulted to 0 and max tokens to 500, and context was not kept between calls. Providers were OpenAI and Azure OpenAI. Today an external model is plugged in through the generic LLM connector: you create credentials, then a record in sys_generative_ai_model_config with Provider set to Custom LLM. The current docs still say the controller supports text generation only.

What AI Skill Kit adds (it was Now Assist Skill Kit until the ServiceNow Otto rebrand; current docs call it AI Skill Kit):

  • A prompt you write and version, with several prompts per skill and usage conditions choosing between them. Prompts are locked before publishing.
  • Typed inputs pulled from records, plus tools (script includes, flow actions and subflows, retrievers, other published skills) that fetch grounding data before the prompt is sent.
  • Pre- and post-processors for masking and unmasking data.
  • Deployment as a UI action, context menu entry, flow action, Virtual Agent topic module or Now Assist panel, with role restrictions.
  • Run tests that show the grounded prompt actually sent, and an Evaluations tab that scores a dataset with an LLM judge.

How to choose. Keep a direct controller call when the job is generic (summarise this free text, translate this reply), the fixed capability prompt is good enough, and the call sits inside a flow you already own. Move to a skill when the prompt carries business rules, needs data from several tables, has to be evaluated before go-live, or end users need to trigger it from a form with role control. For this company, incident summarisation is already an out-of-the-box Now Assist for ITSM skill. The Skill Kit FAQ itself says to try OOTB skills and admin settings first, so the first move is to check the entitlement, not to build anything.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The output keys (response, provider) only exist in foreground mode. A background run fails silently from the script's point of view.
  • Data leaves the instance. The 2023 FAQ states plainly that prompts go to OpenAI or Azure OpenAI under their privacy terms. Masking belongs in a Skill Kit pre-processor or the Data Privacy configuration, not in hope.
  • Azure OpenAI uses the deployment name as the model name. Using the base model name gives a "deployment does not exist" error.
  • Calling a skill from script uses a different API, sn_one_extend.OneExtendUtil.execute, with a capability ID and skill config ID. It is not a drop-in replacement for the FlowAPI call.

Common Mistakes

  • Running LLM calls synchronously in a before or after rule on a high-volume table, which slows every save.
  • Treating "rebuild in Skill Kit" as the fix when the defect is one method call.
  • Ignoring that sub-prod testing hides the transaction cost that shows up in production.
Score points: Say that the controller and Skill Kit are layers, not rivals: skills still route to a provider configured at the controller level, so a provider or credential change affects both.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you stop the summary rule from running on tickets created by integrations?
  • What would you need in place before pointing the controller at a self-hosted model?
  • How do you prove the OOTB incident summarisation skill is good enough before building a custom one?

Sources

  • Getting started with the Generative AI Controller
  • Generative AI Controller - Live Coding Happy Hour
  • AI Skill Kit / Now Assist Skill Kit (NASK) FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • AI Skill Kit (ServiceNow product documentation)
  • Configure a generic large language model (LLM) connector (ServiceNow documentation)

question: A university IT team built a custom AI Skill Kit skill called "Expand request" that turns a student's one-line service request into a structured description. It is called from a Flow Designer action when a request is submitted. In testing inside the skill editor it worked. In the flow, every expanded description comes back about healthy breakfast smoothies, whatever the student typed. The developer has rewritten the prompt three times and stripped the Markdown out of it. Question: How would you debug this, and how would you structure the prompt so the output is predictable once the real bug is fixed?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Suspect the input first, not the model. If the skill behaves in the editor and misbehaves in the flow, the difference is what the flow passes in. You should know where to see the prompt the model actually received, then describe a structured prompt (RISEN or similar, with examples and an output contract) rather than "make the prompt better".

The Answer

This exact bug happened on a Developer Advocate live stream while building the "Promptception" app: Now Assist decided every prompt was about breakfast smoothies. The team spent an hour on flow logs, JSON output and prompt formatting, and even stripped Markdown to test theories. The cause was a wrong data pill in the Flow Designer action. The fix was one line.

Debug in this order:

  1. Compare the two paths. In the editor, Run tests uses whatever test value you typed. In the flow, the input is whatever pill is mapped. When the same skill gives sane output in one and nonsense in the other, the input mapping is the first suspect.
  2. Look at the grounded prompt. Run tests in the prompt editor has a Response tab and a Grounded prompt tab. The grounded prompt is the final text with inputs and tool output substituted. Run the test with the same record the flow used. If the student's text is missing and something else is in its place, you have found it.
  3. Read the flow execution. Open the flow execution details and check the value going into the skill action's input. A pill pointing at a different variable, an empty value, or a field from the wrong record all produce a prompt with no real request in it. With no real content, the model fills the gap with whatever the examples or the role suggested. If the prompt had a sample about a smoothie order, that is where the theme came from.
  4. Check the output side too. If a later step parses the response as JSON, log the raw response first. The same stream ended up building a custom action to reformat the AI's JSON before finding the real cause. Do not change two things at once.

Only after the input is correct is it worth touching the prompt.

Structuring the prompt. The Developer Advocates used the RISEN framework both in that app and in a Skill Kit "sleep analysis" demo:

  • Role: "Act as a service desk analyst at a university IT department."
  • Instructions: "Rewrite the student's request as a clear service request description."
  • Steps: identify the service, the problem or need, urgency clues, and missing details to ask for.
  • Expectation (sometimes given as End goal): the exact output shape, for example JSON with service, summary, details and questions.
  • Narrowing: tone, length, and what not to do: "Use only the information in the request. If the request is empty or unclear, return summary as 'Insufficient information' and do not invent details."

Add one or two worked examples (one-shot or few-shot) that look like real student requests. Keep them visibly separate from the live input with clear delimiters, and do not make them all about one topic, or you teach the model a theme.

Then lock the prompt and publish. Skill Kit requires prompts to be locked before publishing; to refine a locked prompt you copy it, which gives you a natural version history.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Skill inputs have a truncate option. A long description cut at the wrong point can drop the actual question.
  • A prompt with no "if empty, say so" rule invites the model to make something up. That is exactly what an empty input exposed here.
  • Testing in the editor consumes Assists. Debugging by re-running the flow dozens of times also costs, so check the grounded prompt first.
  • Output JSON shape can differ by model. If a post-step parses it, validate before using it.

Common Mistakes

  • Rewriting the prompt repeatedly when the input never reached it.
  • Putting a single example in the prompt that dominates every answer.
  • Asking for "a description" with no output format, then writing brittle string parsing downstream.
Score points: Say you would add an assertion in the flow before the skill step: if the input is empty, stop and log. A guard costs nothing and turns a weird AI answer into an obvious data error.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would you use usage conditions to pick between two prompts in the same skill?
  • How would you test this skill against fifty real requests before switching it on?
  • Where would you strip a student ID number before the prompt leaves the instance?

Sources

  • Building the Promptception App - Four Episodes of Live Coding
  • AI Academy: The RISEN Framework
  • Now Assist Skill Kit - Live Coding Happy Hour
  • AI Skill Kit / Now Assist Skill Kit (NASK) FAQ (ServiceNow Community)

question: A US healthcare provider with 12,000 employees uses HR Service Delivery. Its tax-credit screening vendor (integrated through CIC Plus) needs employee profile data every night. The vendor's developer built a job that calls the HR REST API endpoint get_usa_employee_profile once with no parameters and gets 1,000 records, while the provider has 12,000 employees. They also report that 300 remote employees living in Canada but working for the US entity show up, while some US-based contractors don't. Explain how this endpoint selects and pages employees, which parameters are mutually exclusive, and how the nightly job should be written.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This is a narrow, purpose-built endpoint, and even at Foundation level you should read its contract precisely. It returns employees whose work or home country is the United States. It supports either a single employee_identifier lookup or a delta by updated_after, never both. It pages with sysparm_limit (default 1000) and sysparm_offset, and it signals more data through a Next-Page response header rather than a Link header or a total count. The caller needs the sn_hr_core.usa_employee_only role and the HR Core plugin.

The Answer

Why 1,000 records. sysparm_limit defaults to 1000. The job read the first page and stopped. The response header Next-Page is true when more matching records exist and false when it is done. Loop with sysparm_offset = offset + limit until Next-Page is false.

Who is included. The reference says employees "must either have their work or home country specified as the United States". A Canadian resident working for the US entity has a US work country, so they are included. A contractor without a US work or home country on their profile isn't. That is a data question for HR, not an API bug. If contractors should be in scope, their work or home country needs to be filled in.

Delta, not full load. Use updated_after (format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, or YYYY-MM-DD with time defaulting to 00:00:00) to get employees added or updated on or after that point. Store the job's start time and use it as the next run's updated_after, with a small overlap to cover clock skew. Use employee_identifier only for single-record lookups, such as when the vendor queries one person. The two parameters are mutually exclusive. The reference also notes that to get an identifier you first call with updated_after.

offset=0; limit=500; since="2026-10-22 00:00:00"
while true; do
  resp=$(curl -s -D headers.txt -u "$U:$P" -H "Accept: application/json" \
    "https://instance.service-now.com/api/sn_hr_core/hr_rest_api/get_usa_employee_profile?updated_after=${since// /%20}&sysparm_limit=$limit&sysparm_offset=$offset")
  echo "$resp" >> batch.json
  grep -qi '^Next-Page: *true' headers.txt || break
  offset=$((offset + limit))
done

What comes back. Each record has fields such as EmployeeIdentifier, FirstName, MiddleName, LastName, Email, the Work* address fields, the Residence* address fields, BirthDate, HireDate and Company. ReHire is "for future use", so don't build logic on it.

Running it safely. Give the vendor a dedicated integration user that holds sn_hr_core.usa_employee_only and nothing else. Treat 401 as a credential problem that should page someone. Write each page to staging before loading it, so a run that fails halfway can restart from the last good offset instead of starting again from zero.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The overview lists the CIC Plus parameters as HomeAddress, HomeCity and so on, but the response body table calls them ResidenceAddress, ResidenceCity and so on. Map from the actual response, not from the overview list.
  • The default URL is /api/sn_hr_core/hr_rest_api/get_usa_employee_profile. The section heading shows only /get_usa_employee_profile, and the example uses an upper-case V1 in the path. Confirm the versioned path in the REST API Explorer.
  • The response includes birth dates and home addresses. Grant sn_hr_core.usa_employee_only only to the vendor's integration user, and log access.
  • A 404 is documented. Handle it explicitly for employee_identifier lookups rather than treating it as an outage.

Common Mistakes

  • Sending both employee_identifier and updated_after and expecting a filtered delta.
  • Running a full extract every night when the endpoint was designed for deltas.
  • Looking for X-Total-Count or a Link header to page, when this endpoint uses Next-Page.
Score points: Mention the work-or-home-country rule as the explanation for both the Canadians and the missing contractors, and point to Next-Page as the paging signal specific to this endpoint.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you detect terminations, which a "changed since" feed may not make obvious?
  • How would you restrict which fields the vendor can see if HR objects to birth dates?
  • What would you monitor so a silently failing nightly job is noticed within a day?

Sources

  • HR REST API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A logistics customer's nightly job pushes shipment updates to a carrier API with sn_ws.RESTMessageV2. In a code review you find this pattern: var r = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('Carrier API', 'post'); var res = r.execute(); var data = JSON.parse(res.getBody()); current.u_carrier_ref = data.id;. Last week the carrier had a 20-minute outage and the job left 300 shipments with an empty reference and nothing useful in the logs. Walk through every way this call can fail, which RESTResponseV2 methods tell you about each one, and rewrite the call so failures are caught and logged properly.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You should know that an outbound call can fail in several ways, and each one shows up through a different channel. Some failures throw a JavaScript exception. Some come back as a transport error on the response object. Some come back as a perfectly normal HTTP response with a 4xx or 5xx status. A script that only parses getBody() treats all three as success. I want to hear you separate these cases and name the method that reports each.

The Answer

There are four distinct failure points in that one line of code, and the reference documents each of them.

  1. The constructor can throw. new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2(name, method) reads a REST Message record. The reference notes it "might throw exception if message doesn't exist or not visible due to scope". A typo in the record name, or a scoped app calling a record in another scope, fails before any HTTP traffic.
  2. execute() can throw. The reference says it might throw "if http connection timed out or some issue with sending request itself because of encryption/decryption of password". During the carrier outage this is the most likely path: no exception handling means the script dies, and depending on where it runs you get a stack trace and nothing else.
  3. The transaction can fail without throwing. haveError() returns true when there was an error during the REST transaction. getErrorMessage() returns the text. getErrorCode() returns a numeric code that is specific to the ServiceNow platform, not an HTTP code; the reference gives 1 for a socket timeout and says to quote it to Customer Support.
  4. The provider can answer with an error status. getStatusCode() returns the numeric HTTP status. A 503 page from a load balancer has a body, but it is HTML, so JSON.parse throws on the next line and the record is left half-updated.

The rewrite wraps everything in try/catch, checks the transport error and the status code separately, and only parses a body it expects to be JSON:

function sendShipment(shipmentGr, payload) {
    var result = { ok: false, status: 0, error: '' };
    var rm;
    try {
        rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('Carrier API', 'post');
        rm.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
        rm.setRequestHeader('Accept', 'application/json');
        rm.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify(payload));
        rm.setHttpTimeout(30000);               // socket timeout, ms
        var res = rm.execute();
        result.status = res.getStatusCode();

        if (res.haveError()) {
            result.error = 'code ' + res.getErrorCode() + ': ' + res.getErrorMessage();
        } else if (result.status < 200 || result.status > 299) {
            result.error = 'HTTP ' + result.status + ': ' + res.getBody().substring(0, 500);
        } else {
            var data = JSON.parse(res.getBody());
            if (data && data.id) {
                shipmentGr.setValue('u_carrier_ref', data.id);
                result.ok = true;
            } else {
                result.error = 'Response had no id';
            }
        }
    } catch (ex) {
        result.error = 'Exception: ' + (ex.getMessage ? ex.getMessage() : ex);
    }
    if (!result.ok) {
        gs.error('Carrier push failed for ' + shipmentGr.getValue('number') +
                 ' (' + result.error + ')');
        shipmentGr.setValue('u_sync_state', 'failed');   // so a retry job can find it
    }
    return result;
}

The important design choice is the last block: a failure leaves a state on the record that a later job can query. Logging alone does not get 300 shipments resent.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Do not assume haveError() and the status code always agree. The reference describes haveError() as "an error during the REST transaction" and does not spell out which HTTP statuses set it, so check the status range yourself.
  • getErrorCode() is a platform code. Comparing it to 404 or 500 is a bug.
  • If the message used saveResponseBodyAsAttachment(), calling getBody() on the response causes an error. The reference says to call getErrorMessage() to get the body content when that call fails.
  • getHeaders() returns only the last value of a duplicated header. Use getAllHeaders() when you need every Set-Cookie or similar.
  • setRequestBody() bypasses variable substitution. If the REST Message record body uses ${variables}, a script that also calls setRequestBody() sends the literal string you passed, not the template.
  • setHttpTimeout() is a socket timeout: it only fires if no data arrives within the window, so a slowly streaming response can run longer than the value you set.

Common Mistakes

  • Logging only getBody() on failure. A connection failure may have no response body at all, so also log getErrorMessage() and getErrorCode().
  • Catching the exception and returning silently, which is how 300 records end up with blank references and no trail.
  • Calling JSON.parse() before checking the status, so an HTML error page throws inside the success path.
Score points: Mention setLogLevel('all') for a debugging window (logs land in System Logs > Outbound HTTP Requests) and point out that it may not apply if the endpoint domain is excluded or glide.outbound_http_log.override is true. Then say you would turn it back down afterwards, because the most verbose level can capture payload data you do not want sitting in logs.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you decide which of these failures are worth retrying automatically?
  • Where would you see the request in the platform if the script logged nothing at all?
  • What changes if this message is routed through a MID Server?

Sources

  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global

question: A facilities team built a Scripted REST API so a badge-reader vendor can look up employees: GET /api/x_fac/badges/v1/employee/{id}?fields=name,dept&active=true. The resource script reads request.queryParams.fields.split(','), returns response.setStatus('200'), and when the employee is missing it does response.setBody({error: 'not found'}). The vendor reports TypeErrors in the instance logs, status 0 on some responses, and 'not found' replies that arrive as 200. Explain each defect using what RESTAPIRequest and RESTAPIResponse actually return, and write the corrected resource script.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This checks whether you've read the shape of the objects a Scripted REST resource receives or just copied a sample. The three bugs map to three specific statements in the reference: query parameters arrive as arrays, setStatus() needs a number, and errors should go through setError() so the status and body match.

Diagnosis

  1. The TypeError. request.queryParams is documented as an Array type, and the example shows queryParams.active returning [false] and queryParams.name returning ['now']. Each value is an array, so queryParams.fields.split is calling split on an array. When the vendor omits fields, the value is undefined and the TypeError changes shape. Convert explicitly: String(request.queryParams.fields || ''). That works because a one-element array stringifies to its element. If the vendor sends the parameter twice, you get both values joined with a comma, which happens to suit this case.
  2. Status 0. The reference for setStatus(Number status) says that passing a non-numerical value, such as a string, causes the status code to default to 0. '200' is a string. Some clients treat 0 as a network failure.
  3. "Not found" as 200. setBody() only sets content; it does not change the status. Use response.setError() with an error object. The reference example uses new sn_ws_err.BadRequestError('Missing required parameters.'), and the Scripted REST script samples page also lists NotFoundError, ConflictError and NotAcceptableError.

Path parameters are different from query parameters: request.pathParams is a plain object, so request.pathParams.id is a string. Candidates who mix the two up usually fix one bug and introduce another.

Two other request properties help when debugging a vendor complaint. request.queryString is the raw query exactly as sent, for example active=false&name=now, which shows whether the vendor double-encoded a value. request.uri is the path without the domain, and request.url is the full URL. Logging uri and queryString on a 400 response tells you what the vendor actually called without dumping headers that may carry credentials. Only log them on errors, not on every call, or a busy badge system will fill the log table.

(function process(/*RESTAPIRequest*/ request, /*RESTAPIResponse*/ response) {
    var id = request.pathParams.id;                       // plain string
    var fieldsParam = String(request.queryParams.fields || '');   // array -> string
    var activeOnly = String(request.queryParams.active || 'true') === 'true';

    if (!id) {
        response.setError(new sn_ws_err.BadRequestError('Employee id is required.'));
        return;
    }

    var allowed = { name: 'name', dept: 'department', email: 'email' };
    var wanted = fieldsParam ? fieldsParam.split(',') : ['name', 'dept'];

    var gr = new GlideRecordSecure('sys_user');            // honour ACLs for the API user
    gr.addQuery('employee_number', id);
    if (activeOnly) gr.addActiveQuery();
    gr.setLimit(1);
    gr.query();
    if (!gr.next()) {
        response.setError(new sn_ws_err.NotFoundError('No employee with id ' + id));
        return;
    }

    var out = { id: id };
    for (var i = 0; i < wanted.length; i++) {
        var key = wanted[i].trim();
        if (allowed[key]) out[key] = gr.getDisplayValue(allowed[key]);
    }
    response.setStatus(200);                               // number, not string
    response.setBody(out);
})(request, response);

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • setBody() serializes to JSON or XML based on the request's Accept header. A vendor that sends Accept: application/xml gets XML even though you wrote a JavaScript object. Check request.getSupportedResponseContentTypes() if you need to refuse a format.
  • request.headers is an object keyed by header name, and the reference shows bracket access for names with special characters. request.getHeader('accept') is the safer call.
  • If the call carries a body, data, dataString and dataStream all read the same stream once. Reading data and then dataString returns an empty second value.
  • The allow-list of fields is deliberate. Passing a caller-controlled field list straight into getDisplayValue() lets the vendor read any column the API user can see.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing queryParams.active == 'true' and getting away with it because of loose equality, then breaking when someone switches to ===.
  • Setting the status after starting to write to the stream writer. That is a separate trap: content type and status must be set before getStreamWriter() output.
  • Querying with plain GlideRecord in an API exposed to an external system, which ignores ACLs for the integration user.
Score points: Point out that the version segment v1 in the URL is what lets you change the response shape later without breaking this vendor. You publish v2 with the new contract and leave v1 alone.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you add pagination to a list version of this endpoint?
  • Why might you choose GlideRecordSecure here, and what does it cost?
  • How would you authenticate this vendor without a user password?

Sources

  • RESTAPIRequest - Scoped, Global
  • RESTAPIResponse - Scoped, Global
  • RESTAPIRequestBody - Scoped, Global
  • Scripted REST API example - script samples (ServiceNow docs)

question: A retail chain's HR team uploads one Excel workbook a week to a scoped app record. It has three worksheets (Joiners, Movers, Leavers); each sheet has two title rows above the real column headers, and there is a hidden sheet called Lookups. The developer's script calls new GlideSysAttachment().getContentStream(id) once, then loops over the sheet names calling parser.setSheetName(name) and parser.parse(stream). Joiners loads; Movers and Leavers come back empty, the hidden Lookups sheet gets processed as data, and blank cells land in the target table as the word "null". Question: Explain each symptom and write a correct parsing loop with sn_impex.GlideExcelParser.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need to know that an input stream can only be read once, and that GlideExcelParser has a specific pattern for reading the same workbook more than once: setSource(stream), then parse() with no argument for each sheet. You should also know the switches for header rows and empty cells, that getSheetNames() includes hidden sheets, and that parse() returns a boolean you have to check.

The Answer

Why only the first sheet loads. parse(inputStream) consumes the stream. The second call gets a stream that has already been read, so there is nothing left to parse. The reference is explicit: setSource(inputStream) "defines an input source for parsing multiple times or parsing each worksheet", and the note on parse() says not to pass the stream when you use setSource() to parse the same source multiple times. The pattern is setSource() once, then setSheetName() and a bare parse() per sheet.

Why Lookups is processed. getSheetNames() returns names in left-to-right order and "results include any worksheets marked as hidden". Iterate over an allow-list of the sheets you expect instead of everything the workbook contains.

Why the headers are wrong. By default the parser treats the first row as headers, so with two title rows the column names are the title text. setHeaderRowNumber(n) sets which row holds the headers. The reference does not say whether the number is zero- or one-based (its getTableInfo() example uses 6), so check it against a sample file once and pin it with a comment.

Why "null" appears. A cell that is not present comes back as null. When the script does gr.setValue(field, row[header]) or string concatenation, null becomes the text "null". setNullToEmpty(true) makes missing cells return an empty value instead.

var SHEETS = ['Joiners', 'Movers', 'Leavers'];       // allow-list, not getSheetNames()
var stream = new GlideSysAttachment().getContentStream(attachmentSysId);
var parser = new sn_impex.GlideExcelParser();
parser.setSource(stream);                               // read many times
parser.setNullToEmpty(true);
parser.setHeaderRowNumber(HEADER_ROW);                  // verified against a sample file

var present = parser.getSheetNames();
try {
  for (var i = 0; i < SHEETS.length; i++) {
    if (present.indexOf(SHEETS[i]) == -1) {
      gs.warn('Workbook is missing sheet ' + SHEETS[i]);
      continue;
    }
    parser.setSheetName(SHEETS[i]);
    if (!parser.parse()) {                              // no argument: uses setSource()
      gs.error('Sheet ' + SHEETS[i] + ': ' + parser.getErrorMessage());
      continue;
    }
    var headers = parser.getColumnHeaders();
    if (headers.indexOf('Employee ID') == -1) {
      gs.error('Sheet ' + SHEETS[i] + ' has unexpected headers: ' + headers.join(', '));
      continue;
    }
    while (parser.next()) {
      var row = parser.getRow();                        // { 'Employee ID': '...', ... }
      stageRow(SHEETS[i], row);
    }
  }
} finally {
  parser.close();                                       // release the document
}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The parser handles .xlsx. A legacy .xls or a CSV renamed to .xlsx is not a documented input, so expect parse() to return false (test it on your instance); read getErrorMessage() and tell the uploader, rather than silently loading nothing.
  • If you set both setSheetNumber() and setSheetName(), the name wins. The number example in the reference treats 0 as the first sheet.
  • getRow() keys are the header text exactly as typed. A trailing space in "Employee ID " breaks every lookup. Normalise headers once (trim, lower-case) and map them to field names.
  • getTableInfo(), which reports column types and maximum lengths, is restricted to scoped applications. It is useful for validating a file before loading but will not run in a global script.
  • Large workbooks hold memory while open. Call close() in a finally block so an exception mid-loop does not keep the document in memory.
  • Dates and numbers come back as the parser renders them (the reference output shows 2019-07-29 11:48:43). Convert explicitly with GlideDateTime and validate, rather than assigning the string straight to a date field.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling getContentStream() again inside the loop. It works, but it re-reads the attachment for every sheet; setSource() is the documented approach.
  • Ignoring the boolean from parse() and then wondering why next() returns false.
  • Writing straight into the target table from the parser. Stage the rows into an import set table so a transform map, coalesce and the import log do the matching and error reporting.
Score points: Mention the hidden-sheet behaviour of getSheetNames() unprompted. Few people know it, and it is exactly the kind of thing that turns into a production incident.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you parse a workbook posted directly to a Scripted REST API instead of an attachment? (parser.parse(request.body.dataStream).)
  • Where would the parsed rows go next, and how would you transform them from script?
  • How would you use getTableInfo() to reject a file whose columns are too long for the target fields?

Sources

  • GlideExcelParser API reference

question: A retail company's BI team has built a nightly extract from GET /api/now/table/incident into their warehouse. The first week of reports is confusing: the State column shows 1, 2, 6 and 7 instead of New or Resolved, Assigned to shows 32-character sys_ids wrapped in objects with a link property, and every row carries roughly 90 columns they never use. A developer "fixed" it by adding sysparm_display_value=true, and now the analysts in London say opened_at times look an hour off compared with the timestamps the Singapore team quoted from the same records. Walk me through what each Table API read parameter is doing here and what request you would actually ship.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Show that you know the Table API returns database values by default, that sysparm_display_value has three settings with real consequences for dates and references, and that the reference-link objects and the column bloat each have their own parameter. A strong answer also picks up that display values depend on the user the integration authenticates as, which is where the time-zone complaint comes from.

The Answer

Everything the BI team saw is documented default behaviour.

  • Numbers instead of labels. sysparm_display_value defaults to false, which returns the actual values from the database. For a choice field that is the stored value (1, 2, 6, 7), not the label.
  • sys_id objects with a link. Reference fields return the sys_id plus a link URL to the referenced record through the Table API. sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true removes the link. It does not turn the sys_id into a name; that is still a display-value question.
  • 90 columns. sysparm_fields defaults to all fields. Pass a comma-separated list. sysparm_view exists too, but if both are passed, sysparm_fields takes precedence.

The developer's fix, sysparm_display_value=true, returns display values for every field. The reference states what that means per type: choice fields return the descriptive label, reference fields return the display field of the referenced record, encrypted text is returned decrypted if the caller has the encryption context, and date fields are rendered in the user's time zone while the database value is UTC. The integration account's time zone decides what the warehouse receives. London and Singapore are comparing a value rendered for the service account against values rendered for themselves in the UI, so of course they disagree.

For a warehouse, I want stable keys and UTC timestamps, plus labels for humans. That is sysparm_display_value=all, which returns both the actual and the display value:

GET /api/now/table/incident
  ?sysparm_query=sys_updated_on>=javascript:gs.daysAgoStart(1)^ORDERBYsys_updated_on
  &sysparm_fields=number,state,priority,assignment_group,assigned_to,opened_at,sys_updated_on,sys_id
  &sysparm_display_value=all
  &sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true
  &sysparm_limit=1000
Accept: application/json

With all, each field comes back as an object holding a value and a display_value. The ETL stores opened_at.value (UTC) as the timestamp, state.value as the join key, and state.display_value as a label column. Reference fields give you the sys_id for joins and the name for reports.

The reference also warns that requesting display values can cost performance, because they are not read directly from the database and may involve referencing other fields and records. So I only ask for display values on the fields that need them, which is another reason to keep sysparm_fields tight.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • sysparm_fields silently ignores invalid field names. A typo such as assignment_grp just disappears from the payload; there is no 400.
  • Display values are per user. If someone later changes the integration account's time zone or language, the extract changes with no code deployment.
  • Encrypted fields come back hidden or decrypted depending on the caller's encryption context, so the same request can produce different payloads for two accounts.
  • Name-value pair filters such as &state=closed are an alternative to sysparm_query and accept display values for choice and reference fields. The two are mutually exclusive, so do not mix them.
  • On a valid query with no matches, the current version returns 200 with an empty result array. The reference notes that version 1 of the multi-record GET returned 404 instead, so pinned /api/now/v1/ clients must handle that.

Common Mistakes

  • Using sysparm_display_value=true for machine-to-machine syncs and then joining on names that are neither unique nor stable.
  • Expecting sysparm_exclude_reference_link to return names. It only drops the link.
  • Comparing timestamps across systems without checking whose time zone rendered them.
Score points: Say up front that display values are rendered for the authenticated user, and propose sysparm_display_value=all with UTC values for storage and labels for reporting. That shows you have been burned by this before.

Likely Follow-ups

  • What changes if the warehouse later writes corrections back through PATCH? (Bring up sysparm_input_display_value and the GMT versus user time-zone handling.)
  • How would you page this extract safely across 2 million rows?
  • When would sysparm_view be more useful than sysparm_fields?

Sources

  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A field-service app used by an insurance company uploads damage photos to the incident a technician is working on. The mobile team uses POST /api/now/attachment/upload with multipart form data and keeps getting 400s or files with the wrong type. Another team uses POST /api/now/attachment/file and gets 404 even though the incident definitely exists. Separately, the claims system needs to download every PDF attached to an incident. Explain how the two upload endpoints differ, what is going wrong in each case, and how you would list and download the attachments.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is checking whether you know there are two upload styles with different contracts, that the Attachment API handles one file per request, that the Content-Type header carries real meaning, and that 404 often means "you can't see that record" rather than "it doesn't exist". Knowing the download endpoint and the metadata query is the other half.

The Answer

Binary upload: POST /api/now/attachment/file. The target is described in query parameters: table_name, table_sys_id and file_name are all required. The request body is the raw file, and the Content-Type header is the file's MIME type, for example image/jpeg. The reference calls that header mandatory for this endpoint. An optional encryption_context restricts access to users with that context, and creation_time exists so offline mobile uploads can keep their original timestamp.

curl "https://instance.service-now.com/api/now/attachment/file?table_name=incident&table_sys_id=d71f7935c0a8016700802b64c67c11c6&file_name=front_bumper.jpg" \
  --request POST \
  --header "Accept: application/json" \
  --header "Content-Type: image/jpeg" \
  --data-binary "@front_bumper.jpg" \
  --user "svc_fieldapp:..."

Multipart upload: POST /api/now/attachment/upload. This endpoint takes no query parameters. table_name and table_sys_id go in the form body, the request Content-Type is multipart/form-data, and the file's own Content-Type must be declared inside the file part, not in the form data. The reference adds one more rule: the file content must be in the final part of the message, and earlier parts carry only metadata. Mobile HTTP libraries that order form fields alphabetically or put the file first break that rule. That is the most likely cause of the 400s, and a missing per-part Content-Type explains the wrong file types.

curl "https://instance.service-now.com/api/now/attachment/upload" \
  --request POST \
  --header "Accept: application/json" \
  --header "Content-Type: multipart/form-data" \
  -F 'table_name=incident' \
  -F 'table_sys_id=d71f7935c0a8016700802b64c67c11c6' \
  -F 'uploadFile=@front_bumper.jpg;type=image/jpeg' \
  --user "svc_fieldapp:..."

The 404 on /file. For this endpoint, 404 means the record named by table_name and table_sys_id does not exist or is not accessible to the current user. The reference states the role requirement plainly: the account needs whatever roles are required to create sys_attachment records and to read and write the target table, such as itil for incidents. There is no single out-of-box role that grants attachment creation, though you can create one. So I would check the service account's access to that incident before suspecting the URL.

Listing and downloading. GET /api/now/attachment returns metadata and queries the sys_attachment table, so the filter is written against its columns:

GET /api/now/attachment?sysparm_query=table_name=incident^table_sys_id=<incident sys_id>^content_type=application/pdf&sysparm_limit=100

Each result's sys_id then goes to GET /api/now/attachment/{sys_id}/file with Accept: application/pdf or */*. That returns the binary, and the X-Attachment-Metadata response header carries the size, name and type. GET /api/now/attachment/{sys_id} without /file returns metadata only, including download_link.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • One file per request. Ten photos means ten calls.
  • Uploads respect com.glide.attachment.max_size (1024 MB by default) and glide.attachment.extensions. A blocked extension is a configuration issue, not a code issue.
  • The Attachment API accepts any Content-Type, and what you send is stored as file metadata. If you send */* or the wrong type, downstream consumers will misidentify the file.
  • The list endpoint defaults to sysparm_limit=1000, not the Table API's 10,000.
  • Renaming is done with PATCH /api/now/attachment/{sys_id} and a file_name body, which returns 204. Alt text and similar metadata go in attachment attributes (POST .../attributes).

Common Mistakes

  • Base64-encoding the file into a Table API POST on a custom field. The Developer Advocate team measured direct binary as about a third smaller than base64.
  • Putting table_name in the URL for the multipart endpoint.
  • Granting the integration user admin to "fix" the 404.
Score points: Mention that a 404 from /attachment/file covers "not accessible to the current user" and that multipart requires the file in the last part. Few candidates know either detail.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you fetch a remote file server-side and store it as an attachment without base64? (RESTMessageV2.saveResponseBodyAsAttachment, from the blog.)
  • How would you restrict who can download a sensitive attachment?
  • Where would you batch many small uploads, and what limits apply?

Sources

  • Attachment API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Beyond JSON: Working with Binary Files and Alternative Content Types in ServiceNow REST APIs (Developer Advocate blog)

question: A consumer electronics company wants its public support website (a Next.js site on its own domain) to search and display ServiceNow knowledge articles without customers logging in. A developer has the Knowledge Management REST API working from Postman, but the browser calls fail with CORS errors. Security is alarmed that the same endpoint returned internal-only articles when called with an agent's credentials, and marketing complains that article view counts never move. Explain how the Knowledge API handles unauthenticated access, CORS, rate limits and view counting, and what you would configure before go-live.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The Knowledge Management REST API (plugin sn_km_api) is publicly accessible by default. Any knowledge base that is publicly readable is exposed to unauthenticated callers. Authenticated callers see whatever their user can read. At this level you should know that you lock it down per endpoint with the Requires Authentication flag (version 1.0.1 and later), that a browser on another domain needs a CORS rule, and that unauthenticated and snc_external callers are limited to 500 requests an hour by default. You should also know which call actually increments a view count.

The Answer

Who sees what. The API returns what the calling user can read. Postman with an agent's login showed internal articles because the agent can read them, not because of a bug in the API. The website must call it either unauthenticated (public KBs only) or as a dedicated low-privilege user. It should also pass kb (a comma-separated list of knowledge base sys_ids) on every search so results stay within the customer-facing KBs even if someone later makes another KB public by mistake.

CORS. Postman doesn't enforce CORS. Browsers do. The reference says that to let other domains call these endpoints you define a CORS rule for the API. Without one, the site has to proxy calls through its own server, which is also where you would add caching.

Rate limit. The default is 500 requests per hour for unauthenticated and snc_external users. A busy public site will hit that quickly if every keystroke triggers a search. Debounce the search box, cache GET /knowledge/articles/featured results on the server, and review the inbound REST rate limit rules with the platform team.

Searching. GET /api/sn_km_api/knowledge/articles takes query (free text), filter (an encoded query on kb_knowledge), kb, language (ISO 639-1 codes or all), fields, limit (default 30) and offset. Each article in the response has id, number, title, snippet, score and rank, and meta.count gives the total for paging.

View counts. GET /knowledge/articles/{id} increments the view count and writes a Knowledge Use [kb_use] entry only when you pass search_id and search_rank (taken from the search response), or when you pass update_view. The site was calling the article endpoint without either, so nothing was counted.

GET /api/sn_km_api/knowledge/articles?query=bluetooth%20pairing&kb=<public_kb_sys_id>&language=en&limit=10&fields=short_description
GET /api/sn_km_api/knowledge/articles/KB0012345?language=fr&search_id=<id>&search_rank=<rank>

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • update_view is described as true "whether present as a standalone parameter or set to true", and no false value is documented. Do not rely on update_view=false to suppress a view; leave the parameter out and test it. If search_id and search_rank are also passed, update_view is ignored because the view has already been counted.
  • The language parameter on the single-article endpoint only works when id is a KB number, not a sys_id. To serve the French translation, request by number.
  • Attachments and embedded_content are returned only when the article has display_attachments set. The file itself comes from GET /knowledge/articles/{article_sys_id}/attachments/{attachment_sys_id}.
  • Articles in a scoped knowledge base need Restricted Caller Access granting the sn_km_api scope read access from the requesting scope.
  • All filter parameters are case-sensitive, including column names and values, so test the exact filter the site will send.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing with an admin or agent account and assuming the public site will see the same results.
  • Embedding a service account's password in browser JavaScript to "fix" access.
  • Calling search on every keystroke and blaming ServiceNow when the rate limit starts rejecting requests.
Score points: Say plainly that the API's default posture is public and that you would set Requires Authentication on any endpoint the site doesn't need anonymously. Mention that update_view has no documented false value. It shows you read the parameter description, not just its name.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you add "was this helpful?" feedback from the external site?
  • How would you serve article images that are attachments without exposing a login?
  • What changes if the site later needs customer-specific articles after login?

Sources

  • Knowledge Management REST API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A logistics company runs one English-speaking service desk in Kraków for customers in Brazil, Japan, Germany and Mexico. About 30% of incoming incidents are written in Portuguese, Japanese, German or Spanish, and agents paste text into a public website to read it, which the security team has banned. The CIO asks for incoming descriptions to be machine-translated into English automatically inside ServiceNow, with the customer's language recorded so replies can be translated back. Which server-side API would you use, how would you call it, and what failure cases do you need to handle?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants you to name the Dynamic Translation API (sn_dt_api.DynamicTranslation) instead of a hand-built REST call to Azure or Google. A good answer separates detection from translation, keeps the original text, runs the call asynchronously because it goes to an external provider, and handles the numbered error codes instead of assuming success.

The Answer

Dynamic Translation needs the com.glide.dynamic_translation plugin and a translator configured and active in Translator Configuration (sn_dt_translator_configuration), with credentials set up in Connections and Credentials. Microsoft Azure Translator and Google Cloud Translator are the documented providers, IBM appears as a valid translator value, and you can plug in a custom provider. The methods are static on the class:

  • getDetectedLanguage(text, parms) returns detectedLanguage with a code and a confidence between 0 and 1, plus alternatives.
  • getTranslation(text, parms) takes optional sourceLanguage, targetLanguages (an array), translator and additionalParameters, and returns translations[] of {targetLanguage, translatedText} along with the translator used and the detectedLanguage.
  • getDetectedLanguages() and getTranslations() are the batch versions. They return an overall status of Success, Partial or Error and an isError flag per item.
  • isEnabled(translator) tells you which of the four capabilities (translation, detection, batchTranslation, batchDetection) are switched on for a translator.

For the service desk, translate on insert, asynchronously, and put the English text in a work note so the customer's original description stays untouched:

// Async business rule on incident insert (or a flow script step)
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var DT = sn_dt_api.DynamicTranslation;
    var text = current.getValue('description');
    if (!text) return;

    var enabled = DT.isEnabled();                 // default translator
    if (!enabled.translation) return;

    try {
        var det = DT.getDetectedLanguage(text);
        if (det.code) {                           // some errors come back as {code, message}
            gs.warn('Detection failed ' + det.code + ': ' + det.message);
            return;
        }
        var lang = det.detectedLanguage.code;
        current.u_source_language = lang;         // custom field used for routing/reporting
        if (lang == 'en' || parseFloat(det.detectedLanguage.confidence) < 0.6) {
            current.update();
            return;
        }

        var res = DT.getTranslation(text, {
            sourceLanguage: lang,
            targetLanguages: ['en']
        });
        current.work_notes = '[Machine translation ' + lang + ' -> en, ' + res.translator + ']\n' +
                             res.translations[0].translatedText;
        current.update();
    } catch (e) {
        gs.warn('Dynamic translation failed: ' + e.message);   // message holds {code, message} JSON
    }
})(current, previous);

For the reverse direction, when the agent replies, call getTranslation() with targetLanguages set to the stored source language. If you omit targetLanguages it defaults to the current user's preferred language, which is useful in an interactive script and wrong in a background job running as system.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Errors come back in two ways. The documented examples wrap getTranslation() in try/catch and print a {"code":"40054","message":"Target language is invalid"} payload from error.message, while the detection examples show the same kind of payload returned as the result. Handle both.
  • Useful codes: 40001 plugin not installed, 40002 no default translator, 40005 translator inactive, 40009 time limit exceeded (40 seconds by default), 40052 text longer than the provider allows, 40053/40054 unsupported source/target language, 40055 bad credentials, 40014 translator configuration must be migrated to v3 for the batch methods.
  • Short text detects badly. The reference asks for "enough verbiage". A two-word short description can come back as the wrong language with high-looking alternatives, so detect on the description and check the confidence.
  • HTML content. To translate HTML (for example a knowledge article body) with Microsoft you pass an additional parameter for text type with value html; the default is plain. The parameter table spells the key textype while the example uses texttype, so test which one your instance accepts.
  • Partial batches. getTranslations() can return status: "Partial" where one item has isError: true and no translations. Index into the results carefully.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling the provider in a synchronous before business rule, so the caller waits up to 40 seconds when the provider is slow.
  • Overwriting the description with the translation, which loses the customer's wording and any nuance the machine missed.
  • Not labelling machine-translated text, so agents treat it as what the customer actually wrote.
  • Translating every update, including English ones, and paying the provider for nothing.
Score points: Store the detected language on the incident. It gives you routing to language-capable groups, reporting on volume by language, and the target language for replies without detecting again.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you translate 50 comments in one call, and what changes in the response handling?
  • What data-residency questions would you ask before sending customer text to an external translation provider?
  • Where does Dynamic Translation stop and static UI translation (translated text and field labels) take over?

Sources

  • DynamicTranslation

question: A retailer's nightly scheduled job reconciles 5,000 rows from a staging table (u_server_updates) into cmdb_ci_server by serial number. The original script opens a new GlideRecord on cmdb_ci_server inside the staging loop and has started hitting transaction timeouts. A teammate's rewrite, taken from a community post, collects every serial into an array and a lookup object, runs one cmdb_ci_server query with addQuery('serial_number', 'IN', serials), then loops over the CIs: if (serverMap[ci.serial_number]) set u_last_checked, call ci.setWorkflow(false) and ci.update(). Review both versions: explain the complexity change, then point out what is still wrong or risky in the rewrite and give your final version.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Count the queries first: the original makes one per staging row, which gives O(n × m) behaviour and 5,001 round trips. Give the rewrite credit for turning that into a fixed number of queries, then catch what is still wrong: a redundant lookup check, an object key built from a GlideElement, a per-row update loop where one set-based update would do, an unbounded IN list, and a casual setWorkflow(false) on a CMDB table.

Diagnosis

The Developer Advocate post on time and space complexity uses this exact example. For each staging record the original runs a new query against cmdb_ci_server. With 5,000 rows that is 5,001 database calls, and the per-call overhead alone can exceed the transaction limit. The blog calls it O(n × m). The rewrite pays a little memory (an array and a lookup object) to cut the queries to two, which the blog calls O(n + m). That trade is correct, and it is what the DataLoader, RLQUERY and addJoinQuery episodes are all about: stop querying inside loops.

What the rewrite still gets wrong:

  1. The map check adds nothing. The CI query already filters on serial_number IN serials, so every CI returned is in the map. The lookup costs nothing and protects nothing. It just makes the code look safer than it is.
  2. Object key from a GlideElement. serverMap[ci.serial_number] passes a GlideElement as a property name. JavaScript converts it to a string, so it happens to work. But this is the same habit that breaks === comparisons and array lookups. Use ci.getValue('serial_number').
  3. Row-by-row updates. Every CI gets the same value. The GlideRecord reference has a set-based method for that: updateMultiple(), with values set through setValue() (the reference says to use setValue rather than direct assignment for reliable results).
  4. Unbounded IN list. 5,000 serials in one IN clause today could be 200,000 after an acquisition. Chunk the list.
  5. setWorkflow(false) without a reason. The reference warns that disabling business rules, script engines and audit "can have a significant impact" on the instance, and that it cannot be set for cross-scoped applications. On a CMDB table this also skips audit and any downstream logic. Turn workflow off only if you have decided those rules must not run, not as a general speed-up.

The Answer

(function reconcileServers() {
  var CHUNK = 1000;
  var serials = [];
  var stg = new GlideRecord('u_server_updates');
  stg.addNotNullQuery('u_serial');
  stg.query();
  while (stg.next()) {
    serials.push(stg.getValue('u_serial'));
  }
  var now = new GlideDateTime();
  for (var i = 0; i < serials.length; i += CHUNK) {
    var ci = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_server');
    ci.addQuery('serial_number', 'IN', serials.slice(i, i + CHUNK).join(','));
    ci.setValue('u_last_checked', now);
    ci.updateMultiple();                 // one set-based update per chunk
  }
})();

This runs one staging query and one update per chunk. No CI is loaded into memory one by one. If each CI needs different values (for example a status taken from its staging row), keep the lookup object, key it with getValue(), query the CIs once per chunk, and update inside the loop. That is where the map earns its place.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Duplicate serials in staging are harmless for the IN list but point to a data problem. A Set (available in scoped apps since ECMAScript 2021 support arrived in Tokyo) removes them in one line.
  • updateMultiple() does not support adding multiple journal entries. Do not use it for work notes.
  • The reference says not to combine updateMultiple() with setLimit() or chooseWindow() on large tables.
  • Above glide.db.forced.chunk.threshold the platform forces updates into chunks to protect replication. That is separate from your own chunking of the IN list.
  • Index matters. The blog's checklist says to query on indexed fields to avoid full table scans. Confirm serial_number is indexed on this table before relying on the IN lookup.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing the query count but keeping per-row update() calls that each fire business rules.
  • Assuming the fast version is right because it is fast, when the map check shows the author did not reason about what the query already guarantees.
  • Adding setWorkflow(false) everywhere once someone notices it speeds things up.
Score points: Count the database calls out loud for each version (5,001, then 2, then 1 + chunks) and explain that the last step changes the update pattern, not just the query pattern.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you run this as an event-driven script action in batches instead of one long scheduled job?
  • How would you report serials in staging that matched no CI?
  • Would Identification and Reconciliation (IRE) be a better home for this logic?

Sources

  • Beyond Best Practices: Developer's Guide to Time and Space Complexity (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Solving the N+1 Problem with a DataLoader Pattern (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GlideRecord - Scoped (API reference)
  • Learn ECMAScript 2021 with Earl Duque (Developer Advocate Blog)

question: A university's ServiceNow team has 30 hand-built ATF tests and a family upgrade in six weeks. Testers spend two days per upgrade clicking through the incident form and the 20 most-ordered catalog items. The platform owner wants test coverage generated for incident and those 20 items only, the regression suite run every night without someone leaving a browser tab open as a client test runner, and a way to stop a job that runs into the morning. A teammate kicked off generation with only tableEncodedQuery set and it is now generating tests for hundreds of catalog items. Which APIs would you use, how would you call them, and what went wrong with the teammate's job?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to hear that the ATF Test Generator and Cloud Runner can generate and run tests without anyone keeping a client test runner browser open, and that both are scriptable through the CloudRunnerAPI script include. A good answer scopes generation tightly, knows the job is asynchronous and tracked in the Browser Orchestration Queue, and checks the cloud user before blaming the tests.

The Answer

The plugin is ATF Test Generator and Cloud Runner (sn_atf_tg). The CloudRunnerAPI script include exposes three parts, documented as Scoped and Global. In global scope you call them through the sn_atf_tg namespace:

  • TestGenerationAPI: startJob() inserts a record into the Browser Orchestration Queue (sn_atf_tg_sn_boq) and returns its sys_id. progress() returns counts (testsSucceeded, testsFailed, testsPending, testsInProgress, testsSkipped). cancelJob() stops it. Per-test detail, including failure reasons, is in Generated Tests (sn_atf_tg_generated_test).
  • TestRunnerAPI: startJob() runs an existing test or suite (sys_atf_test or sys_atf_test_suite) in the cloud browser and returns a BOQ sys_id. progress() returns a percentage and a state: Pending, Processing, Browsers requested, Running, Completed or Failed. startJobAsync() returns a root tracker id instead, paired with progressFromTracker() and cancelJobByTracker().
  • TestUserAPI: isValidCloudUser() checks a user and selectCloudUser() runs an end-to-end login job and, if it works, sets that user as the cloud user for future runs and generations.

Every method takes one object argument such as {snboqId: "..."} or {username: "..."}, not positional strings, even though the headings read like startJob(String testId).

// Background script / scheduled job in GLOBAL scope (note the sn_atf_tg namespace)
var CR = sn_atf_tg.CloudRunnerAPI;

// 0. Make sure the cloud user can actually log in
if (!CR.TestUserAPI.isValidCloudUser({ username: 'atf.cloud.runner' })) {
    gs.error('Cloud runner user is not valid (inactive, locked out, no admin role, ...)');
} else {
    CR.TestUserAPI.selectCloudUser({ username: 'atf.cloud.runner' });
}

// 1. Generate tests for incident + the 20 most-ordered catalog items, one suite
var boq = CR.TestGenerationAPI.startJob({
    tableEncodedQuery: 'nameINincident',
    catalogEncodedQuery: 'sys_idIN' + topTwentyCatItemIds.join(','),
    maxTestCountPerTable: 10,
    maxTestCountPerItem: 3,
    separateUpdateSetPerScope: false,
    scopeForGeneratingTests: globalScopeSysId,   // required when separateUpdateSetPerScope is false
    email: 'platform-qa@example.com'
});
gs.info('Generation BOQ ' + boq);

// 2. Later: check progress
gs.info(JSON.stringify(CR.TestGenerationAPI.progress({ snboqId: boq })));
// {"testsSucceeded":4,"testsFailed":2,"testsPending":2,"testsInProgress":8,"testsSkipped":0}

// 3. Nightly: run the regression suite in the cloud browser
var runBoq = CR.TestRunnerAPI.startJob({ testId: regressionSuiteSysId });
gs.info(JSON.stringify(CR.TestRunnerAPI.progress({ snboqId: runBoq })));   // {progress, state}

Generation filters are encoded queries: tableEncodedQuery, catalogEncodedQuery and userEncodedQuery. Caps are maxTestCount (1-9999), maxTestCountPerTable (1-10) and maxTestCountPerItem (1-10). By default tests are split into suites and update sets per scope; set separateUpdateSetPerScope to false to get one suite, and then scopeForGeneratingTests becomes required.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Empty means everything. The default for each encoded query is an empty string, meaning all tables, all catalog items, all users, and maxTestCount defaults to 9999. A job started with only tableEncodedQuery also generates tests for every catalog item. The reference examples pass catalogEncodedQuery: "sysIdISEMPTY" to switch catalog generation off.
