  • GlideModalForm - API reference
  • GlideListV3 (deprecated) - API reference
  • GlideList2 (g_list) - API reference
  • GlideRecord (client) - API reference
  • GlideAjax - API reference
  • GlideForm (g_form) - API reference
  • GlideNotification - API reference

question: A bank's change team wants only members of the 'CAB Approvers' group to approve emergency changes. The current server-side check in a UI action is if (gs.hasRole('x_bank_cab.approver')) { ... }. The audit team then finds that every platform admin passed the check, that an admin approved while impersonating a CAB member, and that a nightly integration account approved changes through a script with no user at the keyboard. Using GlideUser and GlideSession, explain what each of these methods really checks and rewrite the guard so it meets the audit requirement.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Expect to explain that a role check and a group-membership check answer different questions, that gs.hasRole() returns true for admins by design, and that the session can tell you whether the person is impersonating and whether anyone is interacting at all. Then build a guard that encodes the audit rule directly instead of relying on a role that admins inherit.

The Answer

What each method checks, per the reference:

  • gs.hasRole(role) returns true if the current user has the role, and the reference adds that it returns true for users with the administrator role. That is why every admin passed.
  • gs.getUser() returns the scoped GlideUser for the current user. The GlideUser reference points out that using it avoids slower GlideRecord queries for user information.
  • GlideUser.isMemberOf(group) takes a group sys_id or name and reports membership in that group. Group membership is the actual audit rule.
  • GlideUser.getRoles() returns explicitly granted, inherited and group-acquired roles. getUserRoles() returns only explicitly granted roles. Useful for diagnosing how someone got a role.
  • gs.getSession().isImpersonating() returns true when the user is impersonating another user.
  • gs.getSession().isInteractive() is true for a user working through the UI and false for programmatic sessions such as a SOAP request.

Rewritten guard, placed in a script include so the UI action, any REST endpoint and any flow call the same rule:

var CabGuard = Class.create();
CabGuard.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {},

    canApproveEmergency: function () {
        var session = gs.getSession();
        var user = gs.getUser();
        if (session.isImpersonating())
            return this._deny('impersonation');
        if (!session.isInteractive())
            return this._deny('non-interactive session');
        if (!user.isMemberOf('CAB Approvers'))      // prefer the group sys_id in real code
            return this._deny('not in CAB Approvers');
        return true;
    },

    _deny: function (reason) {
        gs.warn('Emergency CAB approval denied for {0}: {1}', gs.getUserName(), reason);
        return false;
    },

    type: 'CabGuard'
};

The UI action condition and the server script both call new CabGuard().canApproveEmergency(). Hiding the button is a usability step; the server-side check is the control.

The order of checks matters for the audit story. Impersonation is checked first because an impersonating admin is, for that session, the CAB member they picked, so isMemberOf() would pass. Interactivity comes next because the nightly account has no person behind it, and a membership check alone would let it through if someone once added the service account to the group. Membership is last. Each denial is logged with a reason, which gives the auditors a list of attempts as well as a list of approvals.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Use the group's sys_id rather than its name in production. Names get edited, and a renamed group silently fails the check for everyone.
  • Blocking non-interactive sessions also blocks legitimate automation. If the integration genuinely needs to approve, give it a separate, explicit path with its own audit trail rather than a shared rule with exceptions.
  • Admins still have other ways to change data, such as editing the record directly. The guard proves that the approval path follows the rule; ACLs and audit history cover the rest.
  • gs.hasRole() and GlideUser.hasRole() are documented separately. The admin note appears on the GlideSystem method; test the GlideUser method on your instance before assuming it differs.
  • gs.isInteractive() on GlideSystem and isInteractive() on GlideSession both exist; the documented examples use the session form, which keeps all session checks on one object.
  • Group membership through nested groups, or roles granted through groups, can surprise auditors. getRoles() versus getUserRoles() shows where a role came from.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a role check when the requirement is about group membership.
  • Putting the check only in the UI action condition, so a direct server call or REST request bypasses it.
  • Querying sys_user_grmember with GlideRecord for every check instead of using isMemberOf().
  • Logging the denial with no reason, which leaves the audit team guessing.
Score points: Quote the reference line that gs.hasRole() returns true for administrators, then show that isMemberOf() plus isImpersonating() expresses the audit rule directly.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you enforce the same rule in an approval flow rather than a UI action?
  • Should the guard also check the change's assignment group or CI owner?
  • How would you report all emergency approvals made in the last quarter by people outside the group?

Sources

  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • GlideUser (Scoped)
  • GlideSession (Scoped)

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

There are two separate bugs to find, one cosmetic and one serious. The cosmetic one is that getRecordValues() copies raw values, so references come out as sys_ids and choice fields as stored values. The serious one is that the widget trusts a URL parameter to decide whose data to show. A good answer also explains the widget lifecycle (server script runs first, data goes to the client, input comes back on c.server.update(), options carries instance configuration) and limits how many rows the server sends.

The Answer

Bug 1: values instead of display values. $sp has three copy helpers and they are not interchangeable. getRecordValues(data, from, names) copies values, so cat_item is the catalog item sys_id and state is the stored choice value. getRecordDisplayValues(data, from, names) copies display values, which is what a student wants to read. getRecordElements(data, from, names) copies the element's name, display value and value, which is the right choice when the client needs both (for example, the sys_id for a link and the label for the text).

Bug 2: whose records. $sp.getParameter(name) returns a value from the query string or post body. Anything the browser sends is under the user's control, so it must never decide which person's data the server returns. The requester should come from the session (gs.getUserID()), not the URL.

Bug 3: no read check. A plain GlideRecord in a widget server script does not apply ACLs the way a list does. $sp.canReadRecord(gr) returns true only if the record is valid and the user can read it, and for sc_cat_item, sc_category and kb_knowledge it also checks whether the user can view the item. Calling it per row costs a little, but this list is small once it is filtered to the current user.

Bug 4: unbounded rows. Some staff accounts have hundreds of active items. Put a limit on the query and make the limit an instance option, so a portal admin can change it without editing code. The Developer Advocate pagination post makes the same argument for server-side paging: send the client only the page it needs.

How the three objects move. On first load the server script runs with input undefined, fills data, and the platform serialises data to the client as c.data. When the client calls c.server.update(), it posts c.data back; the server script runs again with that payload in input, and the new data replaces the client's copy. options holds the widget instance's option values; $sp.getValue(name) reads a named value from the request, the widget instance or the portal record.

(function() {
  var limit = parseInt(options.max_items, 10) || 20;
  data.items = [];
  data.filter = (input && input.filter == 'all') ? 'all' : 'active';

  var gr = new GlideRecord('sc_req_item');
  gr.addQuery('request.requested_for', gs.getUserID());  // session, never the URL
  if (data.filter == 'active')
    gr.addQuery('active', true);
  gr.orderByDesc('sys_updated_on');
  gr.setLimit(limit);
  gr.query();
  while (gr.next()) {
    if (!$sp.canReadRecord(gr))
      continue;
    var row = {};
    $sp.getRecordElements(row, gr, 'number,cat_item,state,sys_updated_on');
    row.sys_id = gr.getUniqueValue();
    data.items.push(row);
  }
})();

In the template, bind to the display values the helper produced, and build the link with the record's sys_id rather than anything the user typed.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • getParameter() returns null when there is no request, JSON request or widget, for example when the widget is rendered from a script or embedded. Code that does getParameter('x').toString() throws in those cases.
  • input is undefined on the first run. Guard every read (input && input.filter) or the first page load fails.
  • On c.server.update() the whole c.data object travels to the server. Do not put large arrays in c.data and then call update in a loop; each call re-sends everything.
  • getRecordElements() gives you name, value and display value per field, so the payload is roughly three times larger than display values alone. Use it only for fields where the client needs both.
  • If the requirement is to show a student's own requests, filtering on the session user is the actual security control; canReadRecord() is a second check for items the user should not see, not a replacement for the filter.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing the display problem in the client with a second server call per row to look up names.
  • Copying the requester sys_id into c.data and reading it back from input as if it were trusted.
  • Using $sp.getRecord() here. With no parameters it returns the record identified by the current URL, which is not what a list widget needs.
Score points: Say out loud that every value in input and every URL parameter is attacker-controlled, and that a widget server script is an API endpoint that happens to render HTML.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you add server-side paging with input.page and still keep the limit enforced on the server?
  • When is getRecordDisplayValues() enough and when do you need getRecordElements()?
  • Where would you check whether the user can open the request page itself ($sp.canSeePage())?

Sources

  • GlideSPScriptable API reference
  • Widget API reference (input, data, options, server.update)
  • Building a Custom Pagination Widget for Service Portal (Developer Advocate blog)

question: A facilities management company has a published custom AI Skill Kit skill, "Classify work order", that returns a category and a confidence note. The business now wants it to run automatically when a work order is created from the portal, not from a button. A developer opens a pull request with an after-insert business rule that calls the skill and does current.u_ai_category = resp.capabilities[capId].response;. In UAT the field fills with [object Object] on some records and stays empty on others, and the AI admin says the monthly Assist count jumped. Question: Review the approach, write the corrected server-side call, and explain what you would change around it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You should know that skills are invoked from script through sn_one_extend.OneExtendUtil.execute and where its two IDs come from. The response is a string you have to parse, its shape varies by model, and an LLM call doesn't belong in a synchronous rule. Treat Assist consumption as a design input too.

The Answer

What is wrong with the PR.

  • It assigns the raw response to a string field. The FAQ's sample treats response as a JSON string that has to be parsed (the useful text is under model_output), and warns that output varies by provider. As a string, the field gets the whole JSON envelope instead of a category; if it comes back as an object, assigning it gives [object Object]. The Developer Advocates hit the same problem when mapping a tool's array output in an AI agent stream.
  • It runs synchronously after insert. The portal user waits for a round trip to the LLM before the save returns.
  • It has no error path. When the LLM returns an error, nothing is logged and the field stays empty. That explains the blanks.
  • It runs on every insert, including integration-created and test records, which explains part of the Assist increase.

Calling a skill from script. The AI Skill Kit FAQ documents sn_one_extend.OneExtendUtil.execute(request). The request carries an executionRequests array; each entry has the input payload, a capabilityId and meta.skillConfigId, and the request sets mode to 'sync'. The skill config sys_id is in sn_nowassist_skill_config (the config-id URL parameter in the editor); the capability sys_id is in sys_one_extend_capability (the skill URL parameter). Each input is keyed by the input name you defined, with table name, sys_id and query string for record inputs.

Corrected version, as an async business rule with a condition of "created from portal" and category empty. Keep the IDs in system properties rather than hard-coding them:

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var capId = gs.getProperty('x_fm.ai.classify.capability_id');
    var cfgId = gs.getProperty('x_fm.ai.classify.skill_config_id');

    var payload = {};
    payload['work_order'] = {
        tableName: current.getTableName(),
        sysId: current.getUniqueValue(),
        queryString: ''
    };

    var request = {
        executionRequests: [{
            payload: payload,
            capabilityId: capId,
            meta: { skillConfigId: cfgId }
        }],
        mode: 'sync'
    };

    try {
        var resp = sn_one_extend.OneExtendUtil.execute(request);
        var cap = resp && resp.capabilities ? resp.capabilities[capId] : null;
        if (!cap || cap.error || !cap.response) {
            gs.warn('Classify skill returned no response for ' + current.getValue('number'));
            return;
        }
        var body = (typeof cap.response === 'string') ? JSON.parse(cap.response) : cap.response;
        var out = body.model_output;
        if (typeof out === 'string') {
            try { out = JSON.parse(out); } catch (e) { /* plain text output */ }
        }
        var category = (out && out.category) ? String(out.category) : '';
        if (!category) {
            gs.warn('Classify skill output had no category: ' + JSON.stringify(body));
            return;
        }
        current.u_ai_category = category;
        current.work_notes = 'AI-suggested category: ' + category;
        current.update();
    } catch (ex) {
        gs.error('Classify skill failed for ' + current.getValue('number') + ': ' + ex);
    }
})(current, previous);

The FAQ's own sample parses the response and reads model_output, and warns that LLM output JSON may differ, so the script checks types instead of assuming. Before merging, log the raw response for a few records on your provider and confirm the shape.

What I would change around it.

  • Validate against a choice list. If the model returns a category that is not a valid choice, do not write it. Log it and leave the field for the human. That turns hallucination into a visible data quality metric.
  • Write a suggestion, not a decision. Store the AI category in its own field and let the dispatcher accept it, at least until you have evaluation numbers.
  • Control volume. Condition the rule on source and state, skip records created by integrations, and do not re-run on update. Testing in the skill editor also consumes Assists, so keep test data sets small.
  • Know the security context. The FAQ says the domain resolves from the invoking user's session, so the skill cannot read data that user cannot. Test as a portal user, not as admin.
  • Prefer a flow if the team is low-code. Skills can be deployed as a flow action. A record-created flow with the skill action plus a decision step is easier for admins to maintain than script.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • When the LLM call returns an error, the FAQ says no Assist is charged, but your code still has to handle the missing response.
  • current.update() in an async rule triggers rules again. The condition (category empty) stops a loop.
  • Plan for the skill being rebuilt: the FAQ says a cloned OOTB skill only lets you change the prompt and provider, and that changing inputs, outputs or deployment methods means creating a new custom skill (with new IDs). How far a published custom skill's inputs can be edited varies by plugin version, so test this on your instance. Properties make an ID swap a config change.
  • Guardian prompt injection detection is not on by default for custom skills. Portal text is user-controlled, so configure it on this skill.

Common Mistakes

  • Hard-coding sys_ids that differ between instances after the skill is rebuilt.
  • Assuming the response is always JSON with the same keys.
  • Calling the skill in a before rule to "set the field before save".
Score points: Point out that a deterministic fallback matters more than the AI path: if the skill fails, the work order must still route by the old rules.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you measure whether the AI category is right often enough to auto-apply it?
  • Would you use a tool inside the skill to fetch the asset's history, or pass it as an input?
  • How do you move this skill and its IDs from dev to production?

Sources

  • AI Skill Kit / Now Assist Skill Kit (NASK) FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • Now Assist Skill Kit - Live Coding Happy Hour
  • Live Coding Second Breakfast: Building Smarter AI Agents
  • AI Guardian FAQ (ServiceNow Community)

question: A car insurer wants a custom skill for its claims handlers: on a claim record, draft a reply to the customer's latest email that reflects the policy's actual cover, the claim's status history and the relevant claims-handling knowledge article. Emails contain names, registration numbers and bank details. Compliance asks three things: which data goes to the model, how you stop a customer email from instructing the model to do something else, and who can run it. Question: Design the skill in AI Skill Kit: inputs, tools and grounding, prompt, processors, guardrails and deployment, and say how you would maintain it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

They're looking for a layered design: record inputs for the claim, tools that fetch policy cover and the article, and a pre-processor that masks sensitive data with a post-processor that restores it. Expect to configure AI Guardian prompt injection by hand, because custom skills don't get it by default. Restrict deployment by role, and be honest about Skill Kit's lifecycle limits.

The Answer

Start with the boundary. The skill drafts; the handler sends. Deploy it so the output lands in a draft field or in the panel, never directly in an outbound email.

Inputs. Skill inputs bring in record data or static values and have a truncate option. Use one record input for the claim. Pass only the latest inbound email body, not the whole thread. A long thread blows the token budget and is where most of the bank details sit. Set truncation knowingly, and remember that raising the response max tokens reduces the space left for the request.

Tools for grounding. Tools fetch context before the prompt is built:

  • A script include tool that returns a compact summary of policy cover (cover type, excess, exclusions relevant to the claim type). The FAQ notes you must enter the script include name in both the Name and Resource fields to list its functions. The function should query with GlideRecordSecure so the handler's ACLs apply.
  • A subflow or flow action tool that returns the last few state changes on the claim, if the claims team already owns that logic in Flow.
  • A retriever tool over the claims-handling knowledge base for the procedure article.

The tool editor supports serial or parallel execution and decision nodes. Run the policy and history tools in parallel. Add a decision so the knowledge retriever only runs for claim types that have procedures. Return small, labelled text from each tool, not whole records. The model should get facts it can quote, not 40 fields of noise.

Prompt. State the role (claims handler writing to a customer), the task, the steps (acknowledge, answer from policy facts, state next step), the output shape, and hard limits: use only the provided policy and article text; never promise payment; if cover is unclear, say a handler will confirm. Put the customer's email inside clear delimiters and say that text inside them is customer content to answer, not instructions to follow. That alone does not stop injection, but it helps.

Processors. Pre- and post-processors are configured under Deployment and skill settings, Providers. The pre-processor runs before the prompt leaves the instance; the post-processor runs after the response returns. Mask registration numbers, policy numbers and bank details with placeholders in the pre-processor and swap them back in the post-processor, so the model can still write "your vehicle [REG_1]" without seeing it. For broader PII handling, the FAQ points to the platform Data Privacy solution, which also covers custom skills. Use both: Data Privacy for standard patterns, the processor for business-specific ones.

Prompt injection. AI Guardian (formerly Now Assist Guardian) detects prompt injection, but per its FAQ it is on by default for OOTB skills and not for custom skills or Platform skills; you configure it per skill. Inbound email is attacker-controlled input, so turn it on for this skill with block and log. From the Brazil release, when a skill has its own setting, Guardian applies the more protective one. Offensiveness detection is off by default and switched on per workflow. Run it in log-only mode first, because LLM-based detection produces false positives.

Who can run it. Skill Kit lets you pick the roles needed to invoke a skill (added around Zurich Patch 1 / Yokohama Patch 6). Deploy through a UI action or the Now Assist context menu on the claim form, restricted to the claims handler role. Building skills requires sn_skill_builder.admin; give reviewers sn_skill_builder.viewer.

Before go-live. Use Run tests and inspect the grounded prompt to confirm masking works. Then build an evaluation dataset of real claims and run it in the Evaluations tab, which scores faithfulness and correctness with an LLM judge. A handler-reviewed sample is still the final check.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The FAQ says that for a cloned OOTB skill only the prompt and provider can change, and that changing inputs, outputs or deployment methods means a new custom skill. Whether a published custom skill's inputs can be edited depends on your plugin version (test this on your instance), so get the input list right before publishing rather than counting on adding "include the adjuster's notes" later.
  • There is no in-product delete. Removing the sn_nowassist_skill_config record leaves metadata behind, so build in a named update set to track every record.
  • Chaining another skill as a tool only works once that skill is published.
  • Domain separation resolves from the invoking user's session, so a handler in one brand's domain cannot pull another brand's policy, which is what you want.

Common Mistakes

  • Passing the whole email thread and the whole policy record "for context".
  • Assuming Guardian already protects a custom skill.
  • Querying in the tool script with plain GlideRecord, so the model sees data the handler could not.
Score points: Mention that masking has to survive the round trip: test the post-processor with a response where the model reorders or repeats placeholders, or the customer gets "[REG_1]" in their letter.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a customer writing in Welsh when the article is English only?
  • What would you log so compliance can reconstruct which policy facts a draft was based on?
  • When would this become an AI agent instead of a skill?

Sources

  • Build Custom AI Skills with Now Assist Skill Kit: Step-by-Step Demo
  • AI Skill Kit / Now Assist Skill Kit (NASK) FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • AI Skill Kit (ServiceNow product documentation)
  • AI Guardian FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • Now Assist Guardian / AI Guardian (ServiceNow documentation, Zurich)
  • Latest access control security enhancements for AI Agents and Skill Kit (ServiceNow Community)
  • Protecting Your AI with Now Assist Guardian: Offensive Content

question: An HR shared services team built an AI agent in AI Agent Studio to "help employees with HR cases". Over three months it grew to 14 tools: knowledge search, read case, read employee profile, update case, reassign case, create catalog request, send email, and several script tools that query HR tables with GlideRecord. All tools run autonomously and the agent runs as the invoking user. A security review flags that an employee could put instructions in a case description that the agent later follows when an HR agent asks it to summarise that case. Question: Redesign the agent's tools and guardrails. Be specific about tool count, execution mode, identity and the scripts.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Recognise this as second-order prompt injection: the malicious text arrives through data the agent reads, and the agent then acts with the privileges of whoever invoked it. The fix is structural: fewer and narrower tools, supervised mode on anything that writes or sends, a deliberate run-as identity, role masking, secure queries in scripts, and agent team segmentation. "Add a line to the prompt" is not an answer.

The Answer

Why it is dangerous. AppOmni published exactly this pattern against ServiceNow agents in November 2025. A low-privileged user wrote instructions into a ticket description. When an admin triggered agents that read that ticket, the agents followed them, read a record the attacker could not see and copied it into the attacker's ticket. The agents ran with the admin's rights. ServiceNow confirmed the behaviours were as designed and updated its documentation. Here, the HR agent reads case descriptions written by employees and holds update, reassign and email tools. That is the same setup.

1. Split and shrink. The Developer Advocate guidance for AI Agent Studio is to start small and keep each agent to about 5-7 tools. Split this into:

  • A read-and-draft agent: knowledge search, read case, read the employee fields needed for HR answers, draft a response. No write tools, no email.
  • A fulfilment agent with the write tools (update case, create catalog request), invoked only by HR agents and only through supervised tools.

Narrow tools are also easier for the model to choose correctly. Agentic evaluations score tool choice per step, and fourteen overlapping tools make that score worse.

2. Execution mode. When you create a tool you set its execution mode. Supervised means the user reviews the action before it runs. Put update case, reassign, create request and send email in supervised mode. Read tools can stay autonomous. Check the system property sn_aia.enable_usecase_tool_execution_mode_override: per AppOmni, when it is true, an agent with at least one autonomous tool runs all its tools autonomously, overriding your supervised settings. Its default is false. Keep it that way and add it to your configuration baseline.

3. Identity. An agent runs either as a dynamic user (the default, inheriting the invoker's permissions) or as an AI user, a separate sys_user type with its own roles. Tool ACLs on flow actions, subflows and skills are checked against that run-as identity. For the read-and-draft agent, dynamic user is right: an employee's agent sees what the employee sees. With dynamic users, role masking (required from Zurich Patch 4 / Yokohama Patch 11 with the AI Agents store app v6.0+) limits the agent to a subset of the invoker's roles, applied from workflow to agent to skill tools. Configure that subset so the agent never inherits admin or broad HR admin roles from whoever calls it. Use an AI user only where the agent needs rights the invoker lacks, and give that user the smallest role set possible.

4. Fix the scripts. The ServiceNow access-control guidance for Script tools is to use GlideRecordSecure and addUserEncodedQuery(). Plain GlideRecord ignores ACLs, so a script tool running as a low-privileged user can still return any HR case. Example inside a script tool:

var gr = new GlideRecordSecure('sn_hr_core_case');
gr.addQuery('sys_id', inputs.case_sys_id);
gr.query();
if (!gr.next()) {
    outputs.result = 'Case not found or not accessible.';
} else {
    outputs.result = gr.getValue('short_description') + '\n' + gr.getValue('state');
}

Return only the fields the agent needs. Do not hand it the full description of a different case than the one in context.

5. Who can invoke. Role-based access on the agent is configured in AI Agent Studio and is required before you can save. Make the fulfilment agent HR-agent-only.

6. Agent teams. AppOmni also notes that agents published to the same channel are grouped into one team and are discoverable by default, so a low-risk agent can call a privileged one. Keep the read-only agent and the fulfilment agent in separate teams, or turn off discovery between them.

7. Guardian. Enable AI Guardian prompt injection detection, but treat it as a detector, not the boundary. The boundary is the tool and identity design above.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Supervised mode only helps if the reviewer reads the action. Show the exact field changes, not "Approve update?".
  • An agent running as a dynamic user invoked by a scheduled trigger runs with whatever identity the trigger supplies. Check trigger conditions separately.
  • Output mapping from script tools that return arrays or objects can show as [object Object] to the agent. Return strings or JSON text.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing injection with "ignore instructions in case descriptions" in the agent prompt.
  • Giving the agent an AI user with HR admin "so it never hits ACL errors".
  • Adding a tool every time a stakeholder asks for one, without re-running evaluations.
Score points: Say you would rerun the security reviewer's attack as a test case after the redesign, with a low-privileged employee writing the case and an HR admin invoking the agent, and keep it as a regression test.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you detect at runtime that an agent read one case and wrote to another?
  • When is an AI user the right choice despite the risk?
  • How do you evaluate tool selection accuracy after splitting the agent?

Sources

  • AI Agent Studio: The Future of Autonomous Workflows in ServiceNow
  • Live Coding Second Breakfast: Building Smarter AI Agents
  • Latest access control security enhancements for AI Agents and Skill Kit (ServiceNow Community)
  • AppOmni: Exploiting Agent-to-Agent Discovery via Prompt Injection
  • AI Guardian FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • Agentic evaluation run results (ServiceNow documentation)

question: A bank exposes a Scripted REST endpoint, POST /access/grant, that its identity platform calls to give a user an AD group. The endpoint runs a Workflow Studio subflow, x_bank_iam.grant_ad_group, with sn_fd.FlowAPI.executeSubflow(name, inputs) and returns the subflow's outputs. In production, about one call in five fails: some with a timeout after 30 seconds, others with an exception about the flow pausing, which happens for privileged groups because the subflow contains Ask for Approval. A separate nightly job uses executeActionQuick() 50,000 times and nobody can find its errors. Question: Explain the synchronous, asynchronous and quick ways to run flows, subflows and actions from script, what each returns, and redesign both pieces.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need to connect both failure modes to documented behaviour: synchronous execution has a default 30-second limit and throws when it expires, and synchronous flows and subflows cannot pause, so anything with an approval or a wait has to run asynchronously. You should also know what each method returns, that quick methods trade observability for speed, and that the newer getRunner() builder is the documented replacement for the older static methods.

The Answer

The method families. The FlowAPI reference groups them like this:

  • executeAction / executeSubflow(name, inputs, timeout) run synchronously and return the outputs object. executeFlow is synchronous too but returns nothing. The optional timeout is in milliseconds and overrides the 30-second default held in com.glide.hub.flow_api.default_execution_time; when it expires an exception is thrown. executeFlow and executeSubflow also throw if the flow pauses.
  • startAction / startFlow / startSubflow(name, inputs) run asynchronously and return the sys_id of the context record. You read results later with getStatus(contextId), getOutputs(contextId) and getErrorMessage(contextId), and stop a run with cancel(contextId, reason).
  • The ...Quick variants do the same without creating execution details or context records, "regardless of Workflow Studio settings". They cannot pause for waits such as Ask for Approval, cannot run on a MID Server, and getErrorMessage() cannot read their errors because there is no context.
  • sn_fd.FlowAPI.getRunner() returns a ScriptableFlowRunner builder: .flow() / .subflow() / .action() / .datastream(), then .inForeground() (script pauses) or .inBackground() (script resumes immediately), optional .inDomain(), .timeout(ms), .quick(), .withInputs(), and .run(), which returns a result object with getContextId(), getOutputs(), getDomainId() and debug(). The current FlowAPI page says the runner replaces the execute/start/quick static methods.

Diagnosing the endpoint. The timeouts are the 30-second default on a subflow that calls AD through a spoke. The "pause" exceptions are the approval branch: a synchronous subflow cannot wait for a human. No timeout value fixes the second one.

Redesign. Split the contract. Standard groups can complete in the request; privileged groups get an accepted response with a tracking id.

(function process(request, response) {
  var body = request.body.data;
  var inputs = { user_id: body.user_id, group_name: body.group };

  if (!isPrivileged(body.group)) {
    try {
      var res = sn_fd.FlowAPI.getRunner()
        .subflow('x_bank_iam.grant_ad_group')
        .inForeground()
        .timeout(20000)                  // ms; keep below the caller's own timeout
        .withInputs(inputs)
        .run();
      response.setStatus(200);
      response.setBody({ status: 'complete', context: res.getContextId(), outputs: res.getOutputs() });
      return;
    } catch (e) {
      gs.error('grant_ad_group sync failed: ' + e);
      // fall through to async so the request is not lost
    }
  }
  var ctx = sn_fd.FlowAPI.startSubflow('x_bank_iam.grant_ad_group', inputs);
  response.setStatus(202);
  response.setBody({ status: 'accepted', context: ctx });
})(request, response);

Give the identity platform a GET /access/grant/{context} resource that returns getStatus(ctx) and, once complete, getOutputs(ctx); or have the subflow call back when it finishes. Be careful with the fallback: if the synchronous run timed out on the caller side but actually completed, a second start grants twice. Make the subflow idempotent (check membership first) before adding that fallback.

The nightly job. Quick methods are meant for high-volume work where the record-keeping overhead matters, but you lose the context record that holds the error. Wrap each call in try/catch, write failures to your own log table with the inputs, and count successes and failures. If that is not acceptable, use the normal methods for a sample, or for the failures on a retry pass.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Run-as differs by method. Per the FlowAPI page, actions run as the session user, while flows and subflows run as the user set in the flow properties. For quick methods the documentation is not consistent: one page says all quick methods run as the system user, the FlowAPI page says executeFlowQuick/executeSubflowQuick run as the session user and the start-quick variants as System. Test it on your release, and use .quick().asUser() on the runner when you need the triggering user.
  • The reference advises against calling these methods from an asynchronous business rule script; it suggests a scheduled job built in Workflow Studio instead.
  • In domain-separated instances the flow runs in the domain of the user who started the script unless you use .inDomain().
  • Background runs give you a context id, not outputs. Reading getOutputs() right after an inBackground() run returns nothing useful; the Developer Advocate Generative AI post makes the same distinction in its comments.
  • cancel() can lag slightly when the context runs on another node.

Common Mistakes

  • Raising the timeout to five minutes so the approval "has time". The REST transaction holds a thread for that long and the call still fails when the flow pauses.
  • Using quick methods in an integration where support needs execution details to answer "what happened to request X".
  • Passing the flow's sys_id or label instead of the scoped internal name (scope.name).
Score points: Name the system property com.glide.hub.flow_api.default_execution_time and say that synchronous flows throw on pause. That shows you have read the reference, not just copied a snippet.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you return a meaningful error to the caller from getErrorMessage(contextId)?
  • When would you use scheduleCancel() rather than cancel()?
  • How do you keep the subflow idempotent if the caller retries?

Sources

  • FlowAPI - Scoped, Global (ServiceNow docs)
  • ScriptableFlowRunner - Scoped (ServiceNow docs)
  • ScriptableFlowRunnerResult - Scoped (ServiceNow docs)
  • API access to Workflow Studio flows (ServiceNow docs)
  • Getting started with the Generative AI Controller (Developer Advocate blog)

question: An insurer routes claims with a decision table, "Claim Routing", that has three inputs (Claim Amount, Line of Business, Loss Date/Time) and one result column, Assignment Group. A script include calls new sn_dt.DecisionTableAPI().getDecision('Claim Routing', {'Claim Amount': amt, 'Line of Business': lob, 'Loss Date': gr.getDisplayValue('u_loss_date')}). Four problems are reported: every claim gets the same default group; it works for admins but throws for the integration user; claims logged near midnight by Sydney staff land in the wrong band; and the business now wants every matching reviewer group, not just the first. Question: Diagnose each problem and write the corrected call.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer expects the four rules the DecisionTableAPI reference spells out. The first argument is the decision table's sys_id. Input keys are the technical column names (lower case, u_ prefix, spaces replaced by underscores). The caller needs the decision_table_crud_api role. Date/time inputs are compared as literal yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss values with no time zone conversion. You should also know the difference between getDecision() and getDecisions(), and what happens when nothing matches.

The Answer

Problem 1: always the default group. Two mistakes combine. getDecision(decisionID, inputs) takes the sys_id of the sys_decision record, not its name. And the inputs map is keyed by the column name of each Decision Input, which the reference says must be lower case with a u_ prefix and underscores for spaces: "Claim Amount" becomes u_claim_amount. If the engine does not receive the inputs it is evaluating against, the conditions cannot match, and the documented behaviour with no inputs is to return the first default answer. That is the "same group every time" symptom. Do not guess the keys: call getInputs(decisionID) once in a background script and read the name/columnName of each input.

Problem 2: fails for the integration user. The API page states "You must have the decision_table_crud_api role to use this API." Admins pass because of admin. Grant the role to the integration user (or the role the script runs under), and put it in the app's role documentation so the next environment is not a surprise.

Problem 3: midnight claims. getDisplayValue() returns the user's local time in the user's format. The reference says date/time inputs must be yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss, are processed without time zone conversion, and "between" conditions compare the literal values. So a Sydney user's display value is compared as if it were UTC, which shifts the band by ten or eleven hours. Pass GlideDateTime.getValue(), which is the internal UTC value, and make sure the table's boundaries were authored in UTC too.

Problem 4: all matching groups. getDecision() returns one answer record (a GlideRecord from the answer table). getDecisions() returns an array of every correctly evaluated answer, or all default answers when no inputs are given. On a multi-result table, the values of each result column are in result_elements, for example answer.result_elements.u_assignment_group.

var DT_CLAIM_ROUTING = gs.getProperty('x_ins_claims.dt.claim_routing'); // sys_id, not name

function routeClaim(claimGr) {
  var loss = new GlideDateTime(claimGr.getValue('u_loss_date')); // internal UTC value
  var inputs = {
    u_claim_amount: parseInt(claimGr.getValue('u_amount'), 10),
    u_line_of_business: claimGr.getValue('u_lob'),               // choice value, not label
    u_loss_date: loss.getValue()                                 // yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss
  };
  var groups = [];
  try {
    var answers = new sn_dt.DecisionTableAPI().getDecisions(DT_CLAIM_ROUTING, inputs);
    for (var i = 0; answers && i < answers.length; i++) {
      var g = answers[i].result_elements.u_assignment_group;
      if (g) groups.push(String(g));
    }
  } catch (e) {
    gs.error('Claim Routing evaluation failed for ' + claimGr.getValue('number') + ': ' + e);
  }
  return groups;   // caller decides what an empty list means
}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • When no default and no correctly evaluated answer exists, both methods are documented to return an error, not an empty result. Wrap the call and decide explicitly what a no-match means for the business (manual triage queue, not a silent default).
  • The type of each value must match the Decision Input type. Passing a string "25000" to an Integer input or a choice label to a Choice input is a common reason rows never match.
  • The reference's own date example calls getDecision("my_decision_table", { effective_time: ... }), which contradicts both the sys_id parameter and the u_ naming note on the same page. Follow the parameter descriptions, not that snippet.
  • Rows are evaluated by order. If the business adds a broad row above a narrow one, getDecision() starts returning the broad answer; getDecisionTable() or getQuestions() lets you audit order and conditions from script.
  • The same role governs the create/update/delete methods (createInputs, createQuestions, updateQuestion and so on). Granting it to an integration user also lets that user change the table through the API, so scope who holds it.

Common Mistakes

  • Hard-coding the decision table sys_id in the script so it differs between instances. Keep it in a system property or look it up once.
  • Treating the result as a plain object. With getDecision() the answer is a GlideRecord on the answer table; read fields with getValue().
  • Re-implementing the table as an if/else chain "because the API was flaky", which throws away the business-editable rules that justified the table.
Score points: Mention that date/time inputs ignore user and system time zones and that between uses the literal values. Then show the GlideDateTime.getValue() normalisation. That is the bug most teams ship.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would you call the decision table from a flow's Make a Decision step instead of from script?
  • How would you unit-test the table across environments in ATF?
  • How would you build the table itself from script with createDecisionTable(), createInputs() and createQuestions()?

Sources

  • DecisionTableAPI - Scoped, Global API reference

question: A procurement team at a European logistics company keeps a fillable vendor contract PDF (40 form fields, signature line on the last page) attached to each contract record. Today a paralegal downloads it, types in the vendor name, value and effective date, pastes the approving director's signature image, saves it as a locked PDF and re-uploads it. That takes about 15 minutes per contract and they process 300 a month. The director's signature is already stored as a PNG attachment. A developer's first attempt calls fillFieldsAndMergeSignature() but the attached output shows the fields empty and no signature, and the script logged nothing. Design the server-side solution with the PDF Generation Utilities APIs, write the code, and explain why the first attempt failed silently.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Show that you know the PDF Generation Utilities plugin already does form filling, signature stamping and flattening in one call, so you don't need a third-party PDF library or a MID Server. A strong answer reads the result object instead of waiting for an exception, explains the point-based coordinate system for the signature box, and says why flattening matters for a legal document. Spotting the argument-order trap in the published example earns extra credit.

The Answer

The APIs live in the sn_pdfgeneratorutils namespace (plugin com.snc.apppdfgenerator, active by default) and are documented as Scoped and Global. Three methods do the work:

  • PDFGenerationAPI.isDocumentFillable(), getDocumentFields() and getDocumentFieldsType() let you inspect the template without opening it. The type call returns the page number and field type for each field (text, check_box, signature and so on), which is how you find where the signature line actually sits.
  • PdfMergeSignRequestor describes the signature: createRequest(targetSysId, targetTable, tableSysId, targetFileName) points at the source PDF attachment, and addSignatureMapping(pageNumber, leftMargin, topMargin, boxWidth, boxHeight, sysId) places an image attachment (the approver's captured signature) in a box measured in points.
  • PDFGenerationAPI.fillFieldsAndMergeSignature(fieldsMap, sysId, tableName, tableSysId, pdfName, requestor, flatten) fills the fields, stamps the image, flattens, and attaches the result to the record. It returns {attachment_id, message, status}.

For the contract flow I would put this in a script include and call it from a Flow Designer script step or an async business rule when the approval completes:

// Script include in the vendor-contract scope (sn_pdfgeneratorutils is Scoped and Global)
var ContractPdfSigner = Class.create();
ContractPdfSigner.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {
        this.api = new sn_pdfgeneratorutils.PDFGenerationAPI();
    },

    sign: function(contractGr, sourcePdfId, signatureImgId) {
        var table = contractGr.getTableName();
        var id = contractGr.getUniqueValue();

        // 1. Is this really a fillable form? document_editable is a STRING
        var fillable = this.api.isDocumentFillable(sourcePdfId);
        if (fillable.status != 'success' || fillable.document_editable != 'true')
            return this._fail(contractGr, 'Not a fillable PDF: ' + fillable.message);

        // 2. Validate the field names we intend to write
        var known = this.api.getDocumentFields(sourcePdfId).fields || [];
        var map = {
            'Vendor Name': contractGr.getDisplayValue('vendor'),
            'Contract Value': contractGr.getValue('contract_value'),
            'Effective Date': contractGr.getValue('starts')
        };
        for (var f in map) {
            if (known.indexOf(f) < 0)
                return this._fail(contractGr, 'Template field missing: ' + f);
        }

        // 3. Make sure the signature page exists (sizes are in points)
        var sizes = this.api.getPdfPageSizes(sourcePdfId).pages_size || {};
        var lastPage = Object.keys(sizes).length;

        // 4. Signature request: page, left, top, width, height (points), image attachment sys_id
        var req = new sn_pdfgeneratorutils.PdfMergeSignRequestor();
        req.createRequest(sourcePdfId, table, id, 'contract_signed');
        req.addSignatureMapping(lastPage, 72, 640, 180, 40, signatureImgId);

        // 5. Fill, stamp, lock. Argument order per the signature: pdfName BEFORE requestor
        var res = this.api.fillFieldsAndMergeSignature(map, sourcePdfId, table, id,
            'contract_signed', req, { FlattenType: 'fully_flatten' });

        if (res.status != 'success')
            return this._fail(contractGr, res.message);
        return res.attachment_id;
    },

    _fail: function(gr, msg) {
        gs.error('ContractPdfSigner ' + gr.getDisplayValue() + ': ' + msg);
        return null;
    },
    type: 'ContractPdfSigner'
};

Flattening is the part legal cares about. FlattenType accepts donot_flatten, partially_flatten (only the fields you changed) and fully_flatten, which is the default. A signed contract with editable fields invites someone to change the value after signature. I pass fully_flatten explicitly even though it's the default, so the intent is obvious in code review.

If the downstream system wants the bytes instead of an attachment (for example to push to a document management API), getFilledDocumentWithSignatureAsBase64(fieldsMap, sysId, requestor, flatten) returns the filled, signed PDF as Base64.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Failures do not throw. Every method returns status: "failure" with a message such as No editable fields exist with specified names, This request cannot be completed as the requested page does not exist, or a security-scan message. Code that only wraps the call in try/catch will report success on a document that was never produced.
  • Antivirus scanning. The API refuses an attachment that failed or is still pending the security scan. If the template is uploaded and signed in the same transaction you can hit the pending message; signing later in the flow avoids that race.
  • Field names are exact. The keys in fieldsMap are the PDF's internal field names (things like 1LN.7 or Check Box21), not the labels printed on the page. Pull them with getDocumentFields() rather than guessing.
  • Two coordinate systems. addSignatureMapping measures from the left and the top margin. The redact() method measures x and y from the bottom-left corner. Teams that reuse coordinates between the two put the box in the wrong place. Use getPdfPageSizes() (612 x 792 points for Letter) to sanity-check positions.
  • Argument order. The method signature is (..., pdfName, requestor, flatten), but the published example passes the requestor before the file name. Follow the signature.
  • Return values are strings. document_editable comes back as the string "true", not a Boolean.
  • The maximum PDF size is 50 MB.

Common Mistakes

  • Building the contract with convertToPDF() from HTML and drawing a signature image in the HTML. You lose the form fields, and the output is fixed A4 that truncates content which overflows the page.
  • Leaving fields unflattened on a signed document.
  • Pointing tableName and tableSysId at a record the source PDF is not attached to. The reference describes them as the record the PDF is attached to, so attach the template to the contract first.
  • Running the signing synchronously in a before business rule on the approval, so a slow or failed generation blocks the approver's click.
Score points: Mention that getDocumentFieldsType() reports each field's type (including signature) and page number, so you can derive the page for addSignatureMapping() from the template itself instead of hard-coding page 6 and breaking when legal adds a cover page. Check by name too: in the reference output a field called Signature.1 is typed text, because many templates use a plain text box for the signature line.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Legal now wants a redacted copy for the vendor portal with bank details blacked out. Which method, and what limits does it have with JBIG2 images and punctuation in search keywords?
  • How would you produce a branded cover letter with a header logo and page numbers from HTML, and why does that need the header/footer variant?
  • Where would you record the resulting attachment_id so auditors can tie the signed PDF to the approval?

Sources

  • PDFGenerationAPI - Scoped, Global
  • PdfMergeSignRequestor - Scoped, Global

question: An HR team at a 12,000-employee retailer runs a new-hire onboarding playbook against HR cases. Three requests have come in: (1) recruiters want a 'Start onboarding' button instead of the playbook firing automatically, and twice already a double-click started two runs; (2) when a start date moves, the Provisioning stage must be re-run without resending the welcome emails from the earlier stages; (3) when an offer is withdrawn, every onboarding run on that case must stop. The previous developer handled (3) by setting sys_pd_context.state to cancelled with a GlideRecord update, and HR still sees laptop orders being placed. Using the PlaybookExperience API, write the server-side logic for all three and explain the state rules that constrain restart and cancel.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to hear that playbooks are process definitions running against a parent record. sn_playbook.PlaybookExperience is the supported way to start, inspect, restart and cancel them from script; inserting or updating sys_pd_context rows directly is not. Good answers know the state rules for restart and cancel, understand that cancel is two-phase (Pending Cancel, then optionally force), and guard against starting duplicate runs.

The Answer

The API needs the Playbook Experience Core plugin (com.glide.playbook_experience.config), at least one playbook in sys_pd_process_definition, and a caller with the roles needed to view and cancel running processes in Process Automation Designer. All methods are static. Playbooks are addressed by scoped name (scope.name) and runs by their sys_pd_context record.

1. Manual start from a UI action. Since Zurich a playbook does not need a predefined trigger, and the Developer Advocate team calls out APIs and UI actions as the intended way to launch those. triggerPlaybook(scopedName, parentRecord) returns the new sys_pd_context sys_id, or null if no run was created. Check for an existing run first:

// UI action "Start onboarding" on sn_hr_core_case (server side)
var name = 'x_acme_onb.new_hire_onboarding';
if (sn_playbook.PlaybookExperience.parentRecordContainsPlaybook(current, name)) {
    gs.addErrorMessage('Onboarding is already running for this case.');
} else {
    var ctxId = sn_playbook.PlaybookExperience.triggerPlaybook(name, current);
    if (ctxId)
        gs.addInfoMessage('Onboarding started.');
    else
        gs.addErrorMessage('Playbook could not be started. Check the process definition is active.');
}
action.setRedirectURL(current);

2. Start date moved: rewind to a stage. restartPlaybook(playbookContext, laneContextId, activityContextId, playbookExperienceId) restarts the whole run, a stage, or an activity. Lane and activity IDs are mutually exclusive; pass one and leave the other null or empty.

// Async business rule on the case: start date changed
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var PE = sn_playbook.PlaybookExperience;
    var runs = PE.getPlaybooksForParentRecord(current);
    for (var i = 0; i < runs.length; i++) {
        var run = runs[i];
        if (run.scoped_name != 'x_acme_onb.new_hire_onboarding') continue;
        if (['IN_PROGRESS', 'QUEUED', 'PENDING_CANCEL'].indexOf(run.state.value) < 0) continue;

        var ctx = new GlideRecord('sys_pd_context');
        if (!ctx.get(run.sys_id)) continue;

        // Completed "Provisioning" stage execution from Lane Executions [sys_pd_lane_context].
        // findLaneContext() is your own helper; check the lane context columns on your instance.
        var laneId = findLaneContext(run.sys_id, 'Provisioning');
        if (!laneId) continue;
        var res = PE.restartPlaybook(ctx, laneId, null);
        if (res.errors && res.errors.length)
            gs.error('Restart failed: ' + JSON.stringify(res.errors));
    }
})(current, previous);

3. Offer withdrawn: cancel. cancelPlaybooksByParentRecord(parentRecord, reason, scopedName, playbookExperienceId) cancels runs for the record (all playbooks if you omit the scoped name) and returns canceledPlaybookContext and skippedPlaybookContext arrays. The cancellation reason is shown to runtime users, so write it for HR, not for developers.

// Case withdrawn: cancel, then force-cancel anything stuck
var PE = sn_playbook.PlaybookExperience;
var out = PE.cancelPlaybooksByParentRecord(current, 'Offer withdrawn', 'x_acme_onb.new_hire_onboarding');
out.skippedPlaybookContext.forEach(function(s) {
    gs.warn('Skipped ' + s.sys_id + ': ' + JSON.stringify(s.errors));
});
// Later (for example a scheduled check), for contexts still PENDING_CANCEL:
// PE.cancelPlaybook(ctxGr, '', undefined, true);

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Restart rules. Only playbooks that are In Progress, Queued or Pending Cancel can be restarted, and only complete stages or activities can be the restart point. Rewinding to a stage that has not finished yet fails, so check the lane state before you call it.
  • Cancel is two-phase. A normal cancel moves the context to PENDING_CANCEL. Underlying flows for in-progress activities may keep running. cancelPlaybook(ctx, reason, experienceId, true) force-cancels those flows, but only once the context is already Pending Cancel, and the reason is ignored when force is true. The reference warns that force cancel cannot guarantee a clean stop, so treat it as a clean-up tool.
  • Duplicates. triggerPlaybook() will happily start a second run. parentRecordContainsPlaybook() is the cheap guard, but it reports any execution, including completed or cancelled ones, so a case that is cancelled and later re-offered can never be started again through this button. If that matters, check the states from getPlaybooksForParentRecord() instead. Neither check is a lock: two near-simultaneous clicks can both pass, so also disable the button client-side.
  • Custom state mappings. If the team defined custom activity state mappings, pass the sys_playbook_experience sys_id to cancel and restart; the default is the Global Playbook Experience.
  • Visibility. Each returned run carries can_read, can_cancel, can_restart and can_add_activity. Reading a run requires read access to the parent record, and Zurich added playbook- and stage-level runtime permissions, so an API call made as the agent can see less than the same call made as admin.
  • Return objects report problems in an errors array rather than throwing. Log them.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting sys_pd_context.state to cancelled with GlideRecord. That skips the engine's clean-up of the underlying flows.
  • Calling restartPlaybook() from a synchronous before rule on the case, which ties the agent's save to the engine's work.
  • Restarting the whole playbook when only one stage needs to run again, which resends welcome emails and recreates tasks.
Score points: Mention that getPlaybooksForParentRecord() returns the state as {displayValue, value} with values like IN_PROGRESS and PENDING_CANCEL. Comparing against the internal value keeps the logic working for users with a non-English session.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you report on cases with playbooks stuck in Pending Cancel for more than a day?
  • When would you use a scheduled record processing trigger instead of starting the playbook from script?
  • How would you restrict who can see the payroll stage of this playbook?

Sources

  • PlaybookExperience
  • Creator Toolbox: Playbook Triggers & Permissions, Recurrence Triggers and Flow Debugger Enhancements

question: A private bank onboards corporate clients in six countries. The process has a shared core (KYC checks, document collection, account setup) but differs by country and client segment: some segments need an extra sanctions review, two countries need a local regulator notification, and KYC document steps must only be visible to the compliance team. Relationship managers want to see where each onboarding is and act on their steps in the workspace; the operations team wants a daily sweep that chases onboardings stuck for 5 days. Today there are 14 near-duplicate flows. Question: What do you build as playbooks, what stays as flows, and how do you use variants, triggers, permissions and localization to get rid of the duplication?
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This tests whether you know where playbooks end and flows begin: playbooks are for human-facing, staged processes users work through, and flows are for automation nobody needs to watch. You're also expected to know the Yokohama and Zurich playbook features (variants, localization, multiple triggers, scheduled record processing triggers, runtime permissions per playbook and stage) and the Zurich flow Recurrence Trigger, and use them to collapse 14 flows into a small set.

The Answer

Split by audience. A playbook gives users a guided view of a multi-step process, embedded in workspace, mobile or portal, built from stages and activities. Relationship managers and compliance work the onboarding step by step and need to see progress. That is a playbook. The daily chase is automation with no user watching. That is a flow. The individual automated pieces (create the account in the core banking system, send the regulator notification) are flow actions or subflows that the playbook's activities call.

One base playbook plus variants. Playbook variants (Xanadu from November 2024 with Workflow Studio 20.6.2, Yokohama with 20.7.1) let you define a parent playbook with the core activities and child variants that add or change activities, adjust start rules and set display order, without touching the parent. Users do not need to know which variant runs. Design:

  • Parent: KYC, document collection, account setup.
  • Variant per segment that needs sanctions review: adds that activity.
  • Variant per country with regulator notification: adds that activity.

Watch the combinations. If a client is in a sanctions segment and a regulator country, you need a variant that covers both, or conditional start rules on activities inside fewer variants. Two dimensions times six countries can recreate the duplication you were removing. Prefer start-rule conditions for small differences and variants for real process differences. The blog listed mid-process variant evaluation as a roadmap item, so the variant is chosen when the playbook starts. If segment can change mid-onboarding, put that logic in conditional activities, not variants.

Localization instead of copies. Playbook Localization (Yokohama) translates a single playbook at runtime. The steps from the post: instance on version 27.1 or later, enable the required system properties, install the language plugins, create and activate the playbook, and translate UI elements in the Process Definition table. Runtime text uses the getMessage API, so labels show in each user's language. Three of the 14 flows were probably language copies.

Triggers (Zurich). Before Zurich a playbook had one trigger. Now it can have several, so "client record created" and "client re-onboarding requested" can start the same definition. Zurich also allows playbooks with no predefined trigger, launched from an API or a UI action, which suits "start onboarding" as a button on the client record.

The daily chase. Two options:

  • A playbook scheduled record processing trigger, which runs a playbook across a batch of records (up to 1,000 by default), useful if the chase itself is a guided process an operations user works.
  • A flow with the Zurich Recurrence Trigger: run on weekdays at 08:00 in a stated time zone, with an end condition if needed. It shows a plain-language summary and localized times. If the chase is just "find stuck onboardings and notify the owner", this is simpler.

I would use the flow. Use the scheduled playbook trigger when each record needs a human to work through steps.

Permissions. Zurich playbook runtime permissions work at playbook and stage level: who can see the playbook, who can see a stage, restart a stage, add optional activities, or rewind and re-execute steps. Lock the KYC document stage to the compliance role. Restrict rewind and re-execute on account setup, since re-running it could create duplicate accounts. Remember this controls the playbook experience; the underlying records still need ACLs.

Getting started fast. Now Assist can generate a playbook from a text description or from an image of a whiteboard diagram. Use it to draft the base playbook from the current process map, then review stages and activities by hand.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Features depend on Workflow Studio versions from the Store (20.8.1 for the Zurich trigger and permission features), not only the family release. Check both before promising them.
  • Stage permissions do not secure the data. Someone with table access can still read KYC records from a list.
  • A scheduled trigger processing 1,000 records by default may miss records in a large backlog. Know the limit and the order.
  • Translations in the Process Definition table must be maintained when activity labels change, or users see mixed languages.

Common Mistakes

  • Building every automated step as a playbook activity so it "shows up", which clutters the user view.
  • One variant per country per segment, which is the 14-flow problem in a new tool.
  • Using a scheduled flow with a script to approximate "first Monday of the month" when the Recurrence Trigger handles it.
Score points: Draw the decision line clearly: if a person needs to see and act on the step, it is a playbook activity; if not, it is a flow action called from one.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you migrate in-flight onboardings from the old flows to the new playbook?
  • How would you debug a variant that did not get selected?
  • Where would an AI agent fit in this process, and where would you not let one in?

Sources

  • ServiceNow Playbooks Overview and Playbook generation via Now Assist
  • Mastering Playbook Variants in ServiceNow Yokohama
  • Playbook Localization in Yokohama
  • Creator Toolbox: Playbook Triggers and Permissions, Recurrence Triggers and Flow Debugger Enhancements

question: A building supplies distributor receives about 900 supplier invoices a week as PDF email attachments. Accounts payable staff save each PDF, key the invoice into a 15-year-old desktop ERP client that has no API, and paste the ERP document number into a ServiceNow AP case. Some AP agents also look up supplier bank details in a web portal while working cases. The CFO wants this automated with ServiceNow RPA, and a developer has already used Now Assist to generate a bot from the prompt "process invoices". Question: Review that start, then design the bots, covering attended versus unattended, credentials, queues and sensitive data, failure handling and how you will observe them.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Start by asking whether RPA is the right tool (it's the fallback when there is no API). Then design around the RPA Hub controls added in Washington DC and later: external credential vaults, the Set Password component, sensitive queue content, Graceful Stop, bot process restrictions, automation logs and embedded taskbar automation for attended bots. Treat Now Assist bot generation as a draft generator that needs a precise prompt and a review.

The Answer

Is RPA right? For the ERP client, yes: no API, desktop UI only. For reading the email and PDF, check first whether the platform can do it natively. RPA is fragile compared with an integration, so use it only for the step that has no other route.

The generated bot. Now Assist for RPA (Yokohama) generates bot logic from natural language through "Build with Now Assist" in RPA Studio, when creating, extending or adding activities to a project. It needs the Now Assist for RPA Hub installed and the RPA bot generation skill activated. The Developer Advocate post is blunt that a vague prompt ("Create an incident") gives a vague bot. "Process invoices" is that prompt. Rewrite it per automation, for example: "Retrieve unread emails from the AP mailbox with PDF attachments, save each PDF to the folder D:\AP\Inbox named by sender and received date, and mark the email as read." Review the generated preview, accept or refine components, then test. Generation shortens a build that the post says took 1-2 weeks for simple bots and 4+ weeks for complex ones, but it does not replace design.

Design: split into two automations.

  1. Unattended intake bot: reads the mailbox, saves PDFs, extracts header fields, and puts one queue item per invoice into an RPA Hub queue.
  2. Unattended ERP entry bot: takes queue items, keys them into the ERP client, captures the ERP document number, and updates the AP case.

A queue between them gives you retries, a backlog you can see, and the option to scale the entry bot across more robots without touching intake.

Attended bot for the bank details lookup. The portal lookup happens while an agent is working a case, so it is attended. Embedded Taskbar Automation lets support agents trigger attended bots from the task record. If the portal uses Shadow DOM, Washington DC added Shadow DOM support so the bot can find those elements.

Credentials. RPA Hub can keep credentials in external vaults instead of storing them in the instance. Use that for the ERP service account and the mailbox. Inside the bot, use the Set Password component, which passes an encrypted or secure string into the password field so it never appears in clear text during execution.

Sensitive data. Invoices carry bank details. Mark the queue content as sensitive, which RPA Hub supports, so payloads are not exposed in the queue UI. Do not write bank details into the AP case work notes. Use bot process restrictions to control who can access and run these bot processes.

Failure handling.

  • Idempotency: before creating an ERP invoice, search the ERP for supplier plus invoice number. A retry after a timeout must not create a duplicate payment.
  • Graceful Stop: use the Graceful Stop component so that a stop request finishes the current invoice and stops cleanly, instead of killing the bot mid-entry and leaving a half-keyed document.
  • Business exceptions (unknown supplier, totals that do not add up) go back to a human queue with a reason, not into endless retries.

Observability. Track Automation Logs show bot execution inside ServiceNow, so you can troubleshoot without logging on to the robot machine. Report queue depth, items per hour, business-exception rate and system-exception rate per day. A rising system-exception rate usually means the ERP screen changed.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Desktop bots break on screen resolution, pop-ups and ERP client updates. Pin the robot machine image and route ERP client upgrades through change management.
  • A sensitive flag on the queue does not stop the bot writing the same data to a log file on the robot. Review the bot's own logging.
  • Generated bots may pick selectors that work once. Re-record selectors against stable attributes before production.
  • The Connection Manager in RPA Desktop Design Studio logs into the instance without an external browser, but production robots should use their own service identities, not a developer's session.

Common Mistakes

  • One monolithic bot from mailbox to ERP, with no queue and no way to resume.
  • Storing the ERP password as a plain variable in the bot.
  • Shipping a Now Assist-generated bot without reading every step.
Score points: Say the duplicate check against the ERP is the most important line of logic in the design, because the cost of a duplicated supplier payment dwarfs the cost of the whole project.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle invoice formats the extraction step cannot read?
  • How many robots do you need for 900 invoices a week, and how would you measure it?
  • When the ERP is finally replaced, what in this design carries over?

Sources

  • ServiceNow RPA Bot Generation with Now Assist
  • What's New in Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in Washington DC

question: A wealth-management firm licenses market and client-holding data from a provider whose contract says no copies of the data may be stored on third-party systems. Advisors want to see a client's current holdings as a related list on the client account form in ServiceNow, filter it, and occasionally report on it. An earlier team built a nightly import set into a custom table, which compliance has now banned. Design the replacement with Remote Tables on a Washington DC or later instance using the Flow Designer route, and explain the data volume, caching and refresh decisions you would make, including how a scoped app can force fresh data after a trade is booked.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Start with what a remote table is: it behaves like a table in lists, forms and reports, but rows are fetched on access and held only in memory, never stored. Then show you know the Washington DC Flow Designer pieces (the Flow field on the definition, the Remote Table Query trigger, the Create Remote Table Record action inside a For Each). Finally, cut the request down to the data the user needs, cache it for a sensible time, and name the scoped API that flushes the cache.

The Answer

Why remote tables fit. The Developer Advocate post on the Washington DC remote tables trigger uses this kind of contract as its example: "no copies of the data shall be stored on third-party systems." When someone opens a remote table, the instance calls the external system at that moment, and the data stays in memory only while the user is working with it. Lists, forms, reports and other basic operations still work. That meets the compliance rule and keeps the advisor experience.

Building it with Flow Designer.

  1. Create the remote table with columns that match what advisors need: holding id, instrument, quantity, market value, currency, as-of time, and a reference-style column to the client account.
  2. On the Remote Table Definition, use the new Flow field (the pencil opens Flow Designer). Once a flow is set, the script field is hidden so the two methods cannot conflict. The script method from earlier releases still works, so existing definitions keep running.
  3. In the flow, use the Remote Table Query trigger (under Application). Call the provider through an Integration Hub spoke action, either an existing spoke or one you build.
  4. For a list response, loop with For Each and call Create Remote Table Record (Global) for each holding. That action is what fills the in-memory rows.
  5. Add the remote table as a related list on the client account form.

Volume. The blog asks the right question: does Abel need all 100,000 records, or only his territory? Push the filter to the provider. Use the client account id from the query, and ideally the advisor's book of business, so each call returns tens of rows, not the whole firm. In the Washington DC TechNow Q&A, the advocates said the old 1,000-record limit had been removed, with the warning that more records means a longer wait for the user. No limit is not the same as no cost.

Caching. The blog recommends watching how users actually work. If an advisor checks holdings a few times in a 15-minute review, a 15 to 20 minute cache turns many API calls into one. Holdings change when trades book, so a short cache plus a targeted flush works better than no cache.

Forcing fresh data. The scoped RemoteTableCacheManager API flushes a remote table's cache so the next query goes back to the source:

// Inside the same scoped app as the remote table, e.g. a flow action
// or business rule that runs when a trade confirmation arrives.
sn_vtable.RemoteTableCacheManager.flushCache('x_wm_client_holding');

The reference lists the rules: it needs the Remote Tables plugin (com.glide.script.vtable), tableName must be a valid remote table in the current scope, and the result is written to the system log. Errors include "No remote table found with name" and "Current scope ... is not same as table scope". A global script cannot flush a scoped app's remote table.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Read-only. In the TechNow Q&A, the advocates said data brought in through remote tables is read-only. Booking a trade or correcting a holding is a separate outbound integration, not an edit to the remote row.
  • Reporting load. A report over the remote table triggers the same live calls. A dashboard that dozens of advisors open at 9 a.m. can flood the provider. Cache for that peak, or give reporting a different, aggregated source the contract allows.
  • Provider outages. When the API fails, the related list is empty or errors. Handle failures in the flow (the Washington DC Flow Designer also added try/catch) and decide what the advisor sees. "No holdings" and "provider unavailable" must look different.
  • Credentials and allowlists. Keep the provider credential in a connection and credential alias used by the spoke. If the instance restricts outbound hosts with glide.hosts.allowlist (the Fetch reference says it applies to HTTP APIs such as RESTMessageV2), check that the provider host is on the list.
  • Compliance check. Make sure nothing else copies the data, such as an audit, a flow that logs full payloads, or an export. Turn off verbose logging of response bodies in the spoke.

Common Mistakes

  • Fetching the whole dataset every time and filtering in the flow.
  • Setting a long cache "for speed" and then explaining stale holdings to an advisor who just booked a trade.
  • Writing remote rows into a real table for reporting, which brings back the copy compliance banned.
Score points: Name the three Washington DC building blocks exactly (Flow field, Remote Table Query trigger, Create Remote Table Record in a For Each). Then pair a short cache with an event-driven flushCache() from the same scope.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you secure the remote table so advisors only see their own clients' holdings?
  • When would Workflow Data Fabric zero-copy connectors be a better fit than a spoke-backed remote table?
  • How would you test the flow when the provider sandbox is down?
