  • Remote Tables Flow Trigger in Washington D.C. (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • TechNow Ep 97: Washington D.C. Q&A (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • RemoteTableCacheManager - Scoped (API reference)
  • Fetch - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • Workflow Studio and Flow Designer in Washington DC (Developer Advocate Blog)

question: A hosting provider pushes inventory from its hypervisor manager into ServiceNow every four hours: Linux servers (each with a BIOS serial and a chassis serial), the software packages installed on each server, and the Tomcat instances running on them. The first version inserted straight into cmdb_ci_linux_server with GlideRecord, and after a month there are 2,300 duplicate servers and Tomcat CIs with no host. You are asked to rebuild it on sn_cmdb.IdentificationEngine.createOrUpdateCI(). Question: Design the payload for one server with its serials, one software install and one Tomcat instance, and explain what each section (lookup, related, referenceItems, relations, sys_object_source_info) does and why.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Expect to explain why IRE replaces direct writes: identification rules find the existing CI, and reconciliation rules decide which source may update which attribute. Then build a payload that uses each section for its documented purpose: lookup for identification against tables that reference the CI, related for records that hang off the CI but do not identify it, referenceItems for filling a reference field with another payload item, and relations for CI relationships such as Runs on::Runs. You also need to know that the dependent CI (Tomcat) is identified through its host, so the relation has to be in the same payload.

The Answer

Why the duplicates happened. A GlideRecord insert has no idea a server with the same serial already exists. createOrUpdateCI(source, input) runs the identification rules for each item's class, finds a match or inserts, and applies reconciliation rules so a non-authoritative source cannot overwrite attributes it does not own. The reference describes it as the method to use "instead of updating the CMDB directly".

The sections.

  • items[].className and values: the CI class and its fields. Reference fields in values take sys_ids; if you only have display values, put them in display_values instead.
  • lookup: records in tables that reference the CI and are used to identify it, such as cmdb_serial_number or cmdb_ci_network_adapter. The Hardware rule searches cmdb_serial_number on serial_number + serial_number_type before falling back to name, so sending both serials here is what stops duplicates.
  • related: records in a related table that references the CI, governed by Related Entry rules. They are written with the CI but "are not used to identify the configuration item". Software instances go here.
  • referenceItems: fills a reference field on one payload item with another item, by internal_id. The software instance's installed_on must point to the server, which has no sys_id yet on the first run.
  • relations: CI relationships. Use parent/child indexes for top-level items only, or parent_id/child_id with internal_ids for any item including lookup and related ones. type is a name from cmdb_rel_type.
  • sys_object_source_info: the source's own key for the item (source_name, source_feed, source_native_key, source_recency_timestamp in UTC). It gives IRE a stable per-source identity even when attributes change.
var payload = {
  items: [
    { className: 'cmdb_ci_linux_server',
      internal_id: 'srv-4471',
      values: { name: 'web-lon-07', os: 'Linux Red Hat', cpu_count: '8',
                serial_number: 'VMW-56 4d 7a 9e' },
      lookup: [
        { className: 'cmdb_serial_number',
          values: { serial_number: 'VMW-56 4d 7a 9e', serial_number_type: 'bios', valid: 'true' } },
        { className: 'cmdb_serial_number',
          values: { serial_number: 'CHS-88120', serial_number_type: 'chassis', valid: 'true' } } ],
      sys_object_source_info: { source_name: 'HyperMgr', source_feed: 'lon-dc1',
        source_native_key: 'vm-4471', source_recency_timestamp: '2026-10-23 06:00:00' } },
    { className: 'cmdb_ci_spkg',
      values: { name: 'OpenJDK 17', key: 'OpenJDK 17_:::_Red Hat' },
      related: [
        { className: 'cmdb_software_instance', internal_id: 'swi-4471-jdk17',
          values: { name: 'OpenJDK 17-web-lon-07' } } ] },
    { className: 'cmdb_ci_app_server_tomcat',
      internal_id: 'tomcat-4471-8080',
      values: { name: 'Tomcat@web-lon-07:8080', install_directory: '/opt/tomcat',
                running_process_key_parameters: 'org.apache.catalina.startup.Bootstrap start' } }
  ],
  referenceItems: [
    { referencedBy: 'swi-4471-jdk17', referenceField: 'installed_on', referenced: 'srv-4471' } ],
  relations: [
    { parent_id: 'tomcat-4471-8080', child_id: 'srv-4471', type: 'Runs on::Runs' } ]
};
var out = JSON.parse(sn_cmdb.IdentificationEngine.createOrUpdateCI('HyperMgr', JSON.stringify(payload)));

The dependent CI. Tomcat's identity depends on the host it runs on; the reference's "Identify a dependent CI" example sends the application and the server together with a Runs on::Runs relation for exactly this reason. Sending Tomcat alone is what produced hostless Tomcat CIs.

Before go-live, run the same payloads through identifyCI(), which returns the operation it would perform without committing, and compare identificationAttempts against what you expect.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The source argument and every source_name must be a choice value of cmdb_ci.discovery_source. Add "HyperMgr" to that choice list first, and give it reconciliation rules, or its updates may be masked.
  • internal_id must be unique within the payload. Building it from the source key (vm-4471) keeps it deterministic.
  • Relations by index only work between top-level items. Once lookup or related items are involved, use parent_id/child_id.
  • If an existing CI is a different class (for example Windows), IRE may reclassify it, or skip that and report SKIPPED_CLASS_SWITCH in info when a reclassification restriction rule applies. settings.updateWithoutSwitch/Upgrade/Downgrade control this per item.
  • The output is a JSON string. Parse it and check errors per item; the call itself does not throw because one CI failed.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting the serial numbers only in values.serial_number, so identification falls through to name, which is exactly what collides in a hosting estate.
  • Putting software instances in lookup. They do not identify the server and can cause false matches.
  • Sending one CI per call. Batching related items in one payload is what lets IRE resolve references and relations in one pass.
Score points: Read an identificationAttempts array aloud: SKIPPED on cmdb_serial_number means the serial lookup was not provided, MATCHED on cmdb_ci_hardware by name means you are one renamed VM away from a duplicate.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do createOrUpdateCIEnhanced() options change what happens when the Tomcat item is missing its matching attributes?
  • Where would you clean up the 2,300 existing duplicates?
  • How would you show this source's ownership of cpu_count but not assigned_to?

Sources

  • IdentificationEngine API reference

question: An industrial equipment maker runs Salesforce for sales and ServiceNow CSM for support. The integration team wants a nightly sync of accounts and contacts from Salesforce into ServiceNow, plus a near-real-time sync of case updates both ways. Their design document says: "Use the CSM Account API to upsert accounts, the Contact API to upsert contacts, and the Case API for case create, update and activity history." In the pilot, case updates sent to ServiceNow returned 200 but some fields never changed. A partner portal user's updates to priority were silently dropped, and the nightly job pulling cases took 40 minutes. Review the design against the CSM APIs and correct it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The design assumes all three APIs support upserts, and they don't. In the Brazil reference, the Account API (/api/now/account) has only GET endpoints, and the Contact API has GET and POST but no update. The Case API creates and updates, but it doesn't validate parameters: misspelled or unsupported fields are ignored without warning. External users can write only a small set of fields. The 40-minute pull is the cost of reference-field expansion, and you turn that off with sysparm_reference_fields=false.

The Answer

Accounts. GET /api/now/account and GET /api/now/account/{id} are read endpoints, so they can't do the inbound account sync. Use the path the instance already supports for bulk master data, such as an Import Set with a transform that coalesces on the Salesforce ID, or the Table API on customer_account. Use the Account API only for reads (it returns hasMore for paging and its default sysparm_limit is 10).

Contacts. POST /api/now/contact creates a contact and can create a social profile at the same time (social_channel, social_handle, social_handle_url). It has no PUT or PATCH in the reference, so updates go through the same import path as accounts. The POST also "does not perform parameter validation": a misspelled field is ignored without warning. For B2C, the Consumer API (/api/now/consumer) follows the same GET/POST pattern.

Cases inbound. POST /api/sn_customerservice/case accepts all fields as optional, plus custom case fields. If you send contact, the account, contract and entitlement default from the contact and account records unless you override them. PUT /api/sn_customerservice/case/{id} updates a case. Pass sysparm_get_case_details=true to get the updated record back (the default is false), then compare it with what you sent. That check would have caught the "200 but nothing changed" problem, which came from field names Salesforce used that don't exist on sn_customerservice_case.

The partner user. By default, external users with sn_customerservice.customer or sn_customerservice.consumer can set only comments and state through PUT. On create, they are limited to account, asset, comments, consumer, contact, contact_type, partner, partner_contact, priority, product, short_description and state. Priority changes on update were therefore dropped. Admins can extend the list through UPDATE_ALLOWED_FIELDS in the CaseRESTAPIValidatorForExternalUser script include. The reference warns that new fields may have no validators, so add them deliberately.

Cases outbound. GET /api/sn_customerservice/case with sysparm_query=sys_updated_on>=...^ORDERBYsys_updated_on, sysparm_fields limited to what Salesforce maps, sysparm_reference_fields=false (it expands account, contact, consumer and social profile records by default) and paging with sysparm_limit and sysparm_offset. Read X-Total-Count and the Link header. For history, GET /case/{id}/activities?sysparm_activity_type=comments,work_notes.

GET /api/sn_customerservice/case?sysparm_query=sys_updated_on>=2026-10-22 00:00:00^ORDERBYsys_updated_on
    &sysparm_fields=sys_id,number,state,priority,account,contact,short_description
    &sysparm_reference_fields=false&sysparm_limit=500&sysparm_offset=0

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • /case/{id}/activities accepts a sys_id or a case number, but results are "unpredictable" if two cases share a number. Always store and use the sys_id.
  • Every Case API sysparm parameter also works without the prefix (limit, reference_fields). Be consistent so log searches find them.
  • sysparm_display_value=true is convenient for mapping but carries a documented performance cost on large pulls.
  • Use GET /case/field_values/{field_name} to build Salesforce picklist mappings. It applies the dictionary reference qualifiers, accepts sysparm_ref_qual_input for JavaScript qualifiers and sysparm_dependent_value for dependent choices.
  • An invalid sysparm_query part is dropped and the rest still runs, so a typo in the date field returns every case.

Common Mistakes

  • Trusting HTTP 200 from the Case or Contact endpoints as proof the data landed.
  • Running the integration as a customer-role user and fighting the field allowlist, when csm_ws_integration is the role meant for full access.
  • Using the case number as the cross-system key.
Score points: Point out that the Account API is read-only and the Contact API is create-only in the reference before anyone writes code. Then name sysparm_reference_fields=false and sysparm_get_case_details=true as the two parameters that fix the performance and the silent-failure problems.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prevent an update loop when both systems push case changes?
  • Where would entitlement checks happen for cases created from Salesforce?
  • How would you sync attachments on cases?

Sources

  • Case API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Account API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Contact API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Consumer API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A logistics company's release tooling team has been creating change requests with the Change Management API for a year. In a code review you find this call in their Python client: requests.post(f"{base}/api/sn_chg_rest/change", json={"short_description": "Patch WMS", "implementation_plan": plan, "assignment_group": "Warehouse Apps", "state": "Implement"}). Last week's upgrade changed which change model new records defaulted to, and 300 changes created since then followed an unexpected approval path. The assignment group field on those changes is empty too, although the call returned 200. Explain what is wrong with this call, why the upgrade broke it, why assignment_group came back empty, and rewrite it correctly.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The call sets neither chg_model nor type. The reference says that when both are missing, the default "is subject to change by release". That one sentence explains the upgrade incident. The empty assignment group is a values-versus-display-values problem. The endpoint stores what you send through setValue() unless you name the field in encrypted_fields, in which case it uses setDisplayValue(). The interviewer also wants to see that you won't jump a change straight to Implement on create. The change model's transitions are there to stop that, and nextstates tells you what is allowed.

The Answer

1. No model or type. POST /api/sn_chg_rest/change takes the change model by name (chg_model, for example "Normal" or a custom model such as "Cloud Infrastructure") or a type from sys_choice. If both are set, type is only a categorisation and the model drives the lifecycle. If neither is set, the instance uses its default, and ServiceNow documents that this default can change between releases. That is what happened here. Find the model the business actually agreed on with GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/model (filter with name-value pairs or sysparm_query; default_change_model on each record tells you which one is the current default) and send it every time.

2. Display value sent as a value. "Warehouse Apps" is a group name. The endpoint wrote it as the raw value of a reference field, and nothing matched. You have two options. Send the group's sys_id, which is the better choice for an integration because names get renamed. Or list the field in encrypted_fields. The reference says this switches the endpoint to setDisplayValue(), "so you can also use this parameter to pass display values for non-encrypted fields, such as reference or choice fields". The name of the parameter hides that behaviour, and a reviewer should leave a comment explaining it if you use it.

3. Forcing state on create. A model defines transition conditions. Create the change in its initial state, then ask GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{change_sys_id}/nextstates what comes next. For model-driven changes the response lists state_transitions, each with conditions[].passed and transition_available. Your tool can then say exactly why it can't progress. For type-driven and legacy changes that condition detail isn't returned.

4. Only one record per call. The endpoint doesn't support creating several change requests in one call, so the batch job that wraps this client must loop.

model = "Normal"   # agreed with Change Management, never left to default
body = {
    "chg_model": model,
    "short_description": "Patch WMS",
    "implementation_plan": plan,
    "assignment_group": WAREHOUSE_APPS_SYS_ID,   # sys_id, not name
}
r = requests.post(f"{base}/api/sn_chg_rest/change", json=body,
                  auth=auth, headers={"Accept": "application/json"})
r.raise_for_status()
chg = r.json()["result"]
sys_id = chg["sys_id"]["value"]

# verify what was stored, not what was sent
if chg["assignment_group"]["value"] != WAREHOUSE_APPS_SYS_ID:
    raise RuntimeError("assignment_group not applied")

nxt = requests.get(f"{base}/api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/nextstates",
                   auth=auth, headers={"Accept": "application/json"}).json()

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Every field in the response is an object with value and display_value, and dates also carry display_value_internal. Code that reads result["assignment_group"] as a string will break.
  • Query parameters and body can both carry fields. The body overrides URL parameters, but the reference says required parameters must be in the URL. Pick one style per client so reviewers don't have to work out which value won.
  • Name-value filters on the GET endpoints accept display values for choice and reference fields (&state=closed). PATCH and POST don't do this unless you use encrypted_fields. The asymmetry is where this bug came from.
  • An invalid field in sysparm_query is ignored and the rest of the query still runs, unless glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows is true. That property is instance-wide and affects GlideRecord too.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating HTTP 200 as success without reading back the stored values.
  • Hard-coding a model sys_id copied from a sub-production instance. chg_model on this endpoint takes the model name.
  • Using the type-specific endpoints (/change/normal, /change/emergency) for model-driven processes without checking which model they produce on this instance.
Score points: Quote the "subject to change by release" warning as the root cause of the upgrade regression, and explain the encrypted_fields to setDisplayValue() side effect. Most candidates have never noticed it, and it explains both the bug and the fix.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you write a regression test that catches a default-model change before the upgrade reaches production?
  • When would you use /change/normal rather than the generic endpoint with chg_model?
  • How do you surface failed nextstates conditions to a developer in the pipeline log?

Sources

  • Change Management API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A telecoms operator wants change approvers to approve or reject from a Microsoft Teams adaptive card instead of opening ServiceNow. The Teams bot back end holds a single integration account with the change_manager role, and the first prototype called the Change Management API approvals endpoint with that account for every click. In UAT, the audit log showed every approval as made by "svc_teams_bot", one approver approved a change for a CAB they weren't on, and rejections arrived with no reason. Explain how the approvals endpoint decides whose approval it is acting on, what it requires for a rejection, and how you would redesign the bot so the approval record is attributable and valid.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The approvals endpoint "allows the current user to approve or reject a change request approval record". The authenticated identity on the call is the approver. A shared service account therefore can't produce a valid, attributable approval, however many roles it has. Your fix is to move the bot to per-user tokens. You should also know the endpoint's contract: state is required and is either approved or rejected, comments is required on rejection, and a 400 comes back when the user has no authority to approve.

The Answer

How the endpoint behaves. PATCH /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/approvals takes a body such as {"state":"approved"} or {"state":"rejected","comments":"Clashes with core network freeze"}. It acts on the approval that belongs to the calling user for that change. The documented 400 covers "the user not having the authority to approve or reject the change request". The response returns the change's fields, including the new state (the example moves to -2/Scheduled) and type.

What went wrong in UAT.

  • Attribution: every call ran as svc_teams_bot, so the platform recorded that user. The adaptive card's "who clicked" never reached the instance.
  • Wrong approver: the endpoint acts on approvals belonging to the calling user, which was always svc_teams_bot, so the person who clicked was never checked by the platform. The bot's own membership check was the only control, and it had a bug. (Test exactly which approval records a change_manager service account can act on; the reference does not spell it out.)
  • Missing reasons: the card let users reject without text. The API requires comments when state is rejected, so either the call failed and the bot hid the error, or the bot fell back to something else. In both cases the design is wrong.

Redesign.

  1. Authenticate each approver. The bot exchanges the Teams user's identity for a ServiceNow OAuth token for that same user (for example through your IdP's SSO federation), and makes the PATCH with that token. The approval then belongs to the person who clicked, and the platform enforces whether they are an approver.
  2. Make the card require a reason on Reject, and send it as comments.
  3. Before rendering the card, call GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id} as the user to show current state, planned dates and risk, so nobody approves stale information. After the PATCH, show the returned state.display_value.
  4. For model-driven changes, the bot can call GET .../nextstates to explain what happens next ("moves to Scheduled once all approvals are in").
  5. Keep the service account only for read-only lookups, with roles from the GET list (itil, sn_change_read, change_manager or admin). Don't let it touch approvals.
PATCH /api/sn_chg_rest/change/0f4ac6c4b750230096c3e4f6ee11a9fe/approvals
Authorization: Bearer <token issued to the clicking approver>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{"state":"rejected","comments":"Overlaps core network freeze 22:00-02:00"}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference lists the method as PATCH, but its curl example uses --request POST. Build against PATCH and confirm in the REST API Explorer on your instance. Don't copy the sample.
  • The response does not say which approval record changed. If you need the sysapproval_approver sys_id for your own audit trail, read it separately.
  • A user who belongs to several approval groups for the same change still makes one call. Test what that does under your approval rules before go-live; the reference doesn't describe it.
  • Delegation: if approvers use delegates, test that a delegate's token gets the expected result. The reference doesn't document delegate handling for this endpoint.

Common Mistakes

  • Using impersonation-style headers or an admin account to "act as" the approver. The record still shows the service account and auditors will reject it.
  • Assuming change_manager on the integration account is harmless. Every approval made with it is recorded against the service account, and any extra rights the role carries apply to every user the bot fronts.
  • Swallowing 400 responses so the card shows success when the approval never registered.
Score points: Quote "allows the current user" and draw the conclusion: the identity on the HTTP call is the approver of record. Mention the PATCH/POST mismatch in the reference to show you have read the page closely, not skimmed the example.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle an approver whose token has expired when they click the card hours later?
  • Where would you record the Teams message ID so a reviewer can trace the approval back to the conversation?
  • Would you use the same pattern for emergency changes that need an approval within 15 minutes?

Sources

  • Change Management API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A fintech's CI/CD pipeline creates about 900 normal change requests a month through an integration user, and every one waits for the weekly CAB. The head of change wants low-risk changes approved automatically when the implementing team has a strong track record and the change model has a high success rate, with everything else routed to CAB with a reason. A developer prototyped this with getScoresForChange() but in testing every change goes to CAB, even for the best teams, and the log shows score values as undefined. Explain what the ChangeSuccess API returns, why the prototype fails, write the gate logic, and discuss whether withSecurity(false) is acceptable here.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is checking whether you know the Change Success Score is exposed as a script include, not just a card on the form, and that it returns three different scores with different meanings and scales. Strong answers handle the "no score yet" and "cannot read" cases explicitly, understand that the numbers come from Performance Analytics so they lag reality, and have an opinion about bypassing the security check.

The Answer

sn_chg_score.ChangeSuccess needs the Change Management - Change Success Score plugin (com.snc.change_management.change_success_score). For a change request GlideRecord, getScoresForChange(chgGr) returns three objects:

  • team_success_score: the original group-based score, with can_read, a score object, the matching chg_success_score_rating record (rating names are Low, Medium, High, Excellent) and the group.
  • model_success_score: the success rate of the change model, which in the reference example comes from the PA indicator "Change Model: % Successful and Successful With Issues", so it reads as a percentage.
  • type_success_score: the same idea for the change type (normal, emergency and so on).

Each score has value, display_value, has_score, a delta from the previous score and the PA indicator it came from. Helper methods chain in front of the call: withTeamScore(), withModelScore() and withTypeScore() switch individual scores on or off (only valid with getScoresForChange()), withTeamScoreRatings() returns all rating bands, withIndicatorScores() returns the underlying PA indicators, and withSecurity() controls the read check. For a gate you only need team and model:

// Called from the pipeline's change-creation flow (script step), runs as the integration user
var PipelineChangeGate = Class.create();
PipelineChangeGate.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {
        this.MIN_MODEL_PCT = 85;
    },

    evaluate: function(chgGr) {
        var cs = new sn_chg_score.ChangeSuccess();
        var scores = cs.withTypeScore(false).getScoresForChange(chgGr);

        var team = scores.team_success_score;
        var model = scores.model_success_score;
        var reasons = [];

        if (!team || !team.can_read)
            reasons.push('Team score not readable for this user');
        else if (!team.score.has_score)
            reasons.push('Group has no score history yet');
        else {
            var rating = team.chg_success_score_rating &&
                         team.chg_success_score_rating.sys_name ?
                         team.chg_success_score_rating.sys_name.display_value : '';
            if (rating != 'High' && rating != 'Excellent')
                reasons.push('Team rating is ' + (rating || 'unknown') +
                             ' (' + team.score.display_value + ')');
        }

        if (!model || !model.can_read || !model.score.has_score)
            reasons.push('No model success score');
        else if (model.score.value < this.MIN_MODEL_PCT)
            reasons.push('Model success ' + model.score.display_value + '% below ' + this.MIN_MODEL_PCT);

        var auto = reasons.length === 0;
        // caller saves the change after reading the decision
        chgGr.work_notes = auto ?
            'Auto-approval: team and model success scores within policy.' :
            'Routed to CAB: ' + reasons.join('; ');
        return { autoApprove: auto, reasons: reasons };
    },
    type: 'PipelineChangeGate'
};

I gate on the rating rather than a raw number for the team score. The team score is on a scale bounded by system properties: getMinimumPermittedTeamScore() (default 0), getMaximumPermittedTeamScore() (default 850) and getEntryLevelTeamScore() (default 500). If the change manager retunes the bands in chg_success_score_rating, the gate follows without a code change. The model score is a percentage, so a numeric threshold makes sense there.

Only when the gate passes would the flow move the change forward without CAB. Anything else gets a work note listing the reasons, which is what the CAB chair actually wants to read.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • can_read false. By default every method checks the caller can read the group, the change model, or the change type choice. A locked-down pipeline integration user often cannot, so every score comes back unreadable and the naive code treats "unknown" as "bad" or, worse, as "good". Give the integration user read access to the groups and models it needs.
  • withSecurity(false) removes that check for the current object. It is acceptable inside a server-side gate that only returns a yes/no, but not in a scripted REST resource that hands the full score payload back to an external caller.
  • New teams. A group with no history returns has_score: false. That is not a low score. Decide the policy (CAB review is the safe default) and say so in the work note.
  • Latency. These are the latest PA scores. A failed change this morning does not lower the score until the next PA collection, so the gate is a trend signal, not a real-time one.
  • Value types. getMaximumPermittedTeamScore() and getMinimumPermittedTeamScore() are documented as returning strings; convert before comparing.
  • Domain separation. getTeamScoreForGroupId(sys_id, domain_id) and getTypeScoreForType(type, domain_id) take an optional domain, and ratings can be overridden per domain through sys_overrides. An MSP instance needs to pass the right one.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading score.value without checking has_score and can_read first.
  • Treating the team score and the model score as the same scale.
  • Hard-coding "auto-approve above 700" instead of using the configured rating bands.
  • Querying PA tables directly to rebuild what the script include already returns.
Score points: Use getTeamScoreForGroupId() before the change exists. The pipeline can check the deploying team's score at merge time and fail fast, rather than creating a change only to send it to CAB.

Likely Follow-ups

  • The release manager wants to see why a team's score moved. What does withIndicatorScores(true) add, and how would you show the delta?
  • How would you stop teams gaming the gate by marking failed changes "successful with issues"?
  • Where would you put this check: change model state transition condition, flow, or business rule? Why?

Sources

  • ChangeSuccess

question: A wholesaler's suppliers upload a nightly price file (CSV, 40-80 MB) to a staging record in a scoped app through the Attachment API. A script include reads it with new GlideSysAttachment().getContent(attGr), splits on newlines and updates prices. Since the files grew past a few megabytes, imports finish 'successfully' with most rows missing. Suppliers also re-send the same file after network errors, causing double processing, and the team wants to copy each processed file to an audit record. Explain what is happening and rebuild the read, de-duplication and copy steps with the scoped attachment APIs.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The core of this one is the documented 5 MB ceiling on the string-returning attachment methods, and the fact that the streaming path avoids it. You should also know which APIs accept a GlideScriptableInputStream, how to fingerprint a file without loading it, and how to copy or move attachments without base64 round trips. If you can explain how attachments are stored, you can explain why the string methods are expensive.

Diagnosis

getContent(GlideRecord) returns the attachment as a string, supports CSV, JSON and text files, is for scoped applications only (it returns undefined in global), and returns up to 5 MB of data. getContentBase64() has the same 5 MB limit. Past that, the script receives a truncated string, splits it, processes what it got and reports success. Nothing threw, so nobody noticed.

There is also a cost angle. The Developer Advocate write-up on processing 130,000 images describes how the platform stores a file: the binary is base64 encoded, split into chunks, and each chunk becomes a row in sys_attachment_doc. Reading the whole thing into one string reassembles and decodes all of it in memory.

The Answer

Use getContentStream(sysId), which returns a GlideScriptableInputStream, and read it with GlideTextReader. The GlideTextReader reference says that because it works off a stream it is not subject to the 5 MB attachment limit, and readLine() returns null when there is no more content.

var PriceFileImporter = Class.create();
PriceFileImporter.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {
        this.gsa = new GlideSysAttachment();
    },

    fingerprint: function (attId) {
        // fresh stream: do not reuse one that a reader has consumed
        return new GlideDigest().getSHA256HexFromInputStream(this.gsa.getContentStream(attId));
    },

    alreadyProcessed: function (hash) {
        var a = new GlideRecord('sys_attachment_attribute');   // written via addAttribute(); confirm key/value column names on your instance
        a.addQuery('key', 'x_whs_sha256');
        a.addQuery('value', hash);
        a.setLimit(1);
        a.query();
        return a.hasNext();
    },

    run: function (stagingGr) {
        var att = this.gsa.getAttachments(stagingGr.getTableName(), stagingGr.getUniqueValue());
        while (att.next()) {
            var attId = att.getUniqueValue();
            var hash = this.fingerprint(attId);
            if (this.alreadyProcessed(hash)) {
                gs.info('Skipping duplicate price file {0}', att.getValue('file_name'));
                continue;
            }
            var reader = new GlideTextReader(this.gsa.getContentStream(attId));
            var line, n = 0;
            reader.readLine();                          // header
            while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
                n++;
                this.applyRow(line);                    // batch updates, see follow-up
            }
            this.gsa.addAttribute(attId, 'x_whs_sha256', hash);
            this.gsa.addAttribute(attId, 'x_whs_rows', String(n));
        }
        // copy() copies every attachment on the record (with attributes), so call it once, after the loop
        this.gsa.copy(stagingGr.getTableName(), stagingGr.getUniqueValue(),
                      'x_whs_import_audit', this.auditFor(stagingGr));
    },

    type: 'PriceFileImporter'
};

Points worth explaining in the interview:

  • GlideDigest has ...FromInputStream variants for MD5, SHA1, SHA256 and SHA512, so the file is hashed without becoming a string. SHA-256 is the sensible choice for de-duplication; MD5 and SHA1 are offered but are weak choices for anything security-related.
  • Attachment attributes are scoped-API calls that take the attachment sys_id: addAttribute(sysAttachmentID, key, value), fetchAttribute(), fetchAllAttributes() and so on. They land in Attachment Attributes, which gives you a place to record the hash and row count without a custom table.
  • copy(sourceTable, sourceID, targetTable, targetID) copies all attachments on the source record, returns the array of new attachment sys_ids, and copies their attributes too. The audit copy therefore carries the hash.
  • If you need a single file on another record, writeContentStream(record, fileName, contentType, getContentStream(id)) copies bytes stream to stream, as the reference example shows.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • A stream is consumed as you read it. Get a new one from getContentStream() for each consumer (hash, reader); the documented APIs give you no rewind.
  • The documented consumers of GlideScriptableInputStream are GlideDigest, GlideExcelParser, GlideTextReader and XMLDocument2. A supplier switching to XLSX means GlideExcelParser, not a text reader.
  • getContent() returning undefined in global scope is a common migration surprise when a script include is moved out of the app.
  • write() returns null when the attachment was not added. Check it; a silent null leaves an image or file field pointing at nothing.
  • Line-by-line reading solves memory, not transaction time. Tens of thousands of single-row updates in one transaction can still hit the maximum execution time described in the Developer Advocate performance post. Collect keys, query in bulk, and split the work across async chunks.
  • Deleting an attachment deletes its attributes. If you purge staging files, the de-duplication history goes with them unless the audit copy keeps it.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating 'no exception' as 'whole file processed'. Record and compare row counts.
  • Base64-decoding files manually with getContentBase64() to move them between records.
  • Using filename plus size as the duplicate key; suppliers rename files and identical sizes happen.
  • Hashing with MD5 'because it is faster' and then reusing the same helper for something security-sensitive later.
Score points: Quote the 5 MB limit on getContent() and getContentBase64() and the GlideTextReader statement that streaming is not subject to it. Then mention that copy() carries attributes, so the fingerprint follows the file.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you split a 600,000-row file across several async workers and report a single result?
  • The supplier sends a corrupt last line. How do you detect a partial upload before applying any prices?
  • When would you stop storing these files in ServiceNow at all?

Sources

  • GlideSysAttachment (Scoped)
  • GlideTextReader (Scoped)
  • GlideScriptableInputStream - Scoped, Global
  • GlideDigest (Scoped)
  • Working with Image Attachments in ServiceNow: Lessons from Processing 130,000 Images (Developer Advocate blog)
  • Beyond Best Practices: Developer's Guide to Time & Space (Developer Advocate blog)

question: A utility company's incident form has an after-update business rule that calls an on-premises asset database through a MID Server: var r = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('AssetDB', 'get'); r.setMIDServer('mid-dc1'); var res = r.execute();. Service desk agents complain that saving a P1 incident sometimes hangs for 30 seconds or more, and occasionally the save completes with a blank asset owner. The developer says 'but RESTMessageV2 is fast'. Explain what actually happens when a REST message goes through a MID Server, why execute() versus executeAsync() plus waitForResponse() doesn't fix the root problem, and design the asynchronous version properly.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need to know that a MID-routed call never goes straight from the instance to the endpoint. It is written to the ECC queue, the MID Server picks it up on its next poll, makes the call inside the network, and writes the result back. ServiceNow's own MID Server example says plainly that all REST messages sent through a MID Server are asynchronous. A synchronous wait inside a user's save transaction holds that transaction for the full round trip. A good answer moves the call out of the user's transaction instead of just swapping method names.

The Answer

Step through the timeline. The agent clicks Save. The after business rule runs inside the same transaction. The script queues an ECC output record for mid-dc1. The MID Server sees it on its next check, calls the asset database, and posts an ECC input record. Only then can the instance hand a response back to the script. The agent waits for all of that. If the MID is busy, down, or the database is slow, the wait hits the ECC response timeout. ServiceNow's MID Server example notes the call might throw an exception when it times out waiting for the response in the ECC queue; a script that does not handle that exception or an error response leaves the owner blank.

Switching to executeAsync() followed by response.waitForResponse(60) changes nothing for the user. The reference says waitForResponse() sets how long the instance waits and overrides glide.rest.outbound.ecc_response.timeout for that response. That is still a blocking wait in the save transaction, now with a longer ceiling. The SOAPMessageV2 reference is more direct about the same pattern: if the request must go through the MID Server you generally should not use execute(), because the thread is held both by the request and by waiting for the MID to respond, and it recommends asynchronous calls with a sensor business rule.

The fix has two halves. First, get the call out of the user transaction. Second, handle the reply where it lands.

// 1. Async business rule (or event + script action) on incident, after update
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    // Put 'Configuration item changes' in the rule's Condition field: field.changes()
    // is not reliable inside an async rule's script (previous is not available there).
    if (current.cmdb_ci.nil()) return;

    var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('AssetDB', 'get');
    rm.setMIDServer('mid-dc1');
    rm.setStringParameter('ci', current.cmdb_ci.getRefRecord().getValue('asset_tag'));
    // Correlator lands in the Agent correlator field of the ECC response record
    rm.setEccCorrelator('incident_owner:' + current.getUniqueValue());
    rm.executeAsync();                 // no waitForResponse: do not block
    // u_owner_lookup = 'pending' is set by a separate before rule, so no current.update() here
})(current, previous);
// 2. Business rule on ecc_queue: after insert,
//    condition: queue is input AND agent_correlator starts with incident_owner:
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var incId = String(current.agent_correlator).split(':')[1];
    var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
    if (!inc.get(incId)) return;
    // Parse the payload of the ECC input record here and set the owner,
    // or mark the lookup failed so the form can show it.
    inc.update();
})(current, previous);

Now the save returns immediately, the lookup completes a few seconds later, and failures are recorded on the incident instead of silently blanking a field.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • getQueryString() on the response is documented as not supported for asynchronous requests or requests sent through a MID Server. Code that logs it for debugging breaks when routing changes.
  • The correlator must be unique per request. The reference says to provide a unique correlator so the right ECC result is associated with the right request. Reusing a constant string means two incidents read each other's answers.
  • If the endpoint URL is longer than the REST endpoint field allows, setEccParameter('source', url) overrides it in the MID payload. It only applies to MID-routed messages.
  • setMIDServer() takes a MID Server name, and the instance must have an active MID with that name. Hard-coding mid-dc1 means a MID rename or failover breaks the integration. Prefer the MID selection on the REST Message record, or read the name from a property.
  • saveResponseBodyAsAttachment() through a MID requires the MID Server user to have roles to read and write attachments and the target table.
  • An after business rule that calls current.update() to write the pending state re-triggers business rules. Set the state in a before rule or have the async rule write it.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating executeAsync() plus waitForResponse() as non-blocking.
  • Raising glide.rest.outbound.ecc_response.timeout globally to hide the symptom, which makes every MID wait longer.
  • Forgetting that MID-routed calls depend on MID capacity, so a Discovery schedule on the same MID can slow ticket saves.
Score points: Say that the user experience requirement decides the pattern: if the agent must see the owner before saving, the call belongs in a UI action or client-triggered async call with a spinner, never in a server-side save path. If the owner can arrive later, use the correlator and an ECC sensor.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you build the same thing in Flow Designer and what do you gain?
  • How do you detect requests that never got an ECC response?
  • What changes if the endpoint is reachable from the cloud and the MID is only there for historical reasons?

Sources

  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global
  • SOAPMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTMessageV2 MID server example (ServiceNow docs)

question: A retail customer's payroll integration posts timesheets to a vendor API that is slow at month end. A developer 'fixed' timeouts by setting setHttpTimeout(600000) and wrapping execute() in a five-attempt loop with gs.sleep(10000) between tries, all inside a scheduled job that handles 4,000 employees. Now the job runs for hours, the vendor reports duplicate timesheets, and other scheduled jobs on the node are delayed. Explain what setHttpTimeout() really controls, how to classify failures for retry using the response API, and design a retry approach that won't create duplicates.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Three things. First, the timeout is a socket inactivity timer, not a total request budget. Second, you separate failures that are safe to retry from ones that aren't, using the status code, the platform error code and thrown exceptions. Third, a retry of a POST that may have succeeded is how duplicates happen, so retries need an idempotency strategy, not just a loop.

The Answer

What the timeout means. The reference for setHttpTimeout(Number timeoutMs) notes that it sets a timeout on the socket and only fires if the socket does not receive data within that time. For streamed responses a connection can last much longer than the value. So a 600-second value does not mean "give up after ten minutes"; it means "give up after ten minutes of silence". The SOAPMessageV2 page documents two instance properties that control outbound HTTP timeouts, glide.http.timeout at 175 seconds and glide.http.connection_timeout at 10 seconds (documented there for SOAP execute(); check how they interact with RESTMessageV2 on your instance), and warns that long synchronous timeouts can bring the instance to a standstill. A worker thread waiting up to ten minutes, five times, per employee, is exactly that.

Classifying failures. Each attempt ends in one of four ways, and only some are retryable:

  • execute() throws. The reference lists connection timeout and problems sending the request. Usually transient; retry later.
  • haveError() is true with a platform getErrorCode(), for example 1 for socket timeout. Transient, but the vendor may have received and processed the request before the socket went quiet. Retrying a POST here is the duplicate risk.
  • Status 429 or 5xx. Retry later; read getHeader('Retry-After') if the vendor sends it.
  • Status 4xx other than 429. Not retryable. The payload or credentials are wrong, and sending it again just repeats the failure.

Making retries safe. Generate an idempotency key per timesheet once, store it on the record, and send it on every attempt. If the vendor supports an idempotency header, it will drop the second copy. If it does not, the retry path should first query the vendor for that external reference before posting again.

// Called per timesheet by a queue processor, not in a sleep loop
function pushTimesheet(ts) {
    if (!ts.getValue('u_idem_key')) {
        ts.setValue('u_idem_key', gs.generateGUID());
    }
    var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('Payroll', 'post');
    rm.setRequestHeader('Idempotency-Key', ts.getValue('u_idem_key'));
    rm.setRequestBody(buildBody(ts));
    rm.setHttpTimeout(60000);
    var outcome;
    try {
        var res = rm.execute();
        var sc = res.getStatusCode();
        if (sc >= 200 && sc < 300 && !res.haveError()) outcome = 'done';
        else if (sc === 0 || sc === 429 || sc >= 500) outcome = 'retry';  // transport error, throttled, server error
        else outcome = 'fail';                                           // other 4xx: fix the request, don't resend
        if (outcome === 'retry' && res.getHeader('Retry-After')) {
            ts.setValue('u_retry_after_s', parseInt(res.getHeader('Retry-After'), 10) || 0);
        }
    } catch (ex) {
        outcome = 'retry';
    }
    var attempts = parseInt(ts.getValue('u_attempts') || '0', 10) + 1;
    ts.setValue('u_attempts', attempts);
    if (outcome === 'retry' && attempts >= 5) outcome = 'fail';
    ts.setValue('u_sync_state', outcome);
    var wait = Math.pow(2, attempts) * 60;          // seconds: 2, 4, 8, 16 minutes
    var next = new GlideDateTime();
    next.addSeconds(Math.max(wait, parseInt(ts.getValue('u_retry_after_s') || '0', 10)));
    ts.setValue('u_next_attempt', next);
    ts.update();
}

A scheduled job then picks a batch of records where state is pending or retry and u_next_attempt has passed, processes them, and exits. No thread sleeps. A slow vendor delays a few records, not the whole node.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • A timeout on a POST is ambiguous. The request may have been committed on the vendor side. Without an idempotency key or a lookup, the retry is a guess.
  • gs.sleep() in a scheduled job holds a worker thread. Several sleeping jobs starve other scheduled work on that node.
  • Header names and value formats for idempotency and Retry-After are vendor contracts, not platform features. Confirm them; Retry-After can also be an HTTP date rather than seconds.
  • If the call goes through a MID Server, the effective wait is governed by the ECC response timeout and waitForResponse(), not just the socket timeout.
  • getRequestHeaders() on the message does not show system-set headers unless glide.http.log_debug is true, which matters when you are trying to prove what was sent.

Common Mistakes

  • Raising the timeout to make the error go away, which converts failures into stuck threads.
  • Retrying 400 and 401 responses.
  • Fixed-interval retries that hit a recovering vendor at the same moment from every record.
Score points: Point out that Flow Designer and Integration Hub REST steps give you retry policies and execution history without hand-written state fields. Then explain what you would still need on the record, such as the idempotency key, because the platform retry does not know whether the vendor already accepted the first attempt.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you alert on records stuck in retry?
  • How would you test the ambiguous-timeout path?
  • What would you change if the vendor publishes a rate limit of 10 requests per second?

Sources

  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global
  • SOAPMessageV2 - Scoped, Global

question: Your team is starting a new scoped app that calls three external services: a public weather API, a SaaS ticketing tool that uses OAuth 2.0, and an on-premises inventory system only reachable through a MID Server. A developer proposes using the new server-side fetch() API everywhere because 'it's the modern standard, and we already know it from Node'. Compare fetch() with sn_ws.RESTMessageV2 on what the reference documents for each: error semantics, host control, authentication, MID routing, binary handling and logging. Recommend which to use for each of the three calls and show a correct fetch() call for the one where it fits.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This question is about comparing the two APIs on what the reference documents rather than on taste. fetch() is a smaller, promise-based API whose error model follows the web standard. RESTMessageV2 carries the platform integration features: REST Message records, authentication profiles, mutual TLS profiles, MID routing, ECC correlation, attachments and outbound logging control. The right answer is a split, and the reasons should be specific.

The Answer

Error semantics. The Fetch reference says a fetch() promise only rejects when the request fails, for example a badly formed URL or a network error. It is not rejected for HTTP statuses like 404 or 504; you check the ok and status properties on the response. A Node developer knows this, but a reviewer used to haveError() may not. Every fetch() call needs an explicit ok check.

Host control. Both are governed by glide.hosts.allowlist. The Fetch reference says the property controls which hosts a fetch method can access and that it applies to HTTP APIs like RESTMessageV2 too. Neither API bypasses it.

What only RESTMessageV2 documents. setAuthenticationProfile('oauth2', profileSysId) and 'basic' profiles; setMutualAuth(profileName); setMIDServer(), setEccCorrelator() and setEccParameter(); saveResponseBodyAsAttachment() and setRequestBodyFromAttachment(); setLogLevel() for Outbound HTTP Requests logging; setAllowedRedirectURIs(); and the ability to build from a REST Message record so endpoints and auth live in configuration, not code. The Fetch reference shows Basic auth built by hand with btoa() in an Authorization header. It documents no MID, mutual-auth or attachment options, so you should not assume they exist.

Recommendation.

  • Weather API: public, simple JSON GET, API key in a header. fetch() fits. Keep the key in a credential or property, not in source.
  • SaaS ticketing with OAuth: RESTMessageV2 with setAuthenticationProfile('oauth2', ...), so the platform handles token acquisition and reuse.
  • On-premises inventory: RESTMessageV2 with a MID Server. fetch() has no documented MID routing.
// Scoped script include method; fetch() returns a promise
async getForecast(lat, lon) {
    const key = gs.getProperty('x_acme_wx.api_key');
    const url = 'https://api.weather.example.com/v1/forecast?lat=' +
                encodeURIComponent(lat) + '&lon=' + encodeURIComponent(lon);
    let response;
    try {
        response = await fetch(url, {
            method: 'GET',
            headers: { 'Accept': 'application/json', 'X-Api-Key': key }
        });
    } catch (networkErr) {           // rejected: bad URL, network failure, blocked host
        gs.error('Weather call failed: ' + networkErr);
        return null;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {             // 4xx and 5xx land here, not in catch
        gs.warn('Weather API returned HTTP ' + response.status);
        return null;
    }
    return await response.json();
}

A practical way to keep the choice reversible is to hide each external service behind a script include method with a plain contract, such as getForecast(lat, lon) returning an object or null. Callers never see which HTTP API is underneath, so moving the weather call to a REST Message record later, or moving the ticketing call to an Integration Hub spoke, changes one file. The developer's Node experience is still useful there: the wrapper is where the ok check, timeout policy and logging live.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Any caller of an async method gets a promise back. Business rules and other synchronous scripts that call getForecast() and use the result directly will read a promise object, not data.
  • The main Fetch reference page does not document a timeout setting; check the Fetch RequestInit page for your release before assuming one exists. If you need a socket timeout today, RESTMessageV2.setHttpTimeout() is documented.
  • The Fetch reference example uses btoa() to build Basic auth by hand. That puts credentials in script. With RESTMessageV2 you reference a Basic Auth Configuration [sys_auth_profile_basic] record instead.
  • Modern syntax such as async, await and const depends on the JavaScript mode of the script and application. Confirm the mode before choosing fetch() in a global or older scoped app.
  • How a host blocked by glide.hosts.allowlist surfaces is not spelled out in the reference. Expect a rejected promise in fetch() and an exception or error response on RESTMessageV2, but test this on your instance so you know where to look for each.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing fetch(url).then(r => r.json()) with no ok check, so a 500 error page is parsed as data.
  • Choosing one API for everything for consistency, then hand-coding OAuth refresh in fetch().
  • Assuming fetch() output appears under Outbound HTTP Requests with the same log-level controls as REST messages; verify before relying on it.
Score points: Close with an operational argument: REST Message records let an admin change an endpoint, credential or MID selection between instances without a code deployment. That alone often decides the choice for enterprise integrations.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you unit-test the fetch() wrapper with ATF?
  • What does glide.hosts.allowlist protect against, and what does it not?
  • How would you move the weather call to a REST Message later without changing callers?

Sources

  • Fetch
  • Fetch - Scoped, Global (ServiceNow docs)
  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global

question: A field-service company is exposing a Scripted REST API so its mobile app partner can create and list work orders. Requirements: create must be safe to retry on flaky mobile networks without creating duplicates, list must page through up to 200,000 records, the partner sends single objects or arrays of up to 500 work orders in one POST, and the contract must be able to change next year without breaking old app versions. A colleague suggests a legacy processor (g_request/g_response) because 'it's simpler'. Design the API: versioning, request body handling, status codes, pagination headers and idempotency, using the documented RESTAPIRequest, RESTAPIRequestBody and RESTAPIResponse methods.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

I'm looking for HTTP design discipline expressed through the platform's own objects: versions in the URL, a create that returns 201 with a Location, a duplicate-safe retry path, pagination that doesn't load 200,000 rows, and correct handling of single-versus-array bodies. I also want a reason to reject the processor that is better than "it's old".

The Answer

Versioning. Scripted REST APIs carry a version segment in the path, for example /api/x_fs/work_orders/v1/.... Ship v1 now. When the contract changes, add v2 resources and leave v1 untouched until the old app versions age out. Clients that call the unversioned path get whichever version is marked default, so the partner should always call an explicit version.

Request body. RESTAPIRequestBody.data may be a single object or an array depending on what was sent. The reference shows the instanceof Array check. For bulk input, hasNext() and nextEntry() iterate entries one at a time and handle both shapes the same way: a single object is one entry. Pick one access style per request, because data, dataString and dataStream read the same stream and only the first read returns content.

Idempotency. Require an Idempotency-Key header from the partner, read it with request.getHeader(), and store it on the work order (or on a per-entry key inside the payload for bulk). Before inserting, look it up. If it exists, return the existing record with 200 rather than creating another. Back it with a unique index so two concurrent retries cannot both insert.

// POST /api/x_fs/work_orders/v1/orders
(function process(request, response) {
    var batchKey = request.getHeader('idempotency-key');
    if (!batchKey) {
        response.setError(new sn_ws_err.BadRequestError('Idempotency-Key header is required.'));
        return;
    }
    var body = request.body;
    var results = [], created = 0, n = 0;
    while (body.hasNext()) {
        var entry = body.nextEntry();
        if (++n > 500) {
            response.setError(new sn_ws_err.BadRequestError('Max 500 work orders per request.'));
            return;
        }
        var key = batchKey + ':' + (entry.client_ref || n);
        var wo = new GlideRecord('x_fs_work_order');
        if (wo.get('u_idem_key', key)) {
            results.push({ client_ref: entry.client_ref, sys_id: wo.getUniqueValue(), status: 'existing' });
            continue;
        }
        wo.initialize();
        wo.setValue('u_idem_key', key);
        wo.setValue('short_description', entry.summary);
        results.push({ client_ref: entry.client_ref, sys_id: wo.insert(), status: 'created' });
        created++;
    }
    if (n === 1 && created === 1) {
        response.setLocation(gs.getProperty('glide.servlet.uri') +
            'api/x_fs/work_orders/v1/orders/' + results[0].sys_id);
    }
    response.setStatus(created > 0 ? 201 : 200);
    response.setBody({ results: results });
})(request, response);

Pagination. Accept limit and an opaque cursor. Remember queryParams values are arrays, so coerce with String() and parseInt(). Cap limit at something like 500. Use a keyset cursor (order by sys_created_on then sys_id and filter past the last seen pair) rather than a growing offset, so page 400 is as cheap as page 1. Return the next cursor in the body and a Link header via response.setHeader(). A total count header such as X-Total-Count is useful but costs an aggregate query; compute it only on the first page or on request.

Why not a processor. GlideScriptedProcessor, GlideServletRequest and GlideServletResponse give you raw servlet access: g_request.getParameter(), g_response.setStatus(), g_processor.writeJSON(). There is no body parser, no Accept-based serialization, no sn_ws_err error objects and no version segment in the URL format (/<path>.do?param=value). Scripted REST also fits the platform's REST access policies, which the API key blog post shows being scoped per REST API, method and version.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Calling nextEntry() after the last entry returns undefined; always guard with hasNext().
  • setStatus() with a string defaults the status to 0.
  • A mixed batch (some existing, some new) needs a clear contract. Per-entry status in the body plus 201 if anything was created is one option; document it.
  • setLocation() only makes sense for a single created resource.
  • Index u_idem_key uniquely. The lookup-then-insert is not atomic on its own.

Common Mistakes

  • Offset pagination with chooseWindow() over 200,000 rows, which gets slower as the partner pages deeper.
  • Returning 200 for creates, which removes the partner's ability to tell a replay from a new insert.
  • Breaking v1 in place because "only one partner uses it".
Score points: Mention REST API access policies and inbound API keys: you can bind an API key profile to this API, restrict it to specific methods and a version, and tie it to a service account, so the partner never holds a user password.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a partial failure halfway through a 500-entry batch?
  • How do you expire idempotency keys?
  • What would you return for Accept: text/csv?

question: A franchise business has 30 franchisees who each send a monthly CSV of store equipment to a Scripted REST endpoint in a scoped app. Column sets differ slightly between franchisees. A developer proposes: for each upload, create a staging table with sn_impex.GlideImportSetTable, build a transform map with GlideImportSetTransformMap, insert the rows, run GlideImportSetTransformer.transformAllMaps(), and return the result to the caller in the same HTTP response. In testing, the response always says "done" before any target records exist, and two months later the transform history from the first loads has disappeared. Question: Walk through the scripted import APIs, explain both symptoms, and say whether you would ship this design.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Interviewers want the four-step sequence the reference gives (table, map, import set record, transformer), and the fact that transforms run asynchronously unless you call setSyncImport(true). They also expect you to know that tables created by GlideImportSetTable are temporary: the Scripted Import Set Deleter job removes them, their maps and their import sets every seven days by default. Then push back on the design: dynamic tables suit ad-hoc loads, not a permanent monthly integration.

The Answer

The APIs.

  • new sn_impex.GlideImportSetTable(label) plus addStringColumn(label, length) (default length 40) and addDateTimeColumn(label); create() returns {tableName, tableLabel, columns}, where columns maps each label to its generated column name (for example "first name": "u_first_name"). At least one column is required, and modifying or deleting the table afterwards is not supported.
  • new sn_impex.GlideImportSetTransformMap(name, importSetTable, targetTable), addTransformEntry(sourceColumn, targetColumn, coalesce) or addDateTimeTransformEntry(source, target, coalesce, format), then create(), which returns the map sys_id and requires at least one entry.
  • An import set record created with GlideRecord on sys_import_set, with table_name set to the staging table.
  • GlideImportSetTransformer: optional setMapID(), setLogger(GlideImportLog), setImportSetRun(), setSyncImport(bool); then transformAllMaps(importSetGr); then isError() and getImportSetRun().

Symptom 1: "done" before data exists. setSyncImport() defaults to false, so the transform runs asynchronously and transformAllMaps() returns immediately. isError() at that point tells you nothing about rows that have not been processed. Call setSyncImport(true) if the caller really needs the outcome in the response, and size the batch so the REST transaction does not run for minutes.

Symptom 2: history disappears. The GlideImportSetTable page states that a scheduled job, Scripted Import Set Deleter, runs every seven days by default and "deletes all Import Sets, Transform Maps, Transform Entries, and drops the Import Set Tables" created by the API. That is the designed lifecycle, not a bug.

Would I ship it? Not as a monthly integration. Create one permanent staging table with the union of columns and one transform map (with coalesce on store + asset tag), map per-franchisee column names in code, and keep the scripted pieces for what they are good at: the synchronous transform and logging.

// Scripted REST resource, scoped app. CSV posted as text, header row first.
var lines = request.body.dataString.split(/\r?\n/);
var csv = new sn_impex.CSVParser();
var headers = csv.parseLineToArray(lines[0]);
var colMap = mapFranchiseeHeaders(franchiseeId, headers);   // header -> u_ column on the permanent table

var isGr = new GlideRecord('sys_import_set');
isGr.short_description = 'Franchise ' + franchiseeId + ' ' + new GlideDateTime().getDate();
isGr.table_name = 'x_frn_equipment_import';
var isId = isGr.insert();

for (var i = 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
  if (!lines[i]) continue;
  var obj = csv.parseLineToObject(lines[i], headers);       // handles quoted commas
  var row = new GlideRecord('x_frn_equipment_import');
  row.setValue('sys_import_set', isId);
  for (var h in colMap) row.setValue(colMap[h], obj[h]);
  row.insert();
}

var run = new GlideImportSetRun(isId);
var log = new GlideImportLog(run, 'Franchise REST');
var t = new GlideImportSetTransformer();
t.setImportSetRun(run);                                   // transform and log share one run history
t.setLogger(log);
t.setSyncImport(true);
t.transformAllMaps(isGr);
response.setStatus(t.isError() ? 207 : 200);
response.setBody({ import_set: isId, run: log.getImportRunHistory(), error: t.isError() });

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The parameter table for addTransformEntry() in the reference has its descriptions shuffled (it lists coalesce as "Target column"). Trust the signature and examples: source, target, coalesce.
  • Column names come back as u_ names from create(); the map's source columns must use those names, not the labels.
  • GlideImportLog writes to import_log and can be tied to a run. GlideTransformLog looks similar but only writes to the node's localhost logs, which nobody will find later.
  • GlideImportSetRun() with no argument creates a new sys_import_set record. Pass your import set sys_id or you end up with an orphan import set per call.
  • CSVParser.parseLineToObject() throws ("Header list is empty") if headers is null. Validate the header row before the loop: a file with a blank first line will not give you usable headers.
  • Splitting the body on newlines breaks if a quoted field contains a line break. If franchisees export notes fields, parse with a stream-aware approach or reject such files.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating isError() after an asynchronous transform as the final answer.
  • Building a new map per upload with coalesce false, which turns every monthly load into inserts.
  • Reading row results from the target table instead of the import set rows and import log, which already record insert/update/ignore/error per row.
Score points: Quote the seven-day Scripted Import Set Deleter behaviour and explain it as the reason the dynamic-table APIs are for one-off loads. Interviewers rarely hear that.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you transform a single row for a retry? (transformAllMaps(importSet, rowSysId).)
  • When would you use the Import Set REST API instead of a Scripted REST endpoint?
  • How would you notify a franchisee of rejected rows?

Sources
