  • GlideImportSetTransformMap API reference
  • GlideImportSetTransformer API reference
  • GlideImportSetRun API reference
  • GlideImportLog API reference
  • GlideTransformLog API reference
  • CSVParser API reference

question: A logistics company exports cmdb_ci_computer nightly to an asset-finance platform. The Python job loops sysparm_offset by 1000 until it gets an empty page. Three problems are open: (1) some nights a few hundred CIs appear twice and others are missing; (2) after security tightened ACLs on the CI table, the job sometimes stops at page 3 with an empty result although X-Total-Count says 48,000; (3) last week someone changed the filter to instal_status=1 (typo) and the export suddenly contained every computer, retired ones included. Diagnose each and show me how you would rewrite the paging loop.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Three separate documented behaviours are at work: offset paging over an unstable sort, sysparm_limit being applied before ACL evaluation, and invalid parts of an encoded query being ignored by default. Name each one, fix the loop, and show you know the Link and X-Total-Count headers and when to suppress them.

Diagnosis

1. Duplicates and gaps. The loop pages without an ORDERBY in sysparm_query. Offset paging only works if every page is cut from the same ordering, and without an explicit sort you have no guarantee of that. Records updated during the run make it worse: if the job orders by sys_updated_on and a CI is touched mid-export, it moves to a later position and is read twice, while the record it displaced is skipped. Pick an immutable, unique sort key. I use ORDERBYsys_id, or ORDERBYsys_created_on^ORDERBYsys_id if I want something readable, and a fixed upper bound such as sys_updated_on<=<job start> so the set does not grow under me.

2. Empty page with 48,000 total. This one is in the reference: sysparm_limit "is applied before ACL evaluation". The instance selects 1000 rows, then removes the ones the user may not read. If a whole window is unreadable, you get an empty array even though readable records exist later. The reference suggests reordering so accessible records come first. In practice I either fix the account's read access or move the ACL's condition into sysparm_query so the database returns only rows the account can see. Never treat an empty page as end-of-data. Stop on the offset reaching the total, or on the absence of a rel="next" link.

3. Typo exports everything. By default, if part of a query is invalid, such as an unknown field name, the instance ignores that part and runs the rest. instal_status=1 was dropped and the query became "all computers". The fix at instance level is glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows=true, but the reference warns it affects every query on the instance, including lists and GlideRecord.query(), so it needs a regression pass first. At job level I add a canary check: if X-Total-Count jumps by more than a threshold against last night's count, the job aborts.

The Rewritten Loop

import requests
from urllib.parse import quote

BASE = "https://acme.service-now.com/api/now/table/cmdb_ci_computer"
q = "install_status=1^sys_updated_on<=" + job_start + "^ORDERBYsys_id"
url = (BASE + "?sysparm_query=" + quote(q, safe="=^<")
       + "&sysparm_fields=sys_id,name,serial_number,asset_tag,install_status"
       + "&sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true&sysparm_limit=1000&sysparm_offset=0")
rows, expected = [], None
while url:
    r = session.get(url, headers={"Accept": "application/json"}, timeout=120)
    r.raise_for_status()
    if expected is None:
        expected = int(r.headers.get("X-Total-Count", "0"))
        if last_night and expected > last_night * 1.2:
            raise RuntimeError("count jumped; check the filter")
    rows.extend(r.json()["result"])
    url = r.links.get("next", {}).get("url")   # Link header, rel="next"
if len(rows) != expected:
    log.warning("read %d of %d; ACL-filtered rows?", len(rows), expected)

Following rel="next" from the Link header means the client never does offset arithmetic itself. The header also carries prev, first and last.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • X-Total-Count comes from a select count(*). On very large tables, sysparm_no_count=true skips that query. You then lose the total and must rely on the Link header or page size to know when to stop.
  • sysparm_suppress_pagination_header=true removes the Link header. Use it for single-page lookups, not for exports.
  • The default sysparm_limit is 10,000, and the reference warns that unusually large values hurt performance. Raising the limit does not replace paging.
  • Negative offsets are explicitly unsupported.
  • Column names, operators and values in sysparm_query are case-sensitive, so Install_status is also an invalid field and will be ignored as well.

Common Mistakes

  • Stopping when a page comes back short or empty.
  • Ordering by sys_updated_on on a table that is being written to during the export.
  • Switching on glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows in production without testing every report and script.
Score points: Quote "limit is applied before ACL evaluation" and explain why that produces empty pages mid-export. Then add a count-delta guard as protection against silently ignored query clauses.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you switch this to an incremental (delta) export without missing late updates?
  • Would the CMDB Instance API's GET /now/cmdb/instance/{className} page any differently? (Same sysparm_limit/sysparm_offset semantics.)
  • How would you prove the ACL theory from the instance side?

Sources

  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)
  • CMDB Instance API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A facilities vendor pushes work orders into a custom table x_fac_work_order through the Table API. Their payload uses names for assignment_group ("Facilities - London"), local date-times for scheduled_start, and a value for an encrypted x_access_code field. Users report three things: the group is always empty, scheduled starts are off by the London offset, and the access code never saves even though the POST returns 201. The vendor also asks to send 500 work orders in one POST and wants to stop receiving 30 KB response bodies. Explain the behaviour and the request changes you would make.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This tests sysparm_input_display_value in depth: how it changes reference and date handling, and the less-known rule that encrypted fields are only saved when it is true and the caller has the encryption context. You should also know that a Table API POST creates one record, what happens to fields you leave out, and how to suppress the response body.

The Answer

Group always empty. sysparm_input_display_value defaults to false, which treats input as actual values and stores them without manipulation. A reference field expects a sys_id, so the string "Facilities - London" is not a valid reference. With true, the endpoint treats inputs as display values and converts them. The reference's own example is sending the display name for a reference field and having the sys_id stored.

Dates off by the offset. The reference is precise here. With true, date-time input is interpreted in the current user's time zone and converted to UTC. With false, it is inserted as GMT. The vendor sends London local time with the default false, so 09:00 local is stored as 09:00 GMT. Either the vendor sends UTC and keeps false, or sends local time with true, in which case the integration user's time zone must be London. I prefer UTC with false for dates, because a profile change on a service account should not move every scheduled job.

Encrypted field never saves. From the reference: "To set the value of an encrypted field, you must set this parameter to true. If this parameter is not set to true, values submitted to encrypted fields are not saved." The requesting user also needs the appropriate encryption context. The 201 is honest about the record; it just didn't store that field.

There is a conflict here. true fixes the reference and the encrypted field but changes date semantics. There is only one flag per request, so pick one convention and make the payload consistent with it: send true, a group name that resolves uniquely, and dates in the service account's configured time zone. Or send false with a group sys_id and UTC dates, and set the encrypted field in a second request with true.

POST /api/now/table/x_fac_work_order?sysparm_input_display_value=true&sysparm_fields=sys_id,number
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
X-no-response-body: true

{"short_description":"Lift 3 out of service",
 "assignment_group":"Facilities - London",
 "scheduled_start":"2026-11-02 09:00:00",
 "x_access_code":"4471"}

500 in one POST. The Table API POST "inserts one record... Multiple record insertion is not supported by this method." Options: loop with keep-alive; wrap groups of POSTs in the Batch API to cut round trips (each item still runs as its own call); or, preferably for a vendor feed, post to an Import Set staging table with insertMultiple so a transform map owns the mapping and coalescing.

Response size. The X-no-response-body: true request header suppresses the body on POST, PUT and PATCH. On POST the Location response header still gives the new record's URL. If the vendor needs the number back, drop the header and use sysparm_fields=sys_id,number instead.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • On POST, fields you do not specify (and that are not system-generated) are set to the data type's null value. Do not POST a "full" object with blank strings expecting defaults to apply.
  • Fields starting with sys_ are typically system-generated and cannot be updated through the body. Older releases documented a sysparm_suppress_auto_sys_field parameter for this area, but it does not appear in the Brazil Table API reference, so I would not design around it.
  • The Table API's PUT is documented as updating the record with the request body and returning all fields, not only the modified ones. Use PATCH for partial updates so intent is explicit.
  • Display-value inputs for references depend on the display value resolving to one record. Two groups called "Facilities - London" in different domains is a data problem the API will not warn you about.
  • Encrypted fields are hidden from users without the context, so a read-back check by a different account will look like data loss.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning on sysparm_input_display_value=true globally and then wondering why every date is shifted.
  • Treating 201 as proof that every field was stored.
  • Letting a vendor write straight to the target table when what they really need is a transform layer.
Score points: Quote the encrypted-field rule and the GMT versus user time-zone rule, and point out that one flag controls both, so the payload convention has to be designed rather than toggled.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Show the same load through POST /now/import/{staging}/insertMultiple. What do you lose and gain?
  • How do you make the vendor's retries idempotent when the Table API has no upsert?
  • Which business rules run on these inserts, and can the vendor tell when one rejected the record?

Sources

  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Batch API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Import Set API (Brazil REST reference)

question: An MSP's customer portal shows, for each of 60 tenants, open incident counts by priority and the average reassignment count per assignment group. Today the portal pulls every open incident through the Table API (about 180,000 rows, 10,000 per page) every five minutes and counts in Node.js. The instance's slow-transaction log is full of these requests. Redesign it with the Aggregate API. Write the calls, explain the response shape, and tell me where the Aggregate API will surprise them.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Move the counting into the database with GET /api/now/stats/{tableName}. Show you know its parameters (sysparm_count, sysparm_<aggregate>_fields, sysparm_group_by, sysparm_having, sysparm_order_by, sysparm_display_value) and the traps: no aggregate is computed unless you ask for one, results are grouped arrays rather than rows, and access is governed by role-based read access to the table.

The Answer

Pulling 180,000 rows to produce a few hundred numbers is the wrong shape of call. The Aggregate API runs GlideAggregate on the instance and returns only the aggregates. Two calls replace the export.

Counts by tenant and priority:

GET /api/now/stats/incident
  ?sysparm_query=active=true
  &sysparm_count=true
  &sysparm_group_by=company,priority
  &sysparm_display_value=all
Accept: application/json

Average reassignment count per group, only for noisy groups:

GET /api/now/stats/incident
  ?sysparm_query=active=true
  &sysparm_avg_fields=reassignment_count
  &sysparm_count=true
  &sysparm_group_by=assignment_group
  &sysparm_having=count^assignment_group^>^20
  &sysparm_order_by=AVG^reassignment_count

Grouped results come back ascending by the order key unless you add ^DESC, which the reference shows on a field (state^DESC). For the "worst groups first" view I simply reverse the small result set client-side.

Response shape. result is an array with one element per group. Each element has a stats object keyed by aggregate (the documented example shows stats.avg.reassignment_count and stats.avg.business_stc) and a groupby_fields array of {field, value} pairs. Values come back as strings, for example "1.2500", so parse them. With sysparm_display_value=all on a grouped reference or choice field you get both the sys_id and the label, which is what the portal needs: sys_id to map to the tenant, label to display.

Caching matters as much as the API. Five-minute refreshes for 60 tenants are fine when each refresh is two aggregate queries rather than eighteen pages of rows.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • If you pass neither sysparm_count nor a sysparm_<aggregate>_fields parameter, the reference says no aggregate operation is performed. You get a 200 with nothing useful in it.
  • The reference lists avg, min, max and sum for the _fields parameters, plus count. Nothing like a distinct count or percentile is documented, so those need a different design.
  • Rows with an empty grouping value come back as their own group with value: "". The documented example shows exactly that for unassigned incidents. Decide whether the portal shows "Unassigned" or hides it.
  • sysparm_having uses aggregate^field^operator^value with commas between clauses, not encoded-query syntax. sysparm_order_by accepts a field or an aggregate (AVG^state, COUNT) and sorts ascending unless ^DESC is added.
  • Security: the reference says the API "only honors read-only queries if read access is defined for the table being called on based on role ownership". Treat it as table-level, role-based access and test with the real integration account. A 403 here is documented as the user lacking access rights. If the counts must be tenant-scoped, the tenant filter belongs in sysparm_query, not in an assumption about row ACLs.
  • Requesting display values for groups has the same performance warning as the Table API. Ask only when you need labels.
  • Name-value pair filters such as &active=true work here too and accept display values for choice and reference fields.

Common Mistakes

  • Using X-Total-Count from a Table API call with sysparm_limit=1 once per tenant per priority. That is 300 count queries instead of one grouped one.
  • Grouping by a high-cardinality field (caller_id, cmdb_ci) and recreating the row export.
  • Assuming the aggregates are numbers in JSON.
Score points: Point out that no aggregate runs unless count or a _fields parameter is supplied, and that the empty-string group is real data, not a bug. Then talk about caching and tenant filtering in sysparm_query.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would you build a Scripted REST API with GlideAggregate instead of exposing the Aggregate API?
  • How would you return the same numbers for 60 tenants in one HTTP round trip? (Batch API, or one query grouped by company.)
  • When is Performance Analytics a better answer than live aggregates?

Sources

  • Aggregate API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)

question: An HR platform at a university sends employee changes to ServiceNow. Version 1 wrote straight into sys_user through the Table API and created duplicate users whenever an employee ID was re-sent. The team now wants to use the Import Set API. The HR vendor can send either one record per call in real time or a batch of 5,000 at 02:00, and the batch must be applied after the department load that runs at 01:30. Explain the sync and async behaviour of the Import Set endpoints, how you would sequence the loads, how the vendor learns what happened to each row, and why this beats the Table API here.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is checking whether you know that POST /now/import/{staging} transforms synchronously and returns per-transform results, that insertMultiple is asynchronous by default (configurable in sys_rest_insert_multiple), and that run_after and multi_import_set_id exist for sequencing. You should also be able to explain how transform maps with coalesce fix the duplicate problem that the Table API created.

The Answer

Why the Import Set API. The Table API writes exactly what you send, and its POST always inserts. Re-sent employees became duplicates because nothing decided "is this an update?". The Import Set API writes to a staging table and runs the transform maps defined for it, so a transform map that coalesces on employee number turns a re-send into an update. You also get a staging record for every inbound row, which is your audit trail, and the mapping logic lives on the instance instead of in the vendor's code.

Real-time, one record: POST /api/now/import/u_hr_staging. "Transformation occurs synchronously." The response includes, per transform map, the target table, transform_map, status (for example inserted), the target sys_id, a display_name/display_value pair and a record_link. Any status_message and error_message set by transform scripts are returned in the response too, so an onBefore script that rejects a row can explain why and the vendor sees it immediately.

Nightly batch: POST /api/now/import/u_hr_staging/insertMultiple. The body is {"records":[{...},{...}]} in staging-column format by default, and in that format the keys are matched to staging column labels unless the mapping is switched to column names (see below). Transformation is asynchronous by default, so the response gives you import_set_id (a sys_import_set record) and multi_import_set_id, not per-row results. To make it synchronous you create a record in Rest Insert Multiples [sys_rest_insert_multiple] for the source table and set the transformation to synchronous. That table is also where you switch column mapping from Label to Column name, or enable the data-source JSON format.

Sequencing. The department load's call returns an import_set_id. The 02:00 user batch passes it as run_after:

POST /api/now/import/u_hr_staging/insertMultiple?run_after=<dept import_set_id>&multi_import_set_id=<tonight's multi set>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{"records":[{"employee_id":"E10442","first_name":"Ana","dept_code":"PHY"}, ...]}

The reference says run_after is only valid for asynchronous transformations, and that is the point: the platform holds the user set until the department set completes. multi_import_set_id groups both into one Multi Import Set so operations can see the night as a single unit.

Per-row outcome for the batch. Because the batch is async, the vendor polls or, better, ServiceNow pushes a summary. Each staging row can later be read with GET /api/now/import/u_hr_staging/{row sys_id}, which returns the transformation result, as long as the row still exists.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Import Set POST bodies must be string name-value pairs. Nested JSON is not mapped; the reference gives the example of ":" becoming "=" in the stored value. Flatten before sending, or use the data-source format with a JSON data source and a configured "Path for each row".
  • Staging tables are cleaned on a schedule, so GET /now/import/... can return 404 once the row is gone. Do not design a reconciliation process that depends on reading staging rows days later.
  • The legacy CMDB Data Ingestion API (/cmdb/ingest/{data_source_sys_id}) is explicitly not recommended. Migrate it to insertMultiple.
  • The reference's security note says ACLs on the tables are still enforced, and that adding a table to sys_public.list allows unauthenticated access. Never do that for a staging table.
  • Sync on insertMultiple makes the HTTP request wait on 5,000 transforms, with the transaction-time risks that brings. Keep big batches async.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming insertMultiple returns per-row target sys_ids the way the single POST does.
  • Using run_after with a synchronous configuration.
  • Putting coalesce logic in the vendor's code and still writing directly to sys_user.
Score points: Name sys_rest_insert_multiple as the switch for sync versus async, and explain that run_after only works async. That shows you have actually configured it.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you return a rejection from a transform script to the caller? (status_message/error_message in the single-record POST.)
  • What happens when two transform maps exist for the same staging table?
  • How would you alert on a nightly set whose error rows exceed 2%?

question: A bank's branch tablet app opens a customer case and, before the screen renders, fires 38 separate REST calls: case header, caller, six reference lookups, related tasks, attachment metadata, KB suggestions, and a couple of POSTs to log the view. On branch Wi-Fi the screen takes 9 seconds. An architect proposes moving everything into one Batch API call, and also suggests using the same mechanism for the overnight push of 20,000 case updates "because it will run them in parallel". Build the batch request for the screen, explain how you would handle the response, and tell me what is wrong with the overnight idea.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need to know the request and response contract of POST /api/now/v1/batch (ids, relative URLs, Base64 bodies, per-item headers, serviced_requests versus unserviced_requests), its size and time limits, and the documented statement that it is not for parallel processing or long-running work. Each item is still an ordinary API call with its own ACLs and status code.

The Answer

The Batch API fits the screen problem. The 9 seconds are mostly round trips and per-request authentication and session setup, and the reference names removing that overhead as the whole purpose. What it does not do is make the work itself cheaper: "The Batch API has the same performance characteristics as individual API requests but avoids the overhead of multiple client-server requests."

Building the request. The body is JSON only (Content-Type: application/json). Each item needs a unique id, a method, and a url relative to the instance including query parameters. headers are per item, and any body must be Base64-encoded. Items can target different APIs and even different formats.

const b64 = s => Buffer.from(s, "utf8").toString("base64");
const json = [{name: "Accept", value: "application/json"},
              {name: "Content-Type", value: "application/json"}];
const batch = {
  batch_request_id: "case-" + caseId + "-" + Date.now(),
  rest_requests: [
    {id: "hdr", method: "GET", headers: json, exclude_response_headers: true,
     url: "/api/now/table/sn_customerservice_case/" + caseId +
          "?sysparm_fields=number,short_description,state,contact,account" +
          "&sysparm_display_value=all&sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true"},
    {id: "tasks", method: "GET", headers: json, exclude_response_headers: true,
     url: "/api/now/table/sn_customerservice_task?sysparm_query=parent=" + caseId +
          "&sysparm_fields=number,state,assigned_to&sysparm_limit=50"},
    {id: "att", method: "GET", headers: json, exclude_response_headers: true,
     url: "/api/now/attachment?sysparm_query=table_sys_id=" + caseId + "&sysparm_limit=20"},
    {id: "viewlog", method: "POST", headers: json, exclude_response_headers: true,
     url: "/api/now/table/u_case_view_log",
     body: b64(JSON.stringify({u_case: caseId, u_branch: branchId}))}
  ]
};
const res = await fetch(instance + "/api/now/v1/batch", {
  method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json", Authorization: auth},
  body: JSON.stringify(batch)});
const out = await res.json();
const byId = {};
for (const r of out.serviced_requests) {
  byId[r.id] = {status: r.status_code, error: r.error_message,
               body: r.body ? JSON.parse(Buffer.from(r.body, "base64").toString("utf8")) : null};
}
if (out.unserviced_requests.length) retryIndividually(out.unserviced_requests);

Handling the response. The outer 200 only means the batch was processed. Every item has its own status_code, status_text, optional error_message, execution_time in milliseconds and a Base64 body. A 403 on the attachment item and a 201 on the log item can sit in the same response, because ACLs are applied to each call in the batch. Anything left in unserviced_requests was never run because the batch hit a limit, so the client must retry those ids.

The reference describes no transaction across items, so I treat each item as independent: if viewlog fails, nothing rolls back the reads, and the reverse is also true.

What Is Wrong with the Overnight Idea

Two documented facts kill it. First, "The Batch API is not intended for parallel transaction processing", so items do not run concurrently and 20,000 updates take as long as 20,000 updates. Second, if a batch request runs longer than 30 seconds, the REST Batch API request timeout transaction quota rule ends it, and raising that quota is flagged as a performance risk. Overnight bulk updates belong in an Import Set insertMultiple load with asynchronous transforms, or in chunked parallel Table API calls the client controls.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Size limits: 5 MB per request item (glide.rest.batch.max.inputSize, maximum 10 MB) and 10 MB per response item (glide.rest.batch.max.outputSize). The X-BATCHREQUEST-MAX-OUTPUT-SIZE header can lower the response limit but never raise it above the property.
  • The reference warns against including long-running requests and requests that retrieve large amounts of data. A careless sysparm_limit on one item can push the whole batch into unserviced_requests.
  • Set exclude_response_headers: true on items whose headers you do not read; it shrinks the response noticeably.
  • Accept: multipart/mixed is supported. Streaming multipart responses needs glide.rest.serialize.disable_response_stream_buffering=true.
  • The documented URL format is versioned (/api/now/{api_version}/batch), so pin v1.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to Base64-encode item bodies, or forgetting to decode responses.
  • Checking only the outer status code.
  • Reusing item ids, which makes the response impossible to correlate.
Score points: Quote "not intended for parallel transaction processing" and the 30-second quota rule, then send the overnight job to Import Sets. Mention that unserviced_requests needs its own retry path.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would a Scripted REST API that returns the whole screen model beat the Batch API?
  • How would you size the batch so it stays under 30 seconds as data grows?
  • How do per-item ACL failures show up to the tablet user?

Sources

  • Batch API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Import Set API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Attachment API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A hospital group's BI team wants to show ServiceNow Performance Analytics KPIs (mean time to resolve, open incidents by priority, SLA breach %) in Power BI next to clinical data. A data engineer wrote a connector against the Scorecards API that pulls every indicator daily. The issues: half the indicators the service desk manager sees in the Analytics Hub are missing from the feed; the "by priority" series comes back as a single number; date filtering seems to be ignored; and the sort order flips when they pass sortdir=desc. Explain how the Scorecards API is parameterised, why each issue happens, and how you would build the extract.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

There is one endpoint, GET /api/now/pa/scorecards, and nearly everything depends on sysparm_uuid. It is a colon-separated chain that starts with the indicator sys_id and can add a breakdown, elements, a second-level breakdown and an aggregate. You should also know the defaults that surprise people: sysparm_display=true (only indicators shown on the Analytics Hub), a single latest score unless sysparm_include_scores=true, date bounds that need include_scores, and sysparm_sortdir values asc and des, not "desc". The caller needs pa_viewer, and ACLs apply.

The Answer

Missing indicators. The listing call returns indicators with sysparm_display=true by default, meaning only those set to show on the Analytics Hub. Pass sysparm_display=all. Paging uses sysparm_per_page (default 10, maximum 100) and sysparm_page, not sysparm_offset. A connector that reads one page gets ten indicators. ACLs also apply to the integration user, so it may not see everything the manager sees. Check the user's PA access as well as the pa_viewer role.

"By priority" is one number. You get a breakdown series by adding the breakdown to the UUID, <indicator>:<breakdown>, optionally followed by an element (for example the sys_id of "2 - High"). The alternative is sysparm_breakdown. Without either you get the overall score. Use sysparm_include_available_breakdowns=true once to discover which breakdowns an indicator supports.

Dates ignored. sysparm_from and sysparm_to (ISO-8601) need sysparm_include_scores=true. Without it, the API returns only the most recent score and the bounds do nothing. sysparm_limit caps the number of scores. sysparm_step skips scores by indicator frequency (3 means every third day for a daily indicator).

Sort flips. Valid directions are asc and des. "desc" isn't a documented value. The default is descending on sysparm_sortby=value.

# 1. discover (weekly)
GET /api/now/pa/scorecards?sysparm_display=all&sysparm_per_page=100&sysparm_page=1

# 2. daily extract per indicator / breakdown
GET /api/now/pa/scorecards?sysparm_uuid=<indicator>:<priority_breakdown>
    &sysparm_include_scores=true
    &sysparm_from=2026-10-01T00:00:00&sysparm_to=2026-10-22T23:59:59
    &sysparm_display_value=false

Aggregates and payload size. If the BI team wants weekly or monthly views of a daily indicator, call once with sysparm_include_available_aggregates=true to list what applies, then append the aggregate sys_id to the end of the UUID chain instead of averaging daily values in Power BI. Set sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true to drop the reference URIs (such as the unit and indicator links) that the connector doesn't need.

Keep a mapping table in the BI layer from indicator and breakdown sys_ids to friendly names, and refresh it from step 1 so renamed indicators don't break dashboards.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • sysparm_uuid must be the first parameter and must start with an indicator sys_id. A domain sys_id is appended after a semicolon, not a colon.
  • If the indicator uses a Default time series, every value the API returns uses that aggregate. Your "daily" numbers may already be weekly averages.
  • sysparm_include_realtime isn't supported for formula indicators.
  • sysparm_contains uses AND logic across its comma-separated terms. Three keywords narrow the result; they don't widen it.
  • sysparm_tags filters by indicator group, but the API can't tell you a group's sys_id. Read it from the group record. Don't combine it with sysparm_uuid.
  • Forecast and trendline scores (sysparm_include_forecast_scores, sysparm_include_trendline_scores) also need include_scores.

Common Mistakes

  • Pulling only the latest score each day and building history in Power BI. Pull a rolling window with sysparm_include_scores=true so the BI history matches what the Analytics Hub shows.
  • Requesting sysparm_display_value=true on large pulls. It is slower and gives labels you will remap anyway.
  • Giving the integration user admin "to make it work", which hides the ACL problem until someone audits it.
Score points: Explain the UUID chain from memory (indicator : breakdown : element : level-2 breakdown : level-2 element : aggregate ; domain) and point out the des spelling. Both show you have used the endpoint, not just read the overview.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would you skip the Scorecards API and extract pa_scores tables through another route?
  • How would you include targets and thresholds so Power BI can colour the tiles?
  • How do you handle a domain-separated instance where each hospital is a domain?

Sources

  • Scorecards API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A media company's scoped app calls an AI image service. The service returns a URL to a generated PNG, which must be stored on an x_med_asset record. Later, a print vendor's system must download those images over HTTPS without being given read access to x_med_asset, and the vendor also wants a nightly CSV listing assets with direct image URLs. A developer has proposed fetching the image body, base64-encoding it in script, writing it with GlideSysAttachment.writeBase64, and returning images inside JSON from a Scripted REST API. Design the three pieces properly with the APIs ServiceNow provides, and explain the failure modes you would guard against.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Keep binary data as streams from end to end. Use saveResponseBodyAsAttachment() for the inbound fetch. Use getContentStream() and the response stream writer for serving. Use writeString() with the right headers for the CSV. Show that you know the ordering rule (content type and status before the stream writer) and the documented 500 error when no content type is set on a binary response. Then cover the security trade-off of serving files from a custom endpoint instead of through record ACLs.

The Answer

This is the design from the developer advocates' C3 series, where they handled thousands of images this way.

1. Fetch and store: skip base64.

saveImage: function (imageUrl, assetSysId) {
  var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2();
  rm.setHttpMethod('get');
  rm.setEndpoint(imageUrl);
  rm.saveResponseBodyAsAttachment('x_med_asset', assetSysId, 'generated.png');
  var resp = rm.execute();
  if (resp.getStatusCode() != 200) {
    throw new Error('Image fetch failed: ' + resp.getStatusCode() + ' ' + resp.getErrorMessage());
  }
  return resp.getResponseAttachmentSysid();
}

The reference says the response body is saved as an attachment on the given record, that it can be any format, and that getErrorMessage() on the response explains a failed save. There is a four-argument version that takes an encryption context. The blog's reasons for avoiding base64 still apply. Direct binary is about a third smaller, and attachment storage already base64-encodes and chunks every file into sys_attachment_doc internally, so encoding in script adds a second, pointless round. Also, scoped getContentBase64() only returns up to 5MB, so a base64 design has a size limit built in.

2. Serve through a Scripted REST resource.

(function process(request, response) {
  var id = request.queryParams.assetId;     // validate format before use
  var att = new GlideRecord('sys_attachment');
  att.addQuery('table_name', 'x_med_asset');
  att.addQuery('table_sys_id', id);
  att.addQuery('file_name', 'generated.png');
  att.setLimit(1);
  att.query();
  if (!att.next()) {
    response.setStatus(404);
    return;
  }
  var stream = new GlideSysAttachment().getContentStream(att.getUniqueValue());
  response.setContentType('image/png');      // must come first
  response.setStatus(200);
  response.setHeader('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="' + id + '.png"');
  response.getStreamWriter().writeStream(stream);
})(request, response);

The RESTAPIResponseStream reference says you must set the content type and status before writeStream() or the response fails, and you cannot change them afterwards. The RESTAPIResponse reference adds that leaving out a content type returns a 500 error for a binary response. In global scope the reference example uses new GlideSysAttachmentInputStream(sysId) instead of the scoped getContentStream().

3. CSV export. Build the string and send it with text/csv and an attachment Content-Disposition, then response.getStreamWriter().writeString(csv). Each row can include an absolute link to the image endpoint built from glide.servlet.uri, as the blog does. Put a quote around every value and double any quotes inside it. The blog's sample does not, and a description containing a quote or comma breaks the file.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • You now own access control. The blog says custom serving lets you make images public "without needing to alter table ACLs". That's why it is risky. Decide how the vendor authenticates (an inbound API key with an access policy limited to GET on this resource is a good fit), never let the client choose table_name, and avoid sequential or guessable IDs.
  • Do not trust the caller's query string as an encoded query. The blog's CSV resource accepts request.queryParams.query and passes it to addEncodedQuery(). Anyone with the endpoint can then read whatever the script user can.
  • Look for attachments in all the places they can be. The blog's query also matches a ZZ_YY-prefixed variant of the table_name alongside the plain one. Check your own sys_attachment rows before hard-coding one value. Image fields store an attachment sys_id, so you must write the attachment and then set the field. Replacing an image means delete, write, then update the reference.
  • Big CSVs: building one string in memory is fine for thousands of rows, not millions. Page the export or write in chunks with repeated writeString() calls.
  • Through a MID Server, the MID user needs roles to write attachments and to write the target table.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling setBody() with base64 inside JSON for images: bigger payloads, extra encoding, and clients that cannot use the URL directly.
  • Setting the content type after getStreamWriter().
  • Using setHeader('Content-Type', ...) and assuming it behaves the same as setContentType() for binary responses. Prefer the documented method.
Score points: Quote the two documented rules (set content type and status before writing the stream, and no content type means a 500 on binary). Then raise the access-control trade-off yourself before the interviewer does.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you produce a low-resolution copy for mobile clients, given the C3 team's lessons about multi-MB images on conference Wi-Fi?
  • How would you accept a binary upload in a Scripted REST API using request.body.dataStream?
  • When would you move image storage outside ServiceNow altogether?

Sources

  • Beyond JSON: Working with Binary Files and Alternative Content Types (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Working with Image Attachments in ServiceNow: Lessons from Processing 130,000 Images (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • GlideSysAttachment - Scoped (API reference)
  • RESTAPIResponse - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • RESTAPIResponseStream - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • RESTAPIRequestBody - Scoped, Global (API reference)

question: A manufacturing customer exposes CMDB computers to a data-lake job through a Scripted REST API that pages through about 1.8 million cmdb_ci_computer rows, 2,000 per call. Each page takes 6 to 9 seconds and the slow-query log shows a COUNT(*) on every request. The current code uses chooseWindow() and then calls getRowCount() to return a total. Explain where the cost comes from, tell me what chooseWindow(20, 30) followed by setLimit(100) returns, and write the page-fetch function you would ship.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants the documented cause: running query() with chooseWindow() triggers a COUNT(*), and getRowCount() does too. They want you to know the three ways to stop it, how setLimit() and chooseWindow() overwrite each other, and that pagination without a stable sort returns duplicates and gaps.

A strong answer separates "fetch a page" from "count the total" and uses the right API for each.

The Answer

Where the time goes. The GlideRecord reference says running query() with chooseWindow() triggers a COUNT(*) query, which can be slow on tables with many records. setNoCount() exists for this: it stops the query from running COUNT(*), and its note names both chooseWindow() and getRowCount() as triggers, citing tables of a million or more rows. On top of that, the endpoint calls getRowCount() to return a total on every page, so it counts 1.8 million rows 900 times per export.

What chooseWindow(20, 30) then setLimit(100) returns. setLimit() implicitly calls chooseWindow(). If chooseWindow() is called first, setLimit() overwrites its window, and the reference says that pair returns 100 records starting at row 1. Reverse the order, setLimit(5) then chooseWindow(20, 30), and the window wins: 10 records starting at row 21. Window bounds are zero-based, first row inclusive and last row exclusive, so chooseWindow(2, 4) returns the third and fourth records.

Ordering. Windowing over an unordered result is not stable between calls. The reference example sorts before windowing, and the Developer Advocate GlideRecord tips post says to combine pagination with sorting to avoid inconsistencies. Sort on something that does not change during the export and add a tie-breaker.

var CmdbExportPager = Class.create();
CmdbExportPager.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {
        this.table = 'cmdb_ci_computer';
        this.filter = 'install_status=1';
        this.fields = ['sys_id', 'name', 'serial_number', 'os', 'sys_updated_on'];
    },

    // Called once per export, not once per page
    total: function () {
        var ga = new GlideAggregate(this.table);
        ga.addEncodedQuery(this.filter);
        ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
        ga.query();
        return ga.next() ? parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) : 0;
    },

    page: function (offset, size) {
        size = Math.min(parseInt(size, 10) || 500, 2000);
        offset = Math.max(parseInt(offset, 10) || 0, 0);

        var gr = new GlideRecord(this.table);
        gr.addEncodedQuery(this.filter);
        gr.orderBy('sys_created_on');
        gr.orderBy('sys_id');                 // tie-breaker
        gr.chooseWindow(offset, offset + size);
        gr.setNoCount();                       // no COUNT(*) per page
        gr.query();

        var rows = [];
        while (gr.next()) {
            var row = {};
            for (var i = 0; i < this.fields.length; i++) {
                row[this.fields[i]] = gr.getValue(this.fields[i]);
            }
            rows.push(row);
        }
        return { offset: offset, size: size, returned: rows.length,
                 more: rows.length == size, rows: rows };
    },

    type: 'CmdbExportPager'
};

The response says whether there is probably another page (more) without counting. The client asks for the total once, through a separate resource that uses GlideAggregate. The GlideRecord reference puts it directly: if you only want the number of records, getAggregate() is the better option because it does not return the rows. getValue() copies strings into the payload so the response holds values, not GlideElement objects.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Calling setLimit() before chooseWindow() also skips the COUNT(*), but the reference says setNoCount() gives the same benefit and reads more clearly.
  • chooseWindow() has a third parameter, forceCount; passing true forces the row count even in cases (such as text search) where it would be skipped. Do not pass it by habit.
  • If any caller filters with sys_id IN and more than 100 sys_ids, getRowCount() can be wrong unless you call disableSysIdInOptimization() or raise glide.db.first_pass_sys_id_list_size.max. The reference also says to call next() before getRowCount() in that case.
  • Offset paging over a table that changes during the export can skip or repeat rows when records are inserted before the current offset. Sorting on creation time limits this to newly created rows, which the next incremental run catches.
  • setCategory() can route read-only queries to a read replica if the Secondary Database Pools plugin is active; results may lag the primary slightly.

Common Mistakes

  • Returning getRowCount() on every page.
  • Paging without orderBy(), then blaming the platform for duplicates.
  • Setting both setLimit() and chooseWindow() and getting a different window than intended.
  • Treating lastRow as inclusive and losing one record per page.
Score points: Explain the overwrite rule between setLimit() and chooseWindow() with the documented 100-from-row-1 result. Few candidates know it, and it is a common cause of "pagination returns the same records" bugs.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you make the export incremental using sys_updated_on?
  • What changes if the consumer needs display values for reference fields?
  • Would you consider GlideQuery here, and what does its conversion to JavaScript objects cost on 1.8 million rows?

Sources

  • GlideRecord (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideAggregate (Scoped) - API reference
  • Developer Advocate blog: 6 GlideRecord Tips to Supercharge Your ServiceNow Development

question: A telecom's platform team wants a GitHub Actions pipeline for their scoped app x_tel_orders: on merge to main, publish from DEV to the application repository, install on TEST, run the regression ATF suite, and roll TEST back if the suite fails. Their first attempt calls install immediately after publish and gets failures; the ATF step reports success after 2 seconds every time; and when two pipelines run at once one of them seems to hang. Design the pipeline against the CICD API, write the polling logic, and explain each symptom.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The CICD API is asynchronous. Each call starts work and returns a links.progress.id, and the pipeline must poll /sn_cicd/progress/{id} until the status reaches 2, 3 or 4. You should know the publish-before-install rule, the numeric status codes, how test results are fetched, the role needed, and the queueing behaviour that explains the "hang".

The Answer

Pipeline shape.

  1. POST /api/sn_cicd/app_repo/publish?scope=x_tel_orders&version=1.4.0&dev_notes=... against DEV. Poll progress until it succeeds.
  2. POST /api/sn_cicd/app_repo/install?scope=x_tel_orders&version=1.4.0 against TEST. Keep rollback_version from the response; it is the previously installed version, or null. Poll progress.
  3. POST /api/sn_cicd/testsuite/run?test_suite_sys_id=... against TEST. Poll progress, then read links.results.id and call GET /api/sn_cicd/testsuite/results/{result_id}.
  4. If the suite failed, POST /api/sn_cicd/app_repo/rollback?scope=x_tel_orders&version=<rollback_version>, then poll again.

Polling.

poll() {  # $1 = progress id, $2 = instance
  for i in $(seq 1 360); do
    body=$(curl -s -u "$CICD_USER:$CICD_PASS" -H "Accept: application/json" \
      "https://$2.service-now.com/api/sn_cicd/progress/$1")
    status=$(echo "$body" | jq -r '.result.status')
    echo "$(echo "$body" | jq -r '.result.percent_complete')% $(echo "$body" | jq -r '.result.status_label')" >&2   # progress to stderr so $(poll ...) captures only the final JSON
    case "$status" in
      2) echo "$body"; return 0 ;;                       # Successful
      3|4) echo "$body" | jq -r '.result.status_detail, .result.error'; return 1 ;;  # Failed / Canceled
    esac
    sleep 10
  done
  return 1
}
run=$(curl -s -X POST -u "$CICD_USER:$CICD_PASS" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "https://tel-test.service-now.com/api/sn_cicd/testsuite/run?test_suite_sys_id=$SUITE&run_in_cloud=true")
pid=$(echo "$run" | jq -r '.result.links.progress.id')
final=$(poll "$pid" tel-test) || exit 1
rid=$(echo "$final" | jq -r '.result.links.results.id')
res=$(curl -s -u "$CICD_USER:$CICD_PASS" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "https://tel-test.service-now.com/api/sn_cicd/testsuite/results/$rid")
fails=$(echo "$res" | jq '.result.rolledup_test_failure_count + .result.rolledup_test_error_count')
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ] || rollback

Symptom 1: install right after publish fails. Publish only starts the work. The reference says an application must be published to the repository before it can be installed, and the install fails otherwise. Calling install before publish's progress reaches 2 means it is not published yet. Publish can also fail outright: it returns 400 if source-controlled tracked files have uncommitted changes, and without version it fails if the current version already exists in the repository.

Symptom 2: ATF "passes" in 2 seconds. They are reading the response of testsuite/run, which reports that the run was accepted, typically with status 0 (Pending). That is not a result. Success means progress status 2 and then zero failures and errors in the results payload (rolledup_test_failure_count, rolledup_test_error_count, with child_suite_results for nested suites). Also, if the suite contains UI tests, a scheduled Client Test Runner must be open or headless execution configured. run_in_cloud=true uses Cloud Runner instead.

Symptom 3: the "hang". Since Tokyo, CICD endpoints that need the instance-wide lock queue requests instead of rejecting them. The second pipeline's install is Pending in the Application Operation Queue behind the first. That is by design. An admin can inspect, pause or resume the queue under System Diagnostics, and a queued operation that cannot start within com.glide.update_operation.job_cancel_timeout_minutes (48 hours by default) is cancelled. Give the polling loop its own timeout and print status_message so people can see it is queued.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Pass version on publish. If you do, the publish uses it and updates the local application version to match. If you leave it out, the current local version is used, and the call fails when that version already exists in the repository. That makes reruns of the same pipeline fail in a confusing way.
  • The account needs sn_cicd.sys_ci_automation or admin. A 403 from any endpoint means it has neither.
  • Status values are 0 Pending, 1 Running, 2 Successful, 3 Failed, 4 Canceled. They arrive as strings, so compare carefully in typed languages.
  • Rollback is only available after the install completes, and its version is the version you expect to end up on. For app customizations, it is the base app version.
  • Two hours before a scheduled upgrade, the queue goes into an upgrade-paused state unless com.glide.update_operation.queue_upgrade_window overrides it. Pipelines will sit Pending.
  • For multi-app releases, /sn_cicd/app/batch/install returns links.rollback.id, and batch rollback reverts every package. Packages with no previous version are uninstalled.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating HTTP 200 from an initiating call as success.
  • Using a personal admin account in the pipeline secrets.
  • Skipping rollback_version and then guessing which version to roll back to.
Score points: Explain the queue-instead-of-reject behaviour and show a poller that fails on status 3 or 4 and on its own timeout. Then mention that ATF success is decided by the results endpoint, not the run endpoint.

  • How do you handle source-control stashes from sc/apply_changes?
  • When would you use the CICD Update Set API instead of the app repository?

question: A public-sector agency has three developers working on one scoped permits app across two dev instances. Changes move by update set and keep getting lost or overwritten. The instances are on Zurich, and the team wants Git (GitHub) through ServiceNow Studio's new source control. Walk through the setup end to end (token, credential, linking, branch choice), then explain what happens on commit, pull, stash, branch switch and tag, and the operational gotchas you would put in the team's runbook. They also ask whether Yokohama developer sandboxes change the picture.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Walk through the concrete Studio flow: a fine-grained GitHub token stored as a Basic Auth credential, Link to source control from App details, and the default sn_instances/<instance> branch. Make clear that commits are deliberate snapshots separate from update records, that pulls overwrite the app in the instance (so local changes must be committed, stashed or discarded), and that switching branch is a pull. Know the limits: case sensitivity, binaries, force pushes, long-lived branches, token expiry. Then place developer sandboxes as the answer to "one shared instance, one branch".

The Answer

Setup, from Earl Duque's complete walkthrough and the Zurich Studio post:

  1. Create a GitHub repository per app (a README is fine). Studio controls the repository root, so other code in the same repo lives in subfolders and needs a .gitignore.
  2. Create a fine-grained personal access token limited to that repository, with Contents set to read and write (Metadata is added automatically) and an expiry date. The walkthrough says to be as granular as possible, ideally one token per app per instance, so each can be revoked alone.
  3. In ServiceNow, create a Basic Auth credential: user name is the GitHub user name, password is the token. Your GitHub password will not work.
  4. In ServiceNow Studio (not legacy Studio), open the app, go to App details, Source control, Link to source control, and enter the repo URL, branch and credential. The Zurich post lists the requirements: a dedicated repo and token, network access from the instance to the repo (or a MID Server if it is behind a firewall), and the admin role to link. HTTPS or SSH are both supported.
  5. Branch: the default is sn_instances/<instance>. The walkthrough suggests keeping it, then making it the default branch in GitHub settings if this instance is the source of truth.

Daily operations:

  • Commit. Changes still create update records, but nothing reaches Git until someone chooses Commit changes, selects files (creates, updates and deletes), and writes a message.
  • Import to another instance. Create, Import app, with an existing branch name and a credential that can read the repo. The import does not create branches. Refresh the app list afterwards.
  • Pull. Pull from repository makes the instance's app match the current branch's latest commit. If there are uncommitted local changes, Studio offers to discard them (permanent) or stash them. Applying a stash later is done separately from Manage stashes, which differs from legacy Studio. A stash that is never applied just sits there.
  • Branch. Create branch makes it in GitHub and switches to it (refresh App details to see the right name). Switching branch is the same as pulling the whole branch, so the same stash rules apply.
  • Tag. Tags are immutable markers. Tag the commit you are about to promote (for example v1.4.0) so you can compare or roll back to exactly what was deployed.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

From the walkthrough's warnings section, and what to put in the runbook:

  • Case sensitivity. Git is case-sensitive, and ServiceNow names often are not. Renaming a file or scope by case alone can cause conflicts that only show up on push or pull.
  • Binaries. Keep attachments and exports out of the repo.
  • No force pushes. Rewriting history on GitHub leaves the instance out of step with what Git thinks is current.
  • Short-lived branches. The longer a branch lives, the harder the pull. Merge often.
  • Token expiry. Push and pull stop the day the token expires. Track expiry dates and rotate the credential's password before then.
  • Pull = overwrite. Two developers on one instance, one branch, means one developer's uncommitted work gets stashed or discarded by the other's pull. That is the real cause of the "lost changes" they see today.

Developer sandboxes. The Yokohama developer sandboxes post describes up to 30 isolated, lightweight copies of a base instance, each able to work on its own Git branch, with merge conflicts resolved using standard Git tools. Paired with the ServiceNow IDE (diffs and conflict resolution in the IDE) and Fluent syncing for low-code changes, each developer gets their own space. That fixes the shared-instance problem at its source. Sandboxes need entitlement and setup with ServiceNow, so treat them as the next step, not a prerequisite.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a classic token with full account scope and no expiry, shared by the whole team.
  • Choosing "discard local changes" to get past the stash prompt.
  • Mixing update sets and Git for the same app without a rule for which one is the source of truth.
  • Expecting Studio to merge branches. Merging and pull requests happen on the Git side.
Score points: Explain that "pull makes the instance look like the branch", so stash and discard are about protecting uncommitted instance work. Then connect the team's lost-changes problem to one shared instance on one branch, which sandboxes fix.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you promote from Git to test and production: an app repository install, CI/CD APIs, or ReleaseOps?
  • How would you handle a merge conflict in an XML file Studio generated?
  • What belongs in Git versus in update sets for platform-level (global) configuration?

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants you to spot the typo (u_statsu) and, more importantly, to explain the platform rule that turned a typo into mass deletion: invalid parts of an encoded query are dropped and the rest still runs. They also want you to know that setLimit() does not cap deleteMultiple().

A senior answer ends with guard rails that would have stopped this run: validation, a dry-run count with an abort threshold, and an API that fails loudly.

The Answer

Problem 1: the invalid field is silently dropped. The GlideRecord reference repeats this warning on almost every query method: an encoded query with an invalid field name produces an invalid query, and when it runs "the invalid part of the query condition is dropped, and the results are based on the valid part of the query, which may return all records from the table." It then says plainly that using insert(), update(), deleteRecord() or deleteMultiple() on bad query results can cause data loss. Here the status filter vanished and the job deleted everything older than 90 days, processed or not. On a 300-row dev table nobody noticed the count was wrong.

Problem 2: setLimit(5000) is not a safety net. The reference for deleteMultiple() is explicit: setLimit() does not limit the number of records deleted, and all records returned by the query are deleted. It also says not to combine deleteMultiple() with chooseWindow() or setLimit() on large tables.

Problem 3: side effects of bulk delete. deleteMultiple() does not delete attachments, so if messages carried payload attachments you now have orphans in sys_attachment. The reference also says not to use it on tables with currency fields and to delete those records one at a time. Above the threshold in glide.db.forced.chunk.threshold the platform chunks bulk deletes to protect replication, so very large runs take longer than people expect.

Problem 4: no validation, no dry run, no audit. Nothing logged how many rows the query matched before deleting.

A safer version:

(function purgeVendorLog() {
    var TABLE = 'x_acme_vlog_message';
    var QUERY = 'u_status=processed^sys_created_on<javascript:gs.daysAgoStart(90)';
    var MAX_EXPECTED = 200000;          // tune from history
    var DRY_RUN = gs.getProperty('x_acme_vlog.purge_dry_run', 'true') == 'true';

    var probe = new GlideRecord(TABLE);
    if (!probe.isValidField('u_status') || !probe.isValidEncodedQuery(QUERY)) {
        gs.error('Purge aborted: invalid field or query');
        return;
    }

    var ga = new GlideAggregate(TABLE);
    ga.addEncodedQuery(QUERY);
    ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
    ga.query();
    var count = ga.next() ? parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) : 0;
    gs.info('Purge would delete ' + count + ' rows');

    if (count > MAX_EXPECTED) {
        gs.error('Purge aborted: ' + count + ' exceeds ' + MAX_EXPECTED);
        return;
    }
    if (DRY_RUN || count === 0) return;

    var del = new GlideRecord(TABLE);
    del.addEncodedQuery(QUERY);
    del.query();
    del.deleteMultiple();
})();

Two more layers are worth proposing. First, the reference describes the glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows property: set to true, invalid encoded queries return no records instead of the valid remainder. It has a documented hole (an invalid term used with a WHERE operator can still return rows), so treat it as a backstop, not the fix. Second, for code you control, GlideQuery fails loudly. Its reference shows where('id', ...) throwing "Unable to find field 'id' in table 'task'" and listing the known fields, and it checks value types and choice values too. The Developer Advocate GlideQuery session demonstrates this case: a typo of activated for active returned every row with GlideRecord and threw an error with GlideQuery.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • isValidEncodedQuery() is documented as checking that the syntax is correct. Do not assume it validates every field name; check dynamic field names with isValidField() as well.
  • isValidEncodedQuery('') returns false, yet addEncodedQuery('') followed by query() returns all rows. An empty filter built from a blank property is the same disaster with a different cause.
  • The deprecated isEncodedQueryValid() applies the query if it is valid and adds sys_idNotValidnull if not. Its replacement, isValidEncodedQuery(), does not execute anything.
  • setWorkflow(false) is ignored when deleteMultiple() cascades deletes, so business rules on related tables can still fire.
  • GlideQuery cannot read encoded queries directly; GlideQuery.parse() accepts one but supports only a listed subset of operators.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating setLimit() as a cap on bulk deletes or updates.
  • Testing destructive scripts only on tables too small to show a wrong count.
  • Deleting record-by-record in a loop for 4 million rows "to be safe", which runs every delete business rule and takes hours, instead of fixing the query.
  • Building encoded queries by string concatenation from properties without checking for empty strings.
Score points: Quote the platform rule: invalid query terms are dropped and the rest runs. Then pair a GlideAggregate dry-run count with an abort threshold. That combination shows you design destructive jobs to fail closed.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Why does glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows not fully protect you?
  • How would you purge attachments for the deleted messages?
  • When would you choose deleteRecord() in a loop over deleteMultiple()?

Sources

  • GlideAggregate (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global - API reference
  • Developer Advocate blog: Learn efficient scripting with 'GlideQuery'

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

This one checks whether you know how OR binds in GlideRecord: addOrCondition() attaches to the GlideQueryCondition it is called on, and separate addQuery() calls are ANDed. They also want the smaller rules that bite in production: operators for strings must be upper case, and arrays passed to condition methods need at least two elements.

Then they want the clean version, and some judgement about when an encoded query or GlideQuery's nested where() is clearer.

The Answer

What it filters on. Line 2 returns a GlideQueryCondition for active=true and ORs priority=1 onto it, giving (active=true OR priority=1). Line 3 ANDs priority=2. Put together, the first two lines mean "priority is 2, and either active or priority 1". Since a row cannot be priority 1 and priority 2, the OR branch is dead and the whole thing collapses to "active and priority 2". That is why no P1 ever appears. The developer read line 2 as "active AND priority 1", but addOrCondition() always ORs onto the condition object it is called on. The quickest way to see the real logic is gs.info(gr.getEncodedQuery()) after building the query; the reference shows it returning strings such as active=true^priority=1.

Bug 2: lower-case operator. The GlideRecord reference lists string operators and says they "must be in upper case": CONTAINS, STARTSWITH, DOES NOT CONTAIN and so on. It also says to use CONTAINS instead of LIKE. Do not rely on 'contains' behaving.

Bug 3: single-element array. The GlideQueryCondition reference notes that arrays passed in must contain at least two elements and single-element arrays are not supported. ['7'] is exactly that. Use a comma-separated string ('6,7') with NOT IN, which is in the operator list for addQuery().

Bug 4: redundant state logic. state != 6 AND state NOT IN 7 should be one condition.

GlideRecord version with explicit grouping:

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addActiveQuery();
var pri = gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
pri.addOrCondition('priority', 2);
gr.addQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'VPN');
gr.addQuery('state', 'NOT IN', '6,7');
gr.query();
gs.info(gr.getEncodedQuery());

The reference's own example for grouped logic follows this shape: var q1 = addQuery('state', '<', 3); q1.addOrCondition('state', '>', 5); var q2 = addQuery('priority', 1); q2.addOrCondition('priority', 5); gives (state < 3 OR state > 5) AND (priority 1 OR priority 5). Each OR group starts with its own addQuery() and gets its ORs from the condition object that call returned.

When the logic gets more complicated, the GlideQueryCondition reference itself suggests building the filter in a list view, using Copy query, and passing that string to addEncodedQuery(). That is easier to review than five chained calls, as long as you test it, because an invalid term in an encoded query is dropped rather than rejected.

GlideQuery version:

var rows = new global.GlideQuery('incident')
    .where('active', true)
    .where(new global.GlideQuery()
        .where('priority', 1)
        .orWhere('priority', 2))
    .where('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'VPN')
    .where('state', 'NOT IN', [6, 7])
    .select('number', 'priority', 'state')
    .toArray(500);

GlideQuery makes grouping explicit by passing a child GlideQuery to where(), as in the reference example "active = true AND (priority = 1 OR severity = 1)". It refuses ambiguous chains: the reference lists .where('active', true).whereNotNull('name').orWhere('last_name', 'Luddy') as unsupported because the system cannot tell which grouping you meant. It also checks types, so where('priority', 'one') throws an "Expecting type 'integer'" error instead of running.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • addQuery() with two arguments assumes the equals operator; the value match is not case-sensitive.
  • addCondition() adds an AND to the current condition; the reference example output for it looks like an OR string, so verify with getEncodedQuery() rather than trusting the sample.
  • The operator list for GlideQueryCondition spells it DOESNOTCONTAIN while GlideRecord's list says DOES NOT CONTAIN; copy from the page for the method you are calling.
  • orWhere(), orWhereNull() and orWhereNotNull() must follow a where-family call; where() must not follow an or call.
  • GlideQuery parse() accepts encoded queries but supports only a listed subset of operators.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling addOrCondition() on the wrong condition object because it was the last one created, not the one you meant.
  • Never logging getEncodedQuery() during development.
  • Using lower-case operators or LIKE.
  • Passing single-element arrays to condition methods.
Score points: Read the buggy query back as an encoded string before explaining it. Showing that you would debug by printing getEncodedQuery() beats reasoning about it in your head, and interviewers notice.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you express (A AND B) OR (C AND D) with GlideRecord methods alone?
  • When would you choose addJoinQuery() or RLQUERY instead of OR conditions?
  • What does addUserOrCondition() change compared with addOrCondition()?

  • GlideQueryCondition (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global - API reference

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need to know that GlideFilter evaluates an encoded query in memory with different semantics from a database query: case-sensitive by default, and it treats empty values differently. Know that changes() still returns true in after business rules, and call out current.update() in an after rule.

There's also a security point: the conditions are written by service owners, so how they are evaluated matters.

The Answer

Symptom 1: lower-case company names miss. The GlideFilter reference says the API is case-sensitive by default, while GlideRecord queries are case-insensitive. Its own example shows a GlideRecord query for first_name=abel matching Abel Tuter and the same condition in GlideFilter not matching. You can turn this off with setCaseSensitive(false), but only on a GlideFilter instance used with match(). The static checkRecord() has a note that its filter values are case-sensitive and that setCaseSensitive(false) cannot change that.

Symptom 2: routes fire for empty due dates. The reference shows a condition u_date_field<javascript:gs.beginningOfToday() against four rows, one with an empty date. GlideRecord returns 3; GlideFilter.checkRecord() counts 4, because the empty value matches. Its fix is to add ^u_date_fieldISNOTEMPTY to the condition. Rules that look fine in a list filter therefore behave differently in this business rule.

Symptom 3: the event fires twice. The GlideElement reference explains that business rules (before or after) run before the platform resets the internal previous values. So in an after rule, current.assigned_to.changes() is still true. That is fine on its own. The trouble is current.update() inside an after rule: it saves the record again and runs the business rule chain again while changes() still reports the original change, so the event is queued a second time. Setting a field on current belongs in a before rule, where no explicit update is needed.

Symptom 4, not yet reported: performance. The rule queries every active routing rule on every incident update, for all 30 customers. Filter rules by the incident's company first and order them so the first match is the intended one.

Reworked as a before-update rule:

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    if (current.operation() != 'update') return;

    var rule = new GlideRecord('x_msp_route_rule');
    rule.addActiveQuery();
    rule.addQuery('u_company', current.getValue('company'));
    rule.orderBy('u_order');
    rule.query();
    while (rule.next()) {
        var filter = new GlideFilter(rule.getValue('u_condition'), rule.getValue('name'));
        filter.setCaseSensitive(false);
        filter.setEnforceSecurity(true);       // sandbox the filter string
        if (filter.match(current, true)) {     // all conditions must match
            current.setValue('assignment_group', rule.getValue('u_group'));
            break;
        }
    }
})(current, previous);

Keep the event in a separate after rule with the condition current.assigned_to.changes() && !current.assigned_to.nil(), as the reference example does, and pass display values or sys_ids explicitly, not GlideElement objects.

setEnforceSecurity(true) enables sandboxed evaluation of the filter string; the default is false. Condition builders allow javascript: values, and these strings are written by people outside the platform team, so evaluating them in the sandbox is the safer default. Pair it with an ACL or role on who may edit u_condition.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • match(gr, matchAll) defaults to false for the second argument; checkRecord() defaults its match argument to true. Pass the value explicitly in both.
  • changes() works for all data types except journal fields, so current.work_notes.changes() is not a reliable trigger.
  • changesFrom() and changesTo() return false on a record that has only been initialized and read, because before and after values are the same.
  • setAbortAction(true) in a before rule stops the database action but does not stop later business rules from running; isActionAborted() lets later rules check for it.
  • changes() and changesTo() are not supported inside ACL scripts.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming GlideFilter matches what a list filter or GlideRecord query matches.
  • Calling current.update() in a business rule to save a field you just set.
  • Passing current.assigned_to (a GlideElement) as an event parameter instead of a string.
  • Evaluating user-authored conditions without the sandbox.
Score points: Quote the 3 versus 4 row example from the GlideFilter page. Knowing that in-memory filter evaluation counts empty dates differently from SQL is the kind of detail that only comes from debugging it.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you unit-test routing rules with ATF given the case-sensitivity difference?
  • Why might you move rule evaluation to a Decision Table or Flow instead?
  • What does operation() return in a delete business rule?

Sources
