What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Recognise the lost update: read, add in JavaScript, write back. Two workers read 40, both write 41, and one increment disappears. Name the platform's answer, GlideRecord.addValue(), and its documented limits: integer fields only, no prior setValue() on the same field, and the new value is not read back.

After that, show some design sense: an atomic increment does not enforce a cap on its own, so you need a check-and-compensate step or a different source of truth.

The Answer

What goes wrong. The GlideRecord reference describes this exact case. Code that adds to a field value "simply saves the field to the database with the new value, rather than atomically incrementing it." If another user runs identical code concurrently, "the net effect is that u_count only contains 2, with one operation's update actually being lost." With 20 workers, losing 49 increments in a day is unsurprising.

The fix. addValue(field, value) "performs the addition/subtraction in the database when the record is updated as an atomic operation", so two concurrent operations each update the field correctly. Pass a negative number to subtract.

function claimSeat(poolId) {
    var pool = new GlideRecord('x_acme_seat_pool');
    if (!pool.get(poolId)) {
        return { ok: false, reason: 'pool_not_found' };
    }
    pool.addValue('u_seats_used', 1);      // atomic in the database
    if (!pool.update()) {
        return { ok: false, reason: pool.getLastErrorMessage() };
    }

    pool.get(poolId);                       // reload to see the real value
    var used = parseInt(pool.getValue('u_seats_used'), 10);
    var cap = parseInt(pool.getValue('u_seat_cap'), 10);
    if (used > cap) {
        pool.addValue('u_seats_used', -1);  // compensate
        pool.update();
        return { ok: false, reason: 'pool_full' };
    }
    return { ok: true, used: used };
}

Why the reload. The reference notes that the new value is not read back from the database unless you do so explicitly; its examples call get(sys_id) after update() and show the value as "3, if executed concurrently with another user". Without the reload you would compare a stale number with the cap.

Enforcing the cap. addValue() makes the counter correct, but a check before the increment would still race: two workers both see 99 of 100, both increment, and the pool is at 101. Increment first, read back, and roll back with a negative addValue() if you went over. The window where the counter reads 101 is short and self-correcting. If the business cannot tolerate even that, treat the assignment records as the source of truth and recount them with a GlideAggregate COUNT when the cap is close, or serialise claims through a single queue.

Reconcile anyway. Counters drift for other reasons, such as deletes that bypass business rules or manual edits. A nightly job that recounts active assignments per pool with GlideAggregate and corrects u_seats_used gives finance a number they can trust.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The field must be an integer. The reference says addValue() does not support other types, such as longs.
  • If setValue() is called for the field before addValue(), the addValue() call is not processed and an error is logged. Do not mix them on the same field in the same transaction.
  • addValue() takes effect only on a later update() or insert(). On insert(), the field is initialised with the value you passed.
  • update() returns the sys_id or null on failure; a data policy or a before rule calling setAbortAction(true) can stop the save, and the increment never happens.
  • updateMultiple() sets values; it is not an atomic increment across rows, and the reference recommends setValue() over direct assignment with it.

Common Mistakes

  • Wrapping the read-add-write in a try/catch and thinking that makes it safe.
  • Calling addValue() and then reading pool.u_seats_used without reloading.
  • Using a long or decimal field for a counter that needs addValue().
  • Checking the cap before incrementing, which reintroduces the race.
Score points: Mention that addValue() fixes the counter but not the cap, and describe increment-then-verify with compensation. That shows you think about concurrency as a design problem, not a method lookup.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you test this race in a sub-production instance?
  • Would you use a GlideAggregate recount on every claim? What does it cost?
  • How does this change if the claim must also create the assignment record in the same transaction?

Sources

  • GlideRecord (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideAggregate (Scoped) - API reference

question: A field-services company sends technicians a reminder 'same time next week' after each site visit. The business rule does var due = new GlideDateTime(current.u_visit_start); due.add(7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000); current.u_reminder_at = due;. Every March and November, technicians in US/Pacific complain the reminder arrives an hour off, and a second bug report says reminders created by a dispatcher in India land at odd local times for US technicians. Diagnose both problems using the GlideDateTime API and explain how you would make the logic correct across DST and across users.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Separate elapsed time from calendar time. Adding milliseconds moves the instant by a fixed amount, which is right for 'remind me in 168 hours' and wrong for 'same wall-clock time next week' when a DST change sits in between. Also notice that every *LocalTime method works in the session time zone of whoever runs the script, which explains the India dispatcher report. A strong answer admits where the scoped API stops helping instead of inventing a method.

Diagnosis

Problem one. add(Number milliseconds) and addSeconds() shift the stored UTC instant. A week containing the spring-forward change has only 167 local hours, so 168 elapsed hours later is one hour later on the wall clock. In November it goes the other way. The stored value is correct as elapsed time and wrong as a calendar promise.

The scoped GlideDateTime API has two calendar families for this. addDaysUTC(), addWeeksUTC(), addMonthsUTC() work on the UTC date and time. addDaysLocalTime(), addWeeksLocalTime(), addMonthsLocalTime() and addYearsLocalTime() take the local date and time equivalent of the stored value, add on the calendar, and store the result. The reference describes the LocalTime variants in those words. For 'same local time next week' you want addWeeksLocalTime(1) or addDaysLocalTime(7).

Problem two. 'Local' means the current user's time zone; the documented examples say 'uses current user session time zone'. When the dispatcher in India saves the visit, the business rule runs in the dispatcher's session, so the week is added on Indian wall-clock time. India has no DST, so the US shift leaks straight through. The scoped GlideDateTime reference in this release has no setter for an explicit time zone, so you cannot tell the object 'calculate in US/Pacific' from a scoped script.

The Answer

  1. Decide whose clock owns the promise. Here it is the technician's. Record it explicitly, for example by reading the technician's time zone from their user record, rather than assuming the session matches.
  2. Do the calendar math in a session that is in that time zone. The cleanest place is the technician's own action (accepting or closing the visit), because that transaction runs in their session. Use addWeeksLocalTime(1) there.
  3. Guard the business rule: compare gs.getSession().getTimeZoneName() with the technician's zone. If they match, use the LocalTime method. If they do not, compute the elapsed-time value, flag the record for recalculation when the technician next touches it, and log the mismatch. That is honest about what the scoped API can and cannot do.
  4. For diagnostics, isDST(), getDSTOffset() and getTZOffset() tell you whether and by how much the session zone is shifted at a given instant. Logging those three values next to getValue() makes DST tickets quick to triage.
// Runs in the technician's session (e.g. UI action 'Complete visit')
var tz = gs.getSession().getTimeZoneName();
var visit = new GlideDateTime(current.getValue('u_visit_start'));
var reminder = new GlideDateTime(visit);
reminder.addWeeksLocalTime(1);              // same wall-clock time, DST-safe in this session's zone
current.setValue('u_reminder_at', reminder.getValue());
gs.info('Reminder {0} -> {1} in {2} (DST offset {3} ms)',
        visit.getValue(), reminder.getValue(), tz, reminder.getDSTOffset());

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The LocalTime and UTC variants can both be right; they answer different questions. SLA-style 'within 72 hours' is elapsed time and should stay as add() or addSeconds().
  • setDayOfMonthLocalTime() and setDayOfMonthUTC() clamp to the last day of the month when you pass a day that does not exist, per the reference. Month-end schedules built with them do not overflow into the next month.
  • The relative helpers on GlideSystem, such as gs.daysAgoStart() and gs.beginningOfThisWeek(), return a UTC string for a boundary computed in the session time zone. A scheduled job running as a user in a different zone gets a different 'start of today'.
  • getTZOffset() returns a negative number west of UTC (the documented Pacific example is -25200000). Get the sign wrong once and every reminder is out by twice the offset.
  • getWeekOfYearLocalTime() counts weeks from Sunday, while getDayOfWeekLocalTime() uses Monday = 1. Do not mix them to build 'next Monday' logic.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing the March bug by subtracting an hour, which then breaks November and every zone without DST.
  • Assuming business rules run in the record owner's time zone; they run in the session of whoever triggered the transaction.
  • Using getDisplayValue() strings to do math, then parsing them back.
  • Testing DST logic only with dates in August, as most documented examples do.
Score points: Say out loud that the scoped GlideDateTime reference offers no explicit time-zone setter, so the design has to control which session does the calculation. Interviewers trust a candidate who knows the edge of an API more than one who guesses a method name.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you write an ATF or background-script test that proves the reminder is correct across the March change?
  • When is addMonthsLocalTime() the wrong choice for a monthly billing date?
  • How would the design change if the reminder were driven by a schedule record rather than a fixed seven days?

Sources

  • GlideDateTime (Scoped)
  • GlideSession (Scoped)
  • GlideSystem (Scoped)

question: A procurement team's scoped app must email the contract owner 30 days before each contract's end date, and again on the day. The current design: an after-update business rule calls gs.eventQueue('x_acme_ctr.renewal', current, JSON.stringify(currentAsObject), gs.getUserID()) on every save, and a nightly scheduled script queries every active contract and fires the event if 'today' matches. Code review finds duplicate emails, emails for contracts whose end date was moved, and an addInfoMessage() call inside the async rule that never shows. Redesign this using gs.eventQueue and gs.eventQueueScheduled, including how you would design the event parameters.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The question is whether you treat events as small, durable signals that point at a record, rather than as a message bus carrying snapshots. Give the exact difference between the two queueing methods, a parameter design that survives the record changing, and a consumer that re-checks state before acting. Knowing the documented restriction on messages in async rules is a bonus.

The Answer

The two methods, from the reference:

  • gs.eventQueue(name, instance, parm1, parm2, queue) queues an event now. instance is a GlideRecord such as current; parm1 and parm2 are optional strings saved with the event; queue optionally names a queue.
  • gs.eventQueueScheduled(name, instance, parm1, parm2, expiration) queues an event to be processed at a given time. instance may be a GlideRecord or a sys_id string. If you leave parm1 empty and pass a GlideRecord, it defaults to the record's display value. expiration is a GlideDateTime or a date/time element; the default is now. The schedule information is stored in the Events [sysevent] table.

The redesign:

  1. When a contract is inserted, or when u_end_date changes, queue two scheduled events: one at end date minus 30 days and one on the end date. Compute the times with addDaysLocalTime(-30), as the reference example does for a seven-day delay, and skip any time already in the past using before().
  2. Pass identifiers, not data. parm1 carries the contract's end date value as it was when the event was queued; parm2 carries the reminder type (T-30 or T-0). The instance already identifies the record.
  3. In the consumer (a script action or notification condition), re-read the contract and compare its current u_end_date with parm1. If they differ, the end date moved after the event was queued, so the event is stale and should do nothing. The newer events queued by the date change will handle it.
  4. Remove the nightly scan and the every-save eventQueue. Keep a small nightly reconciliation that only reports contracts with no pending reminder, so a failure is visible.
// after insert/update business rule, condition: u_end_date changes OR operation is insert
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    var end = new GlideDateTime(current.getValue('u_end_date'));
    var now = new GlideDateTime();
    var endValue = end.getValue();

    var t30 = new GlideDateTime(end);
    t30.addDaysLocalTime(-30);
    if (now.before(t30))
        gs.eventQueueScheduled('x_acme_ctr.renewal_due', current, endValue, 'T-30', t30);
    if (now.before(end))
        gs.eventQueueScheduled('x_acme_ctr.renewal_due', current, endValue, 'T-0', end);
})(current, previous);
// Script action for x_acme_ctr.renewal_due
(function () {
    var ctr = new GlideRecord('x_acme_ctr_contract');
    if (!ctr.get(current.getUniqueValue()) || ctr.getValue('active') != '1')
        return;
    if (new GlideDateTime(ctr.getValue('u_end_date')).getValue() != event.parm1)
        return;                                   // end date moved after queueing: stale event
    gs.eventQueue('x_acme_ctr.renewal_notify', ctr, event.parm2, ctr.getValue('u_owner'));
})();

The second hop queues an immediate event that a notification listens to, keeping the 'should we send' logic in script and the content in the notification.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Parameters are strings. JSON.stringify of a whole record puts a snapshot in the event that is out of date the moment the record changes, and it bloats the events table. Pass identifiers and re-read.
  • The default for parm1 on eventQueueScheduled is the record's display value only when instance is a GlideRecord. Passing a sys_id gives you null. Consumers that read parm1 blindly behave differently depending on how the producer called the method.
  • The reference states that addInfoMessage() is not supported for asynchronous business rules. There is no session to show it in. Log instead, or show the message from a before or after rule if the user needs it.
  • Naming a custom queue on eventQueue only isolates work if that queue is being processed on your instance. Confirm that before using it to separate heavy work.
  • If you need to run an existing scheduled job immediately instead of waiting for its trigger, gs.executeNow(job) exists, but only for a job in the same application as the calling script, and it returns null for a global job.
  • Queueing on every update with no 'changes' condition is how the duplicates appeared. Put the condition on the business rule, not inside the script.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating parm1/parm2 as a payload channel.
  • Assuming a queued scheduled event is cancelled when the record changes; design the consumer to discard stale events instead.
  • Building 'run once a day and check if today matches' logic, which misses days when the job fails and double-fires when it is re-run.
  • Forgetting that the consumer runs without the original user's session, so anything relying on the user's roles or time zone behaves differently.
Score points: Describe the stale-event check (compare the record's current end date with the value carried in parm1). It turns an awkward cancellation problem into a one-line guard and works no matter how many times the date changes.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you backfill reminders for 20,000 existing contracts without one long transaction?
  • Where would you put retry logic if the notification email fails?
  • How would you test the scheduled path without waiting 30 days?

Sources

  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • GlideDateTime (Scoped)
  • Beyond Best Practices: Developer's Guide to Time & Space (Developer Advocate blog)

question: A pharmaceutical company has a scoped Change Management extension. Before a change request is submitted, a client script must ask the server whether the chosen CI is inside a regulatory freeze window. The current onSubmit script does ga.getXMLWait(); if (ga.getAnswer() == 'frozen') return false;. After the move to a scoped app it throws errors, and in the global version agents complained the form froze for several seconds. Design the replacement. Show the code, explain how you stop the form from submitting until the answer arrives and then submit it with the button the user originally pressed, and say what still has to happen on the server.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants the standard asynchronous onSubmit pattern and the reasoning behind each step: getXMLWait() is not available to scoped applications, an onSubmit function cannot wait for a callback, so you return false, make the call, and resubmit from the callback with a flag that lets the second pass through. They also want you to say that the client check is a courtesy to the user and the real control is a server-side check.

The Answer

Why the old code fails. The GlideAjax reference says getXMLWait() processes the request synchronously, can make the application seem unresponsive, and is not available to scoped applications. That covers both symptoms: the freeze in global and the error in scope.

The pattern. onSubmit must return synchronously. So on the first pass you cancel the submit, start an asynchronous call, and when the answer comes back you either show a message or submit again. The second submit runs onSubmit again, so you need a flag that says the check already passed. The g_aw reference shows this shape: it stores flags such as g_scratchpad._domainCheckPassed, returns false, and later calls gFormRef.submit(gFormRef.getActionName()). The GlideUser reference shows the same idea with g_user.setClientData() and g_form.submit().

function onSubmit() {
    if (g_scratchpad.freezeCheckPassed) {
        g_scratchpad.freezeCheckPassed = false;   // one-shot, reset for next save
        return true;
    }
    var ci = g_form.getValue('cmdb_ci');
    if (!ci) {
        return true;                              // nothing to check
    }
    var action = g_form.getActionName();          // remember which button
    var ga = new GlideAjax('FreezeWindowAjax');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'checkCi');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_ci', ci);
    ga.addParam('sysparm_start', g_form.getValue('start_date'));
    ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
        var res = JSON.parse(answer || '{}');
        if (res.frozen) {
            g_form.showFieldMsg('cmdb_ci',
                getMessage('This CI is in a regulatory freeze window'), 'error');
            return;
        }
        g_form.hideFieldMsg('cmdb_ci', true);
        g_scratchpad.freezeCheckPassed = true;
        g_form.submit(action);
    });
    return false;
}

Points worth calling out:

  • getActionName() returns the most recent action name (for a client script, the sys_id of the UI action clicked, per the reference). Capture it before the asynchronous call so the resubmit uses the same button. submit(verb) needs an action_name of a visible form button.
  • Reset the flag after it is used. If you leave it true, every later save on the same form skips the check.
  • getXMLAnswer() hands the callback the answer string directly, so there is no responseXML parsing. Return JSON from the script include so you can add fields later without changing the protocol.
  • g_scratchpad is a convenient flag holder because it lives for the life of the form. g_user.setClientData() also works but is session-level, so a flag left behind could leak to another record.

Server side. The client check exists to give a fast, friendly message. Anyone can change the record through a list edit, the REST Table API, an import or a script, and none of those run this client script. Put the same freeze rule in a before-insert/update business rule (or the flow that moves the change forward) that aborts the action. Keep the rule in one script include and call it from both the business rule and the GlideAjax method so the two cannot drift, which is the combined client and server callable script include idea from the Developer Advocate blog.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • getActionName() is not available in Wizard client scripts.
  • If the server call fails, the callback may never run and the user sees nothing. Decide whether to fail open or closed. The g_aw domain example fails open (it sets _domainCheckErrorBypass and submits). For a compliance control, fail closed and say so in the message, and rely on the business rule anyway.
  • Double clicks start two asynchronous checks and can submit twice. Disable the button or track an in-flight flag.
  • Validate the parameters inside the script include (CI sys_id format, date present). The client can send anything, including values a user typed into the console.
  • In Workspace, a UI action's workspace client script receives g_form as a parameter and the domain example uses g_modal.confirm; check that your flag and resubmit logic also work there before reusing the script.

Common Mistakes

  • Keeping getAnswer() after switching to an asynchronous call.
  • Returning false from inside the callback and expecting it to cancel the submit; by then onSubmit has already returned.
  • Resubmitting with g_form.submit() without the action name, which can run the wrong UI action (for example Save instead of Request Approval).
  • Treating the client check as the control and skipping the business rule.
Score points: Explain the flag lifecycle (set, consumed, reset) and name the server-side twin of the check. Those two details separate people who have shipped this from people who have read about it.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you show a confirm dialog (continue anyway?) instead of a hard stop, in both core UI and Workspace?
  • Where do you keep the freeze rule so the client and server checks cannot disagree?
  • How do you write an ATF test that proves the business rule blocks the change when the client script is bypassed?

Sources

  • GlideAjax - API reference
  • GlideForm (g_form) - API reference
  • GlideUser (g_user) - API reference
  • GlideAgentWorkspace (g_aw) - API reference
  • Client Callable and Server Callable Script Includes in One (Developer Advocate blog)

question: A utilities company's Incident form takes about four seconds to become usable. Profiling shows five onLoad client scripts each firing their own GlideAjax call: is the caller a VIP, how many open incidents the caller has, whether the current user belongs to the assignment group, the value of a system property that controls a banner, and the caller's preferred contact channel. The architect proposes a single display business rule that fills g_scratchpad. Walk through when g_scratchpad is the right tool and when GlideAjax still is, how you would restructure these five calls, and what you must never put into g_scratchpad.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to hear that a display business rule runs once on the server while the form is being built, so anything known at load time can ride along in g_scratchpad with zero extra round trips. They also want the limits: the data is a load-time snapshot, it does not react to field changes, and everything in it is visible to the user in the browser. A good answer splits the five lookups into load-time facts and change-driven facts.

The Answer

How g_scratchpad works. A display business rule runs on the server when a form is requested. Properties it sets on g_scratchpad are sent down with the form, and client scripts read them in onLoad. Two practical rules: put only plain values in it (never a GlideRecord object), and do not assume a Boolean set on the server arrives as a Boolean on every UI. The rule below stores everything with String() so the client comparisons are predictable.

Split the five calls.

  • Banner property: pure load-time fact. Move to the display rule.
  • Current user is in the assignment group: load-time fact for the record as it was saved. Move to the display rule. If the agent changes the group, an onChange script re-checks with GlideAjax.
  • Caller VIP, open incident count, preferred channel: for an existing record these are known at load, so the display rule computes them from current.caller_id. When the caller changes, one onChange GlideAjax call returns all three as one JSON object, not three calls.
// Display business rule on incident
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    g_scratchpad.showFreezeBanner = gs.getProperty('x_util.freeze_banner', 'false');
    g_scratchpad.inAssignmentGroup = String(
        gs.getUser().isMemberOf(current.getValue('assignment_group')));
    var caller = current.caller_id.getRefRecord();
    if (caller.isValidRecord()) {
        g_scratchpad.callerVip = caller.getValue('vip');
        g_scratchpad.callerChannel = caller.getValue('preferred_contact') || '';
    }
    var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
    ga.addQuery('caller_id', current.getValue('caller_id'));
    ga.addQuery('active', true);
    ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
    ga.query();
    g_scratchpad.callerOpenCount = ga.next() ? ga.getAggregate('COUNT') : '0';
})(current, previous);
// Single onLoad client script
function onLoad() {
    if (g_scratchpad.showFreezeBanner == 'true') {
        g_form.addInfoMessage(getMessage('Change freeze in effect'));
    }
    if (g_scratchpad.callerVip == 'true') {
        g_form.addDecoration('caller_id', 'icon-star', 'VIP');
    }
    // compare strings, not Booleans
    if (g_scratchpad.inAssignmentGroup != 'true') {
        g_form.setReadOnly('work_notes', true);
    }
}

Five network calls become zero at load, and one at most when the caller changes. The server work is the same; you just stop paying five separate HTTP round trips and five script-include dispatches.

Session-level alternative. When a value belongs to the user's session rather than the record (a login language, a feature flag), GlideSession.putClientData() on the server and g_user.getClientData() on the client avoid recomputing it for every form. The GlideUser reference describes that pairing, and GlideSession says putClientData() is used in a server-side script that runs when a form is created.

What never goes in g_scratchpad. Anything the user is not allowed to see. Server-side GlideRecord queries in the display rule do not enforce ACLs, the values travel to the browser, and anyone can type g_scratchpad in the console. Do not push salary, other users' personal data or security decisions you would not show on screen. Hiding a field client-side because g_scratchpad.canSeeSalary is false while also sending the salary in the scratchpad is a data leak, not a control.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The display rule runs only on form load. After an agent changes the caller, g_scratchpad.callerVip still describes the old caller. Every change-driven fact needs an onChange path.
  • On a new record (g_form.isNewRecord()), most fields are empty, so the display rule computes little. Guard the rule against empty references.
  • onChange scripts also run while the form loads, with isLoading true. Return early in that case or you re-fetch what the scratchpad already gave you.
  • With live forms in Core UI, g_form.isLiveUpdating() tells an onChange script that the change came from another session. Skip the GlideAjax refresh or handle it explicitly.
  • The rule above stores strings, so if (g_scratchpad.inAssignmentGroup) is true for the string 'false'. Compare with == 'true'.
  • Workspace scripts can read g_scratchpad too; the g_aw domain example checks typeof g_scratchpad === 'undefined' before using it. Keep that guard in scripts shared across UIs.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting everything into the display rule, including facts that depend on fields the user will change, then shipping stale data.
  • Treating g_scratchpad as private. It is not.
  • Heavy queries in the display rule. You saved round trips but now every form open pays for the slow query. Use GlideAggregate for counts and keep it to what the form needs.
  • Keeping the five onChange GlideAjax calls separate instead of returning one JSON object.
Score points: Draw the line between load-time facts and change-driven facts, and say the security sentence: g_scratchpad is readable by the user, so it is for presentation data only.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you measure the improvement, before and after, in a way the customer accepts?
  • The same form opens in Agent Workspace. What do you check before relying on the display rule there?
  • When would you choose GlideSession.putClientData over g_scratchpad?

Sources

  • GlideForm (g_form) - API reference
  • GlideUser (g_user) - API reference
  • GlideSession (server) - API reference
  • GlideAgentWorkspace (g_aw) - API reference
  • GlideAggregate (server) - API reference
  • GlideUser (server) - API reference

question: A managed services provider is moving its service desk from the core UI to an Agent Workspace experience. Three core UI UI actions must come along: 'Show related change' uses g_navigation.openRecord('change_request', id); 'Pick affected user' calls reflistOpen(...) to show a lookup popup; and 'Resolve and close tab' saves the form then reloads with g_navigation.reloadWindow(). A contractor's first attempt copies the same scripts into the Workspace Client Script field and adds g_aw.openRecord('change_request', id, {view: 'agent', readOnly: true}) copied from an example. Explain what works in Workspace, what does not, and rewrite the three actions.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You should know that Workspace UI actions have their own client script field, receive g_form as a parameter, and use g_aw and g_modal instead of the core UI's frame-based APIs. Read the reference carefully, too: openRecord() documents three params, and the contractor's view and readOnly keys are not among them.

The Answer

Where g_aw runs. The reference says g_aw.openRecord() is only available in the Agent Workspace client scripting environment or in a UI action's workspace client script field. GlideNavigation controls the navigator and main frame of the core UI, which a workspace does not have, so g_navigation calls are the wrong tool there. The reference examples show a workspace UI action as function onClick(g_form) { ... }.

1. Show related change. Open it in a workspace subtab. The documented params are readOnlyForm (all fields read-only regardless of UI policy and ACLs), defaultTab (a related list or related item to show first; names take the table.field form of the reference's sys_user_grmember.user example; list them with g_form.getRelatedListNames()) and hideDetails (hide the details tab and UI actions).

function onClick(g_form) {
    var changeId = g_form.getValue('change_request'); // your related-change field
    if (!changeId) {
        g_form.addInfoMessage(getMessage('No related change on this incident'));
        return;
    }
    g_aw.openRecord('change_request', changeId, {
        readOnlyForm: true,
        defaultTab: 'task_ci.task'   // table.field form; confirm with getRelatedListNames()
    });
}

The contractor's {view: 'agent', readOnly: true} comes from an example on the same reference page, but those keys are not in the parameter table. Expect them to be ignored; use readOnlyForm.

2. Pick affected user. The standalone methods reference says reflistOpen() is not supported in a Workspace client script and to use g_modal.showFrame() instead. So the lookup becomes a modal frame, or, often simpler, a reference field on the form with a proper reference qualifier, which the workspace renders natively.

3. Resolve and close tab. The g_aw reference example saves and then closes the subtab:

function onClick(g_form) {
    g_form.setValue('state', '6');
    g_form.save().then(function() {
        g_aw.closeRecord();
    });
}

Note that in the core UI GlideForm reference save() returns void, while the workspace example chains .then() on it. Code that chains on save() is workspace-only; do not paste it back into a core UI script. Closing the tab replaces the reload; there is no frame to reload.

Other workspace-specific behaviour worth knowing. g_aw.setSectionExpanded('section_name', false) sets a section's default collapsed state, useful for long forms. isSectionVisible() is not supported in Workspace. GlideFlow (client) is incompatible with the Workspace Experience UI, so a core UI action that starts a flow with GlideFlow.startFlow() needs a different route, typically a server-side UI action or a GlideAjax call. g_aw.domainScopeProvider() needs the domain_expand_scope role.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • readOnlyForm: true overrides UI policies and ACL-driven editability for display only. It does not grant anything, and it does not protect data; it just stops the agent editing in that tab.
  • Scripts shared between core UI and workspace should check typeof g_aw !== 'undefined' before calling it, as the reference examples do.
  • defaultTab accepts related lists or related items only. The reference does not say what happens with a wrong name; test it on your instance (the details tab is the documented default when defaultTab is not set).
  • Some reference examples for closeRecord() and openRecord() chain .then(function(response) { response.success ... }), but the method tables document the return as None. Do not build error handling that depends on that response shape without testing it on your release.
  • hideDetails: true also hides UI actions, so do not use it on a record the agent must act on.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying core UI scripts into the workspace field unchanged and assuming g_navigation, reflistOpen() or GlideDialogWindow will work.
  • Trusting example code over the parameter table.
  • Chaining .then() on g_form.save() in the core UI.
  • Using readOnlyForm as a security measure.
Score points: Quote the two reference notes that decide the design: openRecord only runs in the workspace client script environment, and reflistOpen is replaced by g_modal.showFrame. Then point out the undocumented params in the contractor's code.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you write one UI action that works in both core UI and workspace?
  • The customer wants the related change to open on its Affected CIs tab. How do you find the right defaultTab value?
  • How would you replace a core UI GlideModal confirmation inside a workspace UI action?

Sources

  • GlideAgentWorkspace (g_aw) - API reference
  • GlideNavigation - API reference
  • Standalone client methods (reflistOpen) - API reference
  • GlideForm (g_form) - API reference
  • GlideFlow (client) - API reference

question: A global engineering firm runs a custom scoped spend-management app. Each spend line has an FX Currency field and buyers enter amounts in EUR, GBP, JPY and INR. Finance reports in USD. At quarter close the CFO's team finds the USD totals are 2-4% off their ERP. Code review shows a business rule doing parseFloat(current.amount.getDisplayValue()) * 1.08 for EUR lines, a hard-coded table of other rates updated by hand, and conversion done at report time. French users also complain that amounts show as 123,456.12 instead of 123 456,12. Using the sn_currency APIs, redesign the conversion: write the code, explain which rate and date it should use, and how you would make the numbers auditable.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is checking whether you treat money as data with a currency, a rate source and a date, rather than as a number to multiply. A good answer reaches for the sn_currency classes, converts at the business date instead of today, uses the rate table configured for the field, and stores which rate was used. It also keeps parsing and formatting at the edges, so the arithmetic only ever sees unformatted amounts.

The Answer

The bug has three causes. The code converts at today's rate, it multiplies by a hard-coded number instead of reading the rate table, and it feeds a locale-formatted string such as 1.234,56 into the math. I would replace it with the FX Currency APIs in the sn_currency namespace:

  • GlideCurrencyConfig(ed) takes the GlideElementDescriptor of the FX Currency field and returns that field's settings from fx_configuration, falling back to the system defaults. getRateTable() returns the configured rate table (default fx_system_rate), getReferenceCurrency() the reference currency and getConversionDateSource() the field used as the conversion date, if one is set.
  • GlideCurrencyParser.parse() accepts "EUR;1.234,56" or a bare amount and returns a GlideCurrencyValue with getCurrencyCode() and getAmount(). It handles decimal points and decimal commas, using setLocale() or the session locale.
  • GlideCurrencyConverter does the conversion. Set from/to currencies, setAmount(), optionally setRateTable() and setDateTime(), then call convert(). Without setDateTime() it uses the rate for the current date and time, which is exactly the month-end bug.
  • convert() returns a GlideCurrencyExchangeValue with getAmount(), getRate(), getRateSysId() (the fx_conversion_rate record used), getCurrency() and getOriginalCurrency().
  • GlideCurrencyFormatter renders the result for people: a format string with %s (symbol), %v (amount), %c (ISO code), plus setLocale() and setMinFractionDigits()/setMaxFractionDigits().
// Scoped script include: convert a line's FX Currency amount to USD at the order date rate
var SpendFx = Class.create();
SpendFx.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {},

    toUsd: function(lineGr) {
        // Read the per-field FX configuration instead of hard-coding fx_system_rate
        var ed = lineGr.getElement('amount').getED();
        var cfg = new sn_currency.GlideCurrencyConfig(ed);

        // Parse the stored value into code + unformatted amount
        var parser = new sn_currency.GlideCurrencyParser();
        var cv = parser.parse(lineGr.getValue('amount'));   // parse() accepts "CODE;amount"; confirm what getValue() returns for an FX field on your instance

        var conv = new sn_currency.GlideCurrencyConverter(cv.getCurrencyCode(), 'USD');
        conv.setAmount(cv.getAmount());                     // unformatted: 1234.56, not 1,234.56
        conv.setRateTable(cfg.getRateTable());              // custom tables must extend fx_conversion_rate
        conv.setDateTime(new GlideDateTime(lineGr.getValue('order_date')));

        var x = conv.convert();                             // GlideCurrencyExchangeValue
        return {
            usd: x.getAmount(),
            rate: x.getRate(),
            rateSysId: x.getRateSysId(),                    // keep this for audit
            from: x.getOriginalCurrency()
        };
    },

    display: function(amount, code, lang, country) {
        var f = new sn_currency.GlideCurrencyFormatter('%s%v %c');
        f.setLocale(lang, country);                         // fr, FR -> 123 456,12
        f.setMaxFractionDigits(2);
        return f.format(String(amount), code);
    },
    type: 'SpendFx'
};

I would write the USD amount, the rate and the rate sys_id onto the spend line when it is approved. Finance then reports from stored values that match the day the order was placed, and an auditor can open the exact rate record. Re-running conversions at report time means last quarter's numbers move every time a new rate loads.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Unformatted input only. setAmount() and format() accept a decimal point and nothing else: 1234.56 is valid, 1,234.56 is not. Parse first, then convert.
  • Country vs currency codes. The parameter tables for the converter say "ISO 3166 country code", but every example and the returned fCurrency use ISO 4217 currency codes (EUR, USD, JPY). Use currency codes and test it on your instance.
  • Rate date semantics. setDateTime() takes a GlideDateTime. A date-only field converted at midnight UTC can pick up the previous day's rate for users far from UTC, so decide which time zone defines "order date".
  • Custom rate tables must extend fx_conversion_rate; a contract-rate table that does not will not work with setRateTable().
  • Rounding is display-only. setMaxFractionDigits(2) rounds the formatted string (123.456 becomes 123.46). It does not change the stored number, so do not sum formatted values.
  • The docs are inconsistent on a couple of names: the exchange value method is documented as getOriginalValue() while its example calls getOriginalAmount(). Prefer getRate() and getAmount(), which are consistent.
  • With the no-argument GlideCurrencyConfig(), getConversionDateSource() returns null. It only has a value when you pass the field's descriptor.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting in a client script or in the report layer instead of once, server-side, at approval.
  • Using parseFloat() on getDisplayValue() of a currency field, which includes symbols and locale separators.
  • Hard-coding fx_system_rate when the field is configured for a contract rate table.
  • Forgetting that formatting depends on the session locale when setLocale() is not called, so a scheduled job running as a system user formats differently from the UI.
Score points: Say you persist getRateSysId() with every converted amount. It turns "why is this number different from last week" from an argument into a lookup.

Likely Follow-ups

  • Finance loads rates daily from a treasury feed. How would you load them so GlideCurrencyConverter picks them up, and what happens to a conversion dated on a day with no rate?
  • How does the field's aggregation source (as_entered vs reference) change what a sum on a list shows?
  • How would you test the conversion with ATF without depending on live rates?

question: An insurer's scoped claims app has a 600-line GlideRecord utility that an AI assistant generated last year. It receives JSON payloads from a partner, upserts x_ins_claim records by claim_number, returns a dashboard summary (count of open claims per category and average reserve per state), and occasionally bulk-closes claims. The team wants to move it to GlideQuery. Lay out how you would rewrite the upsert, the single-record read with a safe default, the bulk close, and the per-category counts in GlideQuery, and list the GlideQuery limitations and behaviours that would make you keep GlideRecord or GlideAggregate for some parts.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Treat GlideQuery as a safer interface on the same database engine, not a faster one. You should know the terminal and intermediate method split, Optional versus Stream results, immutability, field and type checking, and the documented limitations. Also show that some needs, such as journal fields, cross-scope tables and workflow suppression on scoped tables, push you back to GlideRecord.

The Answer

Start from the facts in the reference. GlideQuery is a script include that works with the Stream and Optional APIs in a builder pattern. Nothing runs until a terminal method such as select(), selectOne(), count() or updateMultiple(). In a scoped app it must be called as global.GlideQuery, and it needs the com.sn_glidequery plugin. The developer advocates' GlideQuery session made the same points: it wraps GlideRecord, it checks field names, it returns plain JavaScript values, and its queries are immutable.

var GQ = global.GlideQuery;

// Shared base: immutable, so every .where() returns a new query.
var claims = new GQ('x_ins_claim');
var openClaims = claims.where('active', true);

// 1. Upsert from partner JSON. insertOrUpdate updates when a sys_id is
//    present in the object, otherwise inserts. Resolve the sys_id first.
function upsertClaim(p) {
  var existing = claims.where('claim_number', p.claim_number)
                       .selectOne('sys_id')
                       .orElse(null);
  var row = {
    claim_number: p.claim_number,
    category: p.category,
    reserve: p.reserve
  };
  if (existing) { row.sys_id = existing.sys_id; }
  return claims.insertOrUpdate(row).orElse(null);
}

// 2. Single read with a safe default (no if/else on next()).
function getClaim(num) {
  return claims.where('claim_number', num)
               .selectOne('claim_number', 'state', 'assigned_to$DISPLAY')
               .orElse({ claim_number: num, state: null });
}

// 3. Bulk close: set-based, returns { rowCount: n }.
function closeStale(cutoff) {
  return openClaims.where('sys_updated_on', '<', cutoff)
                   .updateMultiple({ state: 'closed' });
}

// 4. Open claims per category, computed in the database.
// The reference documents aggregate(type, field) and shows grouped results as
// { group: {...}, sum: { field: n } }; confirm the 'count' form and result shape on your instance.
function countsByCategory() {
  var out = {};
  openClaims.aggregate('count')
            .groupBy('category')
            .select()
            .forEach(function (g) { out[g.group.category] = g.count; });
  return out;
}

Talking points on each:

  • Upsert. The reference examples show insertOrUpdate() inserting when no sys_id is given and updating when one is. They don't say a business key like claim_number is matched, so resolve claim_number to a sys_id first instead of assuming the method finds the record for you.
  • Read. selectOne() returns an Optional. orElse() gives a default object, which is what the blog meant by keeping widgets from crashing when data is missing. The $DISPLAY flag returns display values without a second call.
  • Bulk update. updateMultiple() returns an object with rowCount. The blog says single-record update() is built to need a sys_id so a missing condition cannot turn into a mass update. Use updateMultiple() when you mean bulk.
  • Aggregates. aggregate() plus groupBy() runs in the database. For one value with no grouping, the reference points to count(), avg(), sum() and the others, which return an Optional (avg('reserve').orElse(0)). having() filters groups.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference's limitations list: no tables that block access from other scopes, no encoded query reading (though GlideQuery.parse(table, query) accepts a subset of operators), GlideDate and GlideDateTime come back as JavaScript strings, no FX currency fields, no journal field updates, and no ambiguous AND/OR chains. Nest a child GlideQuery inside where() to group OR logic.
  • disableWorkflow() only works for tables in the global scope. If closing claims must skip business rules on x_ins_claim, this method does not help. Use GlideRecord setWorkflow(false) inside the owning scope, and think hard before you do.
  • GlideQuery bypasses ACLs by default, like GlideRecord. For anything driven by a user, chain withAcls(), which runs through GlideRecordSecure.
  • The reference warns that converting GlideRecords to plain objects can make queries slower, and says to avoid loops over large numbers of records. Selecting fewer fields helps. A 500,000-row export is still a GlideRecord job.
  • Type checking works both ways. Passing a non-numeric value such as 'one' for an integer field throws "Expecting type 'integer'" (the reference's own example); test how numeric strings like '1' are handled on your instance. Partner payloads need cleaning before insert.
  • toGlideRecord() is the escape hatch when a GlideRecord-only method is needed. It returns a GlideAggregate if the query used aggregate().

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the global. prefix in the scoped app and getting "GlideQuery is not defined".
  • Calling .get() on an empty Optional instead of orElse() or isPresent().
  • Re-using a GlideRecord habit and expecting where() to change the original query object.
  • Passing the partner JSON straight to insert() because "keys match field names". Unknown keys and wrong types now throw. That is a feature, but the integration needs error handling for it.
Score points: Name at least three items from the documented limitations, especially "disableWorkflow is global-scope tables only" and "journal fields cannot be updated". These are the ones that block real migrations.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you unit test code built on immutable GlideQuery objects?
  • When is GlideAggregate still the better choice than GlideQuery aggregates?
  • How do Stream methods like chunk(), reduce() and toArray(n) change memory use?

Sources

  • Learn efficient scripting with GlideQuery (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • Optional - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • GlideAggregate - Scoped (API reference)

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is testing whether you know GlideRecord enforces no ACLs at all, and that there are separate controls for three different leaks: reading rows, reading fields, and using a filter on a field to infer its value. They want the matching APIs: GlideRecordSecure or GlideQuery.withAcls() for rows, element-level canRead() or the enforceFieldACL flag for fields, and the addUser* family for query access.

They also want you to treat a client-supplied encoded query as untrusted input, not just as a filter.

The Answer

What the current code enforces: nothing. Server-side GlideRecord runs without ACL checks. The reference points to GlideRecordSecure as "a class that performs the same functions as GlideRecord and enforces ACLs". So the first leak, other people's case titles, is plain row-level exposure.

The second leak is query-based inference. Even if you hide u_salary_band in the output, a user who can filter on it (u_salary_band=B7) learns the value from which rows come back. The GlideRecord reference has a set of methods for this. addUserEncodedQuery(), addUserQuery(), addUserOrderBy() and addUserOrderByDesc(), plus addUserCondition() and addUserOrCondition() on GlideQueryCondition, "enforce query access based on the user" and return only records the current user has query access to. For addUserQuery() the reference adds that "the calling user must have access to perform the specified query operation on the field for this request to be added." Plain addEncodedQuery() notes that you should use addUserEncodedQuery() to enforce query access.

The mirror image is addSystem*. addSystemEncodedQuery(), addSystemQuery(), addSystemOrderBy() and the addSystemCondition() methods explicitly bypass query ACL checks. Use them in code that legitimately runs with system intent, so a reviewer can see the bypass is deliberate rather than accidental.

Field reads. addEncodedQuery(query, enforceFieldACL) takes an optional flag that enforces field ACLs; it defaults to false. In output code, check gr.u_salary_band.canRead() before copying the value, which the GlideElement reference documents as returning true if the field can be read.

(function (data, input) {
    data.rows = [];
    var filter = (input && input.filter) ? String(input.filter) : '';

    var gr = new GlideRecordSecure('x_univ_hr_case');   // row-level read ACLs
    if (filter && !gr.isValidEncodedQuery(filter)) {
        data.error = 'Invalid filter';
        return;
    }
    gr.addUserEncodedQuery('opened_for=' + gs.getUserID()); // own cases only
    if (filter) {
        gr.addUserEncodedQuery(filter);                 // query ACLs on user filter
    }
    gr.addUserOrderByDesc('sys_created_on');
    gr.setLimit(50);
    gr.query();

    while (gr.next()) {
        data.rows.push({
            number: gr.getValue('number'),
            title: gr.short_description.canRead() ? gr.getValue('short_description') : '',
            band: gr.u_salary_band.canRead() ? gr.getValue('u_salary_band') : ''
        });
    }
})(data, input);

The GlideQuery equivalent for a fixed query is new global.GlideQuery('x_univ_hr_case').withAcls()...; the reference says withAcls() executes the query using the GlideRecordSecure API to honour ACLs. GlideQuery is a poor fit for this widget, though, because it does not support reading encoded queries, and GlideQuery.parse() supports only a subset of operators. For a free-form filter, GlideRecordSecure with addUser* methods is the cleaner tool.

Finally, constrain the filter by design. The browser should send structured parameters (status, date range), and the server should build the query. Accepting arbitrary encoded queries invites the invalid-term problem too: an invalid field is dropped and the rest of the query runs.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Table-level canRead() on GlideRecord evaluates all ACL types, including scripted ACLs. Field-level canRead() is on the element. They answer different questions.
  • changes() and changesTo() are not supported inside ACL scripts, so scripted ACLs cannot rely on them.
  • setWorkflow() cannot be set for cross-scope tables, so you cannot use it to turn off query business rules on a global table from a scoped app.
  • The GlideQueryCondition reference text for addUserOrCondition() has a copy error ("To explicitly bypass query ACL checks, use addUserOrCondition()"); the bypassing method is addSystemOrCondition().
  • HistoryWalker has its own record-level and field-level security flags, both true by default; reporting built on it inherits that behaviour.

Common Mistakes

  • Hiding a field from the output and assuming it can no longer leak, while still allowing users to filter on it.
  • Using gs.hasRole() checks in the widget instead of letting ACLs decide.
  • Switching to GlideRecordSecure but keeping addEncodedQuery() for the user's filter, which still skips query access checks.
  • Using addSystem* methods by habit in user-facing code.
Score points: Name the three separate leaks (rows, fields, inference by filtering) and map one API family to each. That shows you understand ACL enforcement as layers rather than a single switch.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do query_match and query_range ACL operations relate to the addUser* methods?
  • What would you change for a Scripted REST API used by an integration user?
  • How would you write an ATF test that proves a staff member cannot filter on salary band?

Sources

  • GlideRecord (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideQueryCondition (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideElement (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global - API reference

question: An insurer lets external loss adjusters approve claim estimates from an emailed link, without logging in. The current link is .../x_ins_approve.do?claim=<claim sys_id>&token=<gs.generateGUID()>, the token is stored in plain text on the claim, it never expires, and a 6-digit SMS code is generated with Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000000). A penetration test flags all of it. Using the platform's random, digest and date APIs, redesign token generation, storage, validation and expiry, and explain the reasoning behind each choice.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Treat the link token as a password: generated from a secure random source, long enough to resist guessing, stored only as a hash, valid for a short time, usable once, and checked against the specific claim. Name the platform APIs for each step and explain why a GUID and Math.random() are the wrong tools.

The Answer

Generation. gs.generateGUID() is documented as a 32-character hexadecimal GUID for when a unique identifier is required. Uniqueness and unpredictability are different properties, and the documented sample output (af770511ff013100e04bfffffffffff6) is visibly structured. Math.random() is a general-purpose generator with no security claim. The platform offers GlideSecureRandomUtil, a static class available in scoped and global scripts:

  • getSecureRandomString(length) returns a random alphanumeric string. At 32 characters from 62 symbols that is roughly 190 bits, far beyond guessing range.
  • getSecureRandomIntBound(bound) returns an integer from 0 inclusive to the bound exclusive. Use bound 1000000 and left-pad to six digits for the SMS code.
  • getSecureRandomInt() and getSecureRandomLong() exist too, but a string or bounded int is easier to use correctly.

Storage. Store new GlideDigest().getSHA256Hex(token), never the token. If the claim table is exported, cloned to a sub-production instance or read by an over-privileged report, the hashes do not let anyone approve anything. Because the token is long and random, a plain SHA-256 is adequate here; slow password hashing matters for human-chosen secrets, not for 190-bit random values.

Validation and expiry. Put an expiry timestamp and a 'used' flag next to the hash, and validate everything server-side in one place.

var ApprovalToken = Class.create();
ApprovalToken.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {},

    issue: function (claimGr) {
        var token = GlideSecureRandomUtil.getSecureRandomString(32);
        var expires = new GlideDateTime();
        expires.addSeconds(48 * 60 * 60);
        var t = new GlideRecord('x_ins_approval_token');
        t.initialize();
        t.setValue('claim', claimGr.getUniqueValue());
        t.setValue('token_hash', new GlideDigest().getSHA256Hex(token));
        t.setValue('expires_at', expires.getValue());
        t.setValue('used', false);
        t.insert();
        return token;                      // goes into the email only, never stored
    },

    smsCode: function () {
        var n = GlideSecureRandomUtil.getSecureRandomIntBound(1000000);
        return ('000000' + n).slice(-6);
    },

    redeem: function (claimId, token) {
        if (!GlideStringUtil.isEligibleSysID(claimId) || !/^[A-Za-z0-9]{32}$/.test(token))
            return false;
        var t = new GlideRecord('x_ins_approval_token');
        t.addQuery('claim', claimId);
        t.addQuery('token_hash', new GlideDigest().getSHA256Hex(token));
        t.addQuery('used', false);
        t.setLimit(1);
        t.query();
        if (!t.next())
            return false;
        if (!new GlideDateTime().before(new GlideDateTime(t.getValue('expires_at'))))
            return false;
        t.setValue('used', true);
        t.setValue('used_from_ip', gs.getSession().getClientIP());
        t.update();
        return true;
    },

    type: 'ApprovalToken'
};

The token record lives in its own table with tight ACLs rather than on the claim, so ordinary claim readers never see even the hash, and several outstanding links per claim are possible.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The GlideSecureRandomUtil reference describes its outputs as pseudo-random. The reference does not name the underlying algorithm, so in a security review call it the platform's secure random utility and confirm the implementation with ServiceNow documentation or support rather than over-claiming.
  • GlideStringUtil.isEligibleSysID() checks for 32 hexadecimal characters. Validating input shape before it reaches a query keeps garbage and injection attempts out of the database layer and the logs.
  • Email security scanners often open links automatically. If merely loading the URL redeems the token, scanners will approve claims. Make the link show a confirmation page and redeem only on the explicit POST.
  • Six-digit codes have only a million values. Limit attempts per token and expire codes in minutes, not days.
  • getClientIP() returns what the platform sees; behind proxies that may not be the adjuster's address. Log it for audit, do not bind the token to it.
  • Do not log the raw token on issue or redeem. A debug gs.info() line undoes the hashing.

Common Mistakes

  • Using gs.generateGUID() or a record sys_id as a secret because 'it is 32 characters'.
  • Comparing the plain token stored on the record, which turns a database read into an approval.
  • Forgetting single use, so a forwarded email can approve twice.
  • Using MD5 or SHA1 because GlideDigest offers them; pick SHA-256 or SHA-512.
Score points: Separate the three properties a token needs (unpredictable, unique, short-lived) and map each to an API: GlideSecureRandomUtil for unpredictability, a hash lookup for uniqueness, GlideDateTime comparison for expiry.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you revoke all outstanding links for a claim when the estimate changes?
  • Which roles and ACLs would protect the token table, and who should be able to read it?
  • How does this compare to inviting the adjusters as external users with proper login?

Sources

  • GlideSecureRandomUtil - Scoped, Global
  • GlideDigest (Scoped)
  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • GlideStringUtil - Scoped, Global
  • GlideDateTime (Scoped)
  • GlideSession (Scoped)

question: A security review of a scoped app finds three things. A UI action builds a confirmation message with gs.addInfoMessage('Created ' + current.short_description), and a tester's short description containing markup rendered as live HTML. The same UI action ends with action.setRedirectURL(action.getURLParameter('sysparm_goto')). A script include builds gr.addEncodedQuery('u_ref=' + input) from a portal parameter. The developer's fix wraps everything in GlideStringUtil.escapeAllQuotes(). Explain why that fix fails, and correct each finding with the right escaping or URL-safety API, stating what each one actually does.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Say up front that escaping depends on the output context. HTML text, a URL, an encoded query and a JavaScript string each need different treatment, and no single 'sanitise' call covers them. You should also know what each GlideStringUtil and GlideSecurityUtils method does according to the reference, including the ones whose names mislead.

Why the Fix Fails

GlideStringUtil.escapeAllQuotes() does not escape anything: the reference says it removes quotes, and its example turns let's into lets. Angle brackets pass straight through, so the markup still renders, and legitimate data with apostrophes is silently changed. If the goal was to make a value safe inside a quoted JavaScript string, escapeTicks() is the method that adds backslashes before quotes.

The Answer

Finding 1: HTML context. Escape user data before it goes into anything rendered as HTML. GlideStringUtil.escapeHTML() converts "<>& into "<>&; the reference says it is meant to stop the UI rendering improperly or a JavaScript or HTML injection. For translated messages, gs.getEscapedMessage(id, args) returns the message with HTML special characters replaced. The reference notes that arguments are inserted verbatim, and its examples only show special characters in the message template being escaped, so escape user-supplied arguments yourself rather than assuming.

var safeDesc = GlideStringUtil.escapeHTML(current.getValue('short_description') || '');
gs.addInfoMessage(gs.getMessage('Created {0}', [safeDesc]));

Finding 2: open redirect. Redirecting to an attacker-supplied URL lets a phishing link start on your instance and land on theirs. GlideSecurityUtils, available in scoped and global scripts, gives three tools:

  • enforceRelativeURL(url) removes the domain and keeps the page and parameters. The documented example turns http://evildomain.com/test.do into test.do.
  • cleanURL(url) removes suspicious encoding aimed at reflected or DOM-based XSS; for javascript%3Aalert(1) the documented output is null.
  • isURLWhiteListed(url) checks the URL against the system allow list.
var target = action.getURLParameter('sysparm_goto');
var safe = target ? GlideSecurityUtils.cleanURL(GlideSecurityUtils.enforceRelativeURL(target)) : null;
if (safe)
    action.setRedirectURL(safe);
else
    action.setRedirectURL(current);          // GlideRecord: go to the record's form

Finding 3: encoded query injection. A caret in user input starts a new query term, so abc^ORactive=false widens the query. GlideStringUtil.escapeQueryTermSeparator() replaces ^ with ^^. Better still, avoid string building: validate the input shape (for a reference, GlideStringUtil.isEligibleSysID()) and use addQuery('u_ref', input).

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The unescape method has different names by scope: unescapeHTML() in scoped apps and unEscapeHTML() in global, per the reference. A script include moved between scopes fails on this.
  • escapeForHomePage() produces percent-style output (%3ctest%3e), which suits URLs rather than HTML text. Using it in a message shows users %3c.
  • getHTMLValue() also converts illegal HTML characters to HTML notation; pick one method per context and use it consistently, or you will double-escape (&lt;).
  • GlideSecurityUtils.escapeScript() escapes a script string so <script> becomes <script>; it is for displaying script text, not for making untrusted code safe to run.
  • GlideStringUtil.dotToUnderBar() only replaces periods: the documented example turns ../../../../../../etc/passwd into __/__/__/__/__/__/etc/passwd, so the slashes survive. It is not path sanitisation on its own; use a strict allow-list pattern for file names built from user input.
  • GlideStringUtil.urlEncode() is documented as global only; in a scoped app use gs.urlEncode().

Common Mistakes

  • Escaping at input time and storing escaped data, which then double-escapes on every display and corrupts exports.
  • Escaping in client scripts only; server-generated messages and redirects are where these findings came from.
  • Allow-listing redirects by checking indexOf('service-now.com'), which evil.com/?x=service-now.com passes.
  • Assuming getEscapedMessage() sanitises the arguments without testing it.
Score points: Point out that escapeAllQuotes() removes quotes rather than escaping them, and name the right method for each of the four contexts: HTML (escapeHTML), URL redirect (enforceRelativeURL plus cleanURL), encoded query (escapeQueryTermSeparator or addQuery), JavaScript string (escapeTicks).

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you add an automated check to stop string-concatenated encoded queries reaching production?
  • Where else in a Service Portal widget can the same HTML injection appear?
  • How do HTML sanitiser settings on HTML fields relate to escaping in script?

Sources

  • GlideStringUtil - Scoped, Global
  • GlideSecurityUtils - Scoped, Global
  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • action - Scoped, Global

question: A healthcare customer integrates with a partner's claims API secured by OAuth 2.0 client credentials. The current scoped script calls the token endpoint with a hand-built RESTMessageV2 on every request, saves the access token into a system property, and logs token.getAccessToken() for troubleshooting. The partner's identity provider has started rate-limiting the instance, and the security team found bearer tokens in the syslog table. Explain how the sn_auth OAuth classes and RESTMessageV2.setAuthenticationProfile() should be used instead, what each object returns, and the traps you'd watch for in the refresh and error paths.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The platform already stores and manages OAuth tokens. A senior developer configures an OAuth Entity Profile, points the REST message at it, and lets the platform fetch and reuse the token. Hand-rolled token code is justified only for unusual grants, and even then it should go through sn_auth.GlideOAuthClient rather than a raw HTTP call. I also want to hear that tokens never go to logs or properties.

The Answer

Default path: let the REST message use the profile. setAuthenticationProfile(type, profileId) takes 'oauth2' and the sys_id of an OAuth Entity Profile [oauth_entity_profile] record. With that set, the platform obtains a token for the profile and uses it on the request. The script stops knowing anything about tokens:

var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('Claims API', 'post');
rm.setAuthenticationProfile('oauth2', gs.getProperty('x_hc_claims.oauth_profile_id'));
rm.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify(claim));
var res = rm.execute();

setRequestorProfile(requestorContext, requestorId) exists for the rare case where a different requestor's token is needed; the reference calls it optional and unnecessary in most configurations. Client credentials is not that case.

When you need the token object. sn_auth.GlideOAuthClient has two different retrieval methods and candidates mix them up:

  • getToken(requestID, oauthProfileID) returns a GlideOAuthToken already stored on the instance. The first argument is a Request ID from the OAuth Requestor Profile [oauth_requestor_profile] table, which references the entity profile. It reads; it does not call the provider.
  • requestToken(clientName, jsonString) and requestTokenByRequest(clientName, GlideOAuthClientRequest) go to the provider and return a GlideOAuthClientResponse, not a token. You call getToken() on that response, which can be empty when the request failed.
var req = new sn_auth.GlideOAuthClientRequest();
req.setGrantType('refresh_token');          // only needed if not defined on the profile
req.setRefreshToken(storedRefreshToken);
req.setScope(null);

var client = new sn_auth.GlideOAuthClient();
var resp = client.requestTokenByRequest('ClaimsPartner', req);
if (resp.getResponseCode() != '200' || !resp.getToken()) {
    gs.error('Token refresh failed: ' + resp.getResponseCode() + ' ' + resp.getErrorMessage());
} else {
    var tok = resp.getToken();
    gs.info('Token refreshed, expires in ' + tok.getExpiresIn() + 's');  // never log the token
}

GlideOAuthToken.getExpiresIn() returns the lifespan in seconds as a Long. If you must decide whether to refresh, compare that against a safety margin rather than waiting for a 401.

Reading the response properly. GlideOAuthClientResponse gives you getResponseCode(), getErrorMessage(), getContentType(), getBody() and getResponseParameters(). When a partner identity provider rejects a request, the useful detail (an invalid_client or invalid_scope error, for example) is usually in the body or the response parameters, not in the generic error message. Log the code and the error field, never the whole body if it might echo a token back.

Clean-up. revokeToken(clientName, accessToken, refreshToken, request) revokes tokens, which matters when you rotate the client secret or decommission the integration. Move the old property-stored token out, revoke it, and delete the property.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • GlideOAuthClientResponse.getResponseCode() is documented as returning a String. A strict === 200 comparison is always false.
  • In global scripts the header setter on GlideOAuthClientRequest is setHead(name, value); the scoped equivalent is setHeader(name, value). Code copied across scopes fails on that one method name.
  • The reference examples log access and refresh tokens with gs.info. They are examples of the API, not of practice. Copying them puts bearer tokens in syslog, which is what the security team found.
  • getAccessTokenSysID() and getRefreshTokenSysID() are deprecated.
  • The requestToken() example uses the password grant with a user name and password in script. Avoid it; it puts credentials in code and is the wrong grant for system-to-system work.
  • Scoped scripts use the sn_auth namespace; the reference states these classes work in both global and scoped scripts.

Common Mistakes

  • Requesting a new token per call, which is what got the instance rate-limited.
  • Storing tokens in sys_properties, readable by anyone with property access and exported in update sets.
  • Treating a 401 from the resource server as a token problem without checking scope, which GlideOAuthToken.getScope() exposes.
Score points: Name the records: OAuth Entity Profile for the profile sys_id, OAuth Requestor Profile for the request ID, and the Application Registry entry that holds the client. Interviewers listen for whether you have configured these, not just scripted around them.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate the client secret without downtime?
  • How do you give a scoped app access to the profile without exposing credentials to end users?
  • When would you build a custom token request with GlideOAuthClientRequest.setParameter()?
