  • GlideOAuthClientRequest - Scoped, Global
  • GlideOAuthClientResponse - Scoped, Global
  • GlideOAuthToken - Scoped, Global

question: A media company wants a scoped app to upload nightly reports to an S3-compatible object store that requires signed requests (signature over method, path, headers, body and a timestamp). A developer put the whole signing flow in a script include using sn_auth.HttpRequestData, RequestAuthAPI and HttpRequestAuthedData. In testing every upload is rejected with a signature mismatch, and when they log the signing result they see status SKIPPED. Walk through the documented signing call order, what each object is responsible for, and the specific reasons this implementation fails.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Signed requests fail with useless errors, so you have to debug from the signing side first. Show that you know the documented sequence, that you read getStatus() and getStatusMessage() before sending anything, and that you can spot the documented restrictions that make this script include approach fail.

The Answer

The reference lists the order explicitly:

  1. HttpRequestData builds the unsigned request: setEndpoint(), setHttpMethod(), setService(), setRegion(), addHeader(), addQueryParam(), setContent().
  2. AuthCredential represents the credential. Usually you load one from a Credentials [discovery_credentials] record with sn_cc.StandardCredentialsProvider().getAuthCredentialByID(); an empty one is filled with setAttribute().
  3. new sn_auth.RequestAuthAPI(httpRequestData, credential).generateAuth() signs it and returns an HttpRequestAuthedData.
  4. HttpRequestAuthedData exposes the result: getStatus(), getStatusMessage(), getHeaderMap(), getQueryMap(), getDirective().
  5. The signed request is sent; the reference names GlideHTTPRequest for this step.

Before any of that works, an authentication algorithm must be configured and associated with the credential. That prerequisite is stated on every page of the set.

Why SKIPPED. getStatus() returns SUCCESS, FAIL or SKIPPED, and SKIPPED means signing was skipped because information was incomplete. The matching message is "Request data is empty. Request auth is skipped". The most likely cause here is documented on setContent(): the method is not supported in script includes or MID Server scripts. The reference does not say exactly what happens when you call it there anyway, but request data that is missing its content fits the SKIPPED status; reproduce it on your instance to confirm. The other two documented messages are worth knowing too: "credential is not valid" (no authentication algorithm on the credential) and "Can't find script includes scope" (algorithm record and its script includes in the wrong scope).

Why the signature mismatches even when signing succeeds. The signature covers exact bytes. If the code signs one body and then sends a re-serialized or differently encoded body, or drops a signed header when copying headers onto the outbound request, the store recomputes a different value. Copy getHeaderMap() and getQueryMap() exactly as returned, and send the same content string you signed.

// Run where setContent() is supported, e.g. a Workflow Studio script step or
// a server script that is not a script include, per the HttpRequestData reference.
var data = new sn_auth.HttpRequestData();
data.setEndpoint('https://store.example.com/reports/2026-10-23.csv');
data.setHttpMethod('PUT');
data.setService('s3');
data.setRegion('eu-west-1');
data.addHeader('Content-Type', 'text/csv');
data.setContent(csvBody);                      // exact bytes you will send

var cred = new sn_cc.StandardCredentialsProvider().getAuthCredentialByID(credSysId);
var signed = new sn_auth.RequestAuthAPI(data, cred).generateAuth();

if (signed.getStatus() != 'SUCCESS') {
    gs.error('Signing ' + signed.getStatus() + ': ' + signed.getStatusMessage());
} else {
    var headers = signed.getHeaderMap();      // send every one of these unchanged
    // ...send with the documented HTTP client, body === csvBody
}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • setDate() is for testing signatures against a known timestamp. The reference warns that setting it in production may make signing fail, because the signing request should use the time the signature was generated.
  • setExpiry() is advisory. The third-party service usually sets expiry, and it overrides yours: if the service says 900 seconds and you set 300, getExpiry() returns 900.
  • setDirective() on HttpRequestData accepts header or query; HttpRequestAuthedData.setDirective() adds credential_value, which applies the signature as a credential value. The related setCredentialValue() method is what the reference says sets the Credential Value data pill for REST, SOAP and Get Connection Info steps in Workflow Studio.
  • getConnectionAliasID() and getConnectionExtendedAttribute() only work inside an Integration Hub REST step.
  • resetAuthCredential() exists for short-lived, limited-privilege tokens (the example sets an Action attribute of aws_sessionToken) and only works if the third party supports such tokens.
  • The AuthCredential.getAttribute() reference lists its return as void while the example reads a value from it. Test the actual return in your release rather than trusting the table.

Common Mistakes

  • Sending the request without checking getStatus(), then debugging the remote 403 instead of the local SKIPPED.
  • Pretty-printing or rebuilding the body after signing.
  • Putting the secret key in a script variable instead of a credential record with an algorithm attached.
Score points: Suggest building this as an Integration Hub REST step with a Connection & Credential alias. The signing algorithm then runs where the APIs are designed to run, and the step's execution details show you the signed request.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate the store's access keys?
  • What would make you choose query-string signing over header signing?
  • How do you prove the clock is not the cause of a mismatch?

Sources

  • HttpRequestData
  • RequestAuthAPI
  • HttpRequestAuthedData
  • AuthCredential

question: A gaming company's community team built a chat bot that posts every Discord message to a scoped Scripted REST API. The resource is set to not require authentication. Its script reads request.getHeader('X-API-Key'), compares it with != to a system property, inserts a row, and an after-insert business rule on that table calls the Discord API synchronously with RESTMessageV2.execute(). The instance runs Washington DC or later. Security has asked you to review it. Explain what is weak about the hand-rolled key check, how you would move it to the platform's inbound API key feature (profile, key, access policy, service user), and what else in the design you would change.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Start with the real problem: an unauthenticated endpoint with a key check in script has no platform identity behind it. Every request reaches your code, the secret sits in a property, and nothing outside the script limits what the key can do. Then walk through the Washington DC inbound API key setup step by step, explain why the key is bound to a non-human user, and catch the synchronous outbound call inside a business rule.

Diagnosis

The Discord walkthrough on the Developer Advocate blog uses this pattern because it is quick to build. In production it is weak:

  • No platform authentication. With "requires authentication" turned off, the platform passes every request to the script. The only control is a string comparison. The script is the security boundary, and any bug in it is an open door.
  • The secret is a property. Anyone with admin or property read access sees it. Rotation means editing a property and redeploying the bot at the same moment. The blog does mark it private, which helps, but it is still not a credential object.
  • No scope limits. The key "works" for whatever the script does. You cannot limit it to one method or one resource without writing more code.
  • Weak record of who called. Requests do not run as a named integration user, so created and updated fields, logs and ACL decisions cannot tell one caller from another.

The Answer

The Inbound REST API Keys post describes the native setup that arrived in Washington DC:

  1. Confirm the API Key and HMAC Authentication plugin (com.glide.tokenbased_auth) is active.
  2. Create an Inbound Authentication Profile of type API Key, choosing the Auth Parameter x-sn-apikey as either a header or a query parameter. Prefer the header, because query strings end up in logs and browser history. The full list of parameters is under REST API Auth Parameter.
  3. Create a REST API Key record and select a user. The key works as that user, so roles and ACLs apply exactly as they would for Basic Auth. The post recommends a service account, not an employee, so the integration does not break when someone leaves. Copy the generated token from the lock icon.
  4. Create a REST API Access Policy for this Scripted REST API. Unchecking the "all" boxes reveals fields to limit it to particular methods, resources, or versions. Here, POST on /message only. Add the authentication profile to the policy.
  5. Turn authentication back on for the resource, remove the script check, and give the service user only the role the resource requires plus create rights on the chat table.

The bot then sends x-sn-apikey: <token>. A wrong key never reaches your script. Revoking access means deactivating one key record, and logs show which user and key made each call. When testing fails, the post lists the usual causes: a typo in the parameter name, a wrong token, or a user without access to the data.

Other Changes

  • The outbound call in the business rule. An after-insert rule that calls execute() holds the inbound transaction open while Discord answers. If Discord is slow, inbound requests pile up. Make it an async business rule, or use executeAsync(). The reference says the instance does not wait for a response with executeAsync(), and suggests processing the response elsewhere. Set setHttpTimeout() either way.
  • Bot token storage. The outbound Discord bot token also lives in a property. Move it into a credential record and read it with sn_cc.StandardCredentialsProvider, as the C3 Replicate integration does with getCredentialByAliasID().
  • Input handling. The script reads request.body.dataString and calls JSON.parse. That is fine, but the RESTAPIRequestBody reference says the body is a stream that can only be read once. Reading data after dataString returns empty, so pick one.
  • Volume. Every Discord message becomes a row and fires a rule that exits early unless the text starts with "!". Filter in the bot so only commands are sent, or check the condition in the rule's filter instead of in script.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • A deactivated or locked service user breaks the key silently from the caller's point of view. Monitor the 401 rate.
  • Access policies are attached per API. A key meant for the bot should not also work on the Table API because someone reused a broad policy.
  • API keys are bearer secrets. Anyone holding one can replay requests. Where the caller can sign payloads, HMAC validation adds tamper detection. The plugin name itself covers both.

Common Mistakes

  • Binding the key to an admin "to make it work".
  • Putting the key in the query string and then sharing request URLs in tickets.
  • Leaving the endpoint unauthenticated "temporarily" after enabling the profile.
Score points: Name all four records in order (plugin, inbound authentication profile, REST API key bound to a user, REST API access policy limited by method or resource). Then add the synchronous-outbound finding without being prompted.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate the key without downtime?
  • When would you choose OAuth client credentials or mutual TLS over an API key?
  • How would you rate-limit a noisy caller?

Sources

  • Inbound REST API Keys (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Discord-ServiceNow Chat Bot - Complete Walkthrough (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • TechNow Ep 97: Washington D.C. Q&A (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • RESTAPIRequest - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • RESTAPIRequestBody - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global (API reference)
  • StandardCredentialsProvider - Scoped, Global (API reference)

question: A logistics company's onboarding app orders three catalog items (laptop, mobile phone, building badge) for every new hire. A scheduled job runs as an integration user and loops over new hires calling sn_sc.CartJS. Since go-live: every request has the integration user as Requested for; on some runs only the last item of the three appears on the request; in UAT the job returns a cart_id and no request is ever created; the phone request arrives with its Data plan variable blank even though the script set it to "Unlimited"; and contractors are getting laptops they are not entitled to. Question: Explain each symptom from the CartJS behaviour and write a safer version of the ordering code.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Four facts carry this answer. CartJS works on the cart of the logged-in user. The methods behave differently when two-step checkout is enabled. Variables take values, not display values. And the reference itself says to create a new CartJS instance per item added in a loop. On top of that, check entitlement with CatItem.isDelegationAllowed() before ordering on someone's behalf instead of relying on the integration user's rights.

The Answer

Requested for is the integration user. new sn_sc.CartJS(cartName) creates a cart "for the user who is currently logged in". Unless you set it, the request is for that user. Use setRequestedFor(userSysId), or pass requested_for to submitOrder(), or sysparm_requested_for to orderNow().

Only the last item. The addToCart() example in the reference notes that new sn_sc.CartJS() is inside the loop: "You must call sn_sc.CartJS() multiple times to be able to add multiple items to the cart." Reusing one instance across adds is the likely cause of a request with one item; the reference states the rule but not the exact failure mode, so confirm it on your instance.

cart_id and no request in UAT. UAT has two-step checkout enabled. With it on, orderNow() "adds the specified item to the cart and returns the sys_id of the cart", and checkoutCart() returns an order summary rather than a request. submitOrder(request) updates special instructions, requested for and delivery address and "performs the cart checkout", returning request_id and request_number. Use it for unattended ordering so behaviour does not depend on a UI setting, and still check that request_id came back.

Blank Data plan. Variables take "Value of the answer (Not the display value)". The choice value is probably unlimited, not "Unlimited".

Contractors get laptops. The integration user can order anything, so ordering on behalf of someone bypasses the entitlement that user criteria would enforce in the portal. CatItem.isDelegationAllowed(userSysId) checks whether that user has acquisition rights to the item; getInvalidDelegatedUsers([ids]) checks a batch and returns the names of users for whom the item cannot be requested.

var ITEMS = [
  { id: LAPTOP_ID, vars: { model: 'standard_14' } },
  { id: PHONE_ID,  vars: { carrier: 'at_and_t_mobility', data_plan: 'unlimited' } },   // values, not labels
  { id: BADGE_ID,  vars: { site: 'lon_hq' } }
];

function orderStarterKit(hireUserId, location) {
  var cartName = 'onboarding_' + hireUserId;           // own named cart, not the integration user's default
  var allowed = [];
  ITEMS.forEach(function (it) {
    if (new sn_sc.CatItem(it.id).isDelegationAllowed(hireUserId)) allowed.push(it);
    else gs.info('Skipping ' + it.id + ' for ' + hireUserId + ': not entitled');
  });
  if (!allowed.length) return null;

  try {
    allowed.forEach(function (it) {
      var cart = new sn_sc.CartJS(cartName);           // new instance per add, per the reference
      cart.addToCart({ sysparm_id: it.id, sysparm_quantity: '1', variables: it.vars });
    });
    var res = new sn_sc.CartJS(cartName).submitOrder({
      requested_for: hireUserId,
      delivery_address: location,
      special_instructions: 'Ready before start date'
    });
    if (!res || !res.request_id) throw 'No request returned: ' + JSON.stringify(res);
    return res.request_number;
  } catch (e) {
    new sn_sc.CartJS(cartName).empty();                // do not leave a half-filled cart behind
    gs.error('Onboarding order failed for ' + hireUserId + ': ' + e);
    return null;
  }
}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Use a named cart per hire. If the script uses the default cart and a person also logs in as that account (or the job runs twice concurrently), items mix between orders.
  • empty() deletes the current cart. Call it on failure so a retry does not order the leftover items twice.
  • getCartItems() returns a GlideRecord on sc_cart_item; it is a cheap way to confirm three lines are in the cart before submitting.
  • canViewRF() tells you whether the current user has the role to edit Requested for. It is useful in a widget that exposes the field, less so in a background job.
  • CartJS needs the Service Catalog Scoped API plugin (com.glideapp.servicecatalog.scoped.api), which is on by default; check it in stripped-down sub-production instances.
  • Quantity is passed as a string in the reference examples; follow that.

Common Mistakes

  • Inserting sc_request and sc_req_item with GlideRecord. You skip pricing, variable records, the item's flow and the delegation check.
  • Impersonating each new hire to make the cart theirs. It works, but it is harder to audit and still bypasses nothing you could not check with isDelegationAllowed().
  • Assuming the same code behaves the same in every environment when two-step checkout differs.
Score points: Quote the reference's note about creating a new CartJS inside the loop, and explain the two-step checkout difference between orderNow(), checkoutCart() and submitOrder(). Those two details explain most "ordering from script" bugs.

Likely Follow-ups

  • When would you use an order guide instead (sn_sc.OrderGuide.init())?
  • How would you update a variable on an item already in the cart? (updateItem(request, cart_item_id).)
  • How would you report which hires were skipped for entitlement?

Sources

  • CartJS API reference
  • CatItem API reference

question: A pharmaceutical company's "Request details" portal page uses a container widget that embeds a child widget with data.vars = $sp.getWidget('rq-variables', { rec: data.ritmId }). The child shows the requested item's variables. It works on first load, but after the user clicks Refresh (which calls c.server.update() in the child) the variables disappear. The child also tried $sp.getRecord() as a fallback and got null, and the debugging calls to $sp.log() show nothing in sp_log when testers reproduce it. Question: Explain all three behaviours and fix the child widget.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

You need the documented limits of embedded widgets: options passed to $sp.getWidget() exist only on the first execution of the child's server script, and $sp.getRecord() returns null when the widget is embedded by another widget. Also know that $sp.log() only records for users with sp_admin or admin. The fix is to carry the identifier through data and input yourself and to re-check access on every server call.

The Answer

Variables disappear on refresh. The reference note on getWidget(sysID, options) says options passed in "will only be available in the embedded widget's server script on the first execution of that script. Any subsequent calls into the server script from the embedded widget will not contain the object properties passed in." On first load, options.rec is set. On c.server.update(), the server script runs again with input from the client and options.rec is gone, so the query finds nothing.

getRecord() returns null. With no parameters it returns the record identified by the current URL, but it "returns null if the widget is embedded by another widget". Even if the page URL contains the sys_id, the embedded child cannot use the no-argument form.

No log entries. $sp.log(message) writes to the Service Portal Log Entries [sp_log] table only when "the logged in user must have the sp_admin or admin role". Testers reproducing as an end user produce nothing. Use gs.debug()/gs.info() with a prefix, or reproduce as an admin with impersonation off.

The fix. Copy the identifier into data on the first run so it travels to the client and comes back in input, and treat the value coming back as untrusted.

(function() {
  // first run: options.rec from the parent; later runs: input.rec from the client
  var ritmId = (input && input.rec) || options.rec || $sp.getParameter('sys_id');
  data.rec = ritmId;
  data.vars = [];
  if (!ritmId) return;

  var ritm = new GlideRecord('sc_req_item');
  if (!ritm.get(ritmId) || !$sp.canReadRecord(ritm)) {   // re-check on every call
    data.error = gs.getMessage('Request not found');
    return;
  }
  data.vars = $sp.getRecordVariablesArray(ritm, false);   // false: skip unanswered variables
  data.number = ritm.getDisplayValue('number');
})();

On the client, keep c.data.rec populated (it is, because the server put it in data) and call c.server.update(). The parent no longer needs to pass anything after the first render.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • getRecordVariablesArray(gr, includeNilResponses) returns an array of variable objects with name, label, value, display_value, type and visibility flags. getRecordVariables() returns the same information as a String; do not try to iterate it as an array.
  • getVariablesArray() reads the record from the URL (table and sys_id parameters), so it has the same embedded-widget problem as getRecord().
  • The record must have catalog variables, such as a requested item or a record created by a record producer. On a catalog task, read the parent RITM.
  • Read access to the RITM does not mean every variable should be shown. Variables have their own visibility flags in the returned objects (visible_summary, visible_standalone); filter on them the way the platform's summary does.
  • If the child should render a catalog item for ordering rather than show an existing item, use $sp.getCatalogItem(sysId, true); for viewing an item's variables, the security check uses write roles when isOrdering is false.

Common Mistakes

  • Making the parent re-embed the child on every refresh with getWidget(), which re-runs both server scripts and resets client state.
  • Trusting input.rec without the canReadRecord() check, which turns the refresh button into a way to read any RITM.
  • Leaving $sp.log() calls in place and assuming they will help support later.
Score points: Quote the first-execution limit on getWidget() options and the null return from getRecord() for embedded widgets. Both come straight from the reference and explain this bug in one sentence each.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would the parent and child widgets talk without a server round trip (events on $rootScope)?
  • How would you render variables of a catalog task, given the variables belong to the RITM?
  • When would you use $sp.getForm() instead of building the view yourself?

Sources

  • GlideSPScriptable API reference
  • Widget API reference (input, data, options, server.update)

question: A university moved its 'Request lab access' catalog item from the classic CMS catalog to the Service Portal. In the core UI catalog view everything works. On the portal, the requester's department never fills in, a star icon next to the supervisor field is missing, a script that reads g_form.getControl('lab').value throws getControl is not a function-style errors, and a helper library loaded with ScriptLoader.getScripts() never runs. The same item must also work for staff who order on behalf of students from a Workspace. Go through which GlideForm and related client APIs behave differently or are unavailable in Service Portal and Workspace, and how you would rewrite the scripts so one version works in all three UIs.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is testing whether you know that g_form is not one implementation. The core UI version exposes DOM-level methods; the Service Portal and Workspace versions do not, and the reference marks which methods are missing or unsupported. They want a concrete list from the reference, a rewrite that sticks to value-level methods, and the right way to share code in portal and workspace (g_ui_scripts) instead of ScriptLoader.

Approach

Find what breaks, method by method. From the GlideForm, ScriptLoader and GlideUIScripts references:

  • getControl(), getElement() and getFormElement() are not available in mobile or Service Portal scripts. Anything that reaches into the DOM (.value, $(), gel()) is core UI only.
  • getDisplayBox() returns the display value in the core UI. In Service Portal the reference says to use getDisplayValue(fieldName). In the core UI, getDisplayValue() with no argument returns the record's display value, not a field's.
  • addDecoration(), removeDecoration(), flash() and setLabelOf() are not supported by Service Catalog. The missing star is expected behaviour, not a bug.
  • addOption() with an index ignores duplicate labels in Service Portal.
  • setVisible() leaves blank space on the desktop UI but collapses it in Service Portal and mobile.
  • onUserChangeValue() does not work for Service Catalog items in the classic environment.
  • ScriptLoader is not available for Service Portal, Mobile or Agent Workspace. GlideURLV3 is not supported in Service Portal, Now Mobile or Agent Workspace either.
  • reflistOpen() is not supported in a Workspace client script; the reference points to g_modal.showFrame().
  • isSectionVisible() is not supported in Workspace.

Rewrite to value-level APIs. Department should come from the server, not from reading a DOM element:

function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading || newValue == '') {
        return;
    }
    var ga = new GlideAjax('LabAccessAjax');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getStudentInfo');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_student', newValue);
    ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
        var info = JSON.parse(answer || '{}');
        if (info.department) {
            // value + display value: no extra round trip, works in every UI
            g_form.setValue('department', info.department, info.department_name);
        }
        if (info.needs_induction == 'true') {
            g_form.showFieldMsg('lab',
                getMessage('Safety induction required before access'), 'info');
        }
    });
}

Replace the decoration with showFieldMsg(), which every UI renders. Replace getControl('lab').value with g_form.getValue('lab'). Where you really need a display value of a reference, prefer having the server return it, which avoids the getDisplayBox versus getDisplayValue split entirely.

Shared helper code. In Service Portal and Workspaces use g_ui_scripts.getUIScript('name'), which returns a promise resolving to whatever the UI script returns. The reference sets the conditions: the UI script must not be Global, and the UI Type on both the client script and the UI script must be Mobile / Service Portal or All, not Desktop. It is not supported in the core UI, so if the core UI also needs the helper, keep the helper tiny or put the logic in a script include behind GlideAjax, which works everywhere.

function onLoad() {
    g_ui_scripts.getUIScript('labAccessUtils').then(function(utils) {
        utils.applyDefaults(g_form);
    }, function() {
        console.log('labAccessUtils did not load');
    });
}

Finally, set each catalog client script's UI Type deliberately. A script marked Desktop never runs on the portal, which is the most common reason a portal script 'does nothing'.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference's own getDisplayValue() example detects the portal by checking window == null, and the same example then alerts an undefined variable (valueCoreUI). Treat it as an illustration; branching on the UI is brittle, so prefer APIs that behave the same everywhere.
  • Client-side GlideRecord has getDisplayValue() in Service Portal, Mobile and Agent Workspace but not on the desktop, so a script that relies on it passes portal testing and fails in the core UI.
  • setVariablesReadOnly() only works on variable editors in the core UI, not on the catalog item form itself.
  • getHelpTextControl() applies to catalog variables only and returns a DOM element, so it is another core UI-only call.
  • GlideUIScripts has an IE11 note: outside an Angular context use g_ui_scripts['name']. Relevant only if you still support that browser.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a script that works in the core UI catalog view will behave the same on the portal.
  • Fixing portal errors with try/catch around DOM calls instead of removing the DOM dependency.
  • Using ScriptLoader or GlideURL in a catalog client script meant for the portal.
  • Leaving the UI Type at Desktop.
Score points: Bring the reference's own notes as evidence (not available in Service Portal scripts, not supported by Service Catalog, not supported in Workspace) and propose a rule for the team: catalog client scripts use only value-level g_form methods and GlideAjax.

Likely Follow-ups

question: A bank's employee portal has a custom 'My open requests' widget. The product owner wants three changes: a Cancel button on each request that asks for confirmation and a reason before cancelling, the list should update by itself when a fulfiller changes a request's state, and a short success message after cancelling that screen-reader users also hear. A junior developer has used window.confirm(), polls the server every ten seconds with $interval and c.server.update(), and uses alert() for the success message. Redesign the widget client script using the Service Portal client APIs and explain what the server script must still check.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Use the portal's own services: spModal for dialogs (it wraps Angular UI Bootstrap's $uibModal), spUtil.recordWatch() for push updates instead of polling, spUtil messages instead of alert(), and spAriaUtil for screen readers. Then make clear that the widget server script, not the button, decides whether this user may cancel this request.

The Answer

Dialog with a reason. spModal.open() takes title, message, input: true (shows an input field), value, buttons, size, backdrop, keyboard and more. With input: true the promise resolves with what the user typed, as in the reference's prompt example. Cancel (or a button flagged cancel: true) rejects the promise, so put the cancellation in the success handler only.

function($scope, spModal, spUtil, spAriaUtil) {
    var c = this;

    c.cancelRequest = function(req) {
        spModal.open({
            title: '${Cancel request}',
            message: '${Why are you cancelling} ' + req.number + '?',
            input: true,
            value: '',
            backdrop: 'static',
            buttons: [
                {label: '${Keep request}', cancel: true},
                {label: '${Cancel request}', primary: true}
            ]
        }).then(function(reason) {
            if (!reason) {
                spUtil.addErrorMessage('${A reason is required}');
                return;
            }
            c.server.get({action: 'cancel', sys_id: req.sys_id, reason: reason})
                .then(function(r) {
                    if (r.data.cancelled) {
                        spUtil.addTrivialMessage('${Request cancelled}');
                        spAriaUtil.sendLiveMessage('${Request cancelled}');
                    } else {
                        spUtil.addErrorMessage(r.data.error);
                    }
                });
        }, function() {
            // user dismissed: do nothing
        });
    };

    // push updates instead of polling
    spUtil.recordWatch($scope, 'sc_req_item',
        'active=true^requested_for=' + c.data.userId,
        function(event, data) {
            spUtil.update($scope);
        });
}

Live updates. spUtil.recordWatch($scope, table, filter, callback) lets a widget react to inserts, updates and deletes on a table filter in real time. The reference notes you must inject $scope into the client script function to pass it. Its P1 example inspects data.changes to refresh only when the state field changed, then calls spUtil.update($scope), which updates the data object on the server like server.update() but for the given scope. That replaces ten-second polling, which costs one server round trip per open browser tab every ten seconds whether or not anything changed.

Messages and accessibility. spUtil.addTrivialMessage() shows a message that disappears after a short time; addInfoMessage() and addErrorMessage() are the heavier variants. spAriaUtil.sendLiveMessage() injects text into an aria-live region; the region is assertive, so it interrupts the screen reader immediately. Use it once per completed action, not on every refresh.

Server script. The widget's server script receives input.action, input.sys_id and input.reason. It must load the request, confirm the current user is the requester (or has a role that allows cancelling), confirm the request is still in a cancellable state, and only then update it. Anyone can call the widget's server endpoint with any sys_id; hiding the Cancel button for closed requests is cosmetic.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference documents the spModal.alert(), confirm() and open() promise as containing true or false, but the custom-buttons example uses the reject handler for the cancel button. Write both handlers so your widget does not depend on which one fires.
  • backdrop: 'static' stops a stray click outside the dialog from closing it; keyboard: false blocks ESC. Use them when the user is typing a reason.
  • message and title accept HTML. Never concatenate unescaped user data (a short description, for example) into them.
  • recordWatch fires for every matching change, including changes the current user makes. Debounce or check data.changes before calling spUtil.update() so one cancel does not trigger two refreshes.
  • spModal.open({widget: 'id', widgetInput: {...}}) embeds a whole widget in the dialog, and shared passes a client-side object to it. Use that when the cancel form grows beyond one text field.

Common Mistakes

  • Polling with $interval when recordWatch exists.
  • Using window.confirm() and alert(), which block the page, ignore portal theming and cannot be translated with ${} message syntax.
  • Forgetting to inject $scope and passing c to recordWatch.
  • Trusting the client to decide whether a request may be cancelled.
Score points: Mention the cost of polling (one call per tab per interval) against recordWatch, and close with the server-side authorization check. Accessibility via spAriaUtil is a nice extra most candidates skip.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you pass widget context (open request count, for example) to Agent Chat on the same page? (spContextManager)
  • How would you track how often users cancel requests in Usage Insights?
  • What changes if the cancellation needs a manager approval instead of happening immediately?

  • spAriaUtil - API reference
  • spContextManager - API reference
  • Widget API reference (ServiceNow product documentation)

question: A university is building a React student-services app that orders ServiceNow catalog items (laptop loans, locker requests, printing credit) through the Service Catalog REST API. The app's backend uses one integration account for all users. In load testing two problems appeared: students occasionally received someone else's locker in their request, and a "request for my whole lab group" feature failed completely when one student in the list had graduated. The product owner also wants the app to show the same mandatory fields and dependent questions as the Service Portal form. Diagnose both defects, explain how the API handles carts, requested-for and delegation, and describe how you would rebuild the ordering flow.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The cart endpoints work on "the cart of the current user". With one integration account, every student shares one cart, so concurrent add_to_cart and submit_order calls mix items. That is the locker bug. The second defect follows the documented rule for sysparm_also_request_for: if any person in the list doesn't qualify, the entire request is rejected. The interviewer wants a flow that avoids shared carts, pre-validates the group, and builds the form from the item metadata the API returns.

The Answer

Defect 1: shared cart. POST /api/sn_sc/servicecatalog/items/{sys_id}/add_to_cart adds to the current user's cart. POST /cart/submit_order and POST /cart/checkout check out that cart. Two students' requests interleave as add A, add B, submit, and one request contains both items. Fix it in one of two ways:

  • Use POST /items/{sys_id}/order_now for single-item orders. It orders directly, takes sysparm_quantity (required), variables and sysparm_requested_for, and returns request_number, request_id and the order's sys_id and table. No cart is involved.
  • Better: call the API as the student, using a per-user OAuth token, so each cart really belongs to one person. Access and requested-for checks then run against the student, not against the integration account.

Defect 2: all-or-nothing group order. sysparm_also_request_for takes up to 50 user sys_ids. If anyone in it doesn't qualify, the whole request is rejected. It also requires the item to have a requested_for variable with "Enable also request for" configured and the caller to have the right roles. Before ordering, call POST /items/{item_sys_id}/get_invalid_delegated_users with the same comma-separated list. It returns invalidUsers, which you remove or show to the student. For a single check, GET /items/{item_sys_id}/delegation/{user_sys_id} returns true or false.

Requested-for rules. Whether the caller can set sysparm_requested_for depends on glide.sc.req_for.roles. If that property is empty, glide.sc.req_for.roles.default decides: deny means nobody can order for others, allow means anyone can. A shared integration account with broad roles can therefore order on behalf of anyone. That is another reason to use per-user tokens.

Rendering the form. GET /items/{sys_id} returns variables, ui_policy, client_script (onLoad/onChange/onSubmit) and data_lookup. These are definitions only. The REST call doesn't run them for your React app, so dependent-question logic either has to be rebuilt or kept deliberately simple. On submit, the server enforces mandatory variables (add_to_cart returns 400 "Mandatory Variables are required") and access ("Security constraints prevent ordering of Item").

// backend, per-user token; single item
POST /api/sn_sc/servicecatalog/items/{locker_item}/order_now
{"sysparm_quantity": 1,
 "variables": {"building": "Library", "duration": "semester"}}
// group order: validate first
POST /api/sn_sc/servicecatalog/items/{lab_kit}/get_invalid_delegated_users
{"sysparm_also_request_for": "id1,id2,id3"}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • submit_order and checkout behave differently when two-step checkout is on. They return cart and order status instead of a request number. Code that expects request_number breaks when an admin enables two-step.
  • GET /items has a default sysparm_limit of 10000, and the limit is "applied before ACL evaluation". A page can come back short, or empty, even though accessible items exist further on.
  • sysparm_type on GET /items only accepts Record Producer or Order Guide. Any other value is silently ignored, so the filter does nothing.
  • Record producers use POST /items/{sys_id}/submit_producer, which returns the created record's Table API path and redirect URLs, not a cart response.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing the shared cart with a mutex in the backend. That serialises every order through one account and leaves the identity problem in place.
  • Sending only mandatory variables because the doc says "name-value pairs of all mandatory cart item variables", and losing the optional answers students gave.
  • Calling DELETE /cart/{sys_id}/empty "to be safe" before each order on a shared account. It deletes other users' in-flight items.
Score points: Connect both defects to identity. Shared credentials create a shared cart and broad requested-for rights. Then name get_invalid_delegated_users as the documented pre-check for the all-or-nothing rule.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle order guides from React (submit_guide and checkout_guide)?
  • Which catalog client script behaviours would you refuse to rebuild, and why?
  • How do you show request status back in the app after order_now?

Sources

  • Service Catalog API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A managed-service provider's support portal lists customer instances and tickets. The current widget loads all 200+ (and for some teams 14,000+) task records into data and paginates in AngularJS, so pages take minutes. You are building a server-side pagination widget like the one published on the Developer Advocate blog: configurable page size (10 to 200), page numbers with ellipses, an out-of-range page sends you to the last page, and an encoded query can be passed in the URL. Describe the server script design, the exact GlideRecord calls for the page window and the total count, and the performance and security traps.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Separate counting from fetching. Get the total with GlideAggregate, fetch one page with chooseWindow() and a deterministic sort, and know the documented interaction between chooseWindow(), setLimit() and the hidden COUNT(*). On security, never trust a query string from the URL; use the user-scoped query methods or GlideRecordSecure.

The Answer

The reasoning comes from the blog post. Client-side paging is fine for small sets, but with hundreds or thousands of rows the page waits for the full payload before rendering. Server-side paging sends only the current page. The GlideRecord reference supplies the details.

(function() {
  var table = options.table || 'task';
  var size = clamp(parseInt(input ? input.pageSize : options.page_size, 10) || 10, 10, 200);
  var userQuery = (input && input.query) || $sp.getParameter('query') || '';

  // 1. Total, counted in the database.
  var ga = new GlideAggregate(table);
  ga.addEncodedQuery(userQuery);            // validated first; see gotchas
  ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
  ga.query();
  var total = ga.next() ? parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) : 0;

  var pages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(total / size));
  var page = clamp(parseInt(input ? input.page : 1, 10) || 1, 1, pages); // 180 of 142 -> 142
  var first = (page - 1) * size;

  // 2. One page of rows.
  var gr = new GlideRecordSecure(table);
  gr.addUserEncodedQuery(userQuery);
  gr.orderByDesc('sys_updated_on');
  gr.orderBy('number');                     // tie-breaker so pages are stable
  gr.chooseWindow(first, first + size);
  gr.setNoCount();                          // skip the COUNT(*) chooseWindow would run
  gr.query();
  data.rows = [];
  while (gr.next()) {
    data.rows.push({ sys_id: gr.getUniqueValue(), number: gr.getValue('number'),
                     short_description: gr.getValue('short_description') });
  }
  data.page = page; data.pages = pages; data.total = total; data.pageSize = size;

  function clamp(n, lo, hi) { return Math.min(Math.max(n, lo), hi); }
})();

Why each line is there:

  • chooseWindow(first, last) takes a zero-based start row (inclusive) and an end row (exclusive), so chooseWindow(first, first + size) returns exactly one page. The reference notes that running a query with chooseWindow() triggers a COUNT(*), which is slow on large tables. setNoCount() skips it. Since GlideAggregate already gives the total, you do not need it twice.
  • Do not mix setLimit and chooseWindow casually. The reference says setLimit() calls chooseWindow() internally. Call chooseWindow(20,30) then setLimit(100) and you get 100 rows from row 1. The other order keeps the window. Pick one.
  • Sort with a tie-breaker. The GlideRecord tips episode says to pair paging with ordering. Without a unique final sort key, rows with equal values can move between pages. The nested-sorting episode shows orderBy() and orderByDesc() chained for multi-level order.
  • Clamp the page. The blog's widget sends page 180 of 142 to the last page. Do it on the server so a hand-edited request cannot ask for row 9,000,000.
  • Ellipsis paging is UI only. Work out the page list on the client from page and pages. No extra server work is needed.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The URL query is attacker input. addEncodedQuery() applies no ACLs and by default does not even enforce field ACLs (its enforceFieldACL argument defaults to false). The reference points to addUserEncodedQuery(), which returns only records the current user has query access to. Combine it with GlideRecordSecure so read ACLs apply to each row. A portal widget otherwise becomes a way to search any table.
  • The scoped GlideAggregate reference lists addEncodedQuery() but not the user-scoped variant, so the total is counted without the user's read ACLs. Either accept that the page count is approximate for restricted users, or write the security condition (for example company or assignment group) into the query so both reads agree.
  • Do not let the table name come from the URL. Take it from widget options or an allowlist.
  • An invalid field in the user's query is dropped and can widen the result. Validate it, or set glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows.
  • Counts and pages are separate reads. A record can be inserted between them, so the last page can be short or a row can appear twice. That is normally acceptable. Say so if the interviewer asks about consistency.
  • Large offsets still make the database skip rows. For very deep paging, keyset paging (where sys_updated_on is less than the last row's value) scales better than a growing window.
  • Page size 200 times wide rows can still be heavy. Send only display columns and load details on click.

Common Mistakes

  • Using getRowCount() on a full GlideRecord query for the total. The reference recommends GlideAggregate when you only need a count.
  • Paging without orderBy, so rows "jump" between pages.
  • Putting the whole table in data "for search" and paging the rest on the server, which brings the original problem back.
Score points: Explain the documented setLimit/chooseWindow precedence and the hidden COUNT(*) fix with setNoCount(). Then raise addUserEncodedQuery as the safe way to accept a filter from the URL.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you keep the current page in the URL so refresh and back work?
  • Would you build this as a Scripted REST or GraphQL endpoint so UI Builder can reuse it?
  • How would you test the out-of-range and empty-result cases with ATF?

Sources

  • Building a Custom Pagination Widget for Service Portal (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • 6 GlideRecord Tips to Supercharge Your ServiceNow Development (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Did You Know - Nested Sorting (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GlideRecord - Scoped (API reference)
  • GlideAggregate - Scoped (API reference)
  • GlideSPScriptable ($sp) - Scoped (API reference)

question: A software company's platform team wants incident resolvers and an AI agent to create and link Jira issues through Atlassian's MCP server instead of the old custom REST integration. The CISO will only agree if no one can point ServiceNow at an unreviewed MCP endpoint, every tool call is attributable to a ServiceNow record, and arguments are validated before they leave the instance. A developer's prototype calls new sn_wdf_mcp_client.MCPClient().getServers() and then loops over result.servers, but it throws 'Cannot read property length of undefined'. Design a governed gateway around the MCPClient API, write it, and explain the prototype failure and the identity the calls should run under.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Open with the fact that ServiceNow ships a governed MCP client (sn_wdf_mcp_client.MCPClient) and that governance is built into the platform: a server cannot be invoked until it is registered and approved through AI Control Tower. Strong answers wrap the client in one gateway that discovers, validates, invokes and audits. They code defensively against the documented response shapes, and they think about which identity makes the call, because the API requires an admin-level role.

The Answer

Prerequisites that are the governance story. The MCP Client plugin (sn_wdf_mcp_client) and the AI Governance plugin (sn_ai_governance) must be installed. Each server is a record in sn_mcp_server with a connection alias that holds its authentication. A server must pass the AI Control Tower approval workflow and reach approved status before invokeTool() will run against it. That is your answer to security: unapproved endpoints are refused by the platform, not by a convention in a script.

Call order. getServers() lists servers the caller may use (approved by default; status: "pending" shows ones awaiting review), with limit 1-200 and offset paging and a meta.total. listTools(serverId, cursor) lists tools with their input schemas and a pagination cursor. getToolInfo(serverId, toolName) returns one tool's descriptor, including inputSchema.required and annotations. invokeTool(serverId, toolName, toolArguments) calls it and returns status, server_id, tool_name and a tool-specific result.

I would put one gateway script include in front of it, so every flow and agent goes through the same validation, caching and audit:

var McpGateway = Class.create();
McpGateway.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {
        this.client = new sn_wdf_mcp_client.MCPClient();
        this.CACHE = 'mcp_tool_schema';          // defined in sys_scoped_cache (Table Row pair on sn_mcp_server)
    },

    findServer: function(name) {
        var res = this.client.getServers({ limit: 200, offset: 0 });   // approved only, by default
        var body = res.result || res;            // docs show both shapes
        var list = body.servers || [];
        for (var i = 0; i < list.length; i++)
            if (list[i].name == name && list[i].governance.aict_status == 'approved')
                return list[i].server_id;
        return null;
    },

    toolSchema: function(serverId, toolName) {
        var key = serverId + ':' + toolName;
        var hit = sn_scoped_cache.ScopedCacheManager.get(this.CACHE, key);
        if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit);

        var info = this.client.getToolInfo(serverId, toolName);         // name is case sensitive
        if (info.status != 'success') throw new Error(info.errorMessage);
        // flushes automatically when the sn_mcp_server row is updated
        sn_scoped_cache.ScopedCacheManager.putRow(this.CACHE, key,
            JSON.stringify(info.tool.inputSchema), serverId);
        return info.tool.inputSchema;
    },

    call: function(serverId, toolName, args, sourceRecord) {
        var schema = this.toolSchema(serverId, toolName);
        var missing = (schema.required || []).filter(function(p) { return !(p in args); });
        if (missing.length) throw new Error('Missing arguments: ' + missing.join(','));

        var res = this.client.invokeTool(serverId, toolName, { inputs: { toolArguments: args } });
        this._audit(sourceRecord, toolName, res.status, res.errorMessage);
        if (res.status != 'success') throw new Error(res.errorMessage);
        return res.result;                       // tool-specific shape
    },

    _audit: function(rec, tool, status, err) {
        rec.work_notes = 'MCP ' + tool + ': ' + status + (err ? ' - ' + err : '');
        rec.update();
    },
    type: 'McpGateway'
};

The tool descriptor rarely changes but is fetched over the network, so I cache it with ScopedCacheManager. putRow() ties the entry to the server's sn_mcp_server sys_id: if that record is updated, the entry is flushed automatically. That needs a cache defined in sys_scoped_cache with a table-row pair on sn_mcp_server. Cache values are strings, hence the JSON.stringify.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Response shapes disagree. getServers() is documented as returning {result: {meta, servers}}, yet its example reads result.meta.total straight off the return value. listTools() documents both next_cursor and nextCursor, and its failure object sits under result while the example checks a top-level status. That mismatch is why the prototype threw on servers. Normalise once in the gateway.
  • Who is calling. The calling user must hold sn_mcp_client.admin. Giving that role to every requester is wrong, so the gateway should run in a controlled context (for example a flow running as a dedicated system user) with the requesting user recorded in the audit note.
  • Paging tools. Large servers return tools in pages. Loop on the cursor until it is null, or a tool on page two looks "not found".
  • Case sensitivity. Tool names are case sensitive in getToolInfo() and invokeTool().
  • Argument wrapping. The documented example wraps arguments as {inputs: {toolArguments: {...}}}, and the reference says the shape is defined by the target tool's schema. Test each tool once and lock the shape in the gateway.
  • Transport. transport is documented with one value, SSE.
  • No exceptions. Failures come back as status: "error" with errorMessage (invalid server, missing tool name, tool not found, server not approved). Check the status every time.
  • Annotations from getToolInfo() are the place to look for hints such as whether a tool changes data; treat write tools differently from read tools in your approval design.

Common Mistakes

  • Hard-coding a server sys_id copied from a dev instance; sys_ids differ per instance, so resolve by name.
  • Passing the language model's raw output straight into invokeTool() without checking it against inputSchema.required.
  • Logging full tool results that contain customer data into the system log.
  • Passing status: "pending" to getServers() in production code to "make it work".
Score points: Separate discovery from invocation. Discovery (servers, tools, schemas) can be cached and reviewed; invocation is what needs approval rules, per-record audit and rate awareness.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you expose this gateway to an AI agent as a single tool rather than one tool per MCP operation?
  • A server's approval is revoked. What happens to in-flight calls and cached schemas?
  • How would you test the gateway without calling the real Jira server?

Sources

  • MCPClient
  • ScopedCacheManager

question: A pharmaceutical company is about to release its first AI features into a validated (GxP-adjacent) environment: two custom AI Skill Kit skills (deviation summary, CAPA draft) and one AI agent that triages quality events. Their QA lead says: "Our release gate is ATF. Every change needs a passing suite. How do I write an ATF test that asserts an LLM's answer is correct?" The platform owner also wants to use Now Assist to generate the ATF tests, and asks what happens when those tests start failing after upgrades. Question: Design the test and evaluation strategy for these AI features, and explain which tools you would use for which layer.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Separate deterministic behaviour (which ATF tests well) from generated content (which needs evaluation datasets, scoring and human review), and name the platform tools for each: ATF and Now Assist for Test Creation, ATF Failure Insight, Skill Kit Evaluations, and agentic evaluation runs. Be honest, too, that an LLM judge is itself a model and needs human calibration in a regulated setting.

The Answer

Do not assert generated text in ATF. An exact-match assertion on LLM output is either flaky or so loose it proves nothing. Use ATF for everything around the model and a separate evaluation layer for the model's output.

Layer 1: deterministic wiring, in ATF.

  • The skill's UI action or flow action is visible to the right roles and not to others (impersonate each persona).
  • When the skill returns, the target field is populated, the value is from the allowed choice list, and an audit work note is written.
  • When the skill fails or is disabled, the fallback works: the record saves, nothing is auto-applied, an error is logged. Drive this with a property that switches the AI call off, so the test does not depend on a live model or spend Assists.
  • For the agent, that supervised tools stop for confirmation and that the agent's run-as identity cannot read records outside its scope.

Generating those tests. Now Assist for Test Creation turns a natural-language description into ATF steps. The Developer Advocate guidance is to be specific ("create a user named John Doe and assign the itil role"), use exact values, and say whether each step creates, updates or validates. Treat the output like code from a junior: review every step, then commit it. In a validated environment, a generated test still needs a named human reviewer.

Layer 2: skill output quality, in Skill Kit. The prompt editor's Run tests shows the response and the grounded prompt; use it while developing. For release, the Evaluations tab runs a dataset against the skill and an LLM judge scores faithfulness (does the output stick to the provided data) and correctness. Build the dataset from real, anonymised deviations, including awkward ones: missing fields, very long text, contradictory notes. Keep the dataset versioned and rerun it on every prompt change, provider change and upgrade. Evaluations consume Assists, so size the dataset deliberately.

Layer 3: agent behaviour, in agentic evaluations. Agentic evaluation runs score the agent from its execution logs using an LLM judge. Task completion is scored 1-3 per record (failed, partial, complete). Tool performance is a binary score per step for whether the agent chose the right tool, and a separate check covers whether tool inputs were complete and correctly formatted. Overall results are banded: 90-100% Excellent (safe to deploy), 70-89% Good (deploy with caution), 50-69% Moderate (investigate first), 0-49% Poor (do not deploy). Make "Excellent on the agreed dataset" the release criterion, and treat a tool-performance drop as a regression even if task completion holds.

Layer 4: human calibration. The judge is an LLM. Have quality SMEs blind-score a sample of the same outputs and compare with the judge's scores before you trust it as a gate. Record that comparison as part of validation evidence.

When ATF tests break after an upgrade. ATF Failure Insight (Zurich) compares metadata between the last successful run and the failed one. From a failed result, "Find changes since the last successful run" shows a side-by-side diff. The demo cases were an impersonated user switched to one without roles and a field value changed from "2 - Medium" to "3 - Low". In the first, the error message pointed at a later step than the real cause. A "Create Task" button raises an incident (configurable to problem or any task table) with the failure details. Build Agent's Q4 2025 release also added an ATF Troubleshooting Agent that diagnoses failing tests and suggests likely fixes. Use both, but a human still decides whether the test or the app was wrong.

Production monitoring. Evaluation before release is not enough. Sample live outputs weekly, track thumbs-down or override rates, and rerun the evaluation set on every platform upgrade.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Temperature changes or a model provider swap can shift outputs without any metadata change, so Failure Insight will not see it. Only the evaluation dataset will.
  • A test that impersonates admin hides ACL problems. Generated tests often default to whatever user the prompt names, so name realistic personas.
  • Agentic evaluation reads execution logs. If a tool returns [object Object], the judge scores what the agent actually saw.
  • Evaluation datasets with real patient or employee data need the same privacy handling as production.

Common Mistakes

  • Using contains assertions on generated text and calling it coverage.
  • Calling a live LLM in every ATF run in the pipeline, which is slow, flaky and billed.
  • Treating the LLM judge's score as ground truth without human calibration.
Score points: Propose a release record that lists, per AI feature, the ATF suite result, the evaluation dataset version and score, the human calibration sample and the approver. That is what a validation auditor will ask for.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How large should the evaluation dataset be, and how do you keep it from going stale?
  • What would you do if task completion is Excellent but tool performance drops after an upgrade?
  • How would you test a prompt injection defence repeatably?
