question: A payments provider calls an unauthenticated Scripted REST endpoint in your scoped app with webhook events. Each request carries webhook-id, webhook-timestamp (Unix seconds) and webhook-signature (base64 HMAC-SHA256 over id.timestamp.body using a shared secret). A developer's pull request validates with new GlideDigest().getSHA256Base64(secret + body) == sig and stores the secret in a system property. Review this, then design verification that is correct, resists replay, and keeps the secret out of plain properties, comparing the CertificateEncryption approach from the Developer Advocate blog with KMFCryptoOperation.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Reject the pull request on two grounds: a plain hash of secret plus body is not an HMAC and will never match the provider's signature, and a valid-but-old request can be replayed. Then show which platform APIs actually compute or verify a MAC, the formatting traps around base64, and where the shared secret should live. Bringing in the blog's debugging discipline (known test vectors, exact inputs) is a strong signal.

Review of the Pull Request

  • GlideDigest creates message digests (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA512) from strings or streams. It has no key input. HMAC is a keyed construction, so SHA256(secret + body) produces a different value from HMAC-SHA256(secret, body). The check will fail for every genuine request, and someone will 'fix' it by loosening the comparison.
  • The signed content is id.timestamp.body, not just the body. Missing the id and timestamp breaks verification and also throws away the replay protection the provider designed in.
  • Storing the secret in a system property means anyone who can read properties can forge webhooks. Rotating it with gs.setProperty() also triggers the system-wide cache flush the GlideSystem reference warns about; tolerable for rare rotations, poor as a pattern.

The Answer

Option A: CertificateEncryption.generateMac, as in the Developer Advocate post on HMAC validation. The post builds id.timestamp.body, strips the provider's secret prefix, calls generateMac(secret, 'HmacSHA256', signedContent), and compares with each signature in the header after removing the v1, version prefix. The GlideSystem reference shows the same method with the key passed through gs.base64Encode() first. The blog's fourth mistake was double-encoding a secret the provider already supplied in base64, so check which form your provider gives you.

Option B: KMFCryptoOperation (sn_kmf_ns namespace, scoped and global). The key sits in a Key Management Framework cryptographic module instead of a property. MAC_GENERATION and MAC_VERIFICATION need a module with the Symmetric Authenticity purpose, and the shared secret has to be imported as that module's key. For verification, pass the received MAC with withAdditionalInput(); the reference also says you must call withOutputType('Boolean') for MAC_VERIFICATION or an exception is thrown at execution.

// Scripted REST resource (scoped). Option B sketch.
(function process(request, response) {
    var id = request.getHeader('webhook-id');
    var ts = request.getHeader('webhook-timestamp');
    var sigHeader = request.getHeader('webhook-signature') || '';
    var body = request.body.dataString;            // raw text, exactly as received

    // 1. replay window: 5 minutes
    var sent = new GlideDateTime();
    sent.setValue(parseInt(ts, 10) * 1000);        // Number = ms since epoch
    var skewMs = Math.abs(new GlideDateTime().getNumericValue() - sent.getNumericValue());
    if (isNaN(skewMs) || skewMs > 5 * 60 * 1000) {
        response.setStatus(401);
        return;
    }

    // 2. MAC verification with the key held in KMF
    var signed = id + '.' + ts + '.' + body;
    var input = toUrlSafe(gs.base64Encode(signed));  // default input format is KMFBase64
    var ok = sigHeader.split(' ').some(function (s) {
        var mac = toUrlSafe(s.split(',')[1] || '');
        var op = new sn_kmf_ns.KMFCryptoOperation('x_pay.webhook_mac', 'MAC_VERIFICATION')
            .withOutputType('Boolean')
            .withAdditionalInput(mac);
        return op.doOperation(input) === true;
    });
    if (!ok) {
        response.setStatus(401);
        return;
    }

    // 3. idempotency: record webhook-id, reject if seen before
    // ... process event ...
    response.setStatus(204);

    function toUrlSafe(b64) {
        return String(b64).replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
    }
})(request, response);

Treat this as a sketch to prove against the provider's published test vector before go-live: the exact form KMF expects for the additional MAC input, and whether padding must be kept, are things to confirm on your instance. The blog's advice applies here: test the MAC call alone with known inputs, then work outwards.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The KMF reference says base64 inputs must be URL safe (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore). Providers usually send standard base64 with + and /. Convert before handing values to KMF.
  • Default formats differ per operation. MAC_GENERATION takes KMFBase64 input and returns Formatted output, which is KMF's own wrapping, so comparing its default output with the provider's raw base64 will never match. Set withOutputFormat() deliberately if you generate rather than verify.
  • The blog re-serialises with JSON.stringify(request.body.data). That only works if the provider's JSON round-trips byte for byte; key order or whitespace changes break the MAC. Prefer the raw body string.
  • GlideDateTime.setValue() accepts a JavaScript Number as milliseconds since epoch. Timestamps in seconds need multiplying by 1000, or every request looks 50 years old.
  • The timestamp check stops old replays; storing webhook-id and rejecting repeats stops replays inside the window and also makes provider retries idempotent.
  • Return the same 401 for every failure type. Telling the caller whether the timestamp or the signature failed helps an attacker.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a digest where a MAC is required.
  • Logging the secret or the full signed content while debugging and leaving it in syslog.
  • Passing algorithm names from the provider's docs (SHA-256) instead of the name the platform method expects (HmacSHA256 in the blog's working code).
  • Running business logic before verification completes, for example parsing and inserting records, then rejecting.
Score points: Mention the URL-safe base64 requirement in the KMF reference and the mandatory withOutputType('Boolean') for MAC_VERIFICATION. Few candidates have read that far, and both cause failures that look like a wrong key.

Likely Follow-ups

  • The provider rotates secrets with a 24-hour overlap. How does your verifier accept both?
  • How would you sign outbound webhooks to a partner who verifies with your public key? (JWT_SIGN or SIGNATURE_GENERATION on an asymmetric module.)
  • What would you log on a failed verification so support can debug without exposing secrets?

Sources

  • KMFCryptoOperation - Scoped, Global
  • GlideDigest (Scoped)
  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • GlideDateTime (Scoped)
  • HMAC Validation in ServiceNow: Securing Webhook Integrations with CertificateEncryption (Developer Advocate blog)

question: An energy company must send a nightly export of about 400,000 asset readings (roughly 180 MB as JSON) to a data-lake ingestion API, and the same team needs a Scripted REST endpoint where an analytics tool downloads the latest export file. The first attempt built one giant string with JSON.stringify() in a scheduled job and ran out of memory; the second used sn_ih.JSONStreamingBuilder from a script include and failed immediately. Design the outbound and inbound halves with the documented streaming and attachment APIs, including size limits, where each API is allowed to run, and how you would keep memory flat end to end.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Know the documented constraints of the streaming builders (where they run, their size limits, how their attachments expire) and design around them: chunking, streaming from attachments rather than strings, and serving files through the response stream writer. Building 180 MB in a JavaScript string is the mistake to explain, not repeat.

The Answer

Why the second attempt failed. The JSONStreamingAPI and JSONStreamingBuilder references say you can only use these APIs within the Workflow Studio environment, in a Script step, typically passing the result to a REST step. A script include called from a scheduled job is outside that environment. XMLStreamingBuilder and XMLStreamingAPI have the same restriction.

Size limits shape the design. Payloads built this way cannot exceed 5 MB as a string or 200 MB as an attachment. Without withAttachment() you get a string through getJSONString(), so the 180 MB export must use attachment mode. Since 180 MB is close to the ceiling and data grows, split the export into chunks, for example 50,000 readings per file, and send several requests. Most ingestion APIs prefer that anyway.

// Workflow Studio Script step, inside a flow looping over chunk numbers
(function execute(inputs, outputs) {
    var ttl = new GlideDateTime();
    ttl.addSeconds(6 * 3600);                       // between 2h (default) and 48h
    var w = new sn_ih.JSONStreamingBuilder().withAttachment().expiresAt(ttl).build();
    try {
        w.startObject()
         .writeStringField('batch', inputs.batch_id)
         .writeFieldName('readings')
         .startArray();
        var gr = new GlideRecord('x_en_reading');
        gr.addQuery('u_export_chunk', inputs.chunk);
        gr.query();
        while (gr.next()) {
            w.startObject()
             .writeStringField('meter', gr.getValue('u_meter'))
             .writeStringField('ts', gr.getValue('u_read_at'))
             .writeNumberField('kwh', gr.getValue('u_kwh'))   // value passed as a string
             .endObject();
        }
        w.endArray().endObject();
        outputs.attachment_id = w.getAttachmentId();      // streaming_attachment sys_id
    } finally {
        w.close();                                         // always close the stream
    }
})(inputs, outputs);

The next step in the flow is the REST step that sends the streaming attachment. Records are written as the query iterates, so memory stays flat no matter how many rows a chunk has.

If you must stay in script. Outside Workflow Studio, the documented tool is RESTMessageV2.setRequestBodyFromAttachment(attachmentSysId), which sends an existing Attachment [sys_attachment] record as the body. You still need a way to produce that file without one giant string. Through a MID Server, the MID user must have roles to read attachment records.

Large responses. If the ingestion API returns a large receipt or error report, call saveResponseBodyAsAttachment(table, sysId, fileName) before execute() and read getResponseAttachmentSysid() afterwards. Do not call getBody() on that response; the reference says it causes an error, and to use getErrorMessage() when the save fails. An overload takes an encryption context sys_id if the file must be encrypted at rest.

Inbound download endpoint. Keep the latest export as a normal attachment on an export record and stream it out:

(function process(request, response) {
    var att = new GlideRecord('sys_attachment');
    att.addQuery('table_name', 'x_en_export');
    att.addQuery('file_name', 'latest.json');
    att.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
    att.setLimit(1);
    att.query();
    if (!att.next()) {
        response.setError(new sn_ws_err.NotFoundError('No export available.'));
        return;
    }
    response.setContentType('application/json');   // must be set before writing
    response.setStatus(200);
    response.setHeader('Content-Disposition', 'attachment; filename="latest.json"');
    var stream = new GlideSysAttachment().getContentStream(att.getUniqueValue());
    response.getStreamWriter().writeStream(stream);
})(request, response);

writeStream() copies the attachment input stream to the HTTP response, so the file never becomes a JavaScript string. The global-scope example in the reference uses new GlideSysAttachmentInputStream(sysId) instead.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • expiresAt() takes a GlideDateTime between 2 hours (the default if you do not call it) and 48 hours after creation. A flow that retries the send the next morning finds the attachment gone if you left the default.
  • getAttachmentId() returns a sys_id from the Streaming Attachments [streaming_attachment] table, not sys_attachment. Code that does GlideSysAttachment operations on it looks in the wrong table.
  • writeNumberField(fieldName, encodedValue) takes the number as a string, and writeRaw() writes text unescaped, so it can break the JSON if fed field data.
  • For RESTAPIResponseStream, content type and status must be set before writeStream() or writeString() and cannot change afterwards. setContentType() notes that a binary response without a content type fails with a 500.
  • Each REST step call is still bound by the receiving API's limits. Chunk size should come from their documentation, not from the 200 MB ceiling.
  • Call close() in a finally block. The reference marks it required.

Common Mistakes

  • Using getJSONString() for anything near 5 MB.
  • Reading the whole export with GlideSysAttachment.getContent() into a string in the download endpoint.
  • Leaving pretty print on for machine-to-machine payloads; enablePrettyPrint() adds bytes nobody reads.
Score points: Point out the operational advantage of the flow version: each chunk is a step with its own execution record, so a failure on chunk 6 of 8 can be retried alone. That matters more at 2 a.m. than the elegance of the script.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you make the export restartable if the flow fails halfway?
  • When would you push these readings to a Kafka topic with Stream Connect instead of a nightly file?
  • How would you protect the download endpoint, and should it require ACLs on the attachment?

Sources

  • JSONStreamingAPI
  • JSONStreamingBuilder
  • XMLStreamingAPI
  • XMLStreamingBuilder
  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTResponseV2 - Scoped, Global
  • RESTAPIResponseStream - Scoped, Global
  • RESTAPIResponse - Scoped, Global
  • Beyond JSON: Working with Binary Files and Alternative Content Types in ServiceNow REST APIs

question: A healthcare group's HR SaaS platform pushes worker changes to ServiceNow as JSON: normally a few hundred a day, but up to 5,000 in bursts after a reorganisation. The team is choosing between three designs for the receiving Scripted REST endpoint: (a) write rows to an import set table and let a transform map run, (b) call sn_impex.RTETransformer with an ETL definition, or (c) parse the JSON and write to sys_user and cmn_department with GlideRecord. The security team also requires a per-message audit trail, and support wants to see why a given worker failed. Question: Compare the options, show how you would use RTETransformer, and explain what you would not copy from the reference example.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Explain what RTETransformer is for (transform an array of messages into records using an ETL definition from the Robust Transform Engine), what each constructor argument controls, and what transform() returns per message. Weigh it against classic import sets and direct writes on auditability, error reporting and performance, and notice that the reference example will not run as written.

The Answer

Option (c), direct GlideRecord, is fastest to write and worst to operate: no staging record, no row-level status, and every mapping rule lives in code. It fails the audit requirement unless you rebuild logging yourself.

Option (a), import set + transform map, gives a staging row per message, coalesce, transform scripts and an import log. Run the transform with GlideImportSetTransformer (synchronously with setSyncImport(true) if the caller needs the outcome) and log with GlideImportLog. It is well understood, but a flat transform map gets awkward when one message must produce records in several tables.

Option (b), RTETransformer, takes the same idea and drives it from an ETL definition (sys_rte_eb_etl_definition) that can map one message into more than one target table.

  • new sn_impex.RTETransformer(transformDefinitionId, verboseLogging, source, batchSize): the ETL definition sys_id; whether to enable verbose logging and the creation of import set rows for debugging; the name stored on the import set record; and how many messages to process per batch (10 messages with batch size 2 run as five batch jobs).
  • transform(messages) takes an array of stringified JSON objects whose field names "must match the field/path of the source entity fields".
  • It returns an array of results. Each has data keyed by target table (each entry with the record sys_id and the mapped fields), status (such as processed or error), message (null on success, the error text otherwise), and sourceRecordSysId, the sys_id of the row in JSON Event Sink (imp_json_event_sink).
(function process(request, response) {
  var events = request.body.data;                      // array of worker objects
  if (!Array.isArray(events) || events.length == 0) {
    response.setStatus(400); response.setBody({ error: 'expected a JSON array' }); return;
  }
  var messages = events.map(function (e) { return JSON.stringify(e); });
  var verbose = gs.getProperty('x_hc_hr.rte.verbose', 'false') == 'true';
  var rte = new sn_impex.RTETransformer(ETL_WORKER_ID, verbose, 'HRSaaS worker feed', 200);

  var results = rte.transform(messages), out = [], failed = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < results.length; i++) {
    var r = results[i];
    var ok = String(r.status).toUpperCase() == 'PROCESSED';
    if (!ok) failed++;
    out.push({
      worker: events[i] ? events[i].worker_id : null,  // assumes one result per message, in order
      status: r.status,
      message: r.message,
      sink_row: r.sourceRecordSysId,
      user: (r.data && r.data.sys_user && r.data.sys_user.length) ? r.data.sys_user[0].sys_id : null
    });
  }
  response.setStatus(failed ? 207 : 200);
  response.setBody({ processed: results.length, failed: failed, results: out });
})(request, response);

For the audit trail, the event sink row per message is the record of what arrived; keep the per-message result in your response and, for failures, in your own log table keyed on the worker id and sink row.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The reference example does not compile: two gs.log() calls are missing a closing parenthesis and the wrapper function is never closed or invoked. It also wraps the code in a CTIOperationRequest signature. Write your own resource script rather than pasting it.
  • The reference shows status as PROCESSED in the output while describing it as "processed or error". Compare case-insensitively and treat anything other than processed as a failure.
  • The reference does not promise that results come back in input order. Map failures back through sourceRecordSysId and the sink row if the order matters for your audit, and test it with a deliberately bad message in the middle of a batch.
  • Verbose logging creates import set rows for every message. Turn it on in sub-production or behind a property for diagnosis, not permanently on a 5,000-message burst.
  • A 5,000-message burst in one REST call is a long transaction. Have the sender page at a few hundred per call, or accept the payload, store it, and process it from a scheduled job.
  • If any target were a CMDB class, neither RTE nor a transform map should write it directly; send CIs through IdentificationEngine.createOrUpdateCI().
  • If a partner sends CSV instead of JSON, sn_impex.CSVParser.parseLineToObject(line, headers) turns each line into an object you can stringify into the same message array; it handles quoted fields with embedded commas.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing direct GlideRecord writes for speed and then building a homemade staging table to satisfy audit.
  • Returning 200 for the whole batch when some messages failed. Return per-message status (207 or a body with failures) so the sender can retry only what failed.
  • Passing objects to transform(). The parameter is an array of stringified JSON.
Score points: Point out the broken reference example and the status casing difference, then show defensive result handling. It tells the interviewer you test what you copy.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you retry a single failed worker without resending the batch?
  • How do you version an ETL definition between instances?
  • Where does a transform map still beat RTE?

Sources

  • RTETransformer API reference
  • GlideImportSetTransformer API reference
  • GlideImportLog API reference
  • CSVParser API reference

question: An audit at a domain-separated managed service provider finds a single integration account, svc_integrations, with admin. It is used by the ITSM sync with a customer's Jira, the CMDB collector posting to IRE, the document scanner that attaches PDFs to cases, the GitHub CICD pipeline, and a reporting extract. When the auditors removed admin in a sub-production clone, half the integrations broke in confusing ways, including a Jira sync that suddenly saw no records for tenant B and attachments that returned 404. Design the replacement security model using what the REST reference says about each API, and explain how you would prove what roles the new accounts actually hold.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A good answer splits the work across purpose-built accounts with the documented minimum role per API. It explains the domain behaviour behind the tenant B symptom and the attachment 404, avoids the anonymous-access shortcuts the reference warns about, and verifies effective roles with the User Role Inheritance API. API keys bound to service accounts with access policies earn extra credit.

The Answer

Why things broke.

  • Tenant B invisible. Table API reads respect domain separation. sysparm_query_no_domain defaults to false, which excludes records in domains the user is not configured for. The parameter is only available to system administrators or users with query_no_domain_table_api. With admin gone, either the account's domain no longer covers tenant B or the sync was passing sysparm_query_no_domain=true and lost the right to use it. The right fix is to put the account in the correct domain, or run one account per tenant. Granting query_no_domain_table_api to a cross-tenant sync account should be a deliberate, documented exception.
  • Attachment 404s. POST /now/attachment/file returns 404 when the target record "does not exist or is not accessible to the current user". The reference says the account needs the roles required to create sys_attachment records and to read and write the target table. There is no out-of-box "attach" role, so create one if needed.
  • Silent partial reads. Table API sysparm_limit is applied before ACL evaluation, so a less privileged account can get short or empty pages. That is easy to misread as "no data".

Replacement model, one account per integration.

  • svc_jira_sync: the roles needed for incident read and write (for example itil) in the right domain. Use PATCH with explicit sysparm_fields.
  • svc_cmdb_collector: the reference requires itil or asset for IRE. Data-source choice values plus reconciliation rules limit what this source can overwrite. No Table API writes to cmdb_ci*.
  • svc_doc_scanner: a custom attachment role plus write access to the case table, nothing else.
  • svc_cicd: sn_cicd.sys_ci_automation, which the CICD API accepts instead of admin. It should exist only on instances the pipeline deploys to.
  • svc_reporting: read-only roles on the reported tables. The Aggregate API honours read access based on role ownership, so check grouped counts with this account, not yours.

Things I would refuse: adding tables to sys_public.list to "make imports work" (the Import Set reference says that allows access without authentication, and ACLs still apply but are the admin's responsibility), and lending these accounts the CMDB Data Ingestion API's cmdb_import_api_admin for a deprecated endpoint.

Credentials. From Washington DC onward, inbound REST API keys can be bound to a service account and scoped through REST API Access Policies to a specific API, method, resource or version. The Developer Advocate blog walks through this with the Table API and recommends a non-person service account so a leaver does not break the integration. One key per integration, each tied to its own account, gives you revocation without collateral damage.

Proving effective roles. Direct grants are only part of the picture, because roles also arrive through other roles and through groups. GET /api/global/user_role_inheritance?user_sysid=<sys_id> returns from_role (granted directly or inherited from roles, as paths like /cloud_user/pa_viewer) and from_group (as [Group]/role paths). Run it for each service account in a scheduled audit job and diff the output against an approved baseline. The caller needs user_admin, and the plugin com.glide.role_management.inh_count.rest_api (or the older Role Management Enhancements REST API plugin) must be active.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Encrypted fields: writes need sysparm_input_display_value=true and the encryption context. Reads hide the field without the context. Removing admin can change payloads without any error.
  • Batch API items are each evaluated against ACLs, so a least-privilege batch can return mixed 200s and 403s.
  • Group membership can quietly re-grant broad roles. The from_group output is where that shows up.
  • The reference describes the CICD Application Operation Queue as inspected and paused by a user with the admin role. Keep that with a human operator rather than the pipeline account.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing least privilege with an admin session, or impersonation that inherits elevated rights.
  • One shared account, so one leaked secret exposes every integration.
  • Fixing domain visibility with sysparm_query_no_domain everywhere.
Score points: Tie each symptom to a documented rule (domain default, "not accessible" 404, limit-before-ACL), name the minimum role per API, and close with a User Role Inheritance diff as continuous evidence for the auditors.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate API keys without downtime?
  • Would you use OAuth client credentials for the pipeline instead of an API key? Why?
  • How would you detect an integration account being used interactively?

Sources

  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Attachment API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Identification and Reconciliation API (Brazil REST reference)
  • CICD API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Aggregate API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Import Set API (Brazil REST reference)
  • User Role Inheritance API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Inbound REST API Keys (Developer Advocate blog)

What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A senior reviewer reads the Table API reference into this code: display values going out and actual values coming back in, a full-record PUT, a typo that makes the query match everything, paging that stops on a short page, and 404 meaning "not found or not visible". Then give a corrected design, not just a list of defects.

Diagnosis

  1. Typo widens the query to the whole table. statte is not a field. By default the instance ignores the invalid part of an encoded query and runs the rest, so q becomes "all changes ordered by number". That is the test run that updated every change. Fix the field name. Add a count guard on X-Total-Count, and consider glide.invalid_query.returns_no_rows=true after an instance-wide impact review, because it affects lists and GlideRecord.query() as well.
  2. Date drift. With sysparm_display_value=true, date fields come back in the authenticated user's time zone. The code writes them back with the default sysparm_input_display_value=false, and with false "the date and time value is inserted using the GMT timezone". A 10:00 local value is stored as 10:00 UTC. Every round trip shifts the record by the offset again. That is the drift.
  3. Lost assignment groups. With display values on, reference fields arrive as names ("Network CAB"). The PUT sends the whole object back as actual values, so a group name is written where a sys_id is expected, because false stores input "without manipulation". Choice fields get the same treatment: the label, not the stored value.
  4. Full-object PUT. The code sends every field it read, including read-only and sys_ fields, just to change one date. That widens the blast radius of defects 2 and 3 to the whole record and fires business rules on unrelated field changes. Send a PATCH with only start_date.
  5. Paging stops early and drifts. sysparm_limit is applied before ACL evaluation, so a page can come back with fewer than 500 rows, or none, even though more records follow. The loop then exits. Ordering by number is stable, but rows changing state during the run move in and out of the filter, so offsets shift. Follow the Link header's rel="next", compare against X-Total-Count, and snapshot the sys_ids first if you must update while iterating.
  6. Partner 404s. Single-record GET, PUT and PATCH return 404 when the item is not found, and in a domain-separated instance sysparm_query_no_domain defaults to false, which excludes records outside the user's domains. Changes that "exist" in another domain are invisible to this account. Also check that the sys_id is not a display value object, which is defect 3 in another form.
  7. Minor issues. No sysparm_fields, so every column is fetched. No encodeURIComponent on the query. Updates are serial with no error handling or retry. cal.start is assumed to be in the right format and zone.

Corrected Version

const base = INSTANCE + '/api/now/table/change_request';
const q = encodeURIComponent('state=-2^ORDERBYsys_id');   // use the stored value for Scheduled; verify on your instance
let url = `${base}?sysparm_query=${q}` +
  '&sysparm_fields=sys_id,number,start_date,sys_updated_on' +
  '&sysparm_display_value=false&sysparm_exclude_reference_link=true&sysparm_limit=500';
const targets = []; let expected;
while (url) {
  const res = await get(url);                         // returns {body, headers, links}
  expected ??= Number(res.headers['x-total-count']);
  targets.push(...res.body.result);
  url = res.links.next || null;                      // Link header rel="next"
}
if (expected > MAX_EXPECTED) throw new Error('filter too wide: ' + expected);
for (const chg of targets) {
  const cal = partner.lookup(chg.number);
  if (!cal || !cal.startUtc || cal.startUtc === chg.start_date) continue;
  await patch(`${base}/${chg.sys_id}?sysparm_fields=sys_id`,
              {start_date: cal.startUtc},              // 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss' in UTC
              {'X-no-response-body': 'true'});
}

Reads and writes now both use actual values: UTC dates and sys_ids. Nothing depends on the service account's profile. The PATCH carries one field, and an unchanged date skips the write entirely, which keeps the audit trail and business rules quiet.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • If the partner can only deal in local time, use sysparm_input_display_value=true deliberately and pin the integration user's time zone. That adds an operational dependency, so document it.
  • The stored value behind "Scheduled" is instance data. Confirm it rather than trusting a blog. Name-value filters such as &state=scheduled accept display values, but cannot be combined with sysparm_query.
  • sysparm_fields ignores invalid names silently. A typo there loses columns without an error, the mirror image of defect 1.
  • A pinned /api/now/v1/ path returns 404 for an empty multi-record GET, while v2 returns 200 with an empty array. Check which version the client uses before trusting a 404.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing the drift by subtracting the offset in code, which breaks again at daylight-saving changes.
  • Switching to PATCH but still sending the whole object.
  • Treating empty pages as the end of the data.
Score points: Explain the drift precisely: display value out in user time, actual value in as GMT, repeated on every round trip. Pair it with the ignored-invalid-query rule as the cause of the "updated everything" incident.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you make the partner-to-ServiceNow direction conflict-safe? (Compare sys_updated_on or sys_mod_count before writing.)
  • Would an Import Set with a transform map be a better inbound path here?
  • How would you repair the drifted dates already in production?

Sources

  • Table API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A payments company deploys its card-authorisation service from GitLab about 60 times a week. The CAB has agreed that a pre-approved standard change template, "Deploy card-auth microservice", covers these releases, but only if the pipeline (1) raises the change from that template, (2) links the Kubernetes cluster CIs it touches, (3) proves there is no clash with a blackout window or another change on those CIs before it deploys, and (4) closes the change with the outcome. A contractor's first version raised the change and immediately deployed; the audit team found 11 deployments that overlapped a freeze. You are asked to redesign the pipeline stage using only the Change Management REST API (sn_chg_rest). Walk through the exact sequence of calls, how the pipeline should wait on the asynchronous parts, and what it should do when the conflict check finds something.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to see that you know which parts of the Change Management API are synchronous and which hand you a worker or a job to poll. CI association, impacted-service refresh and scheduling all return a worker. Conflict checking starts a process that you query separately. A pipeline that ignores this will gate on data that hasn't been written yet, and that is exactly how the contractor's version deployed into a freeze. They also want a clear policy for what the pipeline does with a conflict: stop, reschedule, or escalate. Silently carrying on is not one of the options.

The Answer

  1. Look up the template once, not per run. GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/standard/template accepts name-value filters or sysparm_query. Cache the template sys_id in the pipeline's variables so a renamed template fails loudly instead of matching the wrong record.
  2. Create the change. POST /api/sn_chg_rest/change/standard/{standard_change_template_id} creates exactly one standard change (multiple creations per call are not supported). Pass the overrides you are allowed to change, such as short_description with the pipeline ID, and planned start/end. Then read __meta.ignoredFields in the response. Description, backout plan, test plan and implementation plan cannot be overridden from a template, and the API drops read-only or unknown fields without failing the call.
  3. Associate the CIs and wait for the worker. POST /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/ci with association_type: "affected", cmdb_ci_sys_ids (array or comma-separated string) and refresh_impacted_services: true. It returns 202 with a worker.link. Poll GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/worker/{sys_id} until state.display_value is Complete or Error, and fail the stage on anything in messages.errorMessages (for example, an invalid CI sys_id).
  4. Start the conflict check. Only once the CIs are in place, call POST /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/conflict. The result is the sys_id of the conflict-checking process.
  5. Poll the result. GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/conflict returns job_status, last_run, record_count, status and a conflicts array. Wait until the job has finished and last_run is later than the time you started it. Then decide based on the conflicts array.
  6. On conflict: reschedule rather than force. PATCH /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{change_sys_id}/schedule/first_available with duration_in_seconds (and optionally a UTC planned_start_time) moves the change to the first free slot. It also returns a worker, and the worker's messages.infoMessages tells you either that the change was updated or "No slots found for N days from now". At that point the pipeline parks and posts the new planned start back to the merge request. It does not deploy.
  7. Close. After deployment, call GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{change_sys_id}/nextstates. For model-driven changes this shows each transition's conditions and whether they have passed. Then PATCH /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id} with the target state and the closure fields that the transition requires.
# poll helper used for every worker (bash + jq)
wait_worker() {
  link="$1"
  for i in $(seq 1 60); do
    s=$(curl -s -u "$SN_USER:$SN_PASS" -H "Accept: application/json" "$link" \
        | jq -r '.result.state.display_value')
    [ "$s" = "Complete" ] && return 0
    [ "$s" = "Error" ] && return 1
    sleep 5
  done
  return 1
}

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The worker state.value is a number from 1 to 4. The reference lists the labels Complete, Error, In-Progress and Waiting, but its own example returns value: 1 with display_value: "Waiting". Compare on display_value, not on a guessed numeric order.
  • Don't rely on the conflict status string either. The field note says it is set to "Conflict" even when there are no conflicts, and the "no conflicts" example shows exactly that: status: "Conflict" with an empty conflicts array. The array is the signal.
  • If a stale run is still going when the pipeline retries, DELETE /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id}/conflict cancels it.
  • GET .../schedule and first_available need the change to have a CI. The GET variant also needs planned start and end, and returns 400 if they are missing. first_available returns 403 if the integration user can't write the planned dates. Both need the sn_change_writer role, which is separate from the itil/change_manager roles listed for the basic CRUD endpoints.
  • The search window defaults to 90 days and is controlled by change.conflict.next_available.schedule_window.
  • planned_start_time is UTC in yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss. A runner in a different timezone that sends local time will schedule at the wrong hour.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting the conflict check straight after the CI POST. The association hasn't been written yet, so the check runs against no CIs and comes back clean.
  • Treating HTTP 200 from POST .../conflict as "no conflicts". It only means the process started.
  • Putting the implementation plan in the template POST and assuming it was saved. It ends up in __meta.ignoredFields.
  • Using one shared admin account. GET needs only itil or sn_change_read, POST/PATCH need itil or change_manager, DELETE needs change_manager. Scope the service account to what the stage actually does.
Score points: Say plainly that three different async patterns are involved (CI worker, conflict job, scheduling worker) and that the pipeline must wait on each before it moves on. Then point out the two traps in the reference (the worker state numbering versus its example, and a conflict status of "Conflict" even when nothing clashes), and say how your code avoids depending on either.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you cap total wait time so a stuck worker doesn't hold a runner for an hour?
  • When would you switch from this hand-built flow to DevOps Change Velocity's changeControl callback?
  • How do you keep the cached template sys_id correct across clones from production to sub-production?

Sources

  • Change Management API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A retail bank runs 400 Jenkins pipelines. The platform team has two proposals for change control. Proposal A extends an in-house Groovy library that calls the Change Management API (sn_chg_rest) directly to create, poll and close changes. Proposal B adopts DevOps Change Velocity and uses the DevOps API's orchestration endpoints. Security has also raised a concern: the existing Jenkins credentials store a ServiceNow username and password, and they want token-based access per tool. Compare the two approaches at the API level: how the pipeline learns that a change was approved, how the change gets closed, what authentication each supports, and which failure modes each introduces. Recommend one and justify it.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The main difference is who waits. With sn_chg_rest the pipeline owns the change lifecycle and has to poll. With the DevOps API the pipeline registers a callbackURL, and the instance calls Jenkins back once the change decision is made. You should also know the DevOps API's v2 token header and the odd rule that Basic Auth wins if both are sent. Bring up the restrictions on changeRequestDetails and on closing through changeInfo, and that DevOps Change Velocity is a Store application with its own prerequisites (tools, steps, change control enabled on the app stage).

The Answer

Proposal A: Change Management API. The library creates the change (POST /api/sn_chg_rest/change or the standard-template endpoint), associates CIs, runs conflict checks, then loops on GET /api/sn_chg_rest/change/{sys_id} until the state shows it is approved, and finally PATCHes it closed. Authentication is whatever the instance supports for REST; the reference lists Basic credentials in its examples and doesn't define a tool token. You get full control and full responsibility: polling intervals, timeouts, executors held while waiting, and closure logic, all repeated across 400 pipelines through a shared library.

Proposal B: DevOps API.

  • GET /api/sn_devops/devops/orchestration/changeControl?toolId=...&orchestrationTaskName=... tells the step whether it is under change control (changeControl: true/false). testConnection=true checks the round trip.
  • POST /api/sn_devops/devops/orchestration/changeControl?toolId=...&toolType=jenkins registers a callback. Required body: callbackURL, orchestrationTaskURL, and orchestrationTaskDetails.triggerType (scm, upstream or user; upstreamTaskExecutionURL is required for upstream). The instance calls callbackURL when the approval process completes, and the job continues or stops. It returns 201.
  • changeRequestDetails in that body sets fields used when the change is closed. It must not contain impact, number, risk, risk_impact_analysis or sys_id; any of these gives a 400. setCloseCode defaults to true, which writes the job status to close_code and a step-execution link to close_notes.
  • GET /devops/orchestration/changeInfo (toolId and buildNumber required, plus pipelineName/stageName for non-Freestyle jobs) returns the change number, state, approvers and planned dates for a build. Pass branchName for multibranch pipelines or "the response may include incorrect change details".
  • PUT /devops/orchestration/changeInfo/{changeInfo}?changeRequestNumber=CHG... updates fields. For state, only cancel (from Implement, with reason) and closed (from Implement or post-implement, with close_code and close_notes) are supported.
  • Auth: from v2, Authorization: sn_devops.DevOpsToken <tool_sys_id>:<tool_token>, with the token copied from the tool record. If Basic credentials are also sent, Basic Auth takes precedence. If the devops.system user is missing, the property "Switch to this user after token based authentication is successful" maps to a user with sn_devops.integration.

Recommendation: B. The callback releases the executor instead of a polling loop occupying it. Closure is standardised. Security gets per-tool tokens that can be rotated on the tool record. Keep sn_chg_rest for the few cases DevOps doesn't model, such as a standard-change template that a non-Jenkins job raises, or conflict checks.

curl -X POST "https://instance.service-now.com/api/sn_devops/v2/devops/orchestration/changeControl?toolId=$TOOL_ID&toolType=jenkins" \
  -H "Authorization: sn_devops.DevOpsToken $TOOL_ID:$TOOL_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '{"orchestrationTaskURL":"'"$JOB_URL"'",
       "callbackURL":"'"$CALLBACK"'",
       "orchestrationTaskDetails":{"triggerType":"scm","message":"commit '"$GIT_SHA"'"},
       "changeRequestDetails":{"setCloseCode":true}}'

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Jenkins must be able to receive the callback. If callbackURL isn't reachable from the instance, the step has nothing to resume it and waits until a job timeout stops it, so set one. That is a network design task, not a code fix.
  • Setting changeRequestDetails fields that have their own mandatory dependencies doesn't fail at registration. It fails later, during pipeline processing: the change is cancelled and the reason goes into work notes.
  • Leaving an old Basic credential in the Jenkins global config quietly defeats the token, because Basic wins.
  • The orchestration task must already exist (through discovery or POST /devops/orchestration/stepMapping) and be linked to a step with change control enabled. Otherwise there is nothing for the callback to bind to.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing A because "it's just REST" and underestimating 400 copies of polling and timeout logic.
  • Sending risk in changeRequestDetails to "help" the risk calculation and getting 400s.
  • Omitting branchName on multibranch jobs and gating on another branch's change.
Score points: Describe it as "poll versus callback" and attach the operational cost to each. Then mention the Basic-over-token precedence rule. Security teams care about it, and few candidates know it.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate tool tokens without breaking running builds?
  • What happens to a registered callback if the Jenkins controller restarts mid-approval?
  • How do you report change lead time when some pipelines use A and some use B during migration?

Sources

  • DevOps API (Brazil REST reference)
  • Change Management API (Brazil REST reference)

question: A facilities company is rebuilding its desk-booking front end in UI Builder and also keeps a Service Portal view. Today both call a 'kitchen sink' Scripted REST API that returns every reservation with dot-walked requester and location details. Mobile users complain about payload size, and the portal team keeps asking for new endpoint variants (summary, detail, manager view). The architect proposes a custom GraphQL API instead. Make the case for or against with specifics: how ServiceNow GraphQL schemas map to records, why GraphQL can do less server work per request, what it costs, how you test and introspect it, and the operational traps (error handling, introspection properties, outbound GraphQL).
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Explain that in GraphQL the server publishes what it can return and the client picks what it gets. Resolvers only run for the fields requested. That saves database work and payload size, and removes the need for a new endpoint per view. Be honest about the costs too: routing queries to resolvers is not free, a hand-tuned REST endpoint can still be faster, and errors usually come back with HTTP 200. And know GraphQL Explorer and the two introspection properties.

The Answer

I would back the proposal, with conditions. The Developer Advocate post "Using GraphQL APIs for Better Performance" makes the case using almost this exact Scripted REST endpoint. It loops over records and builds caller and assigned_to objects through dot-walks for every row. That payload is rigid. Every consumer gets every field, and every row pays for two sys_user lookups whether the view shows them or not. New views mean new code.

A schema describes the shape instead, using @source to map GraphQL fields to record fields and reference values:

type Query { reservations(conditions: String): [Reservation] }
type Reservation {
  sysId: GlideElement @source(value: "sys_id")
  number: GlideElement @source(value: "number")
  requester: User @source(value: "requested_for.value")
  location: Location @source(value: "location.value")
}
type User { name: GlideElement @source(value: "name") email: GlideElement @source(value: "email") }
type GlideElement {
  value: String! @source(value: "value")
  displayValue: String! @source(value: "display_value")
}

With resolvers and resolver mappings in place, the mobile summary asks only for number { value } and location { name { value } }. The manager view asks for requester details too. Same endpoint, different queries. The post spells out the performance effect. If displayValue is not requested, getDisplayValue() is not called. If requester is not requested, there is no dot-walk and no sys_user query. GraphQL works out which resolvers to run and runs the minimum. Nested types also let one round trip return what a screen needs, which shortens the request waterfall that slows UIs.

The costs, stated honestly. The same post admits that a well-tuned REST API may beat a well-tuned GraphQL API, because routing a query to resolvers has a cost. GraphQL wins on typical, real-world endpoints, not on a carefully tuned one. You also take on schema design, resolver code, and versioning discipline.

Testing and discovery. GraphQL Explorer (System Web Services, GraphQL, GraphQL Explorer) is based on GraphiQL. It has prettify, merge fragments, history, variables and headers panes, and tabs. Name your operations (query activeReservations { ... }). Named queries label the tab, and with several named queries in one tab, Execute asks which one to run. Introspection, which feeds the Docs panel, is off by default. glide.graphql.introspection_enabled controls custom schemas, and glide.graphql.glide_record_schema.introspection_enabled controls the built-in GlideRecord schema. The Explorer post warns that turning on the latter can add about a minute to Explorer load time for everyone on the instance.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Errors with 200 OK. The Explorer post says most responses return HTTP 200, so clients must check the errors in the response body, not the status code. UI Builder data resources and portal code both need this.
  • Deep queries. Letting the client choose also lets it ask for a lot (all reservations, every nested field). Require condition arguments, cap result size in resolvers, and keep the GlideRecord schema's introspection off in production.
  • ACLs. Decide whether resolvers use GlideRecordSecure. A flexible API that skips ACLs is a flexible data leak.
  • Outbound GraphQL. In the TechNow Washington DC Q&A, the advocates explained that GraphQL requests are HTTP POSTs with a JSON payload (the query plus variables). Calling a third-party GraphQL API from a spoke or script therefore means building that JSON body. Explorer is for testing inbound schemas only.
  • Caching. POST-based queries do not benefit from simple HTTP caching the way GET resources do. Plan caching in the client or the resolvers.
  • Keep both front ends on the same API. That was the reason the author moved logic out of widget server scripts in the first place: reuse when the front-end framework changes.

Common Mistakes

  • Porting the kitchen-sink logic into a single resolver that always dot-walks, which loses the benefit.
  • Turning on GlideRecord schema introspection in production "for the developers".
  • Treating HTTP 200 as success.
Score points: Say "the server declares what it can return, the client decides what it gets", then tie that to concrete savings: no getDisplayValue and no sys_user query when those fields are not requested. Then volunteer the REST-can-still-win caveat and the 200-with-errors trap.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you paginate a GraphQL list field?
  • How would you handle mutations (create and cancel a booking) and their validation?
  • How would you keep the schema backward compatible as fields are renamed?

Sources

  • Using GraphQL APIs for Better Performance (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GraphQL Explorer in Washington D.C. (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Two ways to save multiple GraphQL Queries in GraphQL Explorer (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • TechNow Ep 97: Washington D.C. Q&A (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • RESTAPIResponse - Scoped, Global (API reference)

question: A bank's problem-management team has a nightly script that takes 3 hours and often hits the transaction timeout. It loops over 280,000 problem records, runs an incident query per problem to see whether any active incidents are linked, computes how long each linked incident has been open in JavaScript with GlideDateTime, and finally collects problem sys_ids into an array to update a flag with addQuery('sys_id', 'IN', ids), checking getRowCount() to log how many were flagged. The log says 100 every night. Diagnose every performance and correctness problem and redesign the job using platform APIs that push work to the database.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants you to spot the N+1 query pattern and replace it with set-based queries: addJoinQuery() or RLQUERY to filter problems by related incidents, GlideAggregate to count per problem in one query, and GlideDBFunctionBuilder to compute values in SQL instead of JavaScript.

The correctness trap is the "100 every night": getRowCount() with more than 100 sys_ids in an IN clause is wrong unless you disable the sys_id optimisation. At Expert level you should know that by name.

The Answer

Diagnosis.

N+1 queries. 280,000 problems means 280,001 queries before any computation. Each incident query is cheap; the round trips are not.

Row-by-row date maths in JavaScript. Loading every linked incident and building GlideDateTime objects moves data out of the database that the database could compute.

The count of 100. The GlideRecord reference describes an optimisation that avoids an extra query when you pass a large sys_id list. If the list exceeds glide.db.first_pass_sys_id_list_size.max (default 100) and you do not call disableSysIdInOptimization(), "the returned value from GlideRecord.getRowCount() may be incorrect." The reference also says to call next() before getRowCount() in this case. The job may be flagging the right rows and logging the wrong number; you cannot tell from the log.

Redesign, step 1: problems that have active incidents, in one query. addJoinQuery() adds a subquery. The reference is careful: it is "not a true database join", the result set is limited by the related table, but you only get fields from the base table. That is all this step needs.

var prob = new GlideRecord('problem');
prob.addActiveQuery();
var sub = prob.addJoinQuery('incident', 'sys_id', 'problem_id');
sub.addCondition('active', true);
prob.query();
// Flag them set-based instead of collecting sys_ids
// (or reuse the same conditions with updateMultiple, see below)

The Developer Advocate post on RLQUERY and addJoinQuery() shows the encoded-query alternative, for example ^RLQUERYsys_user_grmember.group,>=1,m2m^user.active=true^ENDRLQUERY, which also lets you say "at least N related rows". Its tip for getting the syntax right is to build the related-list condition in a report and copy the encoded query.

Step 2: per-problem counts in one query.

var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addActiveQuery();
ga.addNotNullQuery('problem_id');
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.groupBy('problem_id');
ga.query();
var counts = {};
while (ga.next()) {
    counts[ga.getValue('problem_id')] = parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10);
}

Step 3: compute open duration in the database. GlideDBFunctionBuilder builds an SQL function that you attach with addFunction(), filter on with addQuery(), and read with getValue(). The reference shows datediff() taking two date/time fields. Note what its documented example measures: opened_at to sys_updated_on, which is time to the last update, not time open until now. The builder documents no current-time function, so if you need age as of the run, test on your instance whether a constant can stand in for now, or bucket by age with date filters on opened_at instead.

var fb = new GlideDBFunctionBuilder();
var openFor = fb.datediff();
openFor = fb.field('sys_updated_on');
openFor = fb.field('opened_at');
openFor = fb.build();

var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
inc.addActiveQuery();
inc.addNotNullQuery('problem_id');
inc.addFunction(openFor);
inc.setCategory('reporting');          // only if Secondary Database Pools is active
inc.query();
while (inc.next()) {
    var duration = inc.getValue(openFor);   // computed by the database
    // aggregate per problem_id in memory if needed
}

Step 4: the flag update. Do not collect sys_ids at all. Run updateMultiple() on a GlideRecord built with the same join query, using setValue() for the flag. If you keep a sys_id list for some reason, call disableSysIdInOptimization() before relying on getRowCount(), and log the count from a GlideAggregate instead.

Read replica. setCategory() routes the query to a secondary database when the Secondary Database Pools plugin is active and a matching category exists in sys_db_category. Results can lag the primary slightly, which is acceptable for a nightly report. Writes, including update(), always go to the primary.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • addJoinQuery() defaults primaryField to sys_id and joinTableField to the first reference field on the join table that points at your table; name both explicitly so a new reference field does not change the join.
  • Function results have database-specific behaviour: dayofweek() works on MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server only, and on Oracle needs NLS_TERRITORY set to a Sunday-first territory. Check the format of datediff() output on your instance before you depend on units.
  • position() returns 0 when the term is not found and NULL if a required argument is NULL; substring() and position() map to SQL functions, not JavaScript ones.
  • GlideAggregate orderBy() adds the field to the group-by list, so ordering by something other than the grouped field changes the groups.
  • GlideQuery converts results to JavaScript objects, and its reference warns this can be slower on loops over many records; it is not the tool for the 280,000-row pass.

Common Mistakes

  • Optimising the inner query with indexes while keeping 280,000 round trips.
  • Expecting fields from the joined table after addJoinQuery().
  • Trusting getRowCount() with large sys_id lists.
  • Routing writes through setCategory() and expecting them to hit the replica.
Score points: Name disableSysIdInOptimization() and glide.db.first_pass_sys_id_list_size.max when you see a suspicious round number in a log. Then show the set-based rewrite. Linking a symptom to a documented platform behaviour is what interviewers look for at this level.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you verify that the join query uses an index on incident.problem_id?
  • When would you move this calculation to Performance Analytics or a database view instead?
  • How would you make the job resumable if it still runs long?

  • GlideDBFunctionBuilder - Scoped, Global - API reference
  • GlideQueryCondition (Scoped) - API reference
  • Developer Advocate blog: Mastering RLQUERY & addJoinQuery()
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global - API reference

question: A hospital's service desk dashboard calls a Scripted REST API that returns the 40 most recent P1/P2 incidents with caller name, caller email, caller's department, assignment group name, and whether that group has at least one active member. Transaction logs show about 120 queries per call: the script dot-walks incident.caller_id.name, .email and .department.name per row, and for each group opens a new GlideRecord on sys_user_grmember. Under morning load the endpoint takes 4 to 6 seconds. Explain where the N+1 patterns are, then redesign the endpoint using batching (a DataLoader-style script include), RLQUERY or addJoinQuery where they fit, and GlideAggregate, and say precisely what each technique can and cannot do.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Start by counting where the extra queries come from. Each dot-walk through a reference loads the referenced record, and each per-group membership check is its own query. Then match tools to needs. Batching (collect keys, run one IN query, map results) is for loading related data. RLQUERY and addJoinQuery are for filtering by related records, and they return only base-table fields. GlideAggregate answers "how many" without loading rows. Know the limits as well: addJoinQuery is a subquery, not a real join.

Diagnosis

One query loads 40 incidents. Then, per row: caller_id.name and caller_id.email trigger a sys_user lookup (the GraphQL performance post makes this point: dot-walked caller and assigned_to data means extra queries to sys_user). caller_id.department.name adds a department lookup. The group membership check runs one more query per group. With 40 rows that comes to about 120 queries, which is the N+1 shape the "Did You Know" DataLoader episode shows (39 caller queries reduced to one).

The Answer

1. Batch related records (DataLoader pattern). Collect unique keys during the first pass, load each related table once with an IN query, and look them up from a map.

var BatchLoader = Class.create();
BatchLoader.prototype = {
  initialize: function () {},
  /** Loads rows from table where keyField IN keys; returns map key -> plain object. */
  loadMany: function (table, keys, fields, keyField) {
    var map = {};
    keyField = keyField || 'sys_id';
    if (!keys.length) return map;
    var gr = new GlideRecord(table);
    gr.addQuery(keyField, 'IN', keys.join(','));
    gr.query();
    while (gr.next()) {
      var row = {};
      for (var i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
        row[fields[i]] = gr.getDisplayValue(fields[i]);  // display text, e.g. department name
      }
      map[gr.getValue(keyField)] = row;
    }
    return map;
  },
  type: 'BatchLoader'
};

// Resource script
var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
inc.addEncodedQuery('active=true^priorityIN1,2');
inc.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
inc.setLimit(40);
inc.query();
var rows = [], callerIds = {}, groupIds = {};
while (inc.next()) {
  var c = inc.getValue('caller_id'), g = inc.getValue('assignment_group');
  rows.push({ number: inc.getValue('number'), caller: c, group: g,
              group_name: inc.getDisplayValue('assignment_group') });
  if (c) callerIds[c] = true;
  if (g) groupIds[g] = true;
}
var loader = new BatchLoader();
var callers = loader.loadMany('sys_user', Object.keys(callerIds), ['name', 'email', 'department']);

getDisplayValue('department') returns the department's display value from the user row. That avoids writing a separate department query when the display value is all you need, although the platform may still look up the referenced record to build the display value. Check the transaction log rather than assuming it is free.

2. Count active members per group in one aggregate.

var active = {};
var ga = new GlideAggregate('sys_user_grmember');
ga.addQuery('group', 'IN', Object.keys(groupIds).join(','));
ga.addQuery('user.active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.groupBy('group');
ga.query();
while (ga.next()) {
  active[ga.getValue('group')] = parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) > 0;
}

Total: one incident query, one user query, one aggregate. Three queries instead of about 120.

3. Where RLQUERY and addJoinQuery fit. If the requirement becomes "only show incidents whose group has an active member", that is a filter, and the related-list query does it inside the main query. The RLQUERY post's example finds groups with at least one active member:

grGroup.addEncodedQuery('^RLQUERYsys_user_grmember.group,>=1,m2m^user.active=true^ENDRLQUERY');

The post suggests getting the syntax by building the related-list condition in a report and copying the encoded query from its XML. addJoinQuery(joinTable, primaryField, joinTableField) does a similar filter in code, and returns a GlideQueryCondition you can extend with addCondition(). The scoped reference is explicit: it "is not a true database join". It adds a subquery, and only base-table fields are available. Neither technique loads the related data. They only narrow the rows.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Empty key lists. An IN query with an empty string can behave unexpectedly. Return early, as loadMany does.
  • Very large key sets. Chunk IN lists (for example 1,000 keys) when batching thousands of rows.
  • The GlideRecord tips episode mentions addExtraFields() (Washington DC) to fetch related reference fields up front. It is not in the scoped reference I checked, so confirm availability in your scope before relying on it.
  • Typos in RLQUERY strings fail quietly like other encoded queries. Invalid parts are dropped. Test in sub-production, as the post warns.
  • Batching changes security. The original per-row dot-walks ran with the same rights as the batched queries (GlideRecord ignores ACLs either way), but if you switch to GlideRecordSecure, apply it to every batch query, not just the first.
  • Index the filter columns. The IN on sys_id is cheap. Filtering on user.active through the dot-walk may not be.

Common Mistakes

  • Using addJoinQuery and then reading the joined table's fields, which are not there.
  • "Fixing" N+1 by caching in a global object that persists across transactions.
  • Replacing the membership query with getRowCount() per group. Still N+1, and heavier.
Score points: Split the toolbox clearly: batching loads, RLQUERY and addJoinQuery filter, GlideAggregate counts. Quote "not a true database join" from the reference when asked why addJoinQuery cannot return caller email.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would GraphQL resolvers avoid running the caller lookup at all when the client does not ask for caller fields?
  • How would you prove the improvement (transaction logs, slow query log, ATF performance profiling)?
  • How would you make BatchLoader generic across tables while keeping it safe in a scoped app?

Sources

  • Solving the N+1 Problem with a DataLoader Pattern (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Mastering RLQUERY and addJoinQuery() (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • 6 GlideRecord Tips to Supercharge Your ServiceNow Development (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • Using GraphQL APIs for Better Performance (Developer Advocate Blog)
  • GlideRecord - Scoped (API reference)
  • GlideAggregate - Scoped (API reference)
  • GlideQueryCondition - Scoped (API reference)

question: A managed service provider runs one domain-separated instance for 30 customer domains. Its scoped escalation app x_msp_esc reads a threshold with gs.getProperty('x_msp_esc.p1_escalate_minutes'), but three customers now want different thresholds. A developer's fix creates one system property per customer (x_msp_esc.p1_escalate_minutes.acme, ...) and also calls gs.setProperty() from an incident business rule to keep a running count of escalations per customer. Performance degrades during busy hours. Explain what is wrong, and design the configuration model with GlideApplicationProperty, covering domain resolution, scope, failure modes and background jobs.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

They want to see you spot the performance cause straight away: gs.setProperty() in a high-frequency path. Then explain that per-customer configuration on a domain-separated instance has a supported model, GlideApplicationProperty, with its own plugin, tables, naming rules, inheritance and exceptions. Finally, cover what 'current domain' means when no user is driving the session.

Diagnosis

The reference for gs.setProperty() carries a warning: setting a system property causes a system-wide cache flush, each flush can degrade the system while caches rebuild, and values that change often should not be stored as properties. A business rule on incident writing a counter flushes caches on every escalation, which matches 'degrades during busy hours'. Counters belong in a table.

Thirty suffixed properties is a governance smell rather than a crash. Each lookup builds a key by string concatenation, nothing enforces that every customer has one, and nothing ties a value to the domain model the instance already uses.

The Answer

GlideApplicationProperty provides get and set of application property values for a specific domain. Facts from the reference that shape the design:

  • It requires the Domain Support - Domain Extensions Installer plugin (com.glide.domain.msp_extensions.installer).
  • Definitions live in Application Properties [sys_application_property] and per-domain values in Application Property Values [sys_application_property_value].
  • In a non-global app, the name must be prefixed with the application scope, for example x_msp_esc.p1_escalate_minutes.
  • getValue(name, domainSysId) defaults to the session domain. If a child domain has no value, it returns the parent domain's value. If the application property does not exist at all, it returns the same-name system property's value. If the user has no access to the requested domain, it throws.
  • setValue(name, value, domainSysId) returns a Boolean, refuses names containing the protected strings listed in the reference (for example glide.properties.blacklist), refuses when a same-name private system property exists, and cannot be called from a different scope.
var EscalationConfig = Class.create();
EscalationConfig.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {},

    // domainId: pass the record's sys_domain; never rely on the session in async code
    p1Minutes: function (domainId) {
        var name = 'x_msp_esc.p1_escalate_minutes';
        var raw = null;
        try {
            raw = GlideApplicationProperty.getValue(name, domainId);
        } catch (e) {
            gs.error('Config read denied for domain {0}: {1}', domainId, e);
        }
        var n = parseInt(raw, 10);
        return isNaN(n) ? 30 : n;               // explicit, documented default
    },

    type: 'EscalationConfig'
};

// in the escalation business rule
var mins = new EscalationConfig().p1Minutes(current.getValue('sys_domain'));

Define the property once with a sensible default, set overrides only for the domains that differ, and let parent fallback cover the rest. The escalation count moves to a small table keyed by domain, updated with a normal GlideRecord write.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Session domain is not always a sys_id. gs.getSession().getCurrentDomainID() returns null for a user in the global domain who has not used the domain picker, and the string global if they picked global. Code that passes that value straight through will resolve differently for the same user depending on picker history. Pass the record's domain instead.
  • Scheduled jobs and event consumers have no interactive user picking a domain. Resolving 'the session domain' there gives whatever the job's context provides, so always pass the domain explicitly.
  • getValue() throws, rather than returning null, when the caller cannot access the domain. An unguarded call inside a business rule turns a permissions issue into a failed save.
  • Silent fallback to a same-name system property is convenient during migration and confusing later. Once migrated, remove the old system property so a typo in the app property name does not quietly read the old value.
  • gs.getProperty(key, alt) returns a string, and alt applies only when the property is not found. The reference does not say what happens when the property exists but is empty; test this on your instance, and parse and default explicitly either way.
  • gs.setProperty() only works for properties within the calling script's scope, so a scoped app cannot quietly rewrite another app's properties with it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using properties as mutable state (counters, last-run timestamps, tokens refreshed per call).
  • Encoding customer identity into property names instead of using domains.
  • Calling GlideApplicationProperty.setValue() from a shared global utility on behalf of the app; the reference says it cannot be called from a different scope.
  • Ignoring the Boolean result of setValue() in an admin UI and showing 'saved' when nothing was written.
Score points: Quote the cache-flush warning on gs.setProperty() and connect it to the busy-hour symptom, then mention parent-domain fallback in GlideApplicationProperty.getValue() so only exceptions need configuring.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How do you move per-domain values between instances, and what goes in the scoped app versus data loads?
  • A customer admin in a child domain should edit only their own threshold. How do you expose that safely?
  • How would you audit who changed a threshold and when?

Sources
