  • GlideSystem (Scoped)
  • GlideSession (Scoped)

question: A large retailer's platform team wants to let 30 developers build scoped apps with coding agents: Build Agent for scaffolding inside the instance, then Claude Code with the ServiceNow SDK (Fluent) locally. The CISO and the platform governance board ask: how do we keep control of what reaches production, how do we know what code is on which instance, how do we roll back, and how do we stop people approving whatever the agent proposes? One senior developer also wants to point Claude Code at a five-year-old production app to "modernise it". Question: Design the development workflow and governance model, and list the specific risks of each tool you would address.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is checking whether you know how the SDK workflow actually works (Fluent source, now-sdk build as the compile gate, now-sdk install with auth aliases, credentials outside the project), what Build Agent can and cannot produce, and where the review gates go. You should also treat "git rollback is not instance rollback" and approval fatigue as first-class risks.

The Answer

The workflow.

  1. Requirements first. Each app starts with a short PRD in the repo, referenced from CLAUDE.md so every agent session loads it. Keep CLAUDE.md concise; it is read in full every session.
  2. Scaffold. Either Build Agent in the instance (tables, roles, navigation from a descriptive prompt), then connect source control from within Build Agent and pull locally, or now-sdk init for a blank project.
  3. Build locally with Claude Code and the ServiceNow SDK plugin (/plugin install servicenow-sdk@claude-plugins-official). Install it from inside the project directory: the Developer Advocates found that installing globally means Claude Code does not reliably pick it up. The plugin's metadata documentation versions with the SDK, so pin the SDK version in package.json per app.
  4. Branch, PR, review. Feature branches, PRs with a summary and test plan, review in the GitHub diff view. Plan mode or a task-then-execution plan for anything touching security, data migration or core logic.
  5. Build gate. now-sdk build compiles Fluent into an installable package (use --frozenKeys in CI to fail if generated keys are stale). The SDK series also describes ATF tests and a readiness scan produced at build time; confirm what your SDK version actually does before relying on it as test coverage. A failing build blocks the PR.
  6. Deploy. now-sdk install --auth dev, then uat, then prod. (deploy is an alias; use install in shared tooling because it is the canonical name.) Commit and push before deploying, never after.

Knowing what is where. Git and instances are not in sync by themselves. After each successful deploy, create an annotated tag such as prod/2026-05-21-abc1234 and push with --follow-tags. git tag then shows exactly which commit is on which environment. Restrict the prod auth alias to a release role or a pipeline account, not 30 laptops. now.config.json holds scope and app identity, not instance URLs; credentials are stored by now-sdk auth outside the project, so they are not in the repo, but they are on developer machines.

Rollback. Rolling back a tag and redeploying restores code. It does not undo records created, tables altered or automations that ran. Each production release needs a written rollback plan: which tag to redeploy and what data cleanup is required. Schema changes get extra review because they are the hardest to reverse.

Stopping rubber-stamping. The Developer Advocates' own accountability post describes the problem: the agent asks, you approve, it is usually right, and your finger starts to drift. Controls that do not depend on willpower:

  • A separate human reviewer on every PR, not the developer who ran the agent.
  • An AI-specific risk review in the change process for anything an agent built, as the post recommends.
  • Workflow commands that leave changes uncommitted for review, and per-issue commits instead of git add -A, so one issue can be reverted cleanly.
  • Disclose AI involvement in the PR. The team's other post argues that hiding AI help, not using it, is the problem.

Tool-specific risks.

  • Build Agent can only build what Fluent supports, plus React UIs. Its own FAQ warns it may write scripted code instead of a flow, and that forcing it to build something outside Fluent can make it build it another way or simulate having built it. It can hallucinate. Review generated apps for missing ACLs and fake implementations. Prompt quotas are per instance (the SDK series cites 100 calls for customer instances and 25 for PDIs), so plan its use for scaffolding.
  • Claude Code + SDK: the series says full CI/CD pipelines entirely outside the platform are still evolving, and branch management from external tools is limited if you also use Studio Source Control. Pick one source of truth per app. On Windows, add .gitattributes with LF rules so regenerated TypeScript does not flood diffs. Never commit .env files.

The brownfield app. Use now-sdk init --from <app sys_id> to download the app's metadata as XML into a metadata/ folder, then now-sdk transform --from . to convert it to Fluent. Before any change, have the agent read and summarise existing business rule patterns, and record table relationships, naming conventions and high-risk areas (integrations, rules on every update) in CLAUDE.md. "Modernise it" is not a ticket. Require specific issues with acceptance criteria, and a hardening review looking for missing error handling and silent business rule failures.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Do not edit src/fluent/generated/keys.ts; the SDK regenerates it on every build.
  • Orphaned git worktrees can confuse the SDK build step. Clean them up.
  • Deploy failures are usually credentials, instance version, or a scope conflict with an existing app.
  • If the app includes AI agents, confirm after deploy that they are registered in AI Control Tower.

Common Mistakes

  • Deploying to prod from a developer laptop because "the CLI makes it easy".
  • Assuming a git revert restores the instance.
  • Letting Build Agent output go straight to UAT without a code review.
Score points: Say the deploy tag and the change record should reference each other: the change says which commit went out, the tag says which change approved it.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you handle a hotfix made directly in production Studio while the repo is the source of truth?
  • What would your PR template require for agent-built changes?
  • How do you stop a developer from adding the prod auth alias locally?

Sources

  • Building ServiceNow apps via Claude Code and the ServiceNow SDK
  • Unleash the Power of Build Agents in the #BuildWithBuildAgent Challenge
  • Build Agent is now live on your Personal Developer Instance
  • Build Agent Q4 2025: Planning, Figma Integration, and Smarter Workflows
  • Your Agent Made the Call. Who Answers For It?
  • AI-Written Answers: What Is Your Community Post Worth?

question: A telecoms operator's IT team deployed an AI agent last quarter to resolve low-priority access requests. Over time it was extended: it can now add users to groups, reset MFA, and call an external identity provider API. On Monday it added 40 contractors to a group that grants access to the billing system, following a description in a bulk request that nobody reviewed. No harm was found, but the regulator's question to the CIO is: "Who is accountable for what this agent does, and how would you know if it did this again?" Nobody can name the agent's owner. Question: Walk through the post-incident analysis and the accountability and control model you would put in place.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Treat this as a process failure rather than one person's mistake, and still name an accountable owner. Identify the conditions that made it possible (scope creep, write plus network access, no one reading the audit trail, no owner) and fix each one with a concrete platform control. A strong answer is honest that more AI watching AI does not answer the accountability question.

The Answer

Reconstruct first. From the agent's execution records, establish: who or what triggered the run, the run-as identity (dynamic user or AI user) and its roles at the time, which tools ran, in which execution mode, with which inputs, and what the agent read that led it there. The bulk request description is the likely injection point: the agent followed text in data it read. Pull Guardian logs for prompt injection detections on that run. If the agent was on autonomous mode for the group-membership tool, that is the immediate control gap.

Name the conditions. The Developer Advocate team's accountability post lists the conditions behind an agent incident they discussed: broad instruction scope, network access beyond what the task needed, an audit trail nobody watched, and no named owner. All four apply here:

  • Scope creep: built for low-priority access requests, extended to group membership, MFA reset and an external API. Nobody decided it should reach all of that; its scope became whatever it could reach.
  • Write plus network: it could change access and call out of the platform.
  • Unread audit trail: the platform logged the run, but no one was reviewing it.
  • No owner: the platform gives you somewhere to record who owns the agent; nobody filled it in.

Accountability model. The post's authors disagreed among themselves, and the honest position is both. Treat the failure as a process failure: blaming the developer who extended the agent leaves the process that allowed it in place. But the regulator also needs a name. Assign:

  • A business owner per agent, accountable for what it is allowed to do, recorded in AI Control Tower and reviewed quarterly.
  • A technical owner accountable for its tools, identity and evaluations.
  • A platform AI governance lead accountable for the guardrails existing and being enforced across all agents. This person is the last line of defence, not the first.

Controls.

  • AI-specific risk review in change. Any new tool, new identity role or new external connection for an agent is a change with a risk review, not a config tweak. That alone would have caught the scope creep.
  • Split read from write-plus-network. An agent that reads and drafts is a different risk class from one with write access and a route to an external API. Split this agent. The resolver drafts the access decision; a separate, narrowly scoped tool performs it.
  • Supervised mode on privileged tools. Group membership, MFA reset and the external API call run supervised, so a human confirms the specific change. Confirm the tool execution mode override property is off.
  • Identity. If it runs as an AI user, cut that user's roles to the minimum. If dynamic user, use role masking so it never carries the invoker's full rights.
  • Friction where the stakes justify it. The post suggests cooling-off windows: a delay before high-impact access takes effect, or a change that cannot reach production until a named person confirms. For access to billing systems, a second approver on any bulk group addition is cheap.
  • An audit trail someone reads. "We'll monitor it" is not a mechanism. Define alerts (bulk membership changes, privileged group changes by any agent) that open a task for a named team, with a review SLA.
  • Central oversight. AI Control Tower is ServiceNow's place to inventory agents, models and copilots, including non-ServiceNow ones, and to shut down an agent acting outside its permissions. ServiceNow Otto, launched at Knowledge 2026, routes governance through it. It only helps if it is turned on and someone owns its alerts.

Answer to the regulator. "The business owner of the access agent is X; the guardrails are owned by Y; any agent change that widens its access now needs a risk-reviewed change; privileged actions require a human confirmation; and bulk privileged changes by any agent raise an alert reviewed within N hours."

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Data-rich, repetitive processes like password and MFA resets are the first ones teams give agents, and the post notes they are also what an attacker most wants an agent operating.
  • Adding defensive agents to watch this agent moves the accountability question to whoever owns the watchers. It does not remove it.
  • Supervised confirmation with a vague prompt ("Approve?") becomes a rubber stamp. Show the user list and the group.
  • External API credentials used by the agent should be scoped on the provider side too, so a platform mistake cannot exceed what the identity provider allows.

Common Mistakes

  • Disciplining the developer and changing nothing structural.
  • Answering "the AI did it" or "it was a process failure" without naming an owner.
  • Relying on Guardian alone as the control for a write-capable agent.
Score points: Say you would run an inventory of every agent now in production and ask, for each, the regulator's question: who owns it, what can it reach, and who reads its log. Most organisations find several with no answer.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you set the compute or cost limits that are the second governance gate?
  • What evidence would you keep to show the controls work over time?
  • How do you stop people automating the human confirmation you added?

Sources

  • Your Agent Made the Call. Who Answers For It?
  • Latest access control security enhancements for AI Agents and Skill Kit (ServiceNow Community)
  • AppOmni: Exploiting Agent-to-Agent Discovery via Prompt Injection
  • AI Guardian FAQ (ServiceNow Community)
  • ServiceNow Otto creates the unified AI experience for the enterprise (press release, May 2026)
  • AI Agent Studio: The Future of Autonomous Workflows in ServiceNow

question: A telecom operator must meet a regulator's 24-month retention rule. A scoped table, x_tel_usage_dispute, holds 11 million rows; about 4 million are older than 24 months. Rows carry attachments (call records), an FX Currency field for the disputed amount, and an after-delete business rule that writes an audit entry to a compliance table. A second requirement: 600,000 open disputes from a retired product must be set to state 'closed_retired' and have their resolution notes cleared, without triggering 600,000 customer emails. Design both jobs: which APIs, which flags, and what you expect each to do and not do.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is looking for precise knowledge of what the bulk methods skip or refuse: deleteMultiple() leaves attachments, should not be used on tables with currency fields, and ignores setLimit(); setWorkflow(false) is ignored for cascade deletes and cannot be set across scopes; updateMultiple() has its own rules for clearing values and journals.

They want a plan that meets the regulator's rule, keeps the audit trail the business rule writes, and runs in batches you can resume.

The Answer

Job 1: retention purge. deleteMultiple() is out for this table, for two documented reasons. The reference says not to use it on tables with currency fields and to delete each record individually, and it does not delete attachments, which would leave call records behind and defeat the retention rule. So the purge deletes record by record, in batches, with business rules on, because the after-delete rule writes the compliance audit entry the regulator will ask for.

// Scheduled job, runs every 15 minutes in the off-peak window
(function purgeBatch() {
    var BATCH = 2000;
    var cutoff = 'sys_created_on<javascript:gs.monthsAgoStart(24)';
    var gr = new GlideRecord('x_tel_usage_dispute');
    gr.addEncodedQuery(cutoff);
    gr.orderBy('sys_created_on');
    gr.setLimit(BATCH);                 // fine here: we iterate, we do not bulk delete
    gr.query();
    var n = 0, failed = 0;
    while (gr.next()) {
        // remove attachments explicitly, e.g. via GlideSysAttachment, before the row
        if (gr.deleteRecord()) { n++; } else { failed++; }
    }
    gs.info('Retention purge: deleted ' + n + ', failed ' + failed);
})();

deleteRecord() returns true when the record was deleted and false when no record was found, so the counts are honest. Batches of a few thousand keep each transaction short. The job is naturally resumable because each run re-queries what is left, and ordering by creation date means the oldest data goes first if the window runs out. At roughly 4 million rows this is days of work, so plan it with the regulator's deadline in mind.

Job 2: retire 600,000 open disputes. Here a bulk update fits. Three rules from the reference shape it. First, use setValue() rather than direct assignment with updateMultiple(). Second, updateMultiple() sets values and does not clear existing ones; to clear a field you set it to the string 'NULL'. Third, it does not support adding multiple journal entries, so do not try to write a work note per row this way.

var gr = new GlideRecord('x_tel_usage_dispute');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('u_product', retiredProductSysId);
gr.setWorkflow(false);                       // no BRs, no notifications, no audit
gr.setValue('state', 'closed_retired');
gr.setValue('u_resolution_notes', 'NULL');   // clears the value
gr.updateMultiple();

setWorkflow(false) disables business rules, script engines and audit for this GlideRecord. That stops the customer emails, but it also stops audit history and any rule that sets active=false when the state closes. Decide deliberately: either set those fields yourself in the same update, or keep workflow on and suppress the notification with a condition. Because the table is in your scope, setWorkflow() works; the reference says it cannot be set for cross-scoped applications.

The GlideQuery form reads well and tells you how many rows changed: updateMultiple() returns an object with rowCount. But its disableWorkflow() "only works for tables in the GLOBAL scope", so it does not apply to x_tel_usage_dispute. disableAutoSysFields() would also stop sys_updated_on and sys_mod_count from changing, which you probably do not want for a regulated status change.

For both jobs, above the glide.db.forced.chunk.threshold property the platform forces chunked deletes and updates to avoid replication problems, so large runs are slower than a single SQL statement would be. Do not combine updateMultiple() or deleteMultiple() with setLimit() or chooseWindow() on large tables; the reference warns against it, and setLimit() does not cap a deleteMultiple().

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • setWorkflow() is ignored when deleteMultiple() or deleteProblem() cascade deletes.
  • updateMultiple() on a journal field cannot add multiple entries; GlideQuery's limitations also exclude updating journal fields.
  • GlideQuery does not support FX currency fields, which rules it out for any step that reads or writes the disputed amount.
  • An invalid term in the purge's encoded query is dropped and the rest runs; validate the query and log a GlideAggregate count before the first run.
  • update(reason) takes an optional reason that appears in the audit record; with setWorkflow(false) there is no audit record to carry it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using deleteMultiple() on a table with attachments and currency fields because it is fast.
  • Turning off workflow for the purge and losing the compliance audit entries.
  • Setting a field to an empty string with updateMultiple() and expecting it to clear.
  • Assuming GlideQuery's disableWorkflow() works on scoped tables.
Score points: Separate the two jobs by what they must preserve: the purge must keep business rules (audit) and delete attachments, the retirement must suppress them. Choosing different APIs for each from the documented constraints is the architect-level answer.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prove to the regulator that every purged dispute's attachments were removed?
  • What would you change if the table extended task in the global scope?
  • How would you throttle the purge if replication lag alerts fire?

Sources

  • GlideRecord (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideQuery - Scoped, Global - API reference
  • GlideElementCurrency2 - API reference

question: An insurance company's operational-risk team is investigating whether P1 incidents were downgraded to hide SLA breaches. They want, for a given incident, a timeline of every update where priority or assignment group changed: the update number, timestamp, old and new priority, and the group at that point. It must run from a scheduled job and also on demand from a UI action used by team leads. Write the server-side function using HistoryWalker and explain the walker choice, security behaviour and the traps.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to see that you know HistoryWalker exists and what it does: it rebuilds a GlideRecord as it was at an earlier update using audit or history data. They want a deliberate choice of walker (AUDIT, HISTORY, CHECKPOINT, OFFLINE) and awareness that walkTo(int) does not work with CHECKPOINT. You should also understand that record-level and field-level security are on by default, so the same code returns different results for a scheduled job and for a team lead.

Good answers also flag the subtle data trap: a dot-walk or display value on a walked record reads today's referenced data, not history.

The Answer

Walker choice. The reference describes four retrieval methods. HISTORY builds or reuses a sys_history_set and reads sys_history_line, ordered by update number. AUDIT queries sys_audit directly, ordered by record_checkpoint, and is the least performant, partly because with glide.sys.audit_inserts false (the base setting) there is no update-zero record and the API has to compensate. CHECKPOINT picks between the two based on com.glide.history_walker.max_history_count (default 1,000) and orders by internal_checkpoint, a timestamp, so it is chronological and the reference calls it the most reliable. OFFLINE is for tables with the offline_timestamp_field attribute. If you do not pass a walker, com.snc.walker.default decides, and the reference advises always passing one.

For this investigation I want ordered, reliable history, so CHECKPOINT is the default choice. The catch is that walkTo(int updateCount) is not supported by the checkpoint walker; it has walkTo(String checkpoint) instead. Walking one step at a time works with any walker, so the function rewinds with walkBackward(), processes the starting state, then steps with walkForward(), and never needs an update number. That also makes the result independent of where a new walker starts, which the reference examples do not agree on.

function priorityTimeline(incSysId, asSystem) {
    var hw = new sn_hw.HistoryWalker('incident', incSysId, 'CHECKPOINT');
    if (asSystem) {
        hw.setRecordLevelSecurity(false);   // scheduled job: full history
        hw.setFieldLevelSecurity(false);
    }
    hw.setWithJournalFields(false);         // default, stated for clarity
    hw.setWithChanges(true);                // default; enables element changes()

    while (hw.walkBackward()) {}            // rewind: the start position is not documented consistently

    var out = [];
    var prevPriority = null, prevGroup = null;
    do {
        var rec = hw.getWalkedRecord();
        var pri = rec.getValue('priority');
        var grp = rec.getValue('assignment_group');
        if (pri !== prevPriority || grp !== prevGroup) {
            out.push({
                update: hw.getUpdateNumber(),
                at: rec.getValue('sys_updated_on'),
                fromPriority: prevPriority,
                toPriority: pri,
                groupSysId: grp
            });
        }
        prevPriority = pri;
        prevGroup = grp;
    } while (hw.walkForward());
    return out;
}

Why it is written this way.

getValue() copies plain strings out of the walked record. The reference warns that the object from getWalkedRecord() might be modified after walking to another update number, and says to use getWalkedRecordCopy() if you need to keep record objects. Copying the values avoids that issue and keeps memory flat.

The group is stored as a sys_id, not rec.assignment_group.getDisplayValue(). A display value on a reference is looked up from the referenced record as it is now. If a group was renamed last month, a display value would put today's name on a two-year-old update, which an investigator could misread. Resolve names separately and label them as current names.

Comparing against the previous values works with any walker. With setWithChanges(true), the default, you could instead check rec.priority.changes(), but comparing values is easier to test.

Security. setRecordLevelSecurity() and setFieldLevelSecurity() both default to true. With record-level security on, the walker does not return the walked record if the caller cannot read it; with field-level security on, it leaves fields empty when the caller lacks read access. Called from the UI action by a team lead without access to priority history, the timeline would come back with empty values that look like "no change". The function takes an explicit asSystem flag; only the scheduled job passes true, and the UI action should check the user's role before calling it at all.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • The doc examples are inconsistent about the starting position (one walkForward() example begins at update 0, a walkBackward() example begins at the latest update). Do not assume; walk from a known point and log getUpdateNumber() while testing.
  • getUpdateNumber() returns -1 if the record is not found.
  • Update numbers from HISTORY and AUDIT are loosely tied to sys_mod_count, which clients can overwrite; the reference calls that count unreliable. CHECKPOINT's internal_checkpoint has no link to sys_mod_count.
  • Generating a history set for a record with roughly 10,000 field updates can exceed the transaction timeout; this is why CHECKPOINT switches to sys_audit above the configured threshold.
  • For OFFLINE-walker tables only walkTo(0) and walkForward() are available, and HistoryWalker requires the History Walker plugin (enabled by default) and the sn_hw namespace in both scopes.
  • The changed-field-names helper used in the reference example, GlideScriptRecordUtil, is shown in an example marked as global-scope only.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling walkTo(3) with the CHECKPOINT walker.
  • Storing getWalkedRecord() objects in an array and finding every entry shows the last state.
  • Reading display values or dot-walks from the walked record as if they were historical.
  • Leaving security defaults on in a scheduled job, or turning them off in a user-facing action.
Score points: Point out that display values on a walked record are current, not historical. That one sentence tells the interviewer you have used audit data in an investigation where the details mattered.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you show who made each change (sys_audit user) alongside the timeline?
  • How would you run this across 20,000 P1 incidents without timing out?
  • When would you read sys_audit directly instead of using HistoryWalker?

Sources

  • HistoryWalker - Scoped, Global - API reference
  • GlideRecord (Scoped) - API reference
  • GlideElement (Scoped) - API reference

question: A managed-services provider commits to its customer: 'P2 incidents resolved within 16 business hours, measured on the customer's Mon-Fri 08:00-17:00 Europe/Berlin schedule excluding German public holidays.' A custom scoped app (not the task SLA engine) tracks this for a supplier contract table. Today the code does due.addSeconds(16 * 3600) and calculates 'time used' as GlideDateTime.subtract(opened, now). Agents in Manila and Austin see different due dates for the same record. Design and write the business-time calculation with GlideSchedule and GlideDuration, and explain every time-zone decision you make.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Recognise that there are two separate errors: calendar time used where business time was promised, and a calculation that silently depends on the viewer's session time zone. Pick GlideSchedule for both the due date and the elapsed figure, pin the schedule's time zone to the contract rather than the session, and know the awkward corners of GlideDuration. Also say when the platform's SLA definitions would be the better tool.

Approach

Two numbers matter: the due date (start plus 16 schedule hours) and business time consumed so far. GlideSchedule gives both. add(GlideDateTime startDate, GlideDuration offset) returns a GlideDateTime: the reference's own example adds two days to 2014-01-02 on an empty schedule and prints 2014-01-04 00:00:00, even though the description calls the return value 'the schedule updated with the new segment'. Trust the example. duration(start, end) returns a GlideDuration of in-schedule time between two instants, computed in the schedule's time zone or, if none was given, the session's.

The time-zone decision: the contract is defined in Europe/Berlin, so the schedule must be evaluated in Europe/Berlin no matter who runs the code. The constructor GlideSchedule(sysID, timeZone) takes an optional zone and falls back to the current session's zone when it is omitted. Omitting it is exactly why Manila and Austin disagree: each agent's session evaluated '08:00-17:00' in their own zone.

var ContractClock = Class.create();
ContractClock.prototype = {
    initialize: function (scheduleSysId, tz) {
        this.tz = tz || 'Europe/Berlin';
        this.schedule = new GlideSchedule(scheduleSysId, this.tz);
        if (!this.schedule.isValid())
            throw new Error('Schedule ' + scheduleSysId + ' has no spans');
    },

    dueDate: function (openedGdt, businessHours) {
        var start = new GlideDateTime(openedGdt);
        var dur = new GlideDuration(businessHours * 60 * 60 * 1000);
        return this.schedule.add(start, dur);          // GlideDateTime
    },

    consumed: function (openedGdt, nowGdt) {
        return this.schedule.duration(new GlideDateTime(openedGdt),
                                      new GlideDateTime(nowGdt)); // GlideDuration
    },

    msUntilClockRuns: function (nowGdt) {
        if (this.schedule.isInSchedule(nowGdt))
            return 0;
        return this.schedule.whenNext(nowGdt, this.tz);  // -1 means never
    },

    type: 'ContractClock'
};

var clock = new ContractClock(current.getValue('u_schedule'), 'Europe/Berlin');
var opened = new GlideDateTime(current.getValue('opened_at'));
current.setValue('u_business_due', clock.dueDate(opened, 16).getValue());
var used = clock.consumed(opened, new GlideDateTime());
current.setValue('u_business_used_text', used.getDurationValue());   // d HH:mm:ss

Store the due date as a date/time value (UTC). Each viewer then sees it converted to their own zone, which is correct: the instant is fixed, only its display changes. The disagreement disappears because the calculation no longer depends on the session.

Calendar elapsed time still has a use. GlideDateTime.subtract(start, end) returns a GlideDuration of wall-clock difference; report it next to business time so customers can see both. It should never feed the breach decision.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • whenNext() is documented as meaningful only when the time is outside the schedule, and it returns -1 when no future span exists. Check isInSchedule() first and treat -1 as a configuration incident (for example, a schedule whose spans ended last year).
  • isValid() only says the schedule has at least one span. A schedule with one span in 2019 is 'valid' and useless today.
  • GlideDuration stores the span as an offset from 1970-01-01. getValue() on a 3.5-day duration returns 1970-01-04 12:00:00. Use getDurationValue() (d HH:mm:ss) for storage and logs, keep your own millisecond figure when you need to compare against a threshold, and use getDisplayValue() only for people.
  • getRoundedDayPart() rounds up when the time part is over 12 hours. A report built on it will show '2 days' for 1 day 13 hours of business time, which customers read as a breach.
  • load(sysID, timeZone, excludeSpanID) lets you reuse one object and exclude a span, for example a customer-approved maintenance freeze.
  • If you omit the zone on whenNext(time, timeZone), you reintroduce session dependency in the one method most likely to be called from a scheduled job.

Common Mistakes

  • Constructing new GlideSchedule(id) without a zone and testing only as an admin whose zone happens to match the contract.
  • Computing 'consumed' with GlideDateTime.subtract() and then subtracting nights and weekends by hand.
  • Writing the due date into a string field with getDisplayValue().
  • Rebuilding SLA pause logic in script when the record is a task and the platform SLA definitions already handle schedules, pause conditions and breach notifications. Custom code is justified here only because the target is a non-task supplier table.
Score points: Point out the mismatch between the documented description of GlideSchedule.add() and its example output, and explain that you would confirm the return type with a quick background script before building on it. That shows you read references critically.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you support pause time (awaiting customer) on top of this calculation?
  • The customer moves from Berlin to a follow-the-sun schedule across three zones. What changes?
  • How would you recalculate thousands of open records after a holiday is added to the schedule without hitting transaction limits?

Sources

  • GlideSchedule (Scoped)
  • GlideDuration (Scoped)
  • GlideDateTime (Scoped)

question: A penetration test of an HR services portal at a 20,000-employee retailer produced three findings. (1) A client-callable script include EmployeeLookupAjax, used by a catalog client script to fill a manager's name, returns the full user record including home address and salary band for any sysparm_user passed to it; the tester called it from the browser console with other employees' sys_ids. (2) A 'Bulk close' list UI action hides itself with g_user.hasRole('hr_admin') and sends g_list.getChecked() to a script include that closes every sys_id it receives. (3) Salary fields are hidden on the form by an onLoad script using g_user.hasRole('hr_comp'), and the values are sent down in g_scratchpad for a calculation. Explain the root cause the three share, how you would fix each one with specific APIs, and how you would review client-side code for this class of bug in future.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants one sentence first: anything in the browser is controlled by the user, so client-side checks are user experience, never authorization. Then they want you to locate the real trust boundary (the script include, the business rule, the ACL), fix each finding there, and know the API details that make these bugs easy to write: GlideAjax server code does not apply ACLs the way client GlideRecord does, g_user.hasRole() also returns true for admins, and GlideList2 getChecked() does not check whether the items may be acted on.

Diagnosis

Shared root cause. Each design makes a security decision in the browser and trusts the server to honour it. The client GlideRecord reference spells out the difference: client-side GlideRecord applies ACLs using the credentials of the user, and 'to execute the code on the server without ACLs, use the GlideAjax API'. So a script include behind GlideAjax that uses plain server GlideRecord reads whatever it is asked for. The GlideAjax object a catalog script builds can be built by anyone with a session and a browser console, with any parameters.

Finding 1: over-sharing script include. Fix it on the server:

var EmployeeLookupAjax = Class.create();
EmployeeLookupAjax.prototype = Object.extendsObject(global.AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
    getManagerName: function() {
        var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user');
        if (!/^[0-9a-f]{32}$/.test(userId)) {
            return JSON.stringify({error: 'invalid'});
        }
        // only the requester themselves, or HR staff, may look up someone else
        if (userId != gs.getUserID() && !gs.hasRole('hr_admin')) {
            return JSON.stringify({error: 'forbidden'});
        }
        var u = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
        if (!u.get(userId) || !u.canRead()) {
            return JSON.stringify({error: 'not_found'});
        }
        return JSON.stringify({manager: u.getDisplayValue('manager')});
    },
    type: 'EmployeeLookupAjax'
});

Return only the field the form needs, check the caller's right to ask, and use an ACL-aware check (canRead(), or GlideRecordSecure, which the server GlideRecord reference describes as the class that performs the same functions and enforces ACLs). Validate the parameter shape. Note that the reference example for gs.hasRole() says it returns true for admins, which is usually what you want here.

Finding 2: bulk close. Hiding the button with g_user.hasRole('hr_admin') stops honest users from seeing it; it stops nobody from calling the script include. The GlideList2 reference says getChecked() returns the checked sys_ids and does not check whether the items are allowed to be executed. The script include must re-check the role with gs.hasRole(), then for each sys_id load the record and confirm the user can write it and that it is in a closable state, and skip (and report) the rest. Better still, make the UI action server-side so the platform's UI action condition and record ACLs apply.

Finding 3: salary in g_scratchpad. The display business rule's server-side queries ignore ACLs and its output is delivered to every user who opens the form; hiding the field afterwards changes nothing about what the browser received. Remove the values from the scratchpad, protect the fields with field-level read ACLs so they are never sent to users without hr_comp, and do the calculation on the server (a business rule, or a GlideAjax method that checks the role before computing).

Review checklist for client code.

  • Every client-callable script include: who may call each method, what parameters it trusts, what it returns. Treat it like a public REST endpoint.
  • Every g_user.hasRole*() in client code: is it only hiding UI, and is the same rule enforced by an ACL or server check?
  • Every display business rule: is anything in g_scratchpad data the user could not see on screen?
  • Every list UI action using getChecked(): does the server re-validate each record?

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • g_user.hasRole('x') returns true for admin as well. If a feature must be limited to people who hold the role explicitly, the client equivalent is hasRoleExactly(), but the server must enforce it anyway.
  • The includeDefaults flag on hasRole, hasRoleExactly, hasRoleFromList and hasRoles controls whether snc_internal and snc_external count. g_user.hasRoles() without it can return false for a portal user who only has default roles.
  • The deprecated GlideListV3 documented getChecked() as excluding items not allowed to be executed. Code written against V3 may have relied on that filtering; under GlideList2 it is gone.
  • g_aw.openRecord(..., {readOnlyForm: true}) and g_form.setReadOnly() are display controls. A user can still change the field through any other channel.
  • Client-side GlideRecord does respect ACLs, which is why some legacy code 'felt' safe. Moving it to GlideAjax for scope compatibility without adding checks removes protection that was there before.

Common Mistakes

  • Answering finding 1 with 'make the script include not client callable' when the catalog item genuinely needs it; the fix is to authorize inside the method.
  • Obfuscating parameter names or adding a client-side token as protection.
  • Assuming that because a field is hidden its value was never sent.
  • Re-checking the role in the script include but not checking each record in a bulk action.
Score points: Quote the client GlideRecord note about GlideAjax running without ACLs. It explains why converting legacy client GlideRecord code to GlideAjax, a common upgrade task, can quietly create this exact vulnerability.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you find every client-callable script include on an instance and rank them by risk?
  • How would you write an ATF or automated test that proves EmployeeLookupAjax rejects another user's sys_id?
  • When is it acceptable for a GlideAjax method to return data the caller cannot read through ACLs?

  • GlideListV3 (deprecated) - API reference

  • Client Callable and Server Callable Script Includes in One (Developer Advocate blog)
  • GlideAgentWorkspace (g_aw) - API reference

question: An energy retailer's Case form in the core UI takes six to eight seconds before agents can type, and selecting an account freezes the browser. An audit of the form finds 14 onLoad client scripts, 22 onChange scripts, three getReference() calls without callbacks, a client-side GlideRecord query without a response function, an onChange on short_description that upper-cases the text with setValue, several setValue() calls on reference fields with only a sys_id, 30 separate getMessage() calls, and setMandatory/setDisplay logic duplicated across scripts and UI policies. Lay out how you would measure the problem, the order in which you would fix it, and the specific API changes for each finding.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer is looking for a method, not a list of tips. Measure first, then remove anything that blocks the browser (synchronous server calls), then cut the number of round trips, then fix the logic that runs too often (load-time onChange, recursive setValue), and only then tidy UI policy duplication. They want each step tied to a documented API behaviour.

Approach

1. Measure. Use the browser's network and performance tools to count server calls during load and during an account change, and time individual scripts. In list and form contexts that support it, the client StopWatch API (new StopWatch(), getTime() in milliseconds, toString() as HH:MM:SS.SSS) is a quick way to log slow sections. Record a baseline: time to interactive, number of requests on load, number on account change.

2. Remove synchronous calls first. These freeze the browser and they are why the account change hangs.

  • getReference() without a callback runs synchronously and halts processing, per the GlideForm reference. Add callbacks, or better, replace them with one GlideAjax call.
  • Client GlideRecord query() without a response function is synchronous; the reference says not to make synchronous query calls. Make it asynchronous or move the lookup into a script include.
  • Search for getXMLWait() as well; the GlideAjax reference says it degrades the user experience significantly.

3. Cut round trips.

  • Facts known at load (account tier, entitlement flags, properties) move to one display business rule that fills g_scratchpad, read by one onLoad script.
  • Facts that change with the account become one GlideAjax method returning JSON with everything the form needs, called once from the account onChange, using getXMLAnswer().
  • setValue() on reference fields with only a sys_id makes the browser fetch the display value. The reference says to pass the display value as the third argument to avoid that round trip; have the GlideAjax response include it.
  • Thirty getMessage() calls become one g_i18n.getMessages([...], callback), which returns an object keyed by message key. The i18N reference notes it falls back to English and then to the key itself if no translation exists.
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading || g_form.isLiveUpdating() || newValue == '') {
        return;
    }
    var ga = new GlideAjax('CaseFormAjax');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getAccountContext');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_account', newValue);
    ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
        if (g_form.getValue('account') != newValue) {
            return;                        // stale response, account changed again
        }
        var ctx = JSON.parse(answer || '{}');
        if (ctx.contact) {
            g_form.setValue('contact', ctx.contact, ctx.contact_name);
        }
        if (ctx.asset) {
            g_form.setValue('asset', ctx.asset, ctx.asset_name);
        }
        g_scratchpad.accountTier = ctx.tier;
    });
}

4. Stop logic running when it should not.

  • onChange scripts also run during form load with isLoading true. Twenty-two onChange scripts without that guard are 22 extra executions, several of them server calls, on every open.
  • The upper-casing onChange is the case the GlideForm reference warns about: setValue() inside onChange registers as a change and can re-trigger the script until the stack overflows. Compare first: only call setValue if newValue != newValue.toUpperCase().
  • With live forms, isLiveUpdating() lets onChange skip work caused by another session's update.

5. Consolidate visibility and mandatory logic. The reference says, for setMandatory(), setDisplay(), setVisible() and setReadOnly(), to use a UI policy whenever possible. Pick one owner per field. Duplicated logic in both a script and a policy is slower and order-dependent: setDisplay() cannot hide a mandatory field with no value, and a read-only field cannot be changed with setValue() until it is made editable again, so two rules fighting over one field produce 'random' behaviour.

6. Merge onLoad scripts. Fourteen onLoad scripts that each read a few fields can usually become two or three, ordered explicitly. Re-measure after each step and report against the baseline.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Asynchronous callbacks can arrive after the user has moved on. Always compare the response's key to the current field value before applying it, as in the code above.
  • Removing a synchronous call can change behaviour that silently depended on ordering, for example an onSubmit that assumed a value was already set. Retest submit paths after step 2.
  • getOptions()' getAvailable() returns a promise; if anyone added it to build choice lists, it is another asynchronous path to account for.
  • Message popups added with addInfoMessage() and friends disappear after roughly four seconds and the timeout is not configurable, so do not rely on them for anything the agent must act on.
  • g_scratchpad data is a load-time snapshot. After consolidation, make sure every value that can change on the form has an onChange path.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting with UI policy clean-up because it is visible, while the synchronous calls that cause the freeze remain.
  • Adding callbacks but keeping one server call per field, so the freeze becomes a slow trickle of requests.
  • Fixing the recursive setValue with a global flag instead of a value comparison.
  • Declaring victory without a before and after measurement.
Score points: Present the work as a ranked plan with a measurement at each step, and name the reference behaviour behind each fix (synchronous without callback, round trip without display value, setValue re-triggering onChange). That is what an architect is expected to bring to a customer.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you stop new slow scripts being added after you leave? (Code review rules, instance scan checks, ATF timing tests.)
  • The same form also runs in a workspace. Which of these fixes carry over and which need rework?
  • When would you move logic out of client scripts entirely into a business rule or flow?

Sources

  • GlideAjax - API reference
  • i18N (g_i18n) - API reference
  • StopWatch - API reference
  • Display Business Rule and g_scratchpad (ServiceNow Community)

question: A food manufacturer streams temperature readings from 4,000 cold-storage sensors across 35 plants, one reading per sensor per minute. The previous developer inserted every reading as a row in a custom table: it now holds 50 million rows, the plant-manager dashboard times out, and nightly clean-up jobs run for hours. You are asked to move the readings to MetricBase. Write the ingestion code for a batch REST endpoint and a query that returns hourly average and 95th-percentile temperature per plant for the last 24 hours. Then review this snippet from the old prototype and explain what is wrong: var t = new sn_clotho.Transformer(gr); t.avg(); t.metric('x_acme_mt_temperature'); t.execute(s1, e1); t.execute(s2, e2);
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants to hear that high-frequency numeric readings belong in MetricBase, not in a ServiceNow table with one row per reading, and that you can use the sn_clotho API correctly: write with DataBuilder and Client.put(), read with Transformer and TransformPart chains. At Expert level you should also know the ordering rules of the transform builder, the one-shot execute(), how retention policies down-sample old data, and which Client calls destroy data permanently.

The Answer

Data model. Keep one row per sensor (the subject record) and define a metric field such as x_acme_mt_temperature on that table with a retention policy. Values go into the MetricBase database, keyed by subject and metric, rather than into rows. The 50 million row table and its reports go away.

Write path. DataBuilder collects points for one subject and metric. add(GlideDateTime, Number) adds one point; add(GlideDateTime, Array) adds a run of values where each later timestamp is computed from the retention policy's collection period. Nothing is stored until Client.put(), which accepts one builder or an array, so a REST batch becomes one write:

// Scripted REST resource: POST a batch of readings
// body: [{"sensor":"<sys_id>","ts":"2026-10-23 08:15:00","temp":71.4}, ...]
(function process(request, response) {
    var readings = request.body.data;
    var builders = [];

    for (var i = 0; i < readings.length; i++) {
        var r = readings[i];
        var sensor = new GlideRecord('x_acme_iot_sensor');    // fresh GR per builder; do not share one cursor
        if (!sensor.get(r.sensor)) continue;                   // builder needs a real subject record
        var db = new sn_clotho.DataBuilder(sensor, 'x_acme_mt_temperature');
        db.add(new GlideDateTime(r.ts), parseFloat(r.temp));    // one point; add(start, [..]) for a run
        builders.push(db);
    }
    new sn_clotho.Client().put(builders);                      // one write for the batch
    response.setStatus(202);
})(request, response);

Read path. new sn_clotho.Transformer(glideRecord) takes the subject records to analyse. You chain groupBy(), metric() and transforms, then call execute(start, end), which returns a TransformResult. Transforms never change stored data.

// Hourly average + p95 per plant, last 24 hours
var end = new GlideDateTime();
var start = new GlideDateTime(end);
start.addSeconds(-24 * 60 * 60);

var sensors = new GlideRecord('x_acme_iot_sensor');
sensors.addQuery('active', true);
sensors.query();

var t = new sn_clotho.Transformer(sensors);
var hourly = new GlideDuration('0 01:00:00');               // d HH:mm:ss

// groupBy BEFORE metric; metric BEFORE any transform
var avgPart = t.groupBy('plant').metric('x_acme_mt_temperature')
               .resample('AVG', hourly).avg().label('avg %g:plant:').collect();
var p95Part = t.groupBy('plant').metric('x_acme_mt_temperature')
               .resample('MAX', hourly).fractiles([0.95]).label('p95 %g:plant:');

var result = t.execute(start, end);                         // only once per Transformer

var series = avgPart.getResult().byGroup();                 // Data[] per plant
series.forEach(function(d) {
    gs.info(d.getLabel() + ' ' + d.size() + ' points, first ' + d.getStart());
});

TransformResult gives you getData() (one Data object, or null if empty), byGroup() (one per group, and an error if you did not group), getByLabel() and toArray(). Each Data exposes getValues(), getStart(), getEnd(), getPeriod(), getLabel() and size(). That is what the dashboard widget consumes.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Builder order rules. Call metric() before any transform. You cannot call metric() or groupBy() after a transform, and execute() runs once per Transformer. Reusing a transformer for a second time window is a bug; build a new one.
  • Intermediate results vanish. In avg().add(2) only the final series is returned. Call collect() on the intermediate step if you need both, and to read a part with getResult() the reference says to call collect() on it before execute() and getResult() only after.
  • Retention down-samples. MetricInfo(table, metric).getRetentionSchedulesInMinutes() returns retention duration mapped to sampling period, for example {"11520":1,"135360":10,"571680":60}: one-minute data for 8 days, 10-minute for 94, hourly for 397. A one-minute chart for last quarter cannot exist. isValid() confirms the metric is mapped to the table before you query.
  • accumulate() vs put(). put() overwrites the value at a timestamp; accumulate() adds to it (kWh from several devices). Using put() for additive readings silently keeps only the last one.
  • Destructive calls. deleteSeries() and deleteMetric() remove data with no recovery. Keep them out of anything that runs in production on a schedule.
  • Stale sensors. getSeries(gr, metric, lastUpdateBefore) returns series with no data newer than the given date. That is a cheap "which sensors went quiet" check.
  • Durations. The resample example in the reference writes new GlideDuration("1:00"); the GlideDuration constructor documents the format d HH:mm:ss, so spell it out. Also note Data.getPeriod() is described as milliseconds in one place and seconds in another; check the unit before you divide.
  • The DataBuilder constructor heading lists a subject sys_id argument, but every example passes (glideRecord, metric). Follow the examples and pass a GlideRecord positioned on the subject.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling put() once per reading inside the loop instead of once per batch.
  • Pulling raw values into script and averaging in JavaScript, which is what the transform engine is for.
  • Returning thousands of points to a chart that is 600 pixels wide; resample(count) or resample(min, max) fixes that.
Score points: Use labels with group placeholders ('%g:plant:') so each series names its own plant, then getByLabel() or byGroup() without positional guesswork.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you raise an incident when a plant's p95 stays above a threshold for 30 minutes?
  • How would you migrate 18 months of history from the old table without breaking retention?
  • When would iqr() or stddev() be a better anomaly signal than a fixed threshold?

  • Transformer - Scoped, Global
  • TransformPart - Scoped, Global
  • TransformResult - Scoped, Global
  • Data - Scoped, Global
  • MetricInfo - Scoped, Global
  • GlideDuration

question: A global retailer's HR portal has an "HR case insights" widget for people managers. It shows, for the manager's region, counts of HR cases by category, average days open, and a list of case numbers per category. Managers are not allowed to read Employee Relations cases about themselves; a before-query business rule and read ACLs enforce that on lists. A pen tester shows that a manager can still see the count, and the case numbers, of Employee Relations cases naming them. The widget uses GlideAggregate with COUNT, AVG and GROUP_CONCAT on number. Explain why the existing controls did not apply and redesign the data access.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

The interviewer wants you to explain that GlideAggregate extends GlideRecord and, like it, does not enforce ACLs; that query business rules do not run for aggregate queries unless you turn them on with setAggregateWorkflow(true); and that GROUP_CONCAT returns actual field values, so an "aggregate" widget can leak record identifiers.

At Expert level they also want a design that does not rely on one flag: minimise what is aggregated, apply the same row restrictions explicitly, and decide what to do with small counts.

The Answer

Why the controls did not apply. Read ACLs protect list views and GlideRecordSecure queries; a before-query business rule runs for list views and ordinary GlideRecord queries alike. A GlideAggregate gets neither by default.

ACLs: GlideAggregate is documented as an extension of GlideRecord. Nothing in it evaluates read ACLs, so aggregates run over every matching row.

Query business rules: the GlideAggregate reference for setAggregateWorkflow() says it "activates or deactivates the running of business rules for aggregate queries", with a default of false. Its example shows that enabling it makes the incident query business rule run for the aggregate. With the default, the before-query rule that hides Employee Relations cases never saw this query. The reference adds that the session-level gs.getSession().setWorkflow() overrides the method, so if the session has workflow off, query rules do not run whatever you pass.

GROUP_CONCAT: the aggregate types include GROUP_CONCAT and GROUP_CONCAT_DISTINCT, which concatenate all non-null values in the group into a comma-separated string. On number, that is a list of case numbers. It is a read of the field, with no field ACL check.

Redesign.

function caseInsights(regionId) {
    var out = { categories: [] };
    var ga = new GlideAggregate('sn_hr_core_case');
    ga.setAggregateWorkflow(true);                 // run query business rules
    ga.addQuery('active', true);
    ga.addQuery('u_region', regionId);
    // Restate the restriction explicitly; do not rely on the BR alone
    ga.addQuery('subject_person.manager', '!=', gs.getUserID());
    ga.addQuery('subject_person', '!=', gs.getUserID());
    ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
    ga.addAggregate('AVG', 'u_days_open');
    ga.groupBy('hr_service.category');
    ga.query();
    while (ga.next()) {
        var n = parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10);
        out.categories.push({
            category: ga.getValue('hr_service.category'),
            count: n < 5 ? '<5' : n,                // small-count suppression
            avgDaysOpen: n < 5 ? null : ga.getAggregate('AVG', 'u_days_open')
        });
    }
    return out;
}

Points in that design:

setAggregateWorkflow(true) applies existing query business rules, which closes the gap the pen tester used. It is necessary but not sufficient, because a session that disabled workflow would undo it, and query rules are often written for list behaviour rather than analytics.

The restriction is restated in the query itself, so the widget is safe even if the business rule changes. Review that restatement together with the ACL whenever either changes.

No GROUP_CONCAT. If managers need to drill into cases, link them to a list view, where ACLs and query rules apply to each row. Returning identifiers from an aggregate bypasses all of that.

Small counts are suppressed. A count of 1 in Employee Relations for a team of six is itself a disclosure, even with perfect row security.

If the numbers must match exactly what the user can read, the only fully ACL-faithful approach is to count rows the user can read: GlideRecordSecure, or GlideQuery with withAcls(), which the reference says executes the query with GlideRecordSecure. That costs a row scan. Test whether withAcls() combined with aggregate() or count() applies ACLs on your release before relying on it; the reference documents withAcls() generally, not for aggregates specifically.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • COUNT in GlideAggregate counts non-null values of the expression. addAggregate('COUNT', 'field') groups by that field, which is different from a SQL COUNT(field).
  • orderBy() and orderByDesc() on GlideAggregate add the field to the group-by list, which can split your groups unexpectedly.
  • For FX Currency fields, getAggregate() returns a string such as USD;134.980000, and returns just a semicolon when the values mix currency codes. Aggregation on currency fields uses the reference currency value, so convert before display.
  • setAggregateWindow(first, last) limits which rows are included in the aggregate, not how many groups come back.
  • On-premise instances need the database server time zone set to GMT/UTC for GlideAggregate to work properly, which matters for date trends with addTrend().

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a before-query business rule protects every query on the table.
  • Using GROUP_CONCAT to save a second query and exposing identifiers.
  • Showing exact small counts on sensitive categories.
  • Treating setAggregateWorkflow(true) as the complete fix.
Score points: Explain the default of setAggregateWorkflow() and the session-level override, then argue for restating the filter in the aggregate. Defence in depth plus small-count suppression is what separates an architect's answer from a patch.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you prove with ATF that the widget hides Employee Relations counts from the subject's manager?
  • Would Performance Analytics with breakdown security be a better home for this widget?
  • How do read replicas via setCategory() affect the freshness of these numbers?

question: A payments platform sends webhooks to an unauthenticated Scripted REST endpoint in your scoped app. Each call carries webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature (space-separated v1,<base64> values, HMAC-SHA256 over id.timestamp.body, secret delivered as whsec_<base64>). The current code follows a well-known blog pattern: it rebuilds the body with JSON.stringify(request.body.data), computes new CertificateEncryption().generateMac(secret, 'HmacSHA256', signed), and compares with ==. Roughly 2% of legitimate webhooks fail validation, and a pen-tester replayed a captured webhook an hour later and it was accepted. Diagnose both problems and write a hardened validator.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

A signature is computed over bytes. Any step that parses and re-serializes the body before verification will sometimes produce different bytes from what the sender signed. You should recognise that, know that the request body stream can only be read once (so you take the raw string first), and know that HMAC alone does not stop replay. Bonus points for constant-time comparison and for knowing the base64 key requirement of generateMac().

Diagnosis

The 2% failure. JSON.stringify(request.body.data) does not reproduce what the sender sent. It parses the JSON and writes it out again. Whitespace, escaped Unicode (\u00e9 versus é), escaped slashes, number formatting such as 1.0 versus 1, and any key ordering or duplicate keys the parser normalises will all change the bytes. Most payloads survive the round trip, which is why it passes most of the time. The ones with accented merchant names or decimal amounts are the 2%. The blog that popularised this pattern even lists "use the raw body exactly as received" in its own checklist.

The fix is to read request.body.dataString, which the reference describes as the content of the request body as a String. The same reference warns that data, dataStream and dataString are consumed from one stream and only one can be read: call data then dataString and the second is empty. So read the string once, verify it, then JSON.parse it yourself.

The replay. HMAC proves the message came from someone holding the secret and was not altered. It says nothing about when. The timestamp is inside the signed content, so check it is within a short window (five minutes is common) and record each webhook-id so the same delivery is processed once.

The Answer

var WebhookVerifier = Class.create();
WebhookVerifier.prototype = {
    initialize: function () {
        var raw = gs.getProperty('x_pay.webhook_secret');      // e.g. whsec_C2FV...
        // generateMac() wants a Base64 key. The provider's secret after the prefix
        // already IS Base64, so do NOT base64-encode it again.
        this.key = raw.indexOf('whsec_') === 0 ? raw.substring(6) : raw;
        this.toleranceSec = 300;
    },

    // Constant-time string compare: avoid leaking match length via timing
    _safeEquals: function (a, b) {
        if (!a || !b || a.length !== b.length) return false;
        var diff = 0;
        for (var i = 0; i < a.length; i++) diff |= a.charCodeAt(i) ^ b.charCodeAt(i);
        return diff === 0;
    },

    verify: function (id, ts, sigHeader, rawBody) {
        if (!id || !ts || !sigHeader) return 'missing headers';
        var nowSec = Math.floor(new GlideDateTime().getNumericValue() / 1000);
        var tsNum = parseInt(ts, 10);
        if (isNaN(tsNum) || Math.abs(nowSec - tsNum) > this.toleranceSec) return 'stale timestamp';

        var expected = new CertificateEncryption()
            .generateMac(this.key, 'HmacSHA256', id + '.' + ts + '.' + rawBody);

        var parts = String(sigHeader).split(' ');
        for (var i = 0; i < parts.length; i++) {
            var p = parts[i].split(',');
            if (p[0] === 'v1' && this._safeEquals(p[1], expected)) return '';
        }
        return 'bad signature';
    },

    type: 'WebhookVerifier'
};
(function process(request, response) {
    var raw = request.body.dataString;              // read ONCE, before anything else
    var id = request.getHeader('webhook-id');
    var v = new WebhookVerifier();
    var problem = v.verify(id, request.getHeader('webhook-timestamp'),
                           request.getHeader('webhook-signature'), raw);
    if (problem) {
        gs.warn('Webhook rejected: ' + problem + ' id=' + id);   // no body, no secret
        response.setStatus(401);
        return;
    }
    var seen = new GlideRecord('x_pay_webhook_receipt');      // unique index on u_webhook_id
    if (seen.get('u_webhook_id', id)) { response.setStatus(200); return; }  // duplicate delivery
    var payload = JSON.parse(raw);                       // parse only after verification
    seen.initialize();
    seen.setValue('u_webhook_id', id);
    seen.setValue('u_event_type', payload.type);
    seen.setValue('u_payload', raw);
    seen.insert();
    gs.eventQueue('x_pay.webhook.received', seen, id, '');   // do the work async
    response.setStatus(202);
})(request, response);

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • generateMac(key, algorithm, data) requires the key to be Base64 encoded and returns the MAC in Base64. The reference example encodes a plain-text key first with gs.base64Encode(). When the provider hands you a key that is already Base64, encoding it again produces a valid-looking but wrong MAC. The blog calls this its fourth mistake.
  • The algorithm string is a Java MAC name: HmacSHA256, not SHA-256.
  • In global scope the class is GlideCertificateEncryption with the same generateMac() signature; CertificateEncryption is the scoped API.
  • If the provider signs with a hex digest instead of Base64, you must convert one side; the platform method only returns Base64.
  • Keep the timestamp tolerance small and make sure the receipt table has a unique index, otherwise two simultaneous retries can both pass the duplicate check.
  • Return quickly. Long processing inside the webhook leads the provider to time out and redeliver, which is more load on the duplicate check.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading request.body.data for routing and then dataString for verification, and getting an empty string.
  • Logging the raw body and the computed MAC on failure, which puts payment data and a valid signature for that body in syslog.
  • Storing the secret in a plain property readable by many roles. Use a password-type property or a credential record and limit read access.
Score points: Say why the endpoint can be unauthenticated at all: the HMAC replaces caller authentication, so the resource must do nothing before verification succeeds. Anything it does earlier, including queries driven by the payload, is reachable by anyone on the internet.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate the webhook secret without dropping deliveries?
  • What would you change if the provider sent the signature over the raw bytes of a gzip-compressed body?
  • How would you rate-limit this endpoint if someone floods it with invalid signatures?

Sources

  • RESTAPIResponse - Scoped, Global
  • HMAC Validation in ServiceNow: Securing Webhook Integrations with CertificateEncryption
  • Scripted REST API Webhooks and the Replicate AI Integration in CreatorCon C3

question: A bank's Microsoft Entra ID tenant has banned client secrets for app registrations, so your ServiceNow integration to Microsoft Graph must authenticate with a certificate-based client assertion (a signed JWT carrying the certificate thumbprint in its header). Separately, the bank's internal fraud API requires mutual TLS. The certificate and private key are already in the instance's keystore and X.509 Certificate [sys_certificate] table. Explain how you'd use CertificateEncryption, sn_auth.GlideJWTAPI, the sn_auth OAuth request classes and RESTMessageV2.setMutualAuth() to satisfy both requirements, and call out the encoding and configuration traps that usually cost a day.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

These are two different uses of one certificate. A client assertion is application-level: you sign a JWT and send it to the token endpoint as a form parameter. Mutual TLS is transport-level: the TLS handshake presents the client certificate before any HTTP is exchanged. Keep them apart, name the platform objects that handle each, and know the encoding details that get a correct-looking JWT rejected.

The Answer

Client assertion for Graph. Configuration first: a JWT Provider [jwt_provider] record tied to the signing key, with the standard claims (audience is the tenant token endpoint, issuer and subject are the client ID). sn_auth.GlideJWTAPI.generateJWT(jwtProviderSysId, header, payload) builds and signs the token. The header and payload are optional JSON strings; when you pass them, they add to or override the provider record's claims. The reference shows a custom kid header being merged with alg and typ, and a custom payload overriding iss, with exp, iat and jti still generated.

Entra ID identifies the certificate by thumbprint in the JWT header. CertificateEncryption.getThumbPrint(certificateID, algorithm) returns a hash of the certificate in the Trust Store, and the reference example computes a SHA-1 thumbprint for a certificate named AzureAAD. getThumbPrintFromKeyStore(certificateID, alias, algorithm) does the same for a keystore entry, which is the one to use when the certificate sits in a keystore with its private key.

function graphToken() {
    var cert = new GlideRecord('sys_certificate');
    if (!cert.get('name', 'Graph Client Cert')) throw 'certificate record missing';

    // Base64 SHA-1 thumbprint (reference example uses the static form).
    // If this record is a keystore rather than a Trust Store certificate, use
    // getThumbPrintFromKeyStore(sysId, alias, 'SHA-1') instead.
    var b64 = CertificateEncryption.getThumbPrint(cert.getUniqueValue(), 'SHA-1');
    // JOSE x5t must be base64url: swap alphabet, strip padding
    var x5t = b64.replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');

    var jwt = new sn_auth.GlideJWTAPI().generateJWT(
        gs.getProperty('x_bank_graph.jwt_provider_id'),
        JSON.stringify({ x5t: x5t }),
        null);                               // claims from the JWT provider record

    var req = new sn_auth.GlideOAuthClientRequest();
    req.setGrantType('client_credentials');
    req.setScope('https://graph.microsoft.com/.default');
    req.setParameter('client_assertion_type',
        'urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer');
    req.setParameter('client_assertion', jwt);

    var resp = new sn_auth.GlideOAuthClient().requestTokenByRequest('Graph App', req);
    if (resp.getResponseCode() != '200' || !resp.getToken()) {
        throw 'token request failed: ' + resp.getErrorMessage();
    }
    return resp.getToken();
}

Before writing that script, check whether your release's OAuth entity profile supports this flow declaratively through the JWT provider. If it does, setAuthenticationProfile('oauth2', profileSysId) on the REST message is less code to maintain. The script is the fallback.

Mutual TLS for the fraud API. Create a protocol profile that references the keystore holding the client certificate, then reference it on the REST Message record or set it in script with rm.setMutualAuth('fraud-mtls'). The reference says this overrides the protocol profile selected on the record. The argument is the profile name, unlike setAuthenticationProfile(), which takes a sys_id. SOAP has the same setMutualAuth(), and for WS-Security message signing it has setWSSecurity(keystoreId, keystoreAlias, keystorePassword, certificateId).

Where sign() fits. CertificateEncryption.sign(certificateID, alias, aliaspassword, algorithm, datatosign) signs arbitrary data with a keystore private key and returns Base64. It is the building block if a partner wants a detached signature over a payload. It takes the private key (alias) password as a plain argument, so the value has to come from a protected source, never a literal.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Every thumbprint and signature method returns standard Base64. JOSE headers like x5t use base64url without padding. Pasting the platform output straight in is the most common reason Entra ID rejects the assertion.
  • Use the same hash algorithm the identity provider expects: x5t is SHA-1, while x5t#S256 is SHA-256.
  • getThumbPrint() reads a Trust Store certificate; getThumbPrintFromKeyStore() needs the keystore alias. Picking the wrong one hashes a different certificate.
  • sign() accepts a fixed list of algorithm names such as SHA256withRSA and SHA256withECDSA. A JWT alg of RS256 corresponds to SHA256withRSA.
  • Certificate expiry breaks both flows on the same day. Monitor the sys_certificate expiry date and rotate with an overlap: upload the new certificate to Entra ID before switching the JWT provider.
  • The scoped reference documents CertificateEncryption; global scripts use GlideCertificateEncryption.

Common Mistakes

  • Thinking mTLS replaces OAuth for Graph. Graph needs a bearer token; mTLS is for the fraud API.
  • Generating a new assertion and token for every Graph call instead of reusing the token until near expiry.
  • Hard-coding the keystore password for sign() or setWSSecurity() in script.
Score points: Explain how you would test the JWT offline: decode it, check aud, iss, sub, exp and the x5t value against the thumbprint shown in the Entra ID portal. Most failures are visible before you send anything.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you rotate the certificate with zero downtime for both integrations?
  • What changes if the fraud API is reachable only through a MID Server?
  • How would you restrict which scoped apps can use this keystore?

Sources

  • GlideOAuthClient - Scoped, Global
  • GlideOAuthClientResponse - Scoped, Global
