  • SOAPMessageV2 - Scoped, Global

question: A SaaS vendor's ServiceNow app lets customer admins register a 'notification callback URL'; when a case changes, a scoped script POSTs case data to that URL with sn_ws.RESTMessageV2. A penetration test registered https://callbacks.partner.example/hook, which answered with a 302 redirect to an internal address, and also registered a URL with an embedded query string that smuggled extra parameters. The report rates it as server-side request forgery. Design the controls using sn_ws.UriMatcher, setAllowedRedirectURIs(), glide.hosts.allowlist and MID routing decisions, and explain exactly what each control does and does not cover.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

SSRF defence is layered. Validate the URL when it is saved and again when it is used. Control where redirects may go. Use instance-level host restrictions as the backstop. Never route user-supplied URLs through a MID Server sitting inside the corporate network. You also need the precise semantics of UriMatcher: its path rule is stricter than people assume, and its fragment rule is looser.

The Answer

Layer 1: validate the URL with UriMatcher. new sn_ws.UriMatcher().match(uri, scheme, hosts, paths, fragments, disallowQueryParameters) returns a UriMatcherResponse. The semantics from the reference:

  • scheme is http or https. Require https.
  • hosts is effectively required. Leaving it out gives isError() true with "Hosts rule is null or empty."
  • paths must match the full path, and each must start with /. Allowing /path1 does not allow /path1/more.
  • fragments is permissive. A URI with no fragment still matches; it fails only if it contains a fragment that is not in the list.
  • disallowQueryParameters true turns any query string into an error, "Query parameters are not allowed for matching." That closes the parameter-smuggling finding.
  • Check both isMatch() and isError(). Per-part results come from isSchemeMatches(), isHostMatches(), isPathMatches() and isFragmentMatches(); getErrorMessages() returns an empty string when nothing went wrong.
function validateCallback(url, tenantHosts) {
    // [] is meant as 'no fragment allowed'; the reference only documents omitting the
    // argument (any fragment allowed), so confirm how an empty array behaves on your instance.
    var resp = new sn_ws.UriMatcher().match(String(url), 'https', tenantHosts, null, [], true);
    if (resp.isError()) return 'Invalid callback URL: ' + resp.getErrorMessages();
    if (!resp.isMatch()) return 'Callback host is not on the approved list for this tenant.';
    return '';
}

Run it in a before business rule on the callback record so a bad URL never saves, and again immediately before sending, because the allowed hosts list can change after the URL was registered.

Layer 2: control redirects. The pen-test URL passed host validation and then redirected inward. setAllowedRedirectURIs(Array) on the REST message lists the URIs a redirect may go to; the reference describes it as protection against URL redirect attacks and points to UriMatcher for more thorough checks. Pass only the registered callback itself, which in practice says "do not follow redirects anywhere else". On SOAP, setFollowRedirect() is off by default, and when it is off you receive the 3xx status and handle it yourself.

var problem = validateCallback(cb.getValue('u_url'), allowedHostsFor(cb));
if (problem) { markCallbackFailed(cb, problem); return; }
var rm = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2();
rm.setEndpoint(cb.getValue('u_url'));
rm.setHttpMethod('post');
rm.setAllowedRedirectURIs([cb.getValue('u_url')]);
rm.setHttpTimeout(10000);
rm.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
rm.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify(minimalCasePayload(caseGr)));
var res = rm.execute();

Layer 3: instance-wide host restriction. glide.hosts.allowlist controls which hosts fetch methods can access and, per the Fetch reference, applies to HTTP APIs like RESTMessageV2. It is the safety net when someone writes a new outbound script and forgets the matcher. It is global to the instance, so it is coarse; per-tenant rules still belong in your app.

Layer 4: routing. Never call setMIDServer() for a customer-supplied URL. A MID Server sits inside a network precisely so it can reach internal addresses, which is what an SSRF attacker wants. If the REST Message record you reuse has a MID configured, build a recordless message as above so nothing is inherited.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • UriMatcher checks the string, not where the name resolves. A host on the allow list whose DNS points at a private address passes. Keep allow lists to hosts the tenant has proved it controls, and treat glide.hosts.allowlist as the backstop.
  • Passing null for paths means any path is allowed. That is reasonable for callbacks, but say so explicitly in review.
  • The matcher needs the REST API Provider plugin (com.glide.rest), which is active by default.
  • Send the minimum payload. Even a correct callback URL is a third-party system; do not send fields the tenant did not ask for.
  • Set a short timeout. A hostile endpoint that holds the socket open ties up a worker per case update.

Common Mistakes

  • Validating once at registration and trusting the stored URL forever.
  • Checking isMatch() but not isError().
  • Allowing redirects because the vendor's endpoint "sometimes moves", which reopens the original hole.
Score points: Mention outbound logging: pick the setLogLevel() value (basic, elevated or all) deliberately for this message. Outbound HTTP Requests logs give an incident responder a record of which hosts the instance actually called, but the most verbose level can also capture case data you would rather not keep.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you let a tenant prove ownership of a callback host?
  • What would you do differently if callbacks had to reach on-premises systems?
  • How would you sign callbacks so the tenant can verify they came from you?

Sources

  • UriMatcherResponse
  • RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • SOAPMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
  • Fetch

question: A state agency built a "Quick order" Service Portal widget and a Virtual Agent topic that both call one script include, QuickOrderService.order(itemSysId, variables, requestedFor), which runs new sn_sc.CartJS().orderNow() for item requests and new sn_sc.CatItem(id).submitProducer() for record producers. A penetration test found that by editing the item sys_id in the browser's request payload, an ordinary employee could order items restricted to the Finance team, raise HR record producers they could not see in the portal, and order on behalf of any colleague. Question: Explain why the catalog's normal protections did not apply, and design the server-side checks using the catalog APIs.
answer:
What the Interviewer Wants to Hear

Point out that user criteria and "Available for" lists hide items in the catalog UI, but a server-side script that takes a sys_id and orders it does not ask those questions unless you ask them yourself. The request payload is attacker-controlled. A strong answer builds an explicit authorisation step on the server that checks the item, the catalog and category, the delegation target and the channel, and fails closed.

The Answer

Why it leaked. The widget's list was filtered by visibility, so the UI looked correct. The script include accepted any itemSysId and requestedFor from input and called CartJS or submitProducer(). Those APIs create the request; nothing in the reference says they re-check user criteria for you. The same applies to the Virtual Agent path, where the item id comes from topic variables.

The checks. Put them in the script include, so every channel goes through them:

  • Can this user see the item? $sp.canReadRecord('sc_cat_item', sysId) returns true only if the record is valid and readable, and for sc_cat_item "checks if the user can view the item". In a non-portal context, use the catalog APIs: CatItem.isDelegationAllowed() with no argument checks the calling user's acquisition rights, canViewInDomain() checks the selected domain, and isVisibleServicePortal() checks the item is exposed in Service Portal at all.
  • Can the beneficiary have it? CatItem.isDelegationAllowed(requestedFor) checks the target user's acquisition rights; getInvalidDelegatedUsers() does it for a list.
  • May this user order for someone else? CartJS.canViewRF() says whether the current user has the role to edit Requested for. If false, force requestedFor to gs.getUserID().
  • Is the catalog or category visible? new sn_sc.Catalog(id).canView(false, userId) and new sn_sc.CatCategory(id).canView(false, userId) cover items reachable only through a restricted catalog or category.
  • Is it the kind of thing this endpoint should order? CatItem.getRecordClass() returns the class (sc_cat_item, a producer class and so on); allow-list the classes each channel may submit.
var QuickOrderService = Class.create();
QuickOrderService.prototype = {
  initialize: function () {},

  order: function (itemId, variables, requestedFor) {
    var me = gs.getUserID();
    if (!/^[0-9a-f]{32}$/.test(itemId)) return this._deny('bad id');

    var item = new sn_sc.CatItem(itemId);
    if (!item.isDelegationAllowed()) return this._deny('caller not entitled');   // caller's rights
    if (!item.canViewInDomain())     return this._deny('domain');

    if (!requestedFor || requestedFor == me) {
      requestedFor = me;
    } else {
      if (!sn_sc.CartJS.canViewRF())                 return this._deny('cannot request for others');
      if (!item.isDelegationAllowed(requestedFor))   return this._deny('beneficiary not entitled');
    }

    var cls = item.getRecordClass();
    if (cls == 'sc_cat_item_producer') {
      if (!this._producerAllowed(itemId)) return this._deny('producer not on allow-list');
      return item.submitProducer({ sysparm_id: itemId, variables: this._clean(variables) });
    }
    if (cls != 'sc_cat_item') return this._deny('class ' + cls);

    return new sn_sc.CartJS('quick_' + me).orderNow({
      sysparm_id: itemId, sysparm_quantity: '1',
      sysparm_requested_for: requestedFor, variables: this._clean(variables)
    });
  },

  // _producerAllowed(itemId) and _clean(variables) are app-specific helpers, omitted for brevity
  _deny: function (why) {
    gs.warn('QuickOrder denied for ' + gs.getUserName() + ': ' + why);
    return { error: 'not_allowed' };          // same message for every reason
  },
  type: 'QuickOrderService'
};

In the widget, keep building the form from $sp.getCatalogItem(sysId, true). The isOrdering flag matters: true uses the create-roles security check (ordering), false uses write roles (viewing an existing item's variables). The one-argument form is deprecated and calls it with false.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • Run this as the requesting user. If the script include runs as a system or integration account (common in Virtual Agent fulfilment and in scheduled jobs), the "caller" checks evaluate that account, which can usually order everything.
  • submitProducer() sets field values from variables on the target table. Clean that object to the producer's own variables, or a caller can populate fields the producer form never exposed.
  • canViewOnSearch(isMobile) answers a different question (visible in global search). Do not use it as the order check. Note the reference example passes the string 'false'; pass a real boolean.
  • CatalogSearch.search() returns a GlideRecord you must query(); a search widget built on it still needs per-item visibility checks.
  • Return the same error for every denial so the endpoint does not tell an attacker which items exist.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing it in the client by hiding the sys_id. Anything the browser sends can be changed.
  • Adding an ACL on sc_req_item create. The request is created by the catalog engine; the decision belongs before the order call.
  • Checking the beneficiary but not the caller, which lets anyone order for an entitled colleague.
Score points: Separate the three identities (caller, beneficiary, executing account) and say which API checks which. That structure is what a security reviewer wants to see.

Likely Follow-ups

  • How would you test these checks in ATF with impersonated users?
  • How do you apply the same rules to the Service Catalog REST API?
  • What would you log for audit without logging variable values that may be sensitive?

  • CatalogJS API reference
